Over the last few decades, as one US
president after another tried to look
tough on crime, America's prison
population has exploded. [music]
Today, more than 1.8 million people are
locked up across nearly 5,000 state
[music] and federal prisons, local
jails, and juvenile facilities, giving
the United States both the largest
number of prisons and the largest number
of prisoners anywhere in the world. The
US has only 5% [music] of the world's
population, yet holds about 25% of the
world's incarcerated people. That works
out to 542 prisoners for every 100,000
citizens, one of the highest
incarceration rates on Earth. Only a
handful of nations, Turkmenistan,
Rwanda, and El Salvador, imprison a
larger share of their population. For
comparison, China's rate is 119 per
100,000, and countries like Finland and
Norway sit at just 54. [music]
And of course, incarcerating millions of
people for years, sometimes [music]
decades, comes with enormous costs.
Food, water, clothing, health care,
security, infrastructure, everything
required to keep an inmate alive and
contained.
In fact, as of 2026, running America's
correctional system costs roughly $116
billion
every single year.
Traditionally, taxpayers [music]
at the local, state, and federal levels
shoulder these costs. But as the bills

searching for ways to lighten the load.
That search opened the door to a new
idea.

[music] 1941, the federal government

in 1979, Congress passed [music] the
Justice System Improvement Act, which
said inmates had to be paid at least the

Almost immediately after, the
Corrections Corporation of America, CCA,
was founded. It expanded fast, opening
[music] private prisons across Texas,

an hour. But the law had two enormous

First, the minimum wage rule only

neighboring state, New York state, that

>> [music]

>> [music]
>> they don't trigger the federal rule
requiring minimum wage. California alone
produces more than 40 million plates a
[music] year. If you can profit from
every prisoner, then you'd better make
sure you have plenty of them. And that's
[music] exactly what the most successful
private prison companies have worked to
guarantee.
CCA would eventually rebrand itself into
[music] CoreCivic, but its business
model didn't change. Alongside its main
[music] competitor, it remains one of
the largest private prison operators in
the United States. Together, [music]
these companies have spent more than
four decades lobbying state and federal
agencies, [music] securing contracts
worth roughly $5.5 billion
every year. One of the most [music]
controversial features buried inside
these contracts is the minimum occupancy
clause. These clauses guarantee a prison
operator [music] a certain number of
filled beds, whether the state actually
has that many prisoners or not.
At Florida's Bay Correctional Facility,
CoreCivic [music] is guaranteed payment
for 90% occupancy or 887 inmates,
translating to just [music] over $43,000
per day. Even if the prison is half

And for the inmates who are inside these
[music] facilities, keeping their

Prison phone systems generate an

>> Companies are

And there are companies that are making

incarcerated. [music]
>> Take New Jersey, where inmates can
theoretically earn one of the highest
[music] wages in the country, up to $2
an hour. Meanwhile, a phone call to
family costs about 4 cents per minute,
[music] capped at 15 minutes. That's
roughly 65 cents per call, close to an
entire day's wage for most inmates.
The market [music] is dominated by two
companies who operate on a kickback

[music] can reach 40 to 60% of total

optional.

constitutionally obligated to provide

another source of income for private
[music] prisons and their affiliates.

the amount spent on the actual

text:
London’s housing market has become unaffordable for nearly everyone. In 2000, buyers needed a £44k salary — today it’s £125k, while wages haven’t kept up. Prices jumped 280%, pushing the city to a record affordability ratio of 13.5. From the 2008 crash to ultra-low interest rates and a surge of foreign investment, London’s market shifted away from local buyers, driving prices across every borough.

Now, tighter lending rules, soaring rents, and the collapse of new home construction have frozen the market. With supply at its lowest since 2009 and confidence drained, more Londoners are leaving the city simply to afford a home.

fast. And that has a simple implication.
The typical home in the capital is now
officially unaffordable for everyone.
Housing economists use a benchmark, five
times your annual salary. Anything
higher is considered unaffordable.
London blew past that threshold long ago

£600,000.

£100,000 just to get a standard mortgage

capital is only around £49,000.

a fall on paper. That should make things
easier. Lower real prices should mean
better affordability. But that isn't
what happened.
Even as prices stagnated, demand didn't
disappear. In fact, it grew. London's
population hit a record 8.95 million in
2023. More people than ever trying to
live in a city that was already
struggling to house the ones it had. The
demand was still there, but the ability
to buy wasn't. Higher mortgage stress
tests, tighter lending rules, and bigger
deposits meant buyers were locked out
even as prices stopped rising. So, the
market froze. Homes stop selling,
borrowing becomes harder, and buyers are
pushed into renting, driving rents to
the highest levels the capital has ever
seen. A series of policy shifts in the
last 10 years have only made the
slowdown worse. Began with stamp duty
reforms that pushed up the cost of
expensive homes. Then came extra taxes
on second properties, tighter buy tolet
rules, and the phased removal of
mortgage interest relief. Individually,
these policies might not seem dramatic,
but together they changed the entire
maths of buying a home in London.
Suddenly, it became more expensive to
buy, harder to invest, [music] and
riskier to be a landlord, especially in
lower yield areas where the margins were
already thin. Investors stepped back.
Landlords left the market altogether.
The result is gridlock. Too few buyers,
too, and no incentive for either sides
to move. But the real choke point isn't
the market at all. It's bureaucracy. The
city simply isn't building. Construction
work for just 1,200 new private housing
units started in London in the [music]
first quarter of 2025, the lowest since
2009 and just [music] 5.5%
of the city's quarterly target. In 23
out of 33 burrows, nothing has started
at all. The city needs 88,000 new homes
every year. Recently, it has averaged
just over 38,000. [music]
With supply this low, the outcome is
inevitable. Prices don't fall because
too few homes are being built [music] to
change anything. What we're announcing
today, me and the mayor of London
working together, is a package that is
designed to get London building again by
lowering [music] the cost for developers
so we get spades in the ground and start
to build the homes that Londoners need
to live in.
>> Developers know the economics don't
work. Buyers aren't in the market.
Investors have stepped back and the cost
of [music] construction has soared. This
means projects get shelved, postponed,
or cancelled, removing yet another
future pipeline [music] of supply.
empty, unused, and unavailable for those
who need them. Amid [music] a national
housing crisis in England, almost 34,000
council [music] houses are boarded up
and closed down.
>> This is how the shortage becomes
self-perpetuating. The fewer homes
built, the more expensive the existing
ones become, and the more expensive they
become, the harder it is to justify
building anything new. All of this is
happening in a climate where confidence
is already running thin. Buyers are not
only hesitating because of expense, but
because they don't trust where the
market, the economy or the government
[music] is headed. Taxes, regulation,
living costs, they all feel
unpredictable. And when confidence
disappears, the market freezes. [music]
The government have tried to jumpstart
things. Longer mortgages, higher income
multiples, tweaking lending rules, but
none of it has changed the fundamentals.
Prices remain too high. Supply remains
too low and the cost of building new
homes is still rising.
So people are leaving London not for
bigger gardens or quieter [music] towns,
but because they've run out of options.
Life beyond the M25 may mean fewer late
nights, fewer job opportunities, and
longer commutes. But for many, it's the

You are standing on a wooden crate in
the middle of a dusty town square. A
crowd of farmers and tired workers
stares up at you. They look skeptical.
You need to hook them and you need to
[music] do it fast. You hold up a brown
glass bottle so it catches the sunlight.
Step close. [music]
Don't be shy. I see you rubbing that
shoulder, sir. What ails you? The
[music] gout or just the weight of the
world? You lower your voice to a
whisper, making them lean in. This isn't
just water, folks. This is Dr. Johnson's
golden elixir. It cures backachches,
toothaches, and heartaches. One sip and
you'll feel 20 years younger. Who's
first? It works. A hand shoots up
holding a silver dollar. Then another.
You start snatching coins as fast as you
can, shoving bottles into desperate
hands. Sold. Sold to the lady in the
blue bonnet. Your pockets are getting
heavy with silver. This is the best part
of the job. But then you look toward the
back of the crowd. The sea of people
parts. A man in a clean suit is walking
toward you. There's a metal star pinned
to his chest. It's the sheriff. You stop
smiling. And uh-oh. That's all for
today. We're sold out. Bless you all.
Barnaby the sheriff. Kick the mules. Go,
go, go. You hop in as the wagon starts
to move, leaving the confused crowd in a
cloud of dust. You made $50, but you
also barely made it out alive. The wagon
rattles for miles. Finally, the angry
town is far behind you. You signal
Barnaby to pull over by a slowmoving
creek. It's time to restock the
inventory. You're a chemist of garbage.
You grab a wooden bucket and dip it into
the murky brown stream. That's your
base. Next, you pull out a sack of red
cayenne pepper. You dump a handful into
the bucket because if the medicine
doesn't burn their throat, the farmers
don't think it's working. The burn tells
them it's strong. Then you add a splash
of molasses to give it a dark, rich
color. And finally, the secret weapon.
You pull a small vial from your boot,
opium. You add just a few drops. This is
the only part that actually does
anything. It won't fix a broken bone or
cure a fever, but it will make them feel
dreamy enough to forget they were sick
in the first place. You stir the sludge
with a stick and funnel it into the
empty bottles. "Goodbye, Dr. Johnson,"
you mutter, scraping the old labels off
with a knife. Johnson is a wanted man
back there. You can't use that name
again. You pull a stack of fresh red
labels from a hidden compartment. Dr.
Thunder's Lightning Tonic. New town, new
name, but the same muddy water. Let's
ride Barnaby. We've got money to make.
You roll into Iron Creek. This isn't a
sleepy farm town like the last one. It's
a mining camp, and the vibe is
completely different. It's loud here.
The air smells like cold smoke, sulfur,
and unwashed bodies. The men here work
16 hours a day deep underground. They're
exhausted. Their backs are ruined, and
they are angry at the world. But they
also have pockets full of silver. "Park
the wagon here, Barnaby," you whisper.
"Light the torches. Let's give them a
show." Barnaby lights a couple torches
on the side of the wagon, lighting up
your new banner, Dr. Thunder's Lightning
Tonic. You step out onto a crate. You
don't wear your fancy top hat this time.
You roll up your sleeves. You rub a
little dirt on your face to sell to
these men. You can't look like a city
slicker. You need to look like a friend
of the working man. Listen to me. I know
you're tired. I know your bones ache.
The company doctors won't help you. They
want you weak, so you keep working for
pennies. The miners stop walking. They
turn toward the fire light. You have
their attention. You hold up the bottle.
This isn't some fancy perfume. This is
fuel. It puts the iron back in your
blood. It gives you the strength of a
grizzly bear. A massive minor steps
forward. He slams a coin onto your
crate. You hand him a bottle. The whole
crowd watches as he unccorks it and
takes a massive swig. He freezes. He
coughs violently. His eyes water. The
cayenne pepper is burning his throat.
You hold your breath. If he gets mad,
this mob will tear your wagon apart. It
burns. The minor yells, wiping his
mouth. You point a finger at him. That
means it's burning out the weakness. The
minor grins. I can feel it kicking in
already.
The crowd roars. Suddenly, everybody
wants the burn. They swarm the wagon,
waving cash and gold dust. [music] You
hand out bottles two at a time, moving
faster than you ever have. You look at
Barnaby and wink. This is going to be
the biggest payday of your life. You're
unstoppable.
Or so you think.
Your collection box is so full of coins
that the lid won't even close. You're
grabbing fistfuls of cash, stuffing them
into your pockets, your boots, and even
down your shirt. You've sold 50 bottles
in 10 minutes. Last case. 20 hands shoot
up at once, clutching silver dollars.
But before you can make the sale, a
voice screams out from the darkness.
You, you snake. The crowd freezes. A man
pushes his way to the front of the
crowd, shoving the giant miners aside
like they're nothing. He isn't covered
in cold dust. He's wearing a suit that
used to be nice, but now it's covered in
3 days of road dust. He looks like he
hasn't slept in a week. He points a
shaking finger right at your nose. In
his other hand, he clutches a familiar
brown bottle, but it doesn't say Dr.
Thunder on the label. It says Dr.
Johnson. You sold me this in the valley.
I tracked your wagon tracks for 40
miles. You said it would cure my
stomach. It made me sick for a week.
It's just pepper and pond water. Your
heart stops. You try to laugh it off. My
good sir, I've never seen you before in
my life. You must have me confused with
a cheap imitator. There are many
charlatans out there. But I am liar. The
man screams. He throws the bottle. The
smell hits the crowd instantly. It
doesn't smell like medicine. It smells
like pond water and mud. The big miner,
the one who tasted it first, steps
forward. He looks at the bottle in his
hand. Then he looks at the shattered
glass. He takes a sniff. He doesn't look
like a friend anymore. Is this true,
little man? Are you poisoning us? Now
wait just a moment. It's an experimental
blend. Someone in the back throws a
rock. It whizzes past your ear and
shatters a lantern which starts a fire.
The crowd starts coming for you. They
want blood. Panic takes over. Barnaby.
You dive toward the back of the wagon,
scrambling over crates of glass bottles.
Barnaby is already whipping the mules
into a frenzy. The wagon begins to move,
but you aren't free. Not yet. A man
lunges at the wagon and grabs your
ankle. It's the man in the suit. He's
running behind the moving wagon,
refusing to let go. His eyes are wild.
You aren't going anywhere. You finally
manage to shake him loose. He screams,
his grip slips, and he tumbles backward
into the dust, nearly getting trampled
by the angry mob behind him. Faster,
Barnaby, they're gaining on us. The
wagon picks up speed, running through
the mining camp. You smash through a
wooden fence behind you. The angry roar
of the crowd is getting quieter. But
just then, the wagon hits a massive
pothole. You bounce three feet in the
air. The box stuffed with all your
profits flies out of your hands. Silver
dollars spray everywhere. They fly out
the back of the wagon, vanishing into
the night. You watch in horror as a
trail of shiny coins bounces away into
the dirt. My money, you cry out,
scrambling on your hands and knees,
trying to scoop up the coins sliding
[music] around. Barnaby, stop. We're
losing the cash. Forget the money,
Barnaby yells over the roar of the wind.
We're losing our lives. Hold on. You
rattle across an old wooden bridge. You
look back one last time through the
smoke. The torches of the angry mob are
stopping at the treeine. They aren't
following you into the deep woods. They
know better. Finally, the wagon slows to
a crawl. You collapse against a
surviving crate of product. You are
covered in cuts, bruises, cool dust, and
sticky molasses. You lost half the
money. You lost most of the bottles. But
the silence of the forest is the most
beautiful sound you have ever heard. And
you're alive. The sun rises. You're
sitting on the broken back of the wagon.
Barnaby is asleep on the ground, snoring
loudly. You look at what's left of your
empire. The banner is burned away. The
wheels are wobbly. You have 11 bottles
of Dr. Thunder left and they're all
cracked. You count the money. You
managed to save about $200 that you
earned across your last few stops. It's
not a fortune, but it's enough. Barnaby
wakes up with a jump. What are we doing,
boss? We need to find a creek. We need
to mix a new batch before we hit the
next town. You shake your head. No more
mixing, Barnaby. I'm done with the
bucket. I'm done with the red pepper.
And I'm definitely done with the
running. Barnaby looks confused. So, we
quit. We get jobs on a farm. Farm work.
Look at these hands, Barnaby. These
hands don't plow. These hands sell. I
heard about a chemist down in Atlanta.
He's cooking up something new.
Apparently, it's a syrup. Dark, sweet,
and fizzy. Does it cure anything?
Barnaby asks. He says it cures headaches
and melancholy, you say with a grin. But
here's the genius part. It doesn't taste
like pond water. It tastes like sugar.
And he puts a special leaf in it. The
cocoa leaf makes people feel wide awake.
You stand up and dust off your pants. We
aren't going to trick people anymore,
Barnaby. That's too much work. We're
going to sell them something they
actually want. We'll talk to this
Atlanta fella, buy some of his syrup,
and set up a fountain. They'll come to
us, and they'll come back every single
day for another glass.

transparency, accountability, serving

in the public works department. [music]
You pushed through affordable housing
initiatives. Local newspapers called
[music] you a breath of fresh air. You

for Congress. Bigger stage, bigger

"Nothing," he said. "Just keep being

Washington. You were going to change
everything. Three months in, the
businessman called. There was a vote

Nothing major. "Would you consider

You looked at the bill. It was

of other companies money, too. Job

You voted yes.
Six months later, another call. Another
vote. This one about environmental

manufacturing waste.
You hesitated. This one felt different.
You'd campaigned on environmental
protection. But the businessman
explained it carefully. The regulations
were killing American jobs, forcing
factories overseas. Was that what you
wanted?
Foreign countries with worse
environmental standards doing the
manufacturing instead? When he put it

[music] irresponsible. You voted yes,

Business groups started praising you.
Pragmatic, they called you. Realistic.
The businessman invited you to dinner.
Expensive [music] steakhouse. He had
friends he wanted you to meet, other

much red tape. They just wanted to do
business. You started taking their
calls,
making introductions,
helping navigate the bureaucracy.
Nothing illegal, just helping
constituents. That's what
representatives do.
Four years later, you ran for Senate.
The businessman and and his friends
donated the legal maximum. Then their
wives donated, their children, their
employees, their companies PACs.
Suddenly, you had 3 million in campaign
funds. You won in a landslide. The
Senate was different. More power, more

He showed up at your office unannounced.
Expensive suit. Again, this man made no
appointment. Your assistant tried to

He sat down across from you [music] and
smiled.
"I solve problems," he said, "for people
like you."
You asked, "What kind of problems?"
"The kind that end careers, the kind

He leaned back his chair.

Nothing illegal, just debts, bad

The Fixer smiled.

Real enough for the news and real enough

The Fixer called the next day, said you

Everyone pays.

want money. I want access."

told yourself you'd stop after this one,

work."
That was two years ago. Now you're

leaders. Secret Service agents stand

guys, that you're playing the long game,
that once you reach the top, once you're
president, [music]
you'll cut ties with The Fixer. You'll
go back to your roots. You'll be the

You tell yourself this late at night
when you can't [music] sleep, when the
guilt creeps in. But deep down, you know
the truth.
You know what you've become.
The climb isn't over yet. You're not
done. One more step, one more position,
the presidency. And you'll do whatever
it takes to get there. The phone on your
desk rings. You know who it is before

problem," The Fixer says.
"There's a journalist, young woman,

financial records." "What did she find?"

She knows the right questions to ask."
"What do you suggest?"
The fixer pulls out his phone, shows you
a photo. The reporter. She's leaving her
apartment building, coffee in hand,

photographed.
"I can make her go away. Not

far, sacrificed too much. You're so
close to the presidency, so close to
everything you've worked for. You look

3 days later stories start appearing.
The reporter has been accused of
plagiarism, fabricating sources, ethical
violations.
The accusations are lies, manufactured,
planted, but they work. Her editor puts

now. Nobody will believe her. You watch

sick, but you also feel relief.
You're safe
for now.
The presidential campaign launches 2
months later. The rallies are enormous,
thousands [music] chanting your name.
You shake hands, you make speeches, you
smile for cameras. But at night, you see
the reporter's [music] face, the
accusations that destroyed her, the lies
you let happen.
You win primary after primary. You
secure the nomination. Then 3 months
before election day, something happens.
The reporter resurfaces.
She's been quietly rebuilding, gathering
evidence, finding sources willing to
talk. People who worked with the fixer,
people who know what happened. She
publishes everything, not just the smear
campaign against [music] her,
everything. Your Senate campaign, the
fake photos, the buried investigations,
the fixer's entire operation. She can't
prove all of it, but she proves enough.
The story goes viral. Every outlet picks
it up.
Your opponents [music] call for
investigations. Your allies go silent.
Your poll numbers collapse.
Two weeks before the election, you're
down by 15 points. It's over. Everyone
knows it.
The fixer calls one last time. He can
still fix this, he says. One more play,
something big, something that changes
everything.
You know what he means. Something
drastic. Something that would cross a
line you can never uncross.
You think about it. Really think about
it. For the first time in 15 years,
you say no.
You're done, you tell him. He warns you.
He goes down, you go down. He has

everything.

Thank you for finally doing the right

You stare at the message.
Then the FBI calls. They want to talk
about the fixer, about everything. You
tell them yes, you'll cooperate. Not for

Finally, you think about the kid who

believed in changing the world, who

Maybe there's still a chance to be the

subtitles.plaintext:
You're 11 years old, curled up on a
straw mat in the burned-out shell of
what used to be your home when a woman
in white robes steps through the
doorway. She smells like incense. She
smiles like a mother, and her eyes are
dead as winter water. She brushes the
ash from your cheek and asks if you'd
like to come somewhere warm. You haven't
eaten in 3 days. Your parents are buried
under the rice barn. You say yes. You
don't know it yet, but you just signed
your life away. Welcome to your life as
a kunoichi. The year is 1565. Sengoku
Japan is one giant open wound. Daimyo
carving each other up over rice fields
and salt roads, and you're one of the
orphans the war coughed up by the
thousands. The woman who took you, Lady
Chiyome, says she runs a house for girls
like you, a sanctuary, a mercy. The
villagers nod and don't ask questions
because feeding starving girls is what
holy women do. That's what she wants
them to think. The cart ride to a
mountain compound in Shinano province
takes 4 days. 12 other girls in the
back, all the same hollow stare. One is
a war widow. One was a prostitute sold
by her uncle. One won't say where she
came from. Her name is Hana. You sleep
against her shoulder because the nights
are cold and the future is colder. You
arrive at a compound tucked into the
mountains. Gates of cedar, snow already
on the rooftops. They give you white
robes. They tell you you're going to be
a miko, a shrine maiden. You think it
sounds beautiful, holy, safe. You're
wrong about all three. By 12, you're
memorizing prayers in the morning and
learning to slit a goat's throat in the
afternoon. The instructors are women in
their 30s who never laugh. They teach
you to walk silent on wood floors, to
pour tea so your sleeve never trembles,
to recite Shinto rituals so smooth a
real priest would weep. They also teach
you how to kill a man with a hairpin,
where his neck goes soft, where the
temples cave in, where the artery sits
just under the jaw like a tripwire.
Sounds glamorous, right? Wrong. It's 12
hours a day of bruises, sliced palms,
and a bamboo rod across your shins every
time your accent slips out of noble
dialect. You bleed through your robes.
You learn to bow while bleeding. By 13,
you can mix poison from oleander root in
the dark. You can identify 17 kinds of
noblemen by the cut of their kimono. You
can kneel for 6 hours without your legs
going numb, because Chiome made you do
it every dawn for a year, and the
alternative was a whip. You also learn
the unspoken rule. You have no friends.
The girls beside you are not sisters.
They're competitors, and one day one of
them will be ordered to test if your
cover holds, and she will not blink when
she presses a blade to your throat. Hana
whispers it to you one night in the
dark. "Don't cry when they send me, and
I won't cry when they send you." You
hold her hand under the blanket. You
both pretend not to. By 14, they start
sending you out on practice runs. Walk
into a village, pose as a wandering
priestess, listen for 3 days, bring back
the name of every man who owns more than
10 horses. Get caught and don't come
back, because Chiome won't retrieve you.
You never get caught. You're 16 when
they hand you a scroll with a name on
it. The name belongs to a minor lord in
a province three weeks walk away. He's
plotting against the Takita clan, your
patron, the one whose silver feeds the
compound. Your job is simple. Get inside
his household, listen, confirm the plot,
then if the order comes, kill him. You
walk into his castle town wearing white
miko robes, a wooden chest carried
behind you by a porter, false bottom.
Inside, crushed datura, two iron nekote
claws wrapped in silk, and a hairpin
sharpened to the width of a darning
needle. The porter doesn't know. The
porter never knows. You bless the lord's
wife. She weeps with gratitude. Within a
month, you're a fixture in the
household, the holy girl who sees omens,
who sings the children to sleep, who
pours sake at the lord's elbow when his
retainers come to whisper. You smile.
You bow. You memorize every face, every
name, every hushed word about troop
movements and which gate of which castle
will be opened on which moon. The lord
notices you. Of course he does. They
always do. He requests you for the night
and your stomach turns to ice, but you
smile because Chiome trained you for
this, because flinching is dying. You go
in. The chamber smells of cedar smoke
and old sake. He's already half drunk,
sprawled on the silk, beckoning. You
kneel beside him and pour a fresh cup
and your sleeves grazes the lacquered
tray and the powder you've been carrying
for 3 weeks slides into the wine without
a sound. He drinks. He laughs. He pulls
you closer. You let him. You smile. You
wait. 20 minutes in, his speech starts
to slur. 40 and his eyes won't track
your face. You feel his pulse stutter
under your palm where it rests on his
chest and you count because Chiome
taught you to count, because a kunoichi
who panics is a kunoichi who leaves a
mess. At 60, his breathing goes slow and
shallow. You slide the hairpin from your
hair. You find the soft spot behind his
ear, just under the hairline, where the
bone gives way to nothing and then you
push. A small, wet sound. A twitch.
Nothing else. You come out. He does not.
When the body is found in the morning,
the household will say a sudden illness
took him in his sleep. The toxin in the
sake leaves no trace. The puncture
behind his ear is the size of a sewing
needle, hidden in the hairline and no
one will ever look. You walk out the
side gate at dawn, white robes
unstained, eyes lowered, a holy girl in
mourning. The guards bow as you pass.
You bow back. You vomit in the forest 2
miles later, hands shaking so hard you
drop the hairpin twice trying to clean
it. Then you bury the shaking deep where
it can't reach you, and you keep
walking. By 17, you're Chiyome's top
operative. By 18, you've killed three
more men and seduced two who didn't need
killing, just listening. One morning in
Kai, you wake in a courtesan's room you
don't remember falling asleep in, and
you sit up, and you reach for the
hairpin under the pillow before you
reach for the lamp. The hairpin first,
the light second. You sit there for a
long minute holding it in the dark, and
you don't feel anything about it. Not
pride, not shame, just the weight of
metal, familiar as a finger. That's when
you know. You live a dozen lives. You're
a fortune-teller in Mikawa, a teahouse
girl in Kai, a courtesan in a Kyoto
pleasure district where you pour wine
for samurai who whispered troop counts
between gulps. You sleep in silk one
week and on dirt the next. You stop
dreaming. You stop missing your village,
your mother, the smell of your father's
pipe, because dreaming and missing are
luxuries that get a kunoichi killed.
Hana is sent to Owari Province in the
spring of 1568. She doesn't come back.
Three months later, a porter passing
through the village mentions a wandering
priestess found in a river, hairpin
still in her hair, throat opened ear to
ear. There are no funerals for kunoichi.
You scrub Hana's name off the wooden
tablet in the shrine yourself, because
that's the rule, and you don't cry,
because that's the rule, too. That
night, alone in your cell, you bite your
sleeve until you taste blood, and you
make a sound no one hears. You're 23
when they send you against a man who has
handlers of his own. The mission looks
like the others. Infiltrate, listen,
wait for the kill order. You take your
place in the household of a Hojo
retainer in Eastern Japan, a colder,
grayer country, the kind where the wind
carries salt off the sea and into your
lungs. You charm him. You learn his
routine. You wait. Then, a maid you've
worked beside for 2 months pulls you
aside in the laundry yard and whispers
in flawless Iga dialect that she knows
what you are. She is not your friend.
She's not your sister. She is a Hojo
Kunoichi and she has been watching you
for 6 weeks and the order has just come
down. Run or fight. Your hand is moving
before your mind catches up. The hairpin
slides out of your hair. Two iron claws
snap onto your fingers from your sleep
and the laundry yard becomes a blur of
white robes and red linen and a single,
short, wet sound. Her eyes go wide.
Yours don't. You run for 9 days eating
roots, sleeping in caves, doubling back
to throw off pursuit. By the time you
reach a Takeda outpost, your feet are
black with frostbite. Your robes are
rags and your face is a mask carved from
someone you don't recognize anymore.
Lady Chiyome receives you in silence.
She nods once. She gives you tea. She
tells you to rest for a week and then
she gives you a new name and sends you
to Mikawa. There is no celebration.
There is no thank you. There's only the
next mission. The Takeda clan begins to
fall apart in 1582. Your patron, the man
whose silver feeds the compound, dies
and the network Chiyome built starts to
fracture like ice on a thawing river.
You're 28. You killed 11 men. You've
buried Hana and four others in your
memory and your knees ache from a decade
of kneeling on cold floors. Your final
assignment is the Tokugawa border. You
don't know it's your final assignment.
You never do. You're 3 days into the
cover, a wandering miko blessing a
village shrine. When a farmer recognizes
the sandals of your dead handler in your
pack, he shouts, "The militia comes!"
And you run for the tree line, hairpin
already in your hand. And you almost
make it. The arrow goes through your
back below the left shoulder. You feel
it before you hear it. Your knees hit
the dirt. The Nekotes slip out of your
sleeve and clatter onto the road, two
small iron claws gleaming in the
afternoon sun. You think of Hana. You
think of [music] the woman who pulled
you off the straw mat when you were 11.
The one who smelled like incense and
smiled like a mother. You think she
should have left you there. [music] The
second arrow takes you inside. You don't
feel the third.
The villagers find white robes, [music]
two iron claws, and a hairpin sharpened
to the width of a darning needle. No one
ever learns your name. You buried it
yourself years ago in a forest 2 miles
from a dead lord's castle. Lady Chiome
will scrub a wooden [music] tablet clean
in a shrine far away and assign your
cover identity to a younger girl, a
16-year-old with a hollow stare [music]
on her first mission. You were a shadow
in white. You were a hairpin in the
dark. [music] You were the blade.
She polished the man who carried one.
Click the card to watch your life as a
samurai's wife.

text:
Discover what your life would have been like as a Crusader Knight.

Inspired by Dinzo, James Toland, and Bound.

DISCLAIMER: This video is a fictional dramatization inspired by historical accounts of a crusader's life. While based on real practices, characters and events are exaggerated for storytelling. No one was harmed in the making of this video.

#Crusades #CrusaderKnight #MedievalHistory #yourlifeas

subtitles.plaintext:
You're 18 years old, standing in a muddy
field in France, November 1095, when the
Pope's words hit you like a thunderbolt.
Deus vult, the crowd screams. God wills
it. Jerusalem, the holiest city on
Earth, languishes under Muslim control.
Pilgrims are being slaughtered. Christ's
tomb is in the hands of infidels, and
Pope Urban the Second is promising
something incredible. Anyone who marches
to liberate the Holy Land will have all
their sins forgiven. Every lie, every
theft, every wrong you've ever done,
wiped clean. There's just one problem.
You're a second son. Your older brother
gets the castle, the title, the land,
the future. You get hand-me-down armor
and a lifetime of obscurity. But this,
this is your ticket out. So you do what
thousands of crusaders are doing. You
mortgage your future. You sell the small
piece of land your father carved out for
you. You borrow from money lenders at
crushing interest rates. You pawn your
mother's jewelry, anything that isn't
nailed down. By the time you're ready to
march, you bet everything on a war
thousands of miles away. The night
before you leave, your mother asks if
you'll come back. You look her in the
eyes and say yes. You both know it's a
lie, but she needs to hear it, and you
need to say it. That lie will sit in
your chest like a stone for the next 3
years. Your mother is crying. You don't
look back. You can't afford to. That's
how it starts, your journey as a
crusader knight. You've set to become a
warrior, but not overnight. By 7, you
were shipped off to become a page,
serving food, cleaning armor, getting
beaten by squires who thought teaching
meant trauma. By 14, you were a squire
yourself, carrying a knight's gear,
learning to kill in 40 different ways.
Sword drills at dawn, lance practice
until your shoulders screamed, wrestling
in the mud until you couldn't feel your
face. By 18, your body was a map of
scars and calluses. Your hands knew a
sword better than they'd ever know a
woman's touch. You were built for war,
and now war was calling. Nobody told you
the crusade would start with walking.
Endless, soul-crushing walking. You join
thousands of fighters snaking through
Germany, Hungary, and into the Byzantine
Empire. Behind you trails tens of
thousands more. Pilgrims, priests,
prostitutes, peasants who sold
everything for this holy gamble. The
Byzantine Emperor shuttles you across
the Bosphorus as fast as he can, eager
to get you out of his city before you
loot it. Then, the dying starts. First,
the heat. You grew up in mild France,
and Anatolia is a furnace. Your armor
turns into an oven. Knights collapse,
cooking alive inside their own
protection. You strip to your gambeson,
risking arrows for the chance to
breathe. Then, the water runs out. The
Turks have poisoned the wells,
slaughtered the livestock, burned the
crops. Men start drinking horse blood.
Some drink their own urine. You watch a
knight, a proud, noble knight who talked
of glory around the campfire just a week
ago, die on his knees, tongue black and
swollen, begging God for one more drop
of water. His prayers go unanswered.
Turkish horse archers shadow your column
like wolves. They dart in at dawn, loose
their arrows, vanish before you can form
a charge. Every night, you wonder if
you'll wake up with a Turkish blade at
your throat. Every morning, more bodies
line the road. Your first real battle is
Dorylaeum, July 1097. Tens of thousands
of Turks against your own vanguard
column. You're surrounded, pinned down,
slowly dying under a rain of arrows for
seven brutal hours. Then, the second
Crusader column crashes into the Turkish
flank. The enemy breaks. You charge.
Your sword takes its first life, a
Turkish cavalryman. Eyes wide with shock
as your blade finds his throat. You feel
nothing, just relief it's him and not
you. Welcome to the crusade. Antioch is
a nightmare wearing the skin of a city.
Walls stretching for miles. 400 towers.
The The lords can't storm it, so they
settle in for a siege. Eight months.
Eight endless months of hunger, disease,
and despair. Winter brings starvation.
You eat the horses first, the same
horses you mortgage your future to buy.
Then the dogs. Then the rats. Then
things you don't want to remember.
Disease runs through camp like fire.
Typhoid, dysentery, things with no name
that make men scream until there's
nothing left. The stench of death hangs
over everything. Desertion becomes
epidemic. Knights who swore oaths before
God, who took the cross with tears in
their eyes, slip away in the night. You
understand. You've thought about it.
You've dreamed of home, of cool French
rain, of your mother's face. The lie you
told her burns hotter now. What if you
never make it back? What if the last
thing you gave her was false hope? But
you've come too far. Turning back now
means dying as a failure. Then a
miracle, or betrayal. A guard on the
walls, an insider with a price, agrees
to open a way in. On a June night in
1098, you're part of the first wave
through. What follows isn't war, it's
slaughter. You pour through the streets,
and every man, woman, and child becomes
the enemy. Blood runs in the gutters.
Bodies pile in the squares. You kill,
you loot, you tell yourself it's holy
work. The screaming faces, they'll visit
you in dreams for the rest of your life.
But you've barely washed the blood from
your armor when a massive Muslim relief
army arrives. Suddenly, you're trapped
inside Antioch. The besiegers become the
besieged. A peasant claims visions of
the Holy Lance, the spear that pierced
Christ, buried under the Cathedral of
St. Peter. They dig for days and find
something. Rusted iron that could be
anything, but the army goes insane with
faith. Three days later, starving and
outnumbered, you sally out on June 28th,
and somehow win. Antioch is yours.
You've lost a third of your army, your
horse, and pieces of your soul you'll
never get back. But Jerusalem still
waits. July, 1099. Three years of
marching, starving, fighting. Of the
tens of thousands who left Europe, maybe
12 to 15,000 remain. The rest are bones
on the road, food for crows, footnotes
in a story that isn't finished yet. The
siege lasts five weeks. You build towers
from dismantled ships, dragging timber
from Jaffa through the desert like
slaves building a pharaoh's pyramid. On
July 15, the towers finally touch the
walls. You're in the second wave,
climbing ladders while arrows rain down
and burning oil tries to turn you into a
torch. The man ahead takes an arrow
through the eye and falls, nearly
pulling you with him. You keep climbing.
There's no other direction anymore. Then
you're over the wall and hell opens its
gates. Crusaders flood through Jerusalem
in a frenzy of religious ecstasy and
bloodlust. Muslim defenders cut down in
mosques. Jewish residents burned alive
in their synagogue. Most Eastern
Christians are already gone, expelled
before you arrived because the governor
didn't trust them. Chroniclers will
write of blood up to the horses'
bridles, of men wading ankle-deep
through gore. You were part of this and
then you see her. A woman clutching a
child pressed against a wall, eyes wide
with terror. She's not a soldier, she's
not a threat, she's just a mother like
yours, trying to protect her child. For
one frozen moment you lock eyes. You see
your mother's face in hers, the same
fear, the same desperate love. A
crusader beside you raises his sword.
You could stop him, you could say
something. You don't. You turn away. You
hear the screams behind you, but you
keep walking. That face, those eyes,
they'll follow you longer than any
battle wound. You tell yourself you had
no choice. The battle rage took over.
Everyone else was doing it. Every excuse
sounds hollow, even inside your own
head. By sunset, the streets fall quiet,
except for the moans of the dying. You
walk through the carnage towards the
Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Christ's
tomb, the holiest site in Christendom.
Blood-soaked warriors fall to their
knees around you, weeping, praying,
thanking God for victory. You kneel,
too. You touch the stone. You try to
feel absolution. Instead, you feel
empty. You came for forgiveness. You
found Jerusalem, but somewhere along the
road, you lost something else entirely.
Most Crusaders go home, but what's
waiting for you? The lands you sold are
gone. Your brother holds the family
estate. You're 22 with nothing but a
sword and a reputation written in blood.
So, you stay. The new Kingdom of
Jerusalem needs knights desperately.
Only a few hundred armed men remain to
hold land surrounded by Muslim powers.
You're granted a small fief near Jaffa,
a tower, some olive groves, a village of
mixed Christians, Muslims, and Jews who
eye you with the wariness of people
who've survived conquest before. Life in
Outremer is strange. You eat foods
you've never tasted, lemons, oranges,
sugarcane. You learn bits of Arabic from
your Muslim tenants. Some Crusaders take
local wives. Some just try to survive.
The peace between battles is just
preparation for the next war. You marry,
have children, teach your sons to fight
before they can read. Your wife dies of
fever. Your youngest son dies at 15,
ambushed on a road you'd ridden a
hundred times. You bury him in the
shadow of Jerusalem's walls. The city
you helped conquer, the city that's
taken everything from you. By 45, you're
ancient by Crusader standards. The dream
still come, the woman in Jerusalem, the
eyes you turned away from. You confess
it a thousand times, to priests, to God,
to the darkness of your room at night,
but some sins aren't words deep. They're
carved into bone. In 1124, you join the
siege of Tyre alongside Venetian
Crusaders. You're too old for the front
lines, but you refuse to watch from the
rear. During a sortie your horse goes
down. A blade finds a gap in your armor,
a spot you've protected for 30 years. As
you fall you see the walls weakening.
Another victory for Christ. They bury
you outside Tyre. A simple stone among
thousands. You were 47, a landless
second son who died a lord. A sinner who
killed for forgiveness. A pilgrim who
never quite found what he was looking
for. Were you a hero or a villain? A
saint or a butcher? The answer depends
on who's telling the story. But you
lived, you fought, you believed in
something bigger than yourself, even
when it led you to hell and back. You
told your mother you'd come back. You
didn't. And the last thing you ever gave
her wasn't glory. It was a lie that
turned into a habit. First with words,
then with silence. [clears throat]
The holy land keeps demanding blood and
new crosses keep marching east, hoping
it buys what it never really could,
forgiveness. You just watched a man
chase salvation and find blood. Now
watch a girl get traded like currency in
an empire built on tribute. Your life as
an Aztec concubine is next.

text:
Discover what your life would have been like as a Victorian Noblewoman in 1800s England.

Inspired by Dinzo, James Toland, and Bound.

DISCLAIMER: This video is a fictional dramatization inspired by historical accounts of a Victorian Noblewoman's life. While based on real practices, characters and events are exaggerated for storytelling. No one was harmed in the making of this video.

#VictorianHistory #WomensHistory #VictorianEra

subtitles.plaintext:
You open your eyes for the very first
time, and the world smells of rosewater
and blood. London, 1840. Your mother is
weeping from exhaustion in a four-poster
bed that costs more than most families
earn in a year. A midwife wipes you
clean with warmed linen. Your father
pushes through the doorway, still in his
riding coat, and looks at you the way a
man looks at a ledger that didn't
balance. "A girl," the midwife says.
Your father says nothing for a long
time. Then, "She'll need to marry well."
You're 11 seconds old. Your dowry is
already being calculated. Welcome to
your life as a Victorian noblewoman.
You're born to the Cavendish family,
minor aristocracy with a country estate
in Berkshire, a house in Mayfair, and a
bloodline that goes back four
generations of men who married well and
died richer. Your father is a baron.
Your mother is a baron's ornament. And
you, third child, only daughter, are the
most expensive bargaining chip either of
them will ever produce. You didn't grow
up. You were assembled. By five, your
mother appears at breakfast and bedtime.
Your father appears at Christmas. The
rest belongs to Miss Wren, your
governess, your warden, your entire
emotional universe. She teaches you
posture by balancing books on your head
and corrects your French with a look
that could curdle cream. The first
corset arrives at 10, light stays, they
call it, training wheels for a lifetime
of compression. Within 2 years, your
ribs will start molding inward like soft
clay on a potter's wheel. Doctors will
later call this chlorosis, green
sickness, and blame your pallor on
female weakness rather than the steel
cage redistributing your organs. Your
best friend is Clara, the cook's
daughter. She teaches you to knead
bread, to whistle, to swear in Cockney.
You teach her to read. One afternoon,
your mother catches Clara sitting in
your chair holding your book. Clara's
mother is dismissed by Thursday. You
learn the lesson faster than any French
conjugation. People below you are
furniture, furniture that smiles,
serves, and vanishes when it becomes
inconvenient. You cry about Clara for 3
days. Miss Wren tells you ladies don't
form attachments with servants. You stop
crying. You don't stop missing her, but
you learn to miss people quietly, which
is the most Victorian skill of all. The
only constant is Agnes, your lady's
maid, who arrives when you're 12 and
never leaves. She laces your corset
every morning, brushes your hair every
night, and knows more about your body
than you do. She's 22, plain, sharp, and
earns 12 pounds a year. Every coin is
hers. Remember that. At 17, they present
you at court. Your corset is cinched to
19 inches. Your liver presses against
your stomach. Every breath comes in half
portions. The Queen glances at you for
roughly 4 seconds. Your mother has spent
11 years preparing you for those 4
seconds. Piano, watercolors, French,
embroidery, nothing that would help you
survive alone for a single afternoon,
but everything that proves you never
have to. You curtsy. The Queen nods. And
just like that, you're on the market.
The rules are simple. A gentleman may
send you exactly four types of gifts:
books, flowers, confectionery, or sheet
music. Anything else implies he's trying
to buy your affection, which is
technically your father's job. Lord
Edmund Ashworth sends tulips first, then
Chopin. He's 34, quiet, owns land in
three counties, and opinions on none of
them. He dances adequately and talks
about drainage improvements with genuine
passion. Your mother calls him a serious
man. Your father calls him solvent. You
call him Lord Ashworth because using his
first name before engagement would cause
a scandal roughly equivalent to arson.
Six months of chaperoned walks and
letters inspected by your mother, you've
had exactly one unchaperoned
conversation. 12 minutes in a garden
while your chaperone was distracted by a
wasp. He told you about his dead sister.
You told him about Clara. It's the most
honest either of you has been with
another person in years. He proposes
through your father. Your father
accepts. You're consulted last, which
everyone agrees is a formality. The
engagement is announced. You are now
allowed to hold his hand in public.
Progress. You're 18 when the wedding
happens. It's beautiful. Everybody says
so. What nobody mentions is that the
moment the vicar finishes speaking, you
legally cease to exist. Under coverture,
the law of the land, your identity is
absorbed into your husband's. Every
penny you brought into this marriage,
his. Your inheritance, his. Pearl
earrings your mother gave you, legally
his. You cannot sign a contract, write a
will, or keep a single shilling without
Edmund's permission. Agnes can leave her
position, sign her own contracts, walk
away whenever she wants. She owns more
of herself than you do. The richest
woman in the county is legally less free
than the maid who buttons her dress.
Edmund isn't cruel. That's the thing.
He's decent, distracted, and mildly
baffled by your unhappiness. He gives
you the household to run, which is like
giving someone the keys to a prison and
calling it management. You organize
dinners for men who make laws you can't
vote on. You host charity bazaars for
causes you can't legally fund. You
smile. You pour tea. You are the most
expensive decoration in every room you
enter. And of course, they expect heirs.
You're 20 when your first pregnancy ends
in stillbirth at 7 months. The doctor,
who came from another patient without
washing his hands, because germ theory
is still a decade away from being taken
seriously, calls it God's will. You call
it the worst night of your life. The
servants change the sheets while you're
still bleeding. At 22, your second
pregnancy. You beg for chloroform. Queen
Victoria used it for Prince Leopold's
birth in 1853, and what's good enough
for the queen is good enough for you.
The doctor resists. Some physicians
still believe labor pain is divine
punishment for Eve's sin. Agnes argues
with the doctor on your behalf. Quietly,
carefully, knowing her place even while
overstepping it, he relents. The
chloroform works. A boy, healthy. You
name him William. Then another, then
another. Each pregnancy is a coin flip
against puerperal fever, which kills
indiscriminately, rich or poor, clean
house or workhouse. During the 1850s
alone, roughly 31,000 women die in
childbirth across England and Wales. You
survive. You consider this luck rather
than baseline expectation, which tells
you everything about what century you're
living in. Meanwhile, the nursery walls
are painted Sheila's green, the most
fashionable color in England, a bright
emerald pigment made with copper and
arsenic. In damp weather, the wallpaper
releases arsenic gas that you and your
children breathe every night. Babies
have died in nurseries exactly like
yours. Nobody connects the dots for
another decade. When William develops a
persistent cough, the doctor blames
London air. You move into a different
bedroom anyway, instinct. By 30, the
routine has calcified around you like
plaster. Morning, correspondence, and
menus. Afternoon, social calls, 15
minutes each, announced by calling card.
Evening, dinner, conversation,
performance. Repeat until dead. Your
opinions on Parliament are sharp,
informed, better than half the men at
Edmund's club. The only channel for a
woman's political influence is the right
word at the right dinner to the right

rotting inside. You grab the edge and
lift. The whole thing comes off the
ground. You're holding it overhead.
You set it down. Breathing normal. Heart
rate is normal. You're not even
sweating.
Three steps back and you jump. You clear
the dumpster. Not by a little. 20 ft of
air and you land on the other side so
hard you leave cracks in the asphalt.
Something happened to you. You don't
know what. You don't know why, but your
body is not the same body you went to
sleep with last night.
And the only thought in your head is,
"What else can I do?" Over the next few
days, you find out. Speed. Not just
Olympic fast. Fast enough that the trees
blur and the wind cuts your eyes. You
cover 3 miles in what feels like 30
seconds and barely notice.
Your durability. You drop a cinder block
on your foot from waist height. Nothing.
Not even a bruise.
You try a higher drop. Same thing.
Your senses sharpen. The couple arguing
two apartments over, you hear every
word.
License plates four blocks away, you
read them without squinting.
Now, the big test. You go to the top of
your apartment building.
You jump off.
However, it doesn't go as planned. You
land on the ground. You're not hurt, but
you can't fly. Okay, good to know. You
know what else is good to know? I wrote
a short novel based on the black market
surgeon video, the one with over 4
million views. The book is its own story
though. Same premise, but it's a dark
psychological thriller that goes places
the video never could. It's on pre-order
right now on Amazon for $4.99.
Links in the description.
Nothing from your hands either. No
energy, no heat, no webs. You try
pointing at a wall and concentrating,
and nothing happens. And you feel like
an idiot standing alone in a parking lot
with your arms out. You don't tell
anyone. Who would you tell? And what
would you say?
One thing sits in the back of your head
at night though. It's small and easy to
ignore.
You didn't ask for this, and nothing
about it came with instructions. The
first time happens by accident.
Walking home from the corner store.
Tires screeching two blocks away, and
then a crunch. Then, nothing. You run,
full speed. You're there in seconds.
A sedan ran a red light and T-boned an
SUV. The SUV is on its side. Smoke from
under the hood. A woman inside pinned
and screaming.
Two people on the sidewalk with their
phones out. They're filming. You walk to
the SUV, grab the frame, flip it back
onto its wheels. Then the woman stares
at you through the shattered window. You
rip the door off its hinges and pull her
out. She's shaking. She grabs your arm
and says, "Thank you."
You leave before anyone asks your name.
The next week it becomes a thing. You
stop a mugging behind the laundromat.
You pull a kid off the train tracks. You
catch a dog that bolted into traffic.
You stop a gas station robbery.
You step between two guys outside a bar
at 2:00 a.m. and don't move when the
first punch lands on your jaw. The guy
breaks two knuckles on your face. You
don't feel anything. He looks at his
hand, looks at you, and runs.
Something loosens in your chest after
each one. A tightness you didn't know
you were carrying. The woman at the car,
the kid on the tracks, each one unwinds
something. Like this is what the
strength is for. Like the universe
[music] handed you something and this is
the answer to why.
You start going out at night, listening
for trouble, finding it, and handling
it.
You don't have a costume. You just wear
a hoodie and a baseball cap. You're not
a superhero. You're just a guy who can
do things and chooses to.
The local news picks it up. Not you
specifically, but the pattern.
Mysterious good Samaritan stops armed
robbery.
Witnesses describe man with impossible
strength at crash site.
You see yourself on a grainy phone
camera on the 11:00 news. Your hoodie's
on with your ball cap. Your face is
mostly hidden. They're calling you the
guardian.
You hate it. But you keep going out.
Then something changes.
You're walking home from a late shift
when you feel it. Pressure in the air,
like the drop before a thunderstorm,
except the sky is clear.
You stop. Two blocks ahead, a street
light explodes. Glass is raining down on
the empty sidewalk. Then the next one,
then [music] the next. They all explode,
a line of dead street [music] lights.
You follow the street lights down to a
warehouse. The door has been ripped off
its hinges. Inside, the air is wrong.
It's heavy and warm. A man is standing
in the center of the floor. Average
height, average build,
but his hands are glowing. He's looking
right at you, like he was waiting.
"Took you long enough."
His voice is calm, almost bored. You
don't move. "I've been watching," he
says.
"The car, the mugging, the kid on the
tracks. Very noble, very small."
The glow around his hands brightens. A
metal pipe [music] on the floor starts
to lift up.
"You don't even know what you are, do
you?" The pipe is pointing at [music]
you now. "Let me show you." It fires.
You move faster than you've ever moved.
The pipe grazes your shoulder, tears
through your hoodie, and doesn't break
your skin, but the force knocks you
sideways [music] into a concrete pillar.
You throw a steel drum at him. The drum
stops midair, 3 ft from his face, and
just hangs there. Then it drops. He
smiles. Then he throws it back at you.
You jump out of the way, but when you
look up, he's gone.
You don't know his name. You don't know
where he came from or how he got what he
has, but he's not like you. Your power
is your body, strength, speed,
durability. His is everything else. He
moves things with his mind, and he's not
interested in saving anyone.
Over the next 48 hours, it gets bad. A
section of an overpass collapses during
rush hour. You save seven people from
crushed cars. The news says it was a
structural failure. You know better. You
saw the support beams. They had been
bent. He chooses the place, an
intersection downtown. It's the middle
of the day, and the crowd is huge. You
hear it from three blocks away, cars
lifting off the ground, people running.
By the time you get there, he's [music]
standing in the center of the
intersection, cars floating around him
in a slow orbit, a city bus on its side,
a street light ripped from the ground,
hovering above him like a javelin.
>> [music]
>> "There you are," he says.
The street light comes at you first. You
catch it. The impact drives you back 20
ft, shoes tearing trenches [music] in
the asphalt. You throw it aside and
charge.
"You keep saving them," he says, "one at
a time, and it will never be enough. You
know that, right?" You move.
Your arms come free, and you drive your
fist forward and land a huge one on his
jaw.
He goes backward, through the car,
through the brick wall on the other
side. 3 seconds of silence.
Then he comes through the rubble,
standing. He raises both hands.
Everything metal within 100 yd rips
free. Car doors, street signs, fencing,
it all lifts, spins.
A tornado of jagged edges with you in
the center.
A hundred pieces of metal slam into you
at once. They don't cut, your skin
holds, but the force sends you off your
feet, through the air, through a wall.
Your back hits concrete and the air
leaves your body. Through the gap in the
wall, he's walking toward you. He stops
10 ft away. The glow around his hands is
[music] weaker now. Flickering. His eyes
are almost entirely red. "Stay down." he
says.
His hands come up as he attempts [music]
to hold you in your place. He's burning
out. You can feel it. The pressure is
[music] nothing. You grab his wrist. He
screams and tries to pull free. You
don't let go. "Stop." you say. He
doesn't. You push him to the ground and
hold him there. He's fighting, but he's
just a man now. The glow is gone. The
air is still. The cops take him. You
don't stay. By the time the first
cruiser rounds the corner, you're three
blocks away. Hoodie destroyed, cap lost
somewhere in the fight. Your hands are
shaking, not from the damage. Your body
is already putting itself back together.
Your bruises are fading. Ache is
draining out of your muscles like water.
By morning, there won't be a mark on
you.
You walk home. It takes an hour. You
could run it in seconds, but you walk.
Your apartment is exactly how you left
it. Dishes in the sink, TV remote on the
couch, coffee maker still has grounds in
it.
You close the door and lock it.
And you stand in the hallway.
Silence.
Not the kind from the absence of noise,
the kind from the absence of people.
You turn on the TV,
they're covering it.
Aerial footage of the intersection, the
overturned [music] bus, the craters in
the asphalt. One anchor mentions [music]
The Guardian.
Your phone buzzes.
Tony.
Hey boss, heard there was some kind of
thing [music] downtown. You good?
You type, "Yeah, all good." And you hit
send.
In the bathroom, [music]
you stare in the mirror.
No cuts, no bruises, not a mark.
Same face as this morning.
Same face [music] as before any of this.
You microwave something, then eat it
standing at [music] the counter, looking
at the wall. The woman from the SUV went
home to her husband and her kids.
The people from all the accidents went
home [music] to someone who is worried
about them.
You go to bed, same as every night, same
as before the strength, before [music]
the speed, before any of it. But the
silence is louder now.
You never [music] asked to be a hero,
and now
you don't have a choice.
Quick reminder, the book is up for
pre-order on Amazon. Links in the
description. If you enjoy my
storytelling, you're going to love the
book.

subtitles.plaintext:
You're 6 years old when your mother
leaves you at the door of a children's
home in Kobe with a bag of clothes and a
note that says, "I'm sorry. I can't
anymore." A woman in a white apron holds
your hand. She takes you through a
corridor of small shoes to a room with
five beds and a window facing a concrete
wall. She points to a bed. "This one's
yours. Nobody is coming back for you."
And the country you were born into has
already decided what you are, Burakumin,
Hamlet people, descendants of those who
skinned animals and buried the dead. A
stain that travels through blood like
ink through water, invisible to the eye,
obvious to everyone who checks. And in
Japan, everybody checks. Welcome to your
life as a Yakuza. By eight, the
orphanage is routine. Wake, clean,
school, silence. You learn to eat fast
because the older boys steal from slow
plates. You learn to sleep light because
the staff don't come when somebody
cries. You learn that adults are just
taller versions of people who leave. At
10, a boy 2 years older than you calls
you Eta, filthy, the old word for your
people, the one that means you're not
even human. You hit him so hard his
tooth comes out in your palm. They move
you to a different room. Nobody moves
him. By 12, school is a daily exercise
in disappearing. Teachers skip your
raised hand. Girls change seats when you
sit down. A guidance counselor tells you
to consider factory work. You're 12.
He's already decided your ceiling. By
13, you're skipping more days than you
attend. By 14, you stop going entirely
and nobody comes looking.
You know, researching this story hit
different because kids like this didn't
fail the system. The system never showed
up for them. They had no one to talk to,
no one to help them see a different
path. And that's something I sit a lot
with when writing these scripts. [music]
Honestly, there are moments in the
research where I have to step away from
the screen. When I'm reading about a
6-year-old left at a door with a bag of
clothes [music]
or a man watching his best friend get
erased from existence with no
explanation, something in me doesn't
want to move on to the next paragraph. I
think about how many of these men
started as kids who just needed one
person to show [music] up, one
conversation that went differently. And
I think about how rarely that happened.
>> [music]
>> How many people are stuck in their own
version of that silence right now,
convinced the only [music] options are
to keep going or disappear. That's where
therapy comes. It won't rewrite your
past, but it can help you stop passing
[music] it forward. And BetterHelp, the
sponsor of today's video, makes starting
that process easier. You take a short
quiz, get matched with a [music]
licensed therapist, and you can talk
over the phone, video, or text. If your
therapist isn't the right fit, you can
switch anytime with no extra cost. Over
6 million people have gotten help
through BetterHelp, and it's earned a
4.8 out of five on the App Store. Click
the [music] link in the description or
go to betterhelp.com/lostlegacy
and get 10% off your first month of
therapy. You're 15 when you hear them
before you see them. A thunder of
engines tearing down National Route 2 at
midnight. 40 Bosozoku riders in modified
jumpsuits, exhaust screaming like
fighter jets. They ride past your window
and something in your chest catches
fire. Within a month, you're one of
them. Hair bleached, jumpsuit
embroidered with kanji you can barely
read, riding a stolen Honda [music]
CB400 with baffles ripped out. The gang
doesn't care where you come from. They
just ask, "Can you ride? And are you
willing to bleed?" Your best friend is
Kenji, son of a Korean dockworker,
another kid the system spat out. At 16,
you get arrested together for the first
time. At 17, the second. This time, a
man in a black suit visits you in the
juvenile facility. He gives you a
business card with a chrysanthemum crest
and says, "When you get out, come see
us." Kenji gets the same card. 1/3 of
all Bosozoku end up exactly where that
card leads. You're released 3 months
later. You go straight to the address
because the alternative is a lifetime of
job applications thrown in the trash the
second someone checks your address. The
card's address leads you to a quiet
office above a pachinko parlor. A man
behind a desk looks you over, nods once,
and puts you to work. 18 months of
scrubbing. You wash cars, mop floors,
fetch cigarettes, and stand in hallways
waiting to be told what to do next. You
make no money. You sleep in a back room
with four other recruits. You are not
Yakuza yet. You are an audition. But you
keep your mouth shut and your hands
busy. And at 19, they decide you've
earned your seat. You kneel on a tatami
in a room that smells of cedar and
incense. Three scrolls hang on the wall.
Amaterasu, the sun goddess, Hachiman,
god of war, and the reigning emperor. 12
candles, two sea bream fish, one large,
one small, parent and child, a single
porcelain sake cup. The Oyabun sits
across from you, 56, thin as wire, face
that gives you nothing. A mediator pours
sake into the cup and hands it to the
boss. He drinks. They fill it again,
less this time, and pass it to you. You
drink. The cup is warm. The sake burns.
That's it. You're his child now. He is
your father. Your real family ceases to
exist. You will call him Oyaji. You will
call the other men Aniki, big brother.
This is the Sakazuki goto. The cup you
just drank from is the most important
object you will ever hold. Lose it and
you've lost everything. Kenji kneels
beside you. He drinks from the same cup.
You're brothers now, bound tighter than
blood. They told you the name Yakuza
comes from a card game, 8-9-3, ya-ku-za,
the worst possible hand, a score of
zero, worthless. That's what society
called you before you walked into this
room. The difference is, now you wear
the name like armor. At 20, they send
you to a Horishi, a tattoo master who
works out of a second-floor apartment in
Shin-Okubo and doesn't advertise. He
sits you down and asks one question.
"What's your story?" You don't know how
to answer, so he answers for you. A koi
swimming upstream on your left shoulder
because you're still climbing. Fudo Myoo
across your back, the immovable king,
protector of those who've got nothing
left to protect. The Tebori method, no
machine, wooden handle, silk thread,
metal needles pushing ink under your
skin one puncture at a time. 120 strikes
per minute. Every single one feels like
a cigarette being put out in your ribs.
Sessions last 3 hours. You come back
every week for 2 years. The pain is the
point. Anyone can pay for a tattoo. Not
everyone can survive one. At 22, you
make a mistake. You mouth off to an
Aniki during a meeting. Nothing violent,
just disrespectful. But respect is
currency here, and you just bounced a
check. The Wakagashira calls you into a
back room. White cloth on the table. A
tanto knife. A bandage. He doesn't need
to explain. You wrap your left pinky at
the first joint, press down.
For 1 second, your entire body turns
into a single scream. The finger
separates. You wrap the severed tip in
the cloth, walk it to the Aniki you
disrespected, and present it with a bow.
Yubitsume, finger shortening. Your grip
on a sword just got weaker. Your
dependence on the family just got
stronger. That's not a side effect,
that's the design. You go back to work
the next morning. Nobody mentions it.
Everybody notices. By 25, you've
graduated from errands to collections.
Your territory is six blocks of
Kabukicho, Shinjuku's red-light
district. Every week, you walk into
hostess bars and pachinko parlors, sit
down, drink the tea they pour with
shaking hands, and leave with an
envelope. The money flows upward, always
upward. You hand a cut to your Aniki. He
feeds the Wakagashira. The Wakagashira
feeds the underboss. The underboss feeds
the Oyabun. Everyone eats before you do.
You wear a suit now, Italian. You carry
two phones. You bow to the right people
at the right angle because in this world
about 3° too shallow is an act of war.
By 28, you're managing a construction
front. On paper, site manager. In
practice, you make sure rival firms
don't bid on your territory. Sometimes
that means tea. Sometimes it means
smashed windows at dawn. Kenji works the
gambling side, charming, reckless. He
starts dipping into the take, small
amounts, barely noticeable. You notice.
You tell him to stop. He laughs and says
the old men are too rich to count. He
stopped laughing because you know how
this story ends. Thieves don't get
warnings in this family. They get
subtracted. You're 29 when you meet her
at a ramen shop in Ikebukuro at 2:00
a.m. She's a nurse. She sees the missing
finger, the suit, the way you sit with
your back to the wall. She knows what
you are. She sits down anyway. Her name
is Aiko. She makes you laugh for the
first time in years, real laughter, the
kind that sneaks up on you like
something you forgot you owned. She
never asks about work. You never
volunteer.
By 30, she's pregnant. You buy a ring.
Your Oyabun nods his approval because
even gangsters need heirs. Your son is
born in a hospital where you register
under a false company name because
Yakuza names on a birth certificate
follow a child like a criminal record.
For a while, the two lives hold. The
suit comes off at the door. The second
phone stays in the car. Your son learns
to walk while somewhere across town, men
hand you envelopes full of cash. You're
34 when the calls come in at 3:00 a.m.
Kenji. The money he'd been skimming from
the gambling take wasn't small anymore.
The bosses found the gap in the books,
and the gap had Kenji's fingerprints all
over it. They called him in for a
meeting. He never came home. No funeral,
no explanation, no body. One morning,
his name is on everyone's lips. By
evening, nobody says it. The family
doesn't announce its punishments. It
just erases people. And the silence is
the announcement. You sit in your
apartment at dawn.
He was your brother. He knelt beside you
at the altar. He drank from the same
cup, and the cup didn't save him. Aiko
finds you still sitting there when she
wakes up. She doesn't ask what happened.
She can read it on your face. That
night, after your son falls asleep, she
sits across the kitchen table and says
the words she's never said before.
"Leave." You don't answer because you
don't resign from the Yakuza. You return
the sake cup and beg your Oyabun for
permission to walk away. He might grant
it. He might not. Some men get a clean
break. Some try to leave without asking
and simply vanish. And even if you got
the blessing, the anti-Boryokudan laws
mark you for 5 more years. No bank
account, no lease, no phone contract. A
free man on paper, a ghost in practice.
You tell Aiko you'll think about it. You
don't think about it. You go back to
work. Your son turns 5 that winter. He
grabs your hand one morning and asks why
it looks different. You tell him you had
an accident at work. He believes you. He
won't always. The raid comes on a
Tuesday when officers politely knock at
your door. They don't kick the door down
because this is Japan. And here, they
dismantle your life with paperwork. The
construction front, the accounting
trails, 12 years of envelopes and false
invoices, every one of them documented
by a police task force that's been
building this case since before your son
was born. You're sentenced to 7 years.
The Oyabun doesn't send a lawyer. The
new boss has already replaced you. The
suit they let you wear to court is the
last nice thing you'll own for a long
time. Aiko tries. She holds it together
for 11 months, but the anti-Boryokudan
law freezes her accounts. The landlord
terminates the lease. And her employer
finds out whose wife she is, and her
shifts disappear. So, she's left with no
choice but to leave your son at the door
of a children's home. On his 7th
birthday, your son is standing at the
same door you stood at [music] 30 years
ago. Same bag of clothes, same silence
where a parent should be. Yakuza,
[music]
893,
the worst hand in the deck. They deal it
to you once. You [music] spend your
whole life passing it to your son.
By 2024, active Yakuza membership had
dropped below 20,000, the lowest number
ever recorded. The average member is now
over 50. Some hands aren't dealt by a
card game. They're dealt by a border, a
regime, a name you were born into and
can never put down. If this story stayed
with you, watch what happens when the
system doesn't just ignore you. It owns
you entirely. Watch your life as a North
Korean next.
