subtitles.plaintext:
You're 12 years old. Weaving cotton
outside your family's adobe home in the
Valley of Mexico 1515 when the
matchmaker arrives. She's here for your
older sister, but then she sees you and
your hands quick and steady. Her eyes
change. She whispers to your father
about the noble lord from Tenochtitlan
who needs weavers. Your father nods
once. The matchmaker points at you. That
one. Her cloth is finer. Three days
later you're in a canoe crossing Lake
Texcoco watching your village shrink
into nothing. The towers of Tenochtitlan
rise ahead like stone mountains. Your
mother didn't cry when you left.
Crying's a luxury when you're a commoner
family with six daughters and failing
crops. You're not a wife. You're a
weaver. You're a concubine and
Tenochtitlan doesn't care about the
difference.
Before we continue with what happens to
you in Tenochtitlan, we want to thank
War Thunder for sponsoring this video.
War Thunder is an epic free-to-play
multiplayer military action game where
tanks, [music] aircraft, helicopters,
and warships clash in massive dynamic
battles across realistic maps worldwide.
The game features tons of [music]
vehicles ranging from the mid-20th
century to modern times. The game's like
a museum where you can examine the
machines in the finest detail. In
combined arms modes, ground and air can
fight together while naval battles
feature ship-to-ship combat. [music] War
Thunder offers advanced military
technologies, guided missiles, active
protection systems, night vision
devices, reconnaissance [music] drones,
and even nuclear strikes. You can
upgrade and customize all vehicles with
unique skins. Thanks to the unique
damage model, every hit matters. Disable
a track, immobilize your opponent. Hit a
fuel tank, watch it ignite. Visualize
with x-ray mode. The latest Spearhead
update brings powerful new vehicles
including the French Jaguar, British
Chieftain 900, and Soviet T-34-85
[music] and many other cool vehicles.
Plus revamped Stalingrad and Carpathians
maps with [music] stunning visuals.
Download War Thunder for free on PC,
Xbox, and PlayStation using the link in
the description. And if you're a new
player or haven't played in 6 months
more, [music] get exclusive bonuses
including 100,000 silver lions, a
special Eagle of Valor [music]
decorator, and more. War Thunder Mobile
puts those same epic battles right in
your [music] pocket. Free on iOS and
Android. Now, back to the capital of the
Aztec Empire where the head wife,
Xochitl, meets you at the entrance with
a face like temple stone. Beautiful,
cold, untouchable. Behind her stands
four other concubines. All older, all
watching with the same question. Threat
or not? You'll weave, Xochitl says. No
hello, no greetings. Sunrise to sunset.
Your cloth belongs to this house. You
eat after we eat. You exist to produce
tribute and sons. Do you understand?
You're 12 and alone. What else can you
say? The weaving room's cramped. Five
looms against the wall. The other
concubines don't talk at first. There's
Citlalli, 16, best weaver in the house.
Chalchi, 19, pregnant. Meow, 14,
terrified like you. And Teyacapan, 22,
who watches everything. Your first
night, Chalchi whispers, "Xochitl
decides who gets fed, who gets beat, and
who gets sent to the lord's chamber.
Stay invisible. Weave fast. Up before
dawn grinding maize then straight to the
loom. Hour after hour. Cotton so fine
it's almost see-through. Tribute cloth
worth more than gold. The quota's
brutal. Two full pieces a week. Fall
short, you don't eat. You hit quota,
barely. Citlalli helps because Xochitl
punishes everyone if one person fails."
The lord's a merchant noble, always
traveling. You're invisible to him.
Furniture that makes cloth. Then Xochitl
summons you. Tonight. He's requested
you. Your stomach drops. Meow goes pale.
She knows. They scrub you in the steam
bath, braid your hair, paint your face,
dress you in soft robes. Then they walk
you to his chamber like you're going to
sacrifice. He's 43, over twice your age.
This is normal. This is law. The night's
a blur of fear and pain and silence.
When it's done, he dismisses you like a
used dish. You stumble back where
Chalchi's waiting with water and a rag.
"First time's the worst," she says
quietly. "After a while you stop feeling
it." You don't believe her. Later you
will. Two years pass. You're 14 now.
Good at two things. Weaving and
disappearing. Your cloth's fine enough
that the lord trades it for jade in
Oaxaca, cacao in Maya lands. You're an
asset, but like a tool, not a person.
Chalchi gives birth. A boy. For 2 weeks
she's treated like something precious.
Then the baby dies. Fever. 15 days old.
They bury him in the garden without
ceremony. Chalchi's back at the loom the
next morning. Silent, hollow, like a
bottle just emptied and thrown away. You
learn the rules. Never outshine Xochitl.
Never argue with other concubines. Never
refuse the lord. The lord calls for you
maybe once a month. Mechanical, joyless.
He never asks your name. Either way you
leave feeling hollow. Then Meow gets
pregnant. She's 15. Terrified, hopeful.
For a few weeks she's safe, valued, fed
better. Seven months in she starts
bleeding. The midwife comes, does what
she can.
It's not enough. The baby's born dead,
strangled by its cord, and Meow bleeds
out on the weaving room floor while you
and Citlalli hold her hands and beg gods
who don't answer. They take her body
before dawn. The lord replaces her
within a week. New girl, 13, from a
village near Texcoco. Her name's Xoco.
You see the same fear in her eyes you
had 2 years ago. You teach her the
rules. You teach her to weave fast. You
teach her to be invisible. By 16 you're
numb to most of it. The other concubines
are your rivals and your only family.
But you're alive. You hit quota, you
survive. You're 16, 4 years in this
house. The lord's traveling to the
coast, trading with strange new people,
pale men with metal armor and sticks
that explode like thunder. Gods or
demons, depending on who you ask. You
don't care. Your world's this compound,
this loom, this never-ending cycle of
weave, eat, sleep, serve. Then the lord
comes home with news. The emperor
Moctezuma needs tribute for a massive
ceremony. Hundreds of bolts of cloth.
Dozens of concubines to be honored in
service to the gods. Xochitl's exempt,
but the rest of you, fair game. They
select Chalchi. She's 24, no living
children, expendable. They dress her in
fine robes, paint her face white like
the moon goddess, tells her she'll be
honored, that this guarantees paradise.
She doesn't fight, just looks at you the
night before and whispers, "Tell them I
was brave, even if I wasn't." They take
her at dawn. You watch from the compound
gate as they lead her towards the Templo
Mayor. A line of victims in ceremonial
dress. Four days later you hear the
details from a servant who watched.
Chalchi climbed the pyramid steps. They
laid her on the stone slab, four priests
holding her down. The fifth priest
raised the obsidian blade. One cut below
the ribs through the diaphragm. His hand
plunged into the cavity. Her body
convulsed. He ripped out her heart while
it was still beating. Held it up to the
sun, steaming in the morning air. Then
they threw her body down the steps,
tumbling, breaking, joining the pile at
the bottom. Hundreds sacrificed over 4
days. Hearts fed to the gods. Blood
running down the pyramid in rivers. The
gods are fed. The sun keeps rising.
Chalchi's gone. There's a new girl by
the end of the week. After months of
rumors and gifts sent back and forth,
the pale men finally march into
Tenochtitlan. Hernan Cortes and his men,
metal gleaming, riding horses. Moctezuma
welcomes them. Gives them women, gold,
and food. The lord's excited. New trade
opportunities. Cortes takes everything.
Smiles with teeth like a skull. Then it
starts. Cortes has Moctezuma taken
hostage in his own palace. Later, during
a festival, Spanish soldiers slaughter
dancers in the temple courtyard. After
that, the city explodes. The markets
close. Foods get scarce. Xochitl starts
hoarding maize, feeding her children
first, concubines last. You're hungry
all the time and the city's burning. The
siege. Tenochtitlan's surrounded, cut
off, dying slowly. Causeways blocked.
Aqueducts destroyed. People drinking
from the lake, getting sick, dying in
the streets. You're still weaving
because what else is there? Your hands
shake from hunger. The cloth's not as
fine. Nobody cares. Citlalli dies first.
Smallpox. It's everywhere, killing
thousands. The Spanish brought it.
They're immune. You're not. She's
covered in pustules, burning with fever.
She dies in the weaving room and you
drag her body outside because nobody's
collecting the dead. The lord dies next.
Fever. Same disease. Xochitl's children
get sick. Two of them die.
The compound's falling apart. No
servants, no food. You and the remaining
concubines huddle in the weaving room,
surviving on scraps and lake water that
tastes like death. Then the Spanish
break through. Screams first, then the
smell. Smoke, blood, burning stone.
They're going street by street,
slaughtering everyone. Men,
[clears throat]
women, children. This isn't conquest.
This is extermination. Teyacapan tries
to run. A Spanish soldier catches her at
the gate. You hear it, then nothing. You
and Xoco hide behind baskets of rotting
maize. Boots on stone, Spanish voices,
laughter, looting everything. One finds
you. Young, eyes cold. He grabs Xoco
first. She screams. You try to pull her
back and he backhands you. You hit the
floor tasting blood. Xoco's dragged away
and the soldier looks at you. Decides
you're not worth it. Too skinny. Too
sick. And moves on. You survived that
day by being worthless. August 13, 1521.
Tenochtitlan falls. The Aztec Empire's
gone, erased in 93 days. You crawl out 3
days later. The city's unrecognizable.
Bodies everywhere. Buildings burned.
Spanish soldiers patrol with indigenous
allies from Tlaxcala. The same people
who used to be your enemies. Xochitl is
dead. You see her body in the garden.
Her children are gone, taken by Spanish
priests, forced to convert. You're 18.
You've survived a siege, disease,
starvation, and the end of civilization.
And for what? The Spanish impose new
rules. No more polygamy. No more
concubines. You're illegitimate now,
legally nothing. The cloth you wove, the
years you served, all erased by a single
decree. You try to find work, there's
none. You try to go home, your village
is gone. Smallpox wiped it out. Your
family's dead, all of them. You end up
in a makeshift camp outside what used to
be Tenochtitlan, now being rebuilt as
Mexico City. Hundreds of displaced
women, all survivors, nowhere to go. You
weave cloth from scraps, selling it for
a few cacao beans, barely enough to
scrape by. At 20, you're dying of the
same disease that killed Xitlalli,
smallpox, finally catching up. You're in
the camp, on a mat, alone. [music]
No ceremony, no prayers. Think about
Miahu, bleeding out in the weaving room.
About Chalchi, heart cut out on a
pyramid. About Xoco, dragged away by
soldiers.
>> [music]
>> Six years of weaving, thousands of
hours, beautiful, intricate tribute
cloth, all of it burned or stolen or
[music] rotting. What was it for? Your
last thought, at least you outlived the
empire. Cold comfort, but it's
something. You die at 20, eight years
after being selected as a concubine. You
survived the compound, the siege, and
the fall of Tenochtitlan, but you didn't
survive the new world the Spanish built
on your civilization's ashes. But you
were there to weave beauty, even when
beauty meant nothing.
You survived the fall of an empire,
watching your entire world burn. But
across the Pacific, same-age girls faced
a different kind of empire, one that
turned promises of factory work into
systematic enslavement. Click here to
see what life was like as a Korean
comfort woman during World War II.

subtitles.plaintext:
You're 17 years old in Japanese occupied
Korea in 1941 when they come with their
polished promises. Your village of
Andong shivers on their colonial rule.
Japanese soldiers patrol like wolves.
Your Korean name has been replaced with
Yamamoto Junko. And speaking your mother
tongue earns you bloody knuckles from
the teacher's stick. Your family
starving. Your father works 16-hour
factory shifts for pennies. Your
mother's fingers bleed from endless
mending. and your 14-year-old brother
coughs like he's dying from the inside
out. Winter has been brutal. Rice is
rationed and the rent collector circles
like a vulture. Then two officials
arrive with an interpreter whose eyes
won't meet yours. Factory work in
Manuria, they explain, showing
photographs of smiling girls in clean
uniforms. Good wages, regular meals,
honorable service to the empire. Your
daughter will send money home and return
with valuable skills. The promised wage
is more than your father makes in three
months. Your brother needs medicine.
Your mother counts the advanced payment
with shaking hands. More cash than your
family has seen in years. Many girls
from neighboring villages have already
volunteered. The interpreter continues.
This opportunity won't last long. You
want to refuse. Every instinct screams
against their two smooth promises and
predatory eyes. But your brother coughs
in the next room. Your father's hands
shake from exhaustion, and your mother's
tears have worn permanent tracks down
her cheeks. I'll do it, you whisper. the
words tasting like betrayal. Three days
later, you board a freight train with 11
other girls, clutching a cloth bundle
containing everything you own, a family
photo, your grandmother's silver
hairpin, and a notebook of secret Korean
poems. You don't know you're packing for
hell. The train journey becomes a
nightmare parade of red flags. Guards
with rifles are placed at polite
officials. The promised meals are rice
balls handed out once daily. There's no
toilet, just a bucket for 12 girls. By
day three, Miong from the village north
of yours develops a fever. By day seven,
she dies in your arms. The guards drag
her body out like garbage and leave her
beside the tracks. Clean up the mess,
they tell you, as if she was refu
instead of a person with a name and a
family, waiting for letters that will
never come. The train stops in Burma,
thousands of miles from the promised
manuria. Military trucks transport you
through dense jungle to a compound
surrounded by double rows of barbed
wire. Guard towers rise from each
corner. Search lights already beginning
their evening sweep. Commander Sato
addresses your group with a
matter-of-fact tone of someone reading a
supply manifest. You are here to serve
the sexual needs of the Imperial
Japanese Army. You will serve as
soldiers according to the schedules we
provide. You will not resist, refuse, or
attempt escape. The jungle will kill you
faster than we will, but we will kill
you if necessary. You are assigned
number seven. The name Tanaka Miko and a
room barely large enough for a sleeping
mat and water basin. The wooden plaque
card nailed above your door replaces
your identity. That's who you are now, a
number. The first soldier comes that
very night, young, maybe 20, with soft
features that might have been kind in
another life, but his eyes are empty,
his hands rough, and he speaks Japanese
words you don't understand, while he
destroys everything you thought you knew
about your own body. You try to
disappear into memories of your mother's
garden. Your father reading newspaper by
lamplight. But the pain keeps pulling
you back. When it's over, you lie on
your mat, understanding that the girl
who boarded the train in Andong just
died. By your first week's end, you
serviced 47 soldiers. You count because
your mind needs something to hold on to.
Some way to measure time in a place
where days blur into endless violation.
Time becomes fluid. days measured not by
sunrise, but by soldier rotations, meal
deliveries, weekly medical examinations
that feel like additional violations.
You turn 18 sometime in 1942, though
birthdays don't exist here. You develop
mental compartmentalizations so complete
you learn to separate consciousness from
flesh entirely. While soldiers use your
body, your mind retreats to a small,
clean room where you sit with your
grandmother, embroidering flowers that
will never fade. Su Jin, another
survivor, becomes your lifeline. She
teaches you which guards can be bribed,
which soldiers turn violent when drunk,
how to fake illness convincingly enough
to earn rest without triggering
punishment. Make them see you as
slightly more human than the others, she
whispers. But not so human, you become a
threat. Some girls develop different
coping mechanisms. Kung stops speaking
entirely. Jungi talks to herself in
rapid whispers that sound like prayer,
but use no recognizable words. You
perfect the art of absence, floating
above seams while your body endures what
cannot be survived. By 1944, chronic
pain settles into your joints. Your
teeth loosen from vitamin deficiency.
Infections linger for weeks without
proper medicine. New girls arrive
sporadically. You teach them survival
rules. Don't fight unless fighting will
win. Remember your real name, but only
in your head. Save strength for
surviving, not for gestures that
accomplish nothing. Some listen, others
break within weeks. He performs small
rituals for girls who don't survive,
whispering their real names to jungle
spirits, promising their stories won't
be forgotten. August 1945, Japan
surrenders, but nobody unlocks your
door. Officers burn papers behind the
administrative building, and rumors
spread of some posts disposing of women.
Commander Sato announces, "Transport
will be arranged for your relocation."
Zu Jin overhears guards talking. They're
eliminating evidence before evacuation.
All evidence. You escape during the
darkest pre-dawn hour, cutting through
barbed wire with a stolen kitchen knife,
following Sujin's handdrawn map towards
a river 2 mi northeast. The jungle
swallows you immediately. A wall of
green so dense you lose sight of the
compound within 50 yards. For 4 days,
you follow game trails and stream beds,
eating leaves and bark, drinking from
streams without worrying about disease.
Sujin develops fever on day three,
becomes delirious and dies quietly on
day four. You dig her grave with bare
hands and whisper her real name. Pox Su
Jin from Inon to the spirits. For the
first time since capture, you are
completely alone. The Burmese village
where you finally stumble emaciated and
infected provides rice and fish broth
but treats you with distant weariness.
You represent something they don't want
to acknowledge. War's reality for women.
Allied forces eventually process you
through repatriation camps. A nightmare
of paperwork and bureaucratic
indifference. Mrs. Kim, an older Korean
woman, coaches you through the system.
Tell them you were a factory worker. The
truth makes officials uncomfortable, and
uncomfortable officials don't approve
paperwork. The merchant vessel to
Busousan takes 12 days. You spend most
of it on deck watching the ocean and
trying to prepare for a homecoming that
feels like attending your own funeral.
Nine months later, you're standing in
front of your own home. Your mother
opens the door before you knock, aged
decades in your absence, hair completely
gray, face lined with permanent worry
channels. Zunja, she whispers, using
your real name for the first time in
years. Your family has built a life
during your absence. Your father has
steady work with American supervisors.
Your brother studies engineering in soul
on an American scholarship. There's no
space in their recovered world for the
broken stranger you've become. That
night, listening to your parents whisper
about your hollow eyes and flinching
reactions, you know you can't stay.
Within a week, you leave Andong forever,
carrying a carefully crafted lie about
finding work in Seoul. Soul in 1946 is a
city reinventing itself. Perfect for
someone needing to disappear. You find
factory work, rent corners of boarding
house rooms, perfect the art of existing
without leaving traces. You move seven
times, change jobs 12 times, develop
supernatural abilities to survive chaos
using skills learned in the compound,
reading men's intentions, becoming
invisible when necessary. The Korean War
arrives like returning fever. Chinese
soldiers, North Korean troops, American
forces to women like you, they're all
potential threats. You learn to
recognize army units moving through the
city and disappear until they pass. By
30, you look 50. Malnutrition has left
your teeth loose, hair thin. Chronic
infections have damaged your
reproductive system so severely a back
alley doctor calls it war damage as if
your body were a bombed building.
Sometimes this feels like loss. The
traditional life that might have
provided cover. More often it feels like
mercy. You've become an expert
seamstress. Read voraciously. Write
poetry in your notebook. At 50, you
realize you've spent more years hiding
than you lived before it happened. You
begin wondering if silence honors what
happened to you or if it's another form
of imprisonment. Korea democratizes in
the 1980s. Students occupy universities.
Journalists investigate forbidden
topics. The enforced silence that
protected you begins feeling more like
suffocation than safety. In 1990, you
read about Professor Yun Chung O's
research into comfort women. The
clinical term finally giving name to
your experiences. We need survivor
testimonies, she says. to ensure this
history isn't forgotten. After 17 drafts
over three months, you mail a letter
offering testimony. Three weeks later,
they reply with compassion and
professionalism. In your small
apartment, you tell your story in
fragments to researchers who believe
you. Understand the historical context.
Value your experience as evidence rather
than shame. On August 14, 1991, you
stand outside the Japanese embassy with
12 other survivors. Most wear masks to
conceal identities. You choose to show
your face. After 50 years of hiding, you
want to be seen. Kim Hak's son gives the
first public testimony. When she
finishes, you step forward. My name is
Kim Sununja, you say, using your real
name publicly for the first time since
1941. I was 17 when they took me. I want
the world to know what happened to us.
Your voice shakes, but grows stronger
with each sentence. You describe the
system for what it was. state organized
sexual slavery used as a weapon of war
and a crime that destroyed hundreds of
thousands of lives. We were children
with dreams and families and futures.
You took all of that and tried to erase
us from history. The response is
immediate and overwhelming. Support
letters from women's groups and
individuals expressing admiration, but
criticism, too. Anonymous calls
questioning your motives. Letters
suggesting you maintain dignity through
silence. On January 8th, 1992, you
joined the first of the now weekly
Wednesday demonstrations, growing in
size and international attention. You
become a regular participant, testimony,
becoming part of Korean and
international consciousness. You speak
at universities, the UN, legislative
bodies worldwide. Japan issues partial
acknowledgements but avoids legal
responsibility. They support an Asian
women's fund that offers atonement money
as private charity rather than
government reparations. You join other
survivors in rejecting these payments.
We don't want charity. We want
acknowledgement that crimes were
committed. At 90, you reflect on two
decades of advocacy. Legal goals remain
unfulfilled. Japan hasn't accepted
responsibility or provided adequate
reparations. But cultural transformation
is undeniable. The comfort women issue
is now part of historical consciousness.
Your testimony preserved for future
generations. Museums, memorials, and
educational programs ensure the history
you help reveal will survive. University
courses examine the comfort women system
as a case study in systemic sexual
violence and historical justice. Your
decision to break silence has inspired
other survivors worldwide to find their
own voices. In your final years, you
tell visiting relatives. Everyone faces
moments when they can choose silence or
truth. I chose silence for 50 years. It
protected me but also imprisoned me.
When I chose truth, it was frightening
but also liberating. The important thing
is to choose consciously rather than let
fear decide.

text:
Discover what your life would have been like as a Kisaeng in Joseon Korea.

DISCLAIMER: This video is a fictional dramatization inspired by historical accounts of a gisaeng's life. While based on real practices, characters and events are exaggerated for storytelling. No one was harmed in the making of this video.

#Gisaeng #Kisaeng #Joseon #JoseonDynasty #KoreanHistory #WomenInHistory #YourLifeAs #WhyItSuckedToBe

subtitles.plaintext:
You're born in a gibang, a courtesan
house in Joseon, Korea, 1572. Your
mother holds you for exactly 1 hour
before the haengsu, the head gisaeng,
takes you away to check your fingers,
your feet, your face. She nods once.
You'll do. Your name goes into the
gijeok, the government registry, before
you can even cry for milk. Most children
inherit their father's name. You inherit
your mother's chains. They call it
jongmobop, the law of following the
mother. Daughters of gisaeng become
gisaeng. No exceptions. Your fate was
sealed before you took your first
breath. That's how it starts, your life
as a gisaeng. You're six when training
begins. The haengsu lines up 15 girls in
the courtyard and says, "10 of you will
become first-tier gisaeng. The rest will
be sold to dock taverns, where sailors
pay in rice, cloth, or whatever a
desperate man can barter." Look at the
girl beside you. She's your competition.
The girl beside you is Wolhyang. She's
seven, sold by her father after her
mother died in childbirth. She's
trembling. You take her hand anyway,
because competition is tomorrow's
problem, and loneliness is tonight's.
Your mother visits between performances,
smelling of rice wine and other men's
breath, cheap incense clinging to her
sleeves. She teaches you to hold a
gayageum before you can properly hold a
brush. "Your fingers are your fortune,"
she whispers. "The girls with clumsy
hands end up in the dock taverns. You
know what happens there." You don't, but
the way she says it makes your stomach
clench. Training breaks girls like
kindling. You learn to sit motionless
for 4 hours while your legs scream. You
learn to pour tea without a ripple,
because a ripple cup means the bamboo
rod. A girl named Sonye cries on the
fifth day. By the tenth day, she doesn't
cry anymore. By the twentieth day, she
doesn't speak anymore. They send her
somewhere. No one tells you where.
Inspectors come regularly. They score
your music, your posture, your
obedience. Fail often enough and you're
reassigned, from banquets to backrooms,
from silk stages to cheap taverns.
Alive, but fading. Wolhyang's hands
shake when she plays. You practice with
her every night, correcting her
fingering, drilling her until moonset.
She's your only friend. You won't let
the taverns take her. She fails her
first inspection anyway. "One more
chance," the haengsu says. Then she's
gone. You practice harder, both of you.
Your fingers crack and bleed. You wrap
them and keep playing, because stopping
means the docks, and the docks mean
death, just slower. Second inspection.
Wolhyang passes, barely. You allow
yourself one night of relief. Third
inspection. The inspector is different,
harsher. He fails four girls, including
Wolhyang. You watch them drag her away,
screaming your name. You don't scream
back. You stand perfectly still, face
empty, because showing emotion is
weakness, and weakness is death in the
gibang. Three months later, you hear
she's dead. Sailors, disease, 12 years
old. You stop making friends after that.
By 10, you're learning classical Chinese
alongside the sons of yangban nobles.
You memorize poetry, study philosophy,
train your voice until it can make drunk
men weep. The irony burns. The most
educated women in Joseon are also the
lowest. You have the mind of an
aristocrat and the body of a slave. Your
mother is demoted that year. 30 years
old, too old for first-tier performance.
They give her a sewing needle instead of
a gayageum. You visit her in the
backrooms, where fading gisaeng go to be
forgotten. She looks at you with hollow
eyes and says, "Be better than me. Be so
good they can never throw you away." You
look at her, bent over silk with ruined
fingers, and you see your future, unless
you're exceptional, unless you're
perfect. Are you exceptional? You don't
know, yet. You're 12 when they put up
your hair, the coming-of-age marker that
tells the world you're no longer a
child. The ceremony cost someone a
fortune. A wealthy merchant pays for the
privilege. He's 53, smells like
fermented bean paste, and tonight you
belong to him. You survive it by
counting ceiling beams. 47. You think of
Wolhyang and tell yourself, "This is the
price of not becoming her." Your stage
name is Myeonghwa, bright flower. The
hojang, the government official who
tracks every gisaeng like livestock,
writes it in his register. Twice
monthly, you report to him so he knows
you haven't fled. Where would you go?
Your face is in the registry. The only
way out is death, or a patron rich
enough to buy your freedom. And men like
that don't marry gisaeng. They collect
them, use them, and throw them away like
garbage. Your first real performance is
at the governor's banquet. 30 yangban
nobles watch you dance the geommu, the
sword dance. The blades aren't real, but
they're heavy. One wrong move means no
patron, no protection, no future. You
don't make a wrong move. By 15, you're
the most requested gisaeng in the
province. You're a celebrity in silk
chains, famous for talents that will
never free you. You take a lover, a
young scholar named Junwoo, who writes
you real poetry. He talks about buying
your freedom, running away together. You
let yourself believe him for 3 months.
Then his father finds out. Yangban don't
marry gisaeng. Junwoo is shipped to a
distant posting. His farewell letter is
four lines long. You burn it without
crying. The older gisaeng have a say,
"Love is a luxury for women who own
themselves." You're 17 when the royal
court summons you to perform. You
perform a court jeongjae, slow, exact,
rehearsed until your joints feel carved
from wood, before the ministers who've
read your poetry. The king himself nods
approval. They offer you a position at
court, first-tier gisaeng. You say yes.
What else can you say? Court life is a
different prison. Arrivals spread rumors
you seduced a married minister. Scandal
sticks to gisaeng like ink to paper. You
survive by becoming indispensable,
trading information the chief minister's
spies can't gather. It's not freedom,
but it's power. You're 20 when the
Japanese invade, 1592. Hideyoshi's army
takes Seoul in 3 weeks. The court flees
north. You're left behind, because
entertainers aren't worth saving. You're
assigned to General Keimura's retinue in
Jinju after the fortress falls. 70,000
Koreans lie dead. You're supposed to
smile and pour wine like your country
isn't bleeding. There's another gisaeng
there, Nongae. She lost her husband to
the siege. Her eyes carry that hollow
look you remember from your mother. That
night, Nongae dances for the general.
She leads [music] him to the cliff's
edge to admire the moonlight. Then she
wraps her arms around him, locks her
fingers, and jumps. They fall together.
[music] The river swallows them both.
You raise your cup to the empty air and
drink to the only freedom [music] some
of us ever get. The war doesn't end
quickly. It drags on for years, burning,
retreating, surging back, until the
[music] last withdrawal in 1598. By
then, you're 26. You survive by being
useful to whoever holds the sword. But
survival has a price. At 22, your career
was already fading. There's always a
younger flower. You're demoted to second
tier. At 26, a minister takes interest
in you. He visits twice a week for 3
months. He's not cruel, just
indifferent, which is almost worse. When
your bleeding stops, you know before the
physician confirms it. Pregnancy changes
nothing and everything. You still
perform, belly swelling beneath layered
silk. The other gisaeng whisper, some
with pity, some with relief it isn't
them. The minister stops visiting. He
has a wife, legitimate children, a
reputation. You're a complication he
never asked for. The haengsu lets you
stay. You're still useful for teaching,
for the administrative work younger
girls can't do, but you feel yourself
becoming invisible, fading into the
background machinery of the gibang.
Labor comes in winter, 16 hours on a
thin mat while snow falls outside. No
physician, just an old woman who's done
this a hundred times. Her hands rough,
but steady. You bite through leather to
keep from screaming, because screaming
is weakness, and you've spent 26 years
learning not to be weak. A girl. Of
course it's a girl. You hold her for
exactly 1 hour before the haengsu takes
her back to check her fingers, her feet,
her face. She nods once. She'll do. And
just like that, you understand your
mother in a way you never did before.
The hollow eyes, the desperate whispers,
the way she looked at you like you were
both her greatest joy and her deepest
wound. The hojang comes 3 days later
with his ledger. He writes your
daughter's name in the gijeok before she
can even focus her eyes. You watch the
brush move across paper. Each stroke a
chain link forged. Daughter of gisaeng,
gisaeng. No exceptions. You name her
Yunbi, silver rain, something beautiful,
because her life will give her a little
else. You take students to stay
relevant. One girl, Chunhyang, has real
talent. "Never fall in love," you tell
her. She doesn't listen. A young
nobleman named Yi Mongryong writes her
poems, sneaks into the gibang at
midnight, promises her the moon. You've
heard these promises before. You've
buried girls who believed them. But
something impossible happens. He passes
his examinations, becomes a secret royal
inspector. And when a corrupt magistrate
tries to claim Chunhyang for himself,
Mongryong returns. Not with excuses, or
with a four-line farewell letter. He
returns with power, and he uses it to
save her. They marry, legally. A
gisaeng's daughter and a yangban,
standing as equals before heaven. You
attend the wedding in disguise, face
hidden beneath a commoner's hood. You
watch Chunhyang smile the way you smiled
at Junwoo 20 years ago. But her story
ends differently. Her nobleman came
back. You slip away before the ceremony
ends. You find a quiet corner [music]
behind the kitchen, and you weep like
you haven't wept since you were 12 years
old, watching Wolhyang disappear [music]
through the gibang gates. You weep for
her happiness, and for the version of
yourself who stopped believing such
things were possible. At 31, they force
you out of performance. You become a
haengsu, training the next generation.
Your mother dies that winter. You find
her poetry hidden in her sewing box,
verses she never showed anyone. They're
beautiful. They're heartbreaking. She
was brilliant, and no one ever knew. You
start writing, too. Sometimes your own
lines. Sometimes you borrow safer words.
You copy a sijo attributed to the famous
gisaeng poet Hwang Jini. On that, I
might capture the essence of this deep
midwinter night, and fold it softly into
the warp of a spring moon quilt and
fondly uncoil it the night my beloved
returns. You're 43 when the coughing
starts, consumption. A lifetime of cold
floors and silk that looks beautiful but
offers no warmth. Your students gather
in the final weeks. You tell them about
Nongae and the cliff, about Chunhyang's
impossible love, about your mother's
hidden poetry. "Remember," you whisper,
"we preserve the songs when scholars
forgot them. We carried the dances
through wars. We were the memory of this
kingdom even when the kingdom refused to
remember us. They bury you in the
gisaeng cemetery, no family name, just
your stage name, Myeong-hwa, bright
flower. Your daughter stands at your
grave, 16, old enough to understand what
the registry means. Her name has been in
the gijok since infancy. Now the
training is coming for her, too. The
cycle continues.
You've seen Korea's version. Now meet
Japan's, more polished, more controlled,
and just as unforgiving. Click here to
watch your life as a geisha.

subtitles.plaintext:
You're 7 years old, ankle-deep in frozen
mud outside your family's longhouse in
Norway 859 AD when the screaming starts.
Smoke rises from the eastern farms. Your
mother shoves you behind the woodpile
and presses a hand over your mouth.
Don't move. Through the gaps in the
timber, you watch men pour into your
village. Not foreigners, but Norsemen
from a rival clan. Your father runs out
with his axe. He drops two of them
before the third steps forward. You see
his face, a jagged scar [music] running
from his left eye to his jaw, twisting
his mouth into a permanent sneer.
>> [music]
>> He moves like a man who enjoys killing.
Your father swings. The scarred man
sidesteps, almost [music] lazy, and
opens your father's throat with a single
stroke. Your brothers fall next, one,
two, like wheat before a scythe. Your
mother's hand slips from your mouth as
they drag her into the smoke. You hear
her screaming your name, then nothing.
The scarred man walks past your
woodpile, close enough to touch. His
boots leave bloody prints in the snow.
He's laughing. You want to scream, but
can't scream. You want to cry, but can't
cry. You pick up your dead father's axe.
It's too heavy, but you drag it anyway
for the sake of revenge. And that's how
it starts, your life as a shieldmaiden.
They call you Skjaldmaer in the songs
later. In the real world, most men will
call you a lie until you crack their
shield. Three days later, your uncle
Bjorn finds you eating raw fish by the
fjord, half frozen, still holding your
father's axe. It's too heavy for you.
You've been dragging it everywhere.
Bjorn is a raider. Gone most years to
places you can't pronounce. He has no
wife, no children, no patience for
softness. He looks at your hollow eyes
and says, "You want to weep or you want
to make them weep?" You don't answer
with words. You lift the axe. "There's a
man," you whisper, "a scar on his face.
I'm going to kill him." Bjorn studies
you for a long moment. Then he nods.
"Then we have work to do." Training
starts two days later. Your uncle
doesn't coddle you. He trains you like
he trained a boy, except harder, because
he knows what men will assume when they
see a woman on a battlefield. Weakness,
hesitation, easy prey. You wake before
dawn to haul water, chop wood, run up
mountain trails until your lungs burn
and your legs buckle. First, the spear.
Bjorn says is the weapon of the common
warrior, cheap and deadly. Your
shoulders ache for months. Your palms
blister, crack, blister again, until the
calluses form thick as leather. By nine,
you move to the axe. Not the elegant
swords that Yarls carry. Those cost more
silver than your whole village earned in
a year. The axe is brutal, unforgiving.
You practice on hanging logs until you
can split them clean. Every log wears
the scarred man's face. At 10, traders
pass through with news from the eastern
clans. You ask about a warrior with a
scar, left eye to jaw. They know him.
Halvard the Cruel, they call him. A
Yarl's champion now, rich and
untouchable. Not forever, you think. At
12, your body changes in ways that feel
like betrayal. Your uncle's men start
looking at you differently. One tries to
corner you in the barn. You break his
wrist with a shield edge strike, exactly
as Bjorn taught you. Your uncle finds
out. He doesn't comfort you. He drags
the man outside and makes an example.
Then tells the crew you're coming on the
next voyage. You're ready, he says. The
sea will decide if I'm right. You don't
care about the sea. You care about
getting strong enough to kill the
scarred man. The longship is nothing
like you imagined. Thirty warriors
packed together with no shelter, bailing
seawater while the North Sea tries to
swallow you whole. You sleep wedged
between rowing benches, waking to find
ice crusted on your cloak. You row until
your arms scream. You vomit over the
side when the waves turn cruel. The men
laugh. You wipe your mouth and grab your
oar. What's a little suffering? You've
been suffering since you were seven.
Your target is a monastery on the
English [music] coast, fat with silver,
guarded by a handful of frightened
locals and old men in robes. The night
before the raid, you can't sleep. Fear,
anticipation, the knowledge that
tomorrow you become what you need to be.
Dawn. The ship scrapes onto the beach.
You pour over the sides, shield up, axe
ready. The first monk you see is
praying, kneeling, hands clasped, lips
moving. He looks up at you with eyes
that expect death. You hesitate. He's
not Halvard, he's not the scar, he's
just a frightened man in brown robes.
One heartbeat, two. Then you remember
your father's throat opening, your
mother disappearing into smoke. You
remember why you're here. Your axe
falls.
That night, loading silver onto the
ship, a boy crawls out from behind the
altar. Eight, maybe nine, shaking. He
reminds you of yourself, crouching
behind that wood pile. The others
haven't seen him. You could end him
quietly. You should. Instead, you jerk
your head toward the forest. Go. He
runs. You tell yourself it doesn't
matter. One monk child won't change
anything. You're wrong, but you won't
learn that for years. You raid every
summer, monasteries, villages, trading
ships, but you're not chasing silver.
You're chasing whispers. Every port,
every captive, every drunken warrior.
Have you seen a man with a scar, left
eye to jaw? They call him Halvard.
At 16, you're close. A merchant says
Halvard winters with Jarl Sigurd's clan,
three fjords north. You beg Bjorn to
raid them. Suicide, he says. Sigurd has
200 warriors, we have 30. You wait. You
train harder. You earn a name, Ragnall
the Red, not for your hair, which is
dark as peat, for the blood that seems
to follow you. At 17, you see a man
across a battlefield with a scar on his
face. Your heart stops. You cut through
three enemies to reach him and find a
stranger. Wrong scar, wrong man. The
disappointment nearly breaks you. At 18,
you fall in love. His name is Eric, a
skald, a poet warrior who fights as
beautifully as he speaks. He sees
something in you that others don't, not
just the killer, the girl still burning
for revenge. You carry ghosts, he tells
you one night. I see them in your eyes.
Everyone carries ghosts. Yes, but yours
are hungry. You've been feeding them so
long. I wonder if you remember what else
you could be. You don't answer. You
don't know. He wants to marry you, build
a farm, have children. You let yourself
imagine it, a life where the scar
doesn't own you, where you wake without
the rage. But then word comes. Jarl
Sigurd is feuding with your jarl, a
sanctioned raid. Halvard will be there.
You volunteer before Bjorn finishes
speaking. The battle is chaos. Shield
walls crash together like waves against
rock. Men scream and fall. Rain mixes
with blood until the ground turns to red
mud. Eric fights beside you, his sword
dancing, his voice rising in a battle
song. For a moment, you let yourself
believe you'll both survive this, that
you'll kill Halvard and sail home and
finally rest. Then you see him, the
scar, left eye to jaw, older now, gray
in his beard, but unmistakable. [music]
Halvard the Cruel, cutting through your
warriors like they're children. The
world narrows. 12 years of nightmares.
12 years of dragging your father's
[music] axe. Everything shrinks to one
man. You scream his name. He turns.
Doesn't recognize you. Why would he? You
were seven, a trembling thing behind a
woodpile, beneath notice. Bjorn doll,
you roar, shoving through the press of
bodies. The farm you burned, the family
you slaughtered, remember? Something
flickers in his eyes, confusion,
amusement. I burned many farms, girl.
You'll remember this one. You crash into
him like a wave. He's bigger, stronger,
more experienced, but you've been
training for this moment your entire
life. Every night you trace [music] his
face in the darkness. He cuts your
shoulder. You don't feel it. You hook
his shield with your axe and rip it
away. He stumbles. "My father was
first." You spit, driving him [music]
backward. "Then my brothers, two of
them. One was 5 years old." You bury his
desperate face. "You're faster [music]
than we expected, angrier. My mother you
took. I heard her screaming my name. Do
you remember her screaming?" His back
hits a tree, nowhere to run. "I don't."
He starts. "I do." Your axe takes his
hand. He screams. Your second blow takes
his knee. He drops. And suddenly, he's
looking up at you, just like your father
looked up at him all those years ago.
"Please." He gasps. You lean [music]
close, let him see your eyes, let him
understand. "She screamed for a long
time. I'm going to make sure you scream
longer." You do. When it's over, when
Halvar the Cruel is nothing but meat and
memory, you stand over his body,
breathing hard, waiting for the
satisfaction to flood in. It doesn't
come. The rage that's driven you since
childhood just stops. And underneath it,
there's nothing. A hole where your heart
should be. 12 years of revenge, and all
it bought you was emptiness. Then you
hear the scream. You turn. Eirik is on
his knees 20 ft away, a spear through
his stomach. He's looking at you. His
mouth moves, but no sound comes out. You
run, slip in the mud, crawl the last few
feet to catch him as he falls. "Eirik!
Eirik, stay with me!" Blood bubbles on
his lips. He tries to smile. His hand
finds your face, your cheek, trembling.
"Your ghosts." He whispers. "They're
quiet now. Yes?" You can't speak, can't
breathe. "Good." His eyes are fading.
You can finally live. He dies in your
arms. The battle rages around you. You
don't move. You came here to kill the
man who destroyed your family. You
succeeded, and it cost you the only
person who made you feel like you could
be something other than a weapon. The
gods have a sick sense of humor. You
raid for six more years, but you're not
fighting for silver, not for revenge.
That's done. You fight because it's the
only thing left, because Aric was wrong.
The ghosts aren't quiet. They just have
new faces now. At 26, on a raid to
Northumbria, your ship is ambushed in a
river. Superior numbers, no escape. And
there, among the English soldiers, you
see a face you recognize. The monk child
you spared 13 years ago, grown now,
armored. He's the one who led them here.
Mercy, as it turns out, has a long
memory. Your crew forms a shield wall on
the riverbank, knowing they'll die. You
fight for hours. Your shield splinters.
Your warriors fall one by one. Then, an
arrow takes you in the side. You drop to
your knees. The English close in. And in
that moment, blade in hand, facing
death, you finally understand. You tell
yourself Valhalla isn't a reward,
>> [music]
>> it's a release, an end to the hunger
that's driven you since you were 7 years
old. You rise. Your body is screaming,
but you rise. And you lift your axe, and
you charge. The English hesitate. One
heartbeat at the sight of a wounded
woman running at them with death in her
eyes. That hesitation costs them. You
kill four more before the spear takes
you through the chest. [music] The world
goes white, then red.
Then,
nothing at all.
Mercy has a long memory, and so does the
society that owns you. Click here to
watch your life as a Korean gisaeng.
Same pain, different prison.

text:
The Netherlands — a small country making a massive impact. Despite being one of the most densely populated nations on Earth, this tiny European powerhouse has become the second-largest exporter of food in the world.

How did they do it? Through cutting-edge innovation, collaboration, and a national mindset that turns limitations into leadership. From high-tech greenhouses and water-efficient crops to global partnerships and next-gen seed engineering, the Dutch are rewriting the future of farming.

In this episode, we explore how a nation reclaimed from the sea became a model for sustainable agriculture — and what the rest of the world can learn from it.

📈 Topics covered:

The rise of Dutch AgriTech and industrial greenhouses

How innovation and collaboration fuel the Netherlands’ success

The “triple helix” model: Government, business, and academia in action

The global race to feed 10 billion people sustainably

🌱 The Netherlands proves that ingenuity, not size, will define the farms of tomorrow.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Brimm delivers high-grade animated explainers on business, brands, and the marketing stories shaping our world.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

#Netherlands #DutchInnovation #AgriTech #SustainableFarming
#FoodTechnology #FutureOfFarming #GreenRevolution #AnimatedExplainer #BusinessExplainer #EducationalVideo #InnovationNation
#Sustainability #BRIMM #GlobalAgriculture #TechForGood

subtitles.plaintext:
This is the Netherlands, a small,
tightly packed country with over 1,300
people per square mile, making it the
most densely populated nation in the
European Union. It's known for its
cycling culture, liberal policies, and
worldclass art. But there's another
remarkable quality about this little
nation, one that's earning it global
recognition. Its ability to feed the
world. On paper, the Netherlands seems
an unlikely agricultural [music]
powerhouse, lacking many of the natural
advantages once considered essential for
large-scale food production. Let me
explain.
Ordinarily, producing food on a large
scale demands vast stretches of land for
crops, livestock, and everything in
between. But the Netherlands is a small
country. Most of its territory should be
taken up by towns and cities. [music]
Good farming also needs fertile soil
rich in nutrients. Yet, Dutch farmland
is often reclaimed from the sea, sandy,
pey, even saline, far from ideal for
growing crops. And then there's the
climate. [music]
Instead of warmth and sunshine, the
Netherlands is cool, damp, and cloudy
for much of the year. By all accounts,
it shouldn't work. And yet, against the
odds, the Netherlands is the world's
second largest exporter of food by
value, behind only the United States, a
country nearly 270 times its size. So,
[music] how have the Dutch pulled it
off? Simply put, by using some of the
most efficient agricultural technologies
in the world. Global implications
[music] of doing high-tech indoor farms
is that you can grow a lot more food
with a lot fewer resources [music] and
much less impact on the environment.
>> Across the Netherlands, nearly 24,000
acres of crops grow inside vast
industrial green houses that stretch
across the countryside. To put that into
perspective, that's the equivalent of
18,000 football fields or about 12 times
the size of Central Park. Inside these
green houses, the Dutch have built one
of the most advanced farming ecosystems
on Earth.
>> Less water, we use 50% less energy.
>> A lot of people think it's science
fiction, but it really is not.
>> It's powered by Agrch, a fusion of
artificial intelligence, robotics,
biotechnology, and big data. Seamlessly
integrated with [music] traditional
tools like tractors, sensors, and GPS.
The result, a system so efficient that a
single acre of land under glass can
produce what would normally require 10
acres of open farmland and do it with
far less water and fertilizer. For
example, Dutch technology makes it
possible to grow a pound of tomatoes
using just half a gallon of water
compared to about 15 gallons in the
United States. Over the past 30 years,
the Dutch tomato industry has become the
most productive in the world, growing
more per square mile than any other
country on the planet. But it's not just
tomatoes.
The Netherlands are also the world's top
exporter [music] of potatoes and onions
and the second largest exporter of
vegetables overall in terms of value.
This success has [music] not gone
unnoticed. The Netherlands combination
of innovation, collaboration, and
efficiency has made it the global hub
for agricultural research and [music]
development, attracting many of the
world's leading food corporations. In
fact, 15 out of the top 20 largest agra
food businesses have major research and
development centers [music] in the
Netherlands. The presence of these
global giants has had a profound impact
on the Netherlands economy. Hosting the
research and development centers of the
likes of companies such as Uni Lever,
Nestle and Cargill not only creates
thousands of high-skilled jobs, but also
drives foreign investment, strengthens
the knowledge economy, and fuels
export-led [music]
growth. These firms collaborate closely
with Dutch universities and startups,
ensuring a constant exchange of
innovation and expertise. [music] The
result is a thriving industrial network
that extends beyond agriculture,
influencing biotechnology, logistics,
and sustainable energy. All of this
contributes to the Netherlands being one
of the wealthiest nations in Europe with
high GDP per capita, robust
infrastructure, and a reputation for
resilience and ingenuity. In essence,
the country's agricultural success
doesn't just feed the world, it enriches
[music] the nation itself. Corporate
investment may fuel the economy, but
it's innovation at the [music] smallest
scale, the seed that truly sustains the
Netherlands global leadership in
agriculture. More than a third of all
global trade in vegetable seeds,
originates in the Netherlands. There's
also Seed Valley, a hub that's home to
many of the world's leading seed
companies. Here, researchers and
engineers focus on developing high
yield, climate resilient seed varieties,
pushing the boundaries of what modern
agriculture can achieve. And they do a
good job. A single high-tech greenhouse
tomato seed priced below 50 has been
known to produce a mind-boggling
150 lb of tomatoes. It's important to
remember these achievements aren't
driven by technology alone. They come
from a national mindset, one that values
cooperation just as much as [music]
innovation.
In the Netherlands, collaboration is the
engine of progress. And it's helped the
country stand among Europe's most
forwardthinking nations [music] for
years. The secret, a highly effective
approach to collaboration known as the
Dutch triple helix model. A framework
for forging partnerships between the
private sector, government, and
academia. Each stakeholder plays a
crucial role. Academic institutions fuel
research and expertise. [music]
The government supports with favorable
policies and businesses bring commercial
viability. It's built on a simple yet
powerful idea that the Dutch call 1 + 1
equals 3. The belief that when we
combine talent and resources, challenges
become opportunities and innovation
scales faster. You can see this
philosophy in action at places like the
dairy campus, a living laboratory where
farmers, suppliers, and processors come
together to shape the future [music] of
dairy.
The flurry of interest in agriculture
and food technology is the result of
several powerful [music] trends. Growing
demand for protein, especially from the
developing world, is putting pressure on
food supply. At the same time, consumer
tastes in the Western world are shifting
from mass-produced brands towards
healthier and more unique products. The
goal is clear to meet the world's
growing demand for sustainable protein
while reducing reliance on traditional
resource-heavy farming methods.
The Netherlands may be shaping the
future of farming, but the [music]
stakes extend far beyond its borders.
The world now faces its greatest
agricultural challenge in history.
produce more food in the next four
decades than all farmers in history have
harvested over the past 8,000 years.
That's because by 2050, the Earth will
be home to as many as 10 billion people,
up from today's 7.5 billion. If massive
increases in agricultural yield [music]
are not achieved, matched by massive
decreases in the use of water and fossil
fuels, a billion or more people may face
starvation.
For a country so small, the Netherlands
casts an enormous shadow on the future
of food. Through innovation,
collaboration, and courage, it has
transformed its limitations into
leadership. Showing that sustainability
and prosperity can go hand in hand as
the world races to feed a growing
population. The Dutch example stands as
proof that ingenuity, not size, will
define the farms of tomorrow.

subtitles.plaintext:
You're 3 years old, sitting cross-legged
in a room lit by one flickering lamp,
when a priest sets a freshly cut buffalo
head on the floor in front of you and
leans down to watch your face. The room
stinks of copper and animal fat. More
heads sit in the shadows, dozens of
them. Eyes gone dull, tongues hanging
loose. Somewhere behind you, a man
clangs a bell and chants words you don't
understand. Any normal toddler would be
screaming by now. You don't. You look at
the buffalo head like it's a toy
somebody forgot to put away, and you
wait for whatever comes next. That blank
little stare is exactly what they've
been hunting the whole valley for.
Welcome to your life as Kumari, the
living goddess of Nepal. You're born in
Kathmandu, into the Shakya castle, a
family of goldsmiths and silver workers.
Newar Buddhists whose people have packed
this valley for hundreds of years.
You're nobody special. Then one day,
priests come to your door with a
checklist. To be the goddess, a girl has
32 signs of perfection. Thighs like a
deer, a chest like a lion, a neck like a
shell, eyelashes like a cow's, and a
voice as soft and clear as a duck. Skin
without a single scar, 20 baby teeth,
none of them lost, and above all, a body
that has never once bled. You tick every
single box. Your birth chart lines up.
You pass the dark room without a
whimper. So, the priests wash you, dress
you, and carry you out the door. Your
feet don't touch the ground on the way.
From now on, they mostly never will.
They carry you to a three-story house of
carved wood on Kathmandu's Durbar
Square. It's called the Kumari Ghar, the
house of the goddess, and for the next 9
years, it's your entire world. Nobody
sits you down and reads you the rules.
You learn them the way you learn a hot
stove, by touching the wrong thing once.
You reach up to scratch your itching
pinned-up scalp, and a hand catches your
wrist. Goddesses don't fidget. You laugh
at something and the whole room freezes.
Goddesses don't laugh. You cry and grown
adults panic like you've cursed the
harvest. And whatever else you do, you
keep your bare feet off bare ground.
Because the second they touch dirt
outside these walls, you're not a
goddess anymore. You're just a kid who
needs a bath. Outside, you get carried.
Or you walk on cloth laid down so the
ground never dares to touch you. You
aren't completely alone. The woman who
runs the house is called Lakshmi and she
feeds you, bathes you, and scolds you
when nobody important is watching. She
has a daughter about your age named
Sunita. And Sunita becomes the only real
friend you're allowed to keep. She's
also the only child you ever see up
close who gets to be, well, a child.
Because here's the thing about godhood.
Every morning you watch Sunita bolt out
the door to school and come back with
scraped knees and stories. She wears a
plain cotton dress and cheap plastic
sandals. And you want those sandals so
badly it aches. You've got a throne, a
crown, and a whole country that worships
you. She's got shoes and a door she's
allowed to walk out of. Guess which one
of you feels lucky. By six, you know the
job. Most days, you sit. Devotees climb
the stairs one at a time, kneel, leave
money and sweets and marigolds, and wait
for you to look at them. Stay calm and
that's a blessing. Cry and that's a
warning of disaster coming. So you hold
still for hours while your legs go dead
and the gold saws grooves into your
neck. And you train your face to stay as
flat as that first buffalo head. By
eight, a woman kneels weeping because
her son is sick. Presses her forehead to
your feet and walks out lighter than she
came in. You didn't do a thing. You sat
there. But sitting there is the whole
job. A handful of times a year, they
haul you out on a tall wooden chariot
for Indra Jatra, the biggest festival in
the city. And everyone shoves just to
catch one look at your painted face. For
one afternoon, you're the most important
person in the palace. Even the king
kneels. Once a year, the man who rules
the whole country climbs your stairs,
bows his head, and waits for a little
girl to smear a red mark on his
forehead. The mark that tells his people
the gods still want him on the throne.
You're small enough to lift with one
arm. You can't spell your own name. And
this man commands an army. Yet, he does
not command you. Nobody finds that
strange, except maybe you. There's the
one thing nobody ever hands you, an
education. You're a goddess, and a
goddess already knows everything. So,
why teach her to read? Convince a whole
city the girl knows it all, and you
never have to teach her a thing. For
years, you get an hour of lessons a day,
when someone remembers, when there isn't
a festival or a line of devotees down
the stairs. Mostly, you get nothing. You
learn other things instead. You learn
about Kamala, the girl who sat on your
throne before you. You piece it together
from scraps, carried in at three,
worshipped for years, then one day
simply gone. Packed off home to a family
she barely knew. Her red dress became
your red dress. Her throne became your
throne. The goddess isn't you. The
goddess is the seat. You're just a girl
keeping it warm. During the big autumn
rites, they line buffalo and goats up in
front of you and cut their throats. And
you're not allowed to look away or
flinch. The blade goes in with a wet
crunch again and again. And the animals
thrash and gurgle until they stop. Blood
spreads across the stones. The copper
smell of the dark room floods back. And
the crowd watches to be sure the goddess
doesn't blink. You don't. You've had
practice since you were three. The years
pile up, but the days blur into one.
Same silk, same stillness, same painted
face morning after morning. Sunita is
the one who changes. By 11, she's got
real school friends and homework, and a
life with a door on it. When she visits,
she chatters about buses and classrooms
and boys, things you've never once seen,
and you feel her turning into a stranger
while she's still sitting beside you. A
whole country prays to you every
morning, and you can't hold on to the
one friend you've got. The visits get
shorter, then they mostly stop. The
throne stays warm. You stay still.
You're 12 when it happens. One morning,
there's blood, the ordinary kind every
girl your age eventually gets. You don't
think anything of it. You have no idea
it's about to end your entire life, but
the priests do. To them, a goddess who
bleeds isn't a goddess anymore. The
second you turn into an ordinary girl is
the second they're finished with you.
Lakshmi's face tells you the truth
before her mouth does. Overnight, the
country that worshipped you for 9 years
decides the goddess has left the
building. They lift the gold off your
neck. They wipe the third eye from your
forehead. Across the city, priests are
already sitting in a dark room with
another tiny girl and a fresh buffalo
head, checking her for 32 kinds of
perfect. And then they open the door and
tell you to walk home. Yep, walk. Except
you've been carried for 9 years, and
your legs have forgotten how to handle
stairs, let alone a street boiling with
motorbikes. You've never worn shoes, and
now there are shoes, and they feel like
prisons. The city you once blessed from
a golden chariot is suddenly a roaring,
honking wall of noise, and you're just a
12-year-old in plain clothes that nobody
bows to anymore. Your family loves you,
but they're strangers, and you're a
stranger right back. Handed to a mother
who gave you up at three. Dropped into a
house where everyone shares the chores
and nobody kneels. While you were a god,
nobody thought to explain any of this.
Then there's school. You're 12 and can
barely read, so they sit you in a
classroom of six-year-olds, and you
hunch there, towering over the little
ones, sounding out letters a goddess
never needed. A five-year-old beside you
gets through the alphabet faster than
you do. Nobody in this room bows. Nobody
even knows what you were. The little
kids laugh and cry and throw tantrums,
and you just sit there blank. Because 9
years of holding your face still took
the crying and laughing right out of
you. You forgot how, or maybe you never
learned. It takes years to claw back up
to your own age. Some girls never manage
it. And then, you're old enough for
marriage. There's an old belief that any
man who marries a former Kumari will
cough up blood and die young. So, the
boys keep their distance. The goddess
who once blessed kings sits at home
while the neighborhood whispers that
loving her is a death warrant. But, you
were never really the girl who cried in
the dark room, because you never cried
at all. You learned the letters. You
learned the shoes. Some former goddesses
finish school, hold real jobs, even
write books that finally tell people
what it was like in that house. [music]
The valley took your whole childhood and
handed you a throne for it. Then took
the throne back, too. And somehow you
build a life anyway. Years later, you're
crossing Durbar Square when you see a
crowd outside [music] the Kumari Ghar.
They're carrying a new little girl up
the steps. 3 years old, red silk, gold
heavy on her neck. Her bare feet held
carefully off the ground. You watch her
vanish [music] through the same door you
came out of. Then you turn, on your own
two feet, in your own cheap sandals, and
you walk yourself home across the dirt.
>> [music]
>> The Kumari tradition continues today.
Nepal's current Royal Kumari, Aryatara
Shakya, was installed in 2025 at the age
of two. And since the 2008 Supreme Court
ruling, serving Kumaris are guaranteed
an education and a small pension after
they retire. Rashmila Shakya, a Kumari
in the 1980s who left barely able to
read, later became the first former
living goddess to finish college. If you
think losing your goddesshood at the
first sign of blood sounds brutal, wait
until you hear what happened to Roman
girls who broke the opposite rule. Watch
your life as a Vestal Virgin to see what
happened when a sacred girl's body
betrayed the one vow she couldn't break,
and why buried alive was considered the
merciful option.

You've lived on the same peaceful street
for years. A quiet corner of Japan where
the seasons move gently [music] and life
unfolds at its own pace. Then one day,
your street is discovered. [music] The
perfect spot to capture the city's most
famous landmarks. Now, from sunrise to
[music] sunset, crowds of tourists
gather outside, cameras in hand,
searching for the perfect shot. What was
once your home has become a viewpoint
and your everyday life part of someone
else's postcard?
This scene now plays out daily across
many of the nation's iconic cities. A
record 37 million people visited the
country in 2024, six times more than 20
years ago. The inbound tourism industry
has now become its second largest export
sector behind cars. A weak yen has made
Japan irresistible, and the crowds prove
[music] it. What started as a travel
boom has now tipped into something else
entirely. Packed [music] trains,
overflowing streets, and locals
wondering how much more their towns can
take. [music] At first glance, it looks
like a destination overwhelmed. But the
reality is far more nuanced.
At the heart of this story lies a
powerful economic shift. Since 2010, the
yen has fallen around 45% against the US
dollar, making it one of the cheapest
destinations in the developed world. For
Western travelers, the weaker yen has
made it exceptionally good value.
Hotels, meals, and transport now cost
far less in dollar or euro terms, and
experiences once seen as luxuries are
within easier reach. That's drawn in
record numbers of travelers, especially
from China, Korea, and Southeast Asia.
But it's also made it harder for local
citizens, especially younger
generations, to travel abroad. Japan's
baby boomers, once seen exploring the
world in large tour groups with cameras
in hand during the economic boom of the
1980s, are now in their late7s, more
often caring for aging spouses [music]
than traveling abroad. This
transformation into a global tourism
magnet was no accident. Back in 2005,
the country welcomed just 6.7 million
visitors. By 2024, that number had
skyrocketed to 37 million. The growth
has been driven by targeted policy,
relaxed visa requirements for Asian
travelers, expanded flight routes
through Tokyo's Haneda airport, and
global showcases like the Tokyo Olympics
and the recent Osaka World Expo. For
years, this was seen as a win-win.
Tourists got their fix of sushi, cherry
blossoms, and anime [music] culture,
while local economies reaped the
rewards. But recently that spirit of
omotanashi, the nation's famed [music]
sense of hospitality is being tested.
The sudden influx of visitors has
created friction, [music] especially in
a society that values quiet order and
social harmony. This is a country built
on discipline, [music]
etiquette, and respect for space. Many
locals feel that an uncontrolled influx
of [music] visitors, often unfamiliar
with these norms, threatens that
balance.
Online, this frustration has boiled
over. Foreigners are filmed pushing in
line, sitting in the wrong seats on
trains, or chasing geisha through the
streets of Kyoto. The clips go viral,
feeding a narrative that [music]
outsiders don't understand Japan.
[music]
>> And that frustration isn't just about
etiquette. It's tied to something more
emotional. money, pride, and memory.
Japan is now cheap for outsiders, and
people feel it's being taken advantage
of.
For the older generation, this sentiment
runs deep. Those who remember the 1980s
[music] when the nation was the world's
economic superpower now see backpackers
from abroad boasting about how
affordable everything has become. For
some it feels like a national
humiliation. That mix of pride,
nostalgia, and frustration is now
playing out in public across viral
clips, online arguments, and community
discussions.
In Kamakura, a coastal city south of
Tokyo, tourists now outnumber residents
by more than 90 to1. On weekends,
traffic crawls to a standstill as
visitors cue for photos at the city's
iconic railway crossing. Look a little
closer, though, and a pattern emerges.
The tourism problem isn't everywhere.
It's concentrated along a single
overcrowded trail. Despite signs in
multiple languages urging people do not
go out on the road, many ignored the
warnings.
Most visitors stick to the welltrodden
golden [music] route of Tokyo, Kyoto,
and Osaka, leaving much of the country
overlooked. The result is a
concentration problem. A few overcrowded
hubs surrounded by regions that see
barely any tourists. Take Canazawa,
where visitor numbers are approaching
capacity. Yet just 30 minutes away,
Kamatsu sits almost empty. Or consider
the Lorson convenience store in
Kawagucho, made famous online for its
view of Mount Fuji, swarmed daily by
photographers, even though identical
viewpoints nearby go unnoticed. [music]
So while headlines warn of over tourism,
much of the country remains strikingly
serene. Officials have taken notice
[music] and are responding with creative
new strategies.
The Japanese government chose 139 tours
from 1,000 applicants that could attract
foreign tours.
>> The National Tourism Organization is now
teaming up with social media influencers
to showcase the country's authentic
natural [music] beauty beyond the
typical tourist hotspots. It's a smart
move. Officials have recognized that the
top three sources of travel inspiration
for visitors are friends and family,
social media, and video sharing
platforms. They've partnered with major
influencers like South [music] Korean
creator Chomad, who has over a million
followers on Instagram, and nearly as
many on YouTube. On a recent trip, he
showcased a little known Japanese
village, sharing his experience grilling
fresh seafood alongside Amma,
traditional female divers who harvest
[music] treasures from the sea. His post
resonated widely, earning thousands of
views, likes, and interactions across
his platforms, proving the power of
authentic storytelling in modern travel
promotion. It's a good start, but
turning online buzz into realworld
balance is the harder part. If Japan
wants to ease public [music] anxiety,
tackle overcrowding, and share the
economic benefits of tourism more
evenly, it must focus on two key goals.
First, [music] it needs to encourage
repeat custom. travelers who have
already seen the major attractions and
are ready to venture off the beaten
path. Second, [music] the government
must continue improving infrastructure,
making it easier for tourists to explore
the country's lesserknown [music]
regions. After all, its border spans
more than 3,000 km from Hkaido in the
north to Kagoshima in the south, and
much of it remains relatively untouched
by [music] foreign visitors. That, of
course, is easier said than done. Take
Fukulei northeast of Kyoto, a region
with everything a traveler could want. A
world-class [music] dinosaur museum, a
Zen Buddhist temple, once admired by
Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, and dozens
of traditional sake breweries. On paper,
it's the ideal alternative to
overcrowded [music] Kyoto. Yet, despite
its appeal, Fukui remains Japan's second
least [music] visited prefecture among
foreign tourists, according to hotel
booking data. There's reason for
optimism, though. Last year, the [music]
bullet train line from Tokyo was
extended to Fukulele City, cutting the
journey by an hour and bringing total
travel time to under 3 hours with no
transfers needed. For Fukulele, that
sleek new rail link might finally be the
ticket to a well-deserved place on the
travel map.
Its journey captures both the promise
and the challenge facing the nation. A
land rich in possibility, yet still
learning how to share it. a land caught
between the desire to open its [music]
doors and the instinct to protect its
traditions. So the next time you hear
someone say Japan is too crowded,
remember it's not the whole country.
It's just that everyone's [music] going
to the same few places. And unless it
learns how to balance tourism's rewards
with its realities, that famous
omotanashi spirit might soon reach its
breaking point.

Your heart jumps. Sounds like a fairy

first, he says, eyes drowning in tears.

catching whispers of plots and
betrayals. The emperor steward nods.
You're good. Scary good. But standing
out here is a neon sign saying, "Stab
me." Lee, now the emperor's errand boy,
hates your rise. At a banquet, he bumps
into you, splashing wine on a consort's
silk. She screams treason for a spill
and lays grinning. A stolen jade seal
planted in your mat to frame you. Guards
drag you to a cell. Mold and death
choking the air. The emperor's mother,
face like carved marble, hisses. Confess
or we get creative. But May, now a
trembling concubine who survived three
purges, passes the evidence to a senior
unuk, the one who owes you a favor. He
tucks it into his own sleeve, eyes
unreadable. She's risking her neck for
you, knowing she could be next. The
senior unic believes her, and Lee gets
dragged away, screaming like a kick dog.
You're free, but every victory is just a
fancier cage. They don't kill you, but
they don't let you go either. Mercyy's
not their style. You're stripped to
number 47. A nameless shadow mopping
floors you once commanded. Concubine
step over you like dirt. Their own
misery, no excuse for their cruelty. You
stop flinching at their screams. That
scares you more than the blood ever did.
You're 20. The machine's perfect tool.
Managing the emperor's har like a ledger
of flesh. Tracking periods, scheduling
visits, burying complaints. Concubines
who once spat on you now beg for your
favor. Their whispers soft as silk,
sharp as thorns. The emperor's gaze
weighs like a guillotine. Thrusting you
because you're broken in all the right
ways. A man who's not a man. Loyal
because you've got nothing left. Wrong.
Power is cute till it's a noose. Your
body's crumbling. Joints creek like
haunted gates. Lungs cuff blood from
palace dust. Damp robes your constant
shame. Then purge hits like a machine
malfunction. The emperor is paranoid of
a coup. A snakeeyed unic whispers your
name on the kill list. You're hauled
before the emperor, not as his trusted
adviser, but as suspect number nine.
Prove your worth, he snaps, tossing you
orders to spy on a noble. You expose the
noble's rebel letters, but the emperor
demotes you anyway. Don't forget, mercy
is not their style. Worse, your
treasures, those preserved parts needed
for the afterlife, are burned during the
purge. Without them, no manhood, no
peace, just a ghost carved from ash. The
machine doesn't kill you, it erases you.
You're 25. Number 47 again. Sweeping
floor is where you once ruled. That
snake-eyed unuk passes daily. His smirk,
a blade twisting in your gut. He's
pretending not to recognize the man he
destroyed. The young unuks don't know
you were a king among cogs. You never
trained anyone. You never saved anyone.
May's already dead. Executed last month
for breathing near the wrong noble. Her
bones feed the palace gardens. Another
forgotten spark. You're alone and the
machine doesn't care about your
innocence. Your lungs collapse. Dust and
shame choking your last breaths. No
fever, no drama. Just a quiet fall in a
store room. Body curled like a broken
puppet. You're 27. Ancient for a unic.
Most are dead or promoted. You're
neither, just erased. The palace ticks
on like a poison clock. New boys fed to
the machine. You weren't a villain, not
even a hero, just a screw titan till it
snapped. In your final flicker, you see
that 8-year-old hungry boy dreaming of
warrior glory. You wanted to survive.
Maybe that's enough. Maybe it's all
anyone gets.
Here's the head spinner. The last Ching
Yunuk died in 1996, barely 30 years ago.
His genitals preserved in a jar for his
afterlife was burned during the cultural
revolution, sealing his fate as a female
mule in eternity. Some prices are too
high, even for a shot at heaven.
