text:
Discover what your life would have been like as a front-line WWI nurse! 

Inspired by Dinzo, James Toland, and Bound.

DISCLAIMER: This video is a fictional dramatization inspired by historical accounts of the life of a Frontline Nurse during World War I. While based on real practices, characters and events are exaggerated for storytelling. No one was harmed in the making of this video.

#WWI #WorldWarOne #HistoryDocumentary #WomenInHistory

subtitles.plaintext:
You're 23 years old, standing in a
canvas tent in northern France, 1916,
when the stretcher bearers carry in a
boy with half his face missing. His jaw
hangs by a thread of gristle. One eye
socket is a crater of red pulp. The
other, blue and terrified, finds yours
and won't let go. You move forward, take
his hand, lean close to the ruin of his
ear and whisper, "You're safe now. I've
got you." He dies 14 minutes later,
still holding your hand. You never learn
his name. Welcome to the Western Front.
You're a VAD nurse, a Voluntary Aid
Detachment volunteer. Six weeks of first
aid training, a gray dress and white
apron, and absolutely no idea what
you've walked into. This is your life as
a World War I frontline nurse. Two years
earlier, you're the daughter of a bank
clerk in Birmingham, 1914. Piano
lessons, Sunday church, a life so small
it's suffocating. Then, Archduke Franz
Ferdinand takes a bullet in Sarajevo,
and suddenly the world cracks open. The
newspapers scream for volunteers.
Posters show brave Tommies marching off
to glory. Your brother enlists in
August. Your father cries at the train
station, first time you've ever seen him
weep. Everyone says it'll be over by
Christmas. Christmas comes. The war
doesn't end. Your brothers write letters
about mud and rats and a friend named
Charlie who stepped on something and
simply ceased to exist. You want to
help, but you're a woman, which means
you can't fight. Can't do much of
anything except roll bandages and feel
useless. Then, you see the
advertisements. Voluntary Aid
Detachments wanted. No nursing
certificate required. Pass the courses,
serve your country. You sign up with a
VAD the next morning. Your mother weeps.
Your father calls it unseemly. You don't
care. You've spent 21 years being
decorative and useless. You're done.
But, there's a problem. You're too young
for overseas service, 21, and they want
23. So, they send you to an auxiliary
hospital in Devon, a converted country
house. Officers recovering from wounds.
Technically, you're a nurse's aide. In
practice, you empty bedpans, change
dressings, and learn what gangrene
smells like. It's not the front, but the
men who arrive have seen it. They scream
in their sleep. Some stare at walls for
hours, flinching at sounds only they can
hear. One lieutenant, barely older than
you, weeps when you change his bandages,
not from pain, but from something
deeper. You learn the work, the
exhaustion, the smell of wounds that
won't heal. You learn to keep your face
calm when a man's leg is more pus than
flesh. By the time you turn 23, you've
assisted at dozens of surgeries, held
men while they died, and forgotten what
it feels like to sleep through the
night. You apply for overseas service
the week of your birthday. They accept
you immediately. Your posting is a base
hospital in Etaples, on the French
coast. The wounded arrive by ambulance
train, hundreds of them, thousands over
the weeks, packed into carriages like
broken cargo. They come caked in mud and
blood and worse. Their uniforms are
stiff with filth. Some haven't had their
wounds dressed days. You thought Devon
prepared you. It didn't. The wounds are
beyond anything your training prepared
you for. Shrapnel doesn't make neat
holes. It tears. It shreds. You see boys
with abdomens split open, intestines
glistening like wet rope, boys with legs
attached by skin alone, boys whose lower
halves are simply gone. You work 14-hour
shifts, then 16. You eat standing up,
sleep in snatches, forget what it feels
like to not be exhausted. One night you
assisted 17 amputations, 17 legs and
arms piled in a corner like firewood.
The surgeon's hands shake. Nobody
speaks. There's nothing to say. The
convoys never stop. Ambulance trains
pulls in at all hours, sometimes three,
four in a single night. Each one carries
hundreds of wounded fresh from the
front. You learn to sleep in snatches
between arrivals, to wake at the sound
of wheels on tracks. When a big push is
on, the trains come faster than you can
empty them. Men lie on stretchers in the
rain waiting for beds that don't exist.
You triage in the dark, lantern in hand,
deciding who gets seen first. Walking
wounded to one ward, surgical cases to
another, hopeless cases to a third. You
learn not to look at the hopeless cases.
Spending time on dying men means living
men die instead. But sometimes a boy
grabs your hand and his eyes are so
young, so terrified, and you sit with
him anyway. You hold his hand. You lie.
You tell him he'll be fine. The
surgeon's coming. He'll see his mother
soon. Then you move to the next one and
the next. They keep dying and you keep
moving on. The Battle of the Somme
begins July 1st. On that single day, the
British Army suffers 57,000 casualties.
20,000 dead before lunch. The wounded
pour in like a tide that never ebbs. You
work 36 hours straight, then 40. Men lie
on stretchers in the mud outside because
there's no room in the tents. Surgeons
operate until their hands shake too
badly to hold scalpels. You stop seeing
faces. You see wounds, tasks. Dress
this, clean that. Hold him down while
the morphine takes. A boy, 17 at most,
must have lied about his age, asks if
he's going to die. His belly's torn
open. You can see things that should be
inside. "Of course not." you say
smiling. "The surgeon will fix you right
up." He believes you. He dies believing
you. Later in the latrine, you vomit
until there's nothing left. Then you
wash your face, straighten your apron,
and go back to work. What else is there
to do? In late 1916, you see him, Thomas
Ashford, 19, Lancashire lad with ginger
hair and a gap-toothed smile that
survives even the morphine haze.
Shrapnel tore through his thigh, missing
the artery by a miracle. The surgeon
saved the leg, but infection sets in.
He'll be with you for weeks. You
shouldn't have favorites, but Thomas
tells terrible jokes while you change
his dressings. What do you call a
soldier with no arms and no legs? Names.
And somehow makes you laugh even as
you're picking shrapnel from his
suppurating wound. He talks about home,
his mom's meat pies, his sister who
wants to be a teacher, his spaniel named
Biscuit who sleeps on his bed. "When
this is over," he says one night, fever
bright, "I'm opening a bookshop
somewhere quiet. You could visit." You
laugh. "I'll hold you to that." The
infection spreads. The leg comes off
after all. Thomas survives the surgery,
but something in him dims. He stops
making jokes, stares at the ceiling for
hours. Then you smell it. That sickly
sweet rot. Gas gangrene. He dies on a
Tuesday holding your hand. He's the 47th
soldier you watched die. He's the first
whose name you'll still remember in 50
years. It's 1917. Mustard gas arrives
this year. It comes in artillery shells,
an oily mist you barely notice until
it's too late. Gas victims come in
blinded, eyes swollen shut and leaking.
Their skin is covered in blisters, great
weeping sacks that burst at the
slightest touch. Their lungs are burning
from the inside. The worst part is the
sound. Gas men don't scream. They can't.
They rasp. They wheeze. They drown in
fluid their own lungs produce. You sit
with them at night, these eyeless
gasping boys, and think about the
recruiting posters back home. Your
country needs you. They didn't mention
this part. They didn't mention the piles
upon piles of bodies with legs missing,
torsos broken, fluid seeping, and flies
buzzing. It's 1918 and the war is almost
over. Except when the real enemy
arrives, Spanish flu. It kills faster
than bullets. A man can be healthy at
breakfast and dead by dinner. The
symptoms are unmistakable. Fever, cough,
then mahogany spots on the cheekbones.
Within hours victims turn blue, a
ghastly heliotrope hue as lungs fill
with fluid. You learn to check feet
first. Black feet mean death. Don't
waste time. Nurses start dying, too. The
sister who trained you, gone in 48
hours. Three friends dead in a week.
Bodies stacked in corners like cordwood.
You get sick, burn with fever for 3
days, certain you'll join them. You
don't. You survive. Not everyone gets to
be so lucky, or not so lucky. On
November 11, 1918, the guns stop at
11:00 a.m. The silence is so absolute,
you think you've gone deaf. Somewhere
people are celebrating. Church bells,
cheering crowds. The war is over. You're
standing in a ward full of men who will
never walk again. Men with no faces. Men
whose minds are still trapped in the
trenches. The war isn't over for them.
It never will be. You step outside and
look up at the stars. The same stars
that watch over the Somme. Same stars
that didn't care when Thomas Ashford
died. [music] You should feel relief,
joy, something. You feel nothing at all.
Two months later, your family meets you
at the station. Your mother cries. Your
father says he's proud. Your brother,
who lost three fingers at Passchendaele,
stands apart, watching you with eyes
that understand. You try to explain what
it was like. You can't. How do you
describe the smell of gangrene to
someone who's never left Birmingham? You
stop trying. The local hospital offers
you a position. Civilian nursing, slower
pace, smaller wounds. Patients complain
about headaches and indigestion, and you
want to scream. You don't know what pain
is. You don't scream. You smile. You
pretend you're the same girl who left 4
years ago. You're not. That girl died
somewhere in France, holding a
stranger's hand who was taking his last
breath. You're just what's left. You
never marry. The men your age are dead
or damaged. You never have children.
Some nights you still smell it, the
gangrene, the gas, the copper tang of
blood. You still see Thomas's
gap-toothed smile. Still hear gassed men
drowning in their own lungs. They called
it shell shock when men broke. When you
break, they call it nerves. It doesn't
fixed. It never fixes.

In this video we cover what your life would have been like if you lived as a Shogun in Japan.

DISCLAIMER: This video is a fictional dramatization inspired by historical accounts of Shogun life. While based on real practices, characters and events are exaggerated for storytelling. No shoguns were harmed in the making of this video.

subtitles.plaintext:
It's 1549 Japan and you're born a
daimo's son in a castle crumbling under
war's fist. War drums pound your skull,
but your mother's whisper. Keep your
heart soft, my son. Lights a spark of
hope. Maybe you'll be a hero, not a
butcher. Wrong. Power's a meat grinder
and you're the meat. One misstep, your
clan's ash, your head skewered on a
pike. Your name spit on. Shogun? Sure.
If you claw through blood, betrayal, and
madness. Spoiler. Victory is just a
prettier grave. Every choice scarves
your soul into ribbons. And glory is a
lie that rots with you. You're six, torn
from your mother's arms. Her voice,
don't let them harden you. Drowned by
cartwheels crunching gravel. The
fortress you're dumped in reeks of mold
and piss. Stone walls oozing slime that
chills your bones. Your bed's a straw
pile, sharp as thorns, shredding your
skin, bloody food's rice, crawling with
weevils, sour as vomit. Choke it down or
starve. You're a hostage. A pawn in your
father's war. One rebellion and your
throat slit. Head box for his doorstep.
Guards sneer, their breath rancid as
corpse flesh, promising pain. At night,
shadows slither, footsteps thumping. Rat
or blade. You clutch a wooden horse,
your mother's gift, whispering her words
to keep fear at bay. At 8, they forge
you into a weapon. Dawn hauls you to a
courtyard, feet numb on frozen mud. You
swing a wooden sword till blisters
burst. Blood oozing sticky. Miss a step
and a bamboo rod smashes your spine.
Crack. Agony choking your screams.
Weaklings rot. Your master snars. Spit
flecking your face. Dust stings your
eyes. Air thick with sweat and dread. A
rival kid smashes your wooden horse at
12. Splinter stabbing your heart. Loves
for losers. He laughs. You learn. Care
and you bleed. Your mother's voice
fades, but it lingers in dreams,
pleading for kindness. At 14, you're
sent home. But first, a cruel test.
Bandits swarm a village, their torches
painting the night red, smoke curling
like demons. Amid the chaos, a peasant
girl, barely 10, frail as a sparrow,
huddles in the dirt, her tattered kimono
stained with ash and blood. Her wide
eyes glistening with tears lock onto
yours, pleading for salvation. She
clutches a broken doll, its straw guts
spilling out, and whispers, "Please save
me. I have no one." Her voice trembles,
soft as a dying bird, slicing your
heart. You step forward to help her, but
your father's voice hacks through your
resolve like steel. Clan first, always.
His glare burns colder than the night,
promising death for defiance. The girl's
cries grow frantic as a knife grazes her
cheek, blood trickling like tears. She
sobs, "Please, I'm scared." Each word a
dagger in your chest. But you step back,
blade lowering, her eyes widen, trust
shattering like glass. No, she wales,
her voice breaking as bandits drag her
into the dark. Her small body thrashing,
bare feet scraping mud. Her screams,
shrill and gut-wrenching, echo through
the burning village, fading into the
crackle of flames and hyena-like laughs.
The last you see is her doll, abandoned
in the dirt, soaked in her blood. That
night sleeps a ghost. You lie on your
mat, the girl's sobbs ringing in your
ears, her bloodied face haunting your
lids. Your mother's voice whispers in
the dark. You could have been kind. It's
a knife twisting in your gut. Her words
heavy with the weight of what you've
lost. You clench your fists, nails
biting palms, burying the guilt deep.
Kindness is a blade in your back, a
luxury for fools. You're no boy now.
You're a katana, sharp and hollow,
forged for war's merciless grind. At 14,
your clan's castle stinks of sweat and
treachery. You learn to read lies and
bow. Smell betrayal in a smile. Turn
allies into corpses before breakfast.
Your father tests you. Save the village
or the gold. You pick gold, watching
flames devour homes. Screams curling
like smoke. Guilt naws, but you choke it
down. Your mother's voice is silent, and
you're glad. Heroes die. Monsters rule.
At 15, you lead a skirmish against a
rival clan. Rain pounding your armor
like fists. You hack your first man. His
scream shredding the air. Blood spraying
your face. Hot and coppery. A wounded
enemy. A boy your rage begs for mercy.
Tears streaming. You freeze. Heart
hammering. Then you rip his throat open.
Blood gushing like a river soaking your
boots. That night you vomit. Not from
guilt, but because your heart's a stone.
You've crossed a line. Your first kill.
Your first choice to be cruel. Your
mother's voice doesn't come. You're free
and it's terrifying. At 18, you ambush a
rebel family in a forest. Their defiance
a threat to your clan. Dawn spills red
through twisted trees. Air biting with
pine and dread. You spot them. Father,
mother, boy your age, gaunt and
trembling. Eyes like cornered deer. The
boy's whimper cuts the silence,
clutching his mother. You could spare
them. Let them vanish. For a heartbeat,
mercy flickers. Power doesn't mean
blood, but weakness breeds betrayal. You
raise your hand and your men pounce like
wolves. Katana is splashing. Blood
spraying hot bark stained crimson. The
father's throat gurgles hacked open. The
mother's scream dies as steel rips her
chest. You cut the boy down, his body
crumpling, blood seeping into frost. The
forest stills, gorge dripping, coppery
air stinging your lungs. Nausea chokes
you, but you smirk, muttering, powers of
butcher's game. Your men cheer, eyes
probing. Did you waver? At 20, a vassel
tries to gut you in your sleep. Blade
grazing your ribs. You don't just kill
him. You flay his skin, his screams a
symphony, blood pooling black. His
servant, innocent, begs, eyes wide. You
hack his neck. Gore splattering your
hands warm as lies. Trust no one, you
mutter, wiping blood on your sleeve.
Shadows dance with treachery, and you
clutch your katana. Ears straining for
whispers of death. At 25, Sei Gajara in
1600 is your crucible. The battlefields
a slaughter pit. Blood rivers, heads
rolling like stones. Tempo shots boom,
tearing your ears. Ash chokes your
lungs. You betray your last friend,
burying his men in mud. Their gurgled
screams clawing your soul. A
surrendering ally kneels pleading.
Mercy's weakness. You snarl and butcher
them. Blades hacking flesh to pulp.
Blood misting the air. You stand at top
a corpse mound. Flag high. Shogun to be.
Victory reeks of death and your souls a
cinder. Your mother's voice is gone.
Just wind howling your sins. At 26, the
emperor gifts you the title of Shogun.
His hollow smile masking centuries of
resentment. You're now Shogun. But
Edeto's castle fers with sewage and
fear. Walls dripping deceit. Daimo bow.
Eyes glinting like daggers. You shackle
them with forced stays in Edeto,
draining their gold till their coffers
bleed dry. A spy hisses a poison in your
tea. You don't execute the cook. You
disembowel him. His guts steaming on the
floor. Blood soaking your silk like ink.
His screams echo as you watch. Stomach
churning. How many more plot your end?
You pace your chambers. Katana clutched.
Every creek a killer's step. Every sip a
roll of dice. At 28, you crush rebels
with fire and iron. You torch a village.
Flames devouring homes. Flesh melting.
Whales drowned by crackling roofs. You
ride through its ruins at 30, ashes
swirling, bones snapping under hooves,
the stench of charred death clogging
your throat. You laugh at your younger
self, telling your son, "Fools trust
loyalty." His eyes wide with fear mirror
yours. You forged a throne on terror,
but paranoia is your true master.
Gnawing your mind like rats. At 32, your
son's coded letters betray his plot to
steal your throne. You order his death.
You wheeled the blade, his begging eyes,
your eyes burning into your soul, his
neck splits, blood gushing hot, his
gasps fading into silence. Your wife
screams rips your gut like a spear. Her
curse of venom in your veins. That
night, your mother's voice howls in the
wind. Don't let them harden you. You
roar at the shadows, heart a blackened
husk, too far gone to care. At 35, Edeto
glitters with silk, but reeks of ash and
lies. You crush a samurai plot. Their
heads impaled on spikes. Eyes pecked by
crows. Flies droning like war drums.
Your laws choke Japan, but every cough
feels like a death's claw. At 37,
peasants storm your lands. Torches
blazing. Screams splitting the night.
You trample them. Hooves pulping skulls.
Blood painting your armor crimson. Their
curses sharper than blades. Each corpse
you crush sprawls 10 more rebels. Hate
breeding like maggots. At 40, your
body's rotting alive. Eda's feted air
poisoned your lungs, hands trembling
like dead leaves, skin gray as ash. You
ride past that burned village's ruins,
bones gleaming in moonlight, a ghost of
your sins. Your mother's voice whispers,
"What have you become?" You spit blood,
ignoring her. Your empire's iron, but
you're a walking corpse. Lord circling
like vultures, smelling your decay. At
48, you mold your heir in a training
hall, stinking of sweat and dread. His
sword trembling, brittle as his will.
Your raw voice snarss. Weak kings feed
worms, smashing his arm. Bones grinding,
his flinch hinting fear or treason.
Daimo lurk, eyes glinting like vultures,
sensing your decay. Edeto's toxic air
sears your lungs. Each breath a blade,
joints creaking like rotting wood. Fear
naws. Is your air too weak to rule or
blotting your end? Your mother's voice
begs. Don't break him. But you crush it.
Mercy's a noose and your rotting carcass
won't swing. At 50, your empire's a
mausoleium of memories. Your castle's a
crypt. Silence shrieking louder than
war. Everyone's dead or despises you.
Wife praying for your end. Kids
flinching at your breath. Nightmares
claw at you. Your son's eyes that burned
village. Your mother's voice. You could
have been kind. Your hands shake. Skin
ashen. Every cuff hacking up blood.
You're Japan's god. but king of nothing
but fear and emptiness. At 52, you're a
corpse defying death. Your room reeks of
medicine and rot, skin like soggy
parchment, eyes sunk in pits. You rasp
orders, but lords sneer. Your air looms
in the doorway, cold as frost, likely
dreaming of your grave. Your mother's
voice sigh one last time. I told you to
stay soft. You choke on a laugh, blood
flecking your lips. Too late, old hag.
You die at 53 in 1616. rotting in
Edeto's filth. A god dethroned by your
own decaying flesh. Your empire crumbled
in a generation. Your name dust on the
wind. You were a god. The gods die, too.
You clawed, killed, ruled for what?
Nothing. Was it worth it?

chest. You cut the boy down, his body crumpling,
blood seeping into frost. The forest stills, gorge 
dripping, coppery air stinging your lungs. Nausea
chokes you, but you smirk, muttering, powers of 
butcher's game. Your men cheer, eyes probing.
Did you waver? At 20, a vassel tries to gut you 
in your sleep. Blade grazing your ribs. You don't
just kill him. You flay his skin, his screams 
a symphony, blood pooling black. His servant,
innocent, begs, eyes wide. You hack his neck. Gore 
splattering your hands warm as lies. Trust no one,
you mutter, wiping blood on your sleeve. Shadows 
dance with treachery, and you clutch your katana.
Ears straining for whispers of death. At 25, Sei 
Gajara in 1600 is your crucible. The battlefields
a slaughter pit. Blood rivers, heads rolling 
like stones. Tempo shots boom, tearing your
ears. Ash chokes your lungs. You betray your 
last friend, burying his men in mud. Their
gurgled screams clawing your soul. A surrendering 
ally kneels pleading. Mercy's weakness. You snarl
and butcher them. Blades hacking flesh to pulp. 
Blood misting the air. You stand at top a corpse
mound. Flag high. Shogun to be. Victory reeks 
of death and your souls a cinder. Your mother's
voice is gone. Just wind howling your sins. At 
26, the emperor gifts you the title of Shogun.
His hollow smile masking centuries of resentment. 
You're now Shogun. But Edeto's castle fers with
sewage and fear. Walls dripping deceit. Daimo bow. 
Eyes glinting like daggers. You shackle them with
forced stays in Edeto, draining their gold till 
their coffers bleed dry. A spy hisses a poison
in your tea. You don't execute the cook. You 
disembowel him. His guts steaming on the floor.
Blood soaking your silk like ink. His screams echo 
as you watch. Stomach churning. How many more plot
your end? You pace your chambers. Katana clutched. 
Every creek a killer's step. Every sip a roll of
dice. At 28, you crush rebels with fire and iron. 
You torch a village. Flames devouring homes. Flesh
melting. Whales drowned by crackling roofs. You 
ride through its ruins at 30, ashes swirling,
bones snapping under hooves, the stench of charred 
death clogging your throat. You laugh at your
younger self, telling your son, "Fools trust 
loyalty." His eyes wide with fear mirror yours.
You forged a throne on terror, but paranoia 
is your true master. Gnawing your mind like
rats. At 32, your son's coded letters betray his 
plot to steal your throne. You order his death.
You wheeled the blade, his begging eyes, your eyes 
burning into your soul, his neck splits, blood
gushing hot, his gasps fading into silence. Your 
wife screams rips your gut like a spear. Her curse
of venom in your veins. That night, your mother's 
voice howls in the wind. Don't let them harden
you. You roar at the shadows, heart a blackened 
husk, too far gone to care. At 35, Edeto glitters
with silk, but reeks of ash and lies. You crush a 
samurai plot. Their heads impaled on spikes. Eyes
pecked by crows. Flies droning like war drums. 
Your laws choke Japan, but every cough feels like
a death's claw. At 37, peasants storm your lands. 
Torches blazing. Screams splitting the night.
You trample them. Hooves pulping skulls. Blood 
painting your armor crimson. Their curses sharper
than blades. Each corpse you crush sprawls 10 more 
rebels. Hate breeding like maggots. At 40, your
body's rotting alive. Eda's feted air poisoned 
your lungs, hands trembling like dead leaves,
skin gray as ash. You ride past that burned 
village's ruins, bones gleaming in moonlight,
a ghost of your sins. Your mother's voice 
whispers, "What have you become?" You spit blood,
ignoring her. Your empire's iron, but you're 
a walking corpse. Lord circling like vultures,
smelling your decay. At 48, you mold your heir 
in a training hall, stinking of sweat and dread.
His sword trembling, brittle as his will. Your raw 
voice snarss. Weak kings feed worms, smashing his
arm. Bones grinding, his flinch hinting fear or 
treason. Daimo lurk, eyes glinting like vultures,
sensing your decay. Edeto's toxic air sears your 
lungs. Each breath a blade, joints creaking like
rotting wood. Fear naws. Is your air too weak to 
rule or blotting your end? Your mother's voice
begs. Don't break him. But you crush it. Mercy's a 
noose and your rotting carcass won't swing. At 50,
your empire's a mausoleium of memories. Your 
castle's a crypt. Silence shrieking louder
than war. Everyone's dead or despises you. 
Wife praying for your end. Kids flinching at
your breath. Nightmares claw at you. Your son's 
eyes that burned village. Your mother's voice.
You could have been kind. Your hands shake. Skin 
ashen. Every cuff hacking up blood. You're Japan's
god. but king of nothing but fear and emptiness. 
At 52, you're a corpse defying death. Your room
reeks of medicine and rot, skin like soggy 
parchment, eyes sunk in pits. You rasp orders,
but lords sneer. Your air looms in the doorway, 
cold as frost, likely dreaming of your grave.
Your mother's voice sigh one last time. I told 
you to stay soft. You choke on a laugh, blood
flecking your lips. Too late, old hag. You die at 
53 rotting in Edeto's filth. A god dethroned by
your own decaying flesh. Your empire crumbled 
in a generation. Your name dust on the wind.
You were a god. The gods die, too. You clawed, 
killed, ruled for what? Nothing. Was it worth it?

subtitles.plaintext:
You're 19, tied to a wooden steak, rough
rope cutting into your wrists. The
flames lick at your ankles. You can
smell your own hair singing. Taste smoke
and terror on your tongue. The crowds
roaring, some hurling curses, some
sobbing, but most just hungry for the
show. Your executioner's torch feels
like the sun itself, and all you did was
try to save France. The twisted irony.
This moment was inevitable from the
second you drew your first breath.
Rewind to 1412. Dom Remy, a village so
small it doesn't even have a proper name
on most maps. You're born into a world
that's already marked you for death. You
just don't know it yet. Your village
reeks of fear and cowdom. A charming
combination. You can hear the war drums
echoing from miles away. Feel the ground
shake when English cavalry thunders
past. The church bells don't ring for
prayers anymore. They're warning
signals. Your life. Wake up. Pray. Work
the fields. Repeat. Your diet's stale
bread and prayers. meets for lords who
wouldn't spit on you. Your dad, Jacques,
is a farmer with a temper. Your mom,
Isabelle, is obsessed with saints.
They've got big plans to marry you off
by 16. Spoiler, you're not into it.
You've got bigger fish to fry, like
saving an entire kingdom. At 13,
everything changes. You're in the
garden, dirt under your fingernails,
sweat stinging your eyes from the brutal
summer heat. Then, bang, the air
crackles like lightning, and glowing
figures appear. The temperature drops so
fast that you can see your breath. St.
Michael, Catherine, and Margaret appear
out of thin air. Their voices ringing in
your skull like cathedral bells. Your
knees hit the ground so hard you'll have
bruises for weeks. But you can't look
away from their burning eyes. They tell
you to kick the English out of France
and crown a king. No pressure, right?
Divine voices. Either God's got a wild
plan or you ate some seriously bad rye
bread. You decide it's the former. These
saints keep showing up, nagging you like
celestial helicopter parents to save a
country that's been at war for decades.
France is split. English and Burgundians
on one side, your dolphin Charles on the
other, barely hanging on to his crown
and his sanity. You try telling people
about your voices. Big mistake. Your dad
thinks you're nuts. The neighbors
whisper, "Witch." A teenage girl saving
France. Yeah, that'll go over like a
lead balloon. The Hundred Years War is
torching villages. And you're hearing
actual screams and smell like actual
smoke from raids. Your divine calling
comes with a soundtrack of human
suffering. Your voices aren't just
inspiration. They're a burden that makes
you the village weirdo. Everyone doubts
you, but you're not backing down. You're
Joan, and you're about to turn this war
torn world upside down. Buckle up. It's
going to be a bumpy ride to either glory
or the stake. Fast forward to 16. You're
a peasant girl with voices in your head
trekking to Vakaloo to beg Robert the
Bulgiko for an escort to the dolphin. A
nobody asking a lord for help. He laughs
you off twice. You're back in 1428
spouting prophecies about French defeats
like some medieval Nostradamus. Third
times a charm. You predict the loss at
the Battle of the Herandings and boom,
it happens. Suddenly Brio's not
laughing. He hands you a horse and some
soldiers. Game on. Now 17, you're
dressed in men's clothes. Practical for
survival, sure, but it's going to bite
you in the ass later. You ride 11 days
through enemy territory to Chinan,
dodging English patrols like some
medieval action hero. One wrong move and
you're dead or worse. You reach Charles
II's court, a den of snobby nobles who
smell better than they act. The dolphins
disguise to trick you. Cute party game,
but you walk right up, call him out, and
spill secrets only he knows. Mic drop
moment. You're a teenager with zero
combat training, asking for an army.
Bold move, Joan. Priests and scholars
grill you for weeks, sniffing for heresy
like blood hounds. Here's the kicker.
You're a peasant girl who can't read,
but you're outsmarting them all with
divine confidence and razor sharp wit.
Your voices, they're real, and you're
not backing down. France needs you, and
you're ready to prove it. Time to saddle
up. War is calling. It's May 1429, and
you're 17, strapped into white armor,
waving a banner like a medieval
rockstar. Welcome to the siege of
Orleans. The English have the city
short, but you're dodging arrows,
rallying troops, and screaming at
generals to move faster. No military
training, no problem. You've got divine
guidance. Or maybe just beginner's luck
and balls of steel. 9 days later,
Orleans is free. The French are calling
you the maid of Orleans, and you're
eating up the glory like a starving
peasant at a feast. Next stop,
steamrolling the English at L campaign.
Yago m pate. You're racking up wins like
a pro. The French soldiers follow you
like you're God's personal messenger,
hanging on your every word. Your voices
told you to liberate the law and you're
delivering with interest. By July,
you're standing proud in rims as Charles
II gets his crown on July 17, 1429. You
did it. Mission accomplished, right?
Wrong. The war is still raging and glory
comes with a price tag that you haven't
seen yet. September brings your push for
Paris, charging the gates like a woman
possessed. But reality checks in. An
arrow slams into your leg. And Charles,
that ungrateful bastard you just
crowned, calls it quits. You're
bleeding, begging to keep fighting, but
his majesty says, "No." The first whiff
of betrayal hits your nostrils. France
is buzzing. Your name's on every tongue.
From peasants to nobles. You're a living
legend. The girl who turned the tide of
the hundred years war. But here's the
thing about legends. They make enemies.
The English and their Burgundian allies
are pissed. And they're plotting your
downfall. Your white armor is shining
bright, but the shadows are creeping in.
You're on top of the world, but the
higher you climb, the harder you fall.
May 1430 companion. One moment you're
charging like the fearless smith, banner
high and spirits higher. The next,
Burggonians yank you off your horse like
you're a sack of grain. Captured, they
don't see a hero, just a prize with a
price tag. They sell you to the English
for a fat stack of gold because loyalty
is about as valuable as peasant promises
in medieval politics. You're 18 and the
people you saved France for just cast
you out like a gambling chip. Now you're
locked in a Rowan tower surrounded by
English guards who lear like you're
their next meal. You stick to men's
clothes, not for fashion, but to keep
their grabby hands off. It's your only
armor now. And even that's a crime in
their kangaroo court. Charles, the king
you crowned, he's too busy sipping wine
and playing politics to send a rescue
party. You're on your own, abandoned by
the guys who owe you everything.
Desperation hits hard. You leap from a
70-foot tower, hoping for a miracle
escape. Spoiler alert, you don't stake
the landing. Bruised, battered, and back
in chains. You're staring down a future
that's looking grimmer by the day. The
English want you dead. The Burgundians
are counting their coins. And your
former king has selective amnesia.
You're still hearing your voices urging
you to stay strong. But the walls,
literal and metaphorical, are closing
in. Rock bottom, you're about to find
out it has a basement. January 1431. on.
You're 19, chained in a courtroom facing
70 charges. Heresy, witchcraft, and the
heinous crime of wearing pants. The
English and their puppet bishop, Pia
Kafon, have rigged this trial tighter
than a medieval chassity belt. These
aren't holy men. They're political
assassins and robes, desperate to
eliminate a French icon who's made them
look like fools. Bishops and scholars
throw trick questions to trap you, but
you're dodging their verbal arrows like
a pro. Outsmarting a room of priests at
19. Not bad for a peasant who can't read
but can spot [ __ ] from a mile away.
They scream, "You're a witch for your
voices." You fire back, "My saints are
real and God's on my side." The
courtroom stunned. The koshons seething
crossdressing. They are smoking gun as
they ran out of actual crimes. On May
24th, they drag you to a cemetery,
threaten to burn you immediately. Terror
grips you. You're still human after all.
You sign a paper saying you lied about
your voices, hoping to buy time. But the
moment you do, your world crumbles. Your
saints feel distant, your purpose
hollow. The betrayal of your own beliefs
cuts deeper than any sword. For days,
you wrestle with crushing guilt and
spiritual emptiness. Then clarity
strikes. You'd rather die true to
yourself than live as a lie. You ditch
the dress, put the men's clothes back
on, and reclaim your identity. May 30,
1431. You're tied to a stake in Ruan's
marketplace. The English love you so
much they're throwing you a bonfire. As
flames climb, you're shouting for God,
clutching a cross, unyielding to the
end. The crowd's sobbing, some soldiers,
too. But it's too late. You're 19 and
the fire takes you. You saved France,
defied a king, and shook an empire. But
this isn't Hollywood. Heroes don't
always get happy endings, especially
when there are inconvenient truths
wrapped in peasant clothes. Your voices
fall silent, but your name, it's about
to echo through eternity. You're gone,
but the world can't let you go. In 1456,
Pope Kixtus III calls your trial a sham.
Innocent, huh? Thanks for the memo,
church. Only 25 years late to the party.
By 1920, you're St. Joan, patron of
France, soldiers, and every dreamer with
guts. Most teenagers can't handle doing
laundry. You became a saint. You're a
feminist icon spitting in the face of
medieval patriarchy. War hero. You
flipped the hundred years war. Pop
culture star. From Christine Deazan's
poems to the passion of Joan of Arc,
you're everywhere. Statues, films,
French flags waving in your honor. It's
2025 and six centuries later, we're
sprawled on fluffy couches, scrolling
6-in smartphones, still talking about
you. You saved France at 19, gave
Charles's crown, and sparked the
nation's fight for independence. But you
paid with your life, burned for being
authentically, uncompromisingly
yourself. Your fire, it's still blazing
through every rebel and underdog who
hears your name and thinks, "If she
could do it, Joan, you're eternal and
eternally pissed off at how unfair it
all was.

text:
💻💰 The Billion-Dollar Hard Drive Buried in a Landfill

Under the grey skies of Wales lies one of the most expensive mistakes in tech history. In 2013, James Howells accidentally threw away a hard drive containing over 8,000 Bitcoins — now worth nearly a billion dollars.

This documentary-style video tells the incredible true story of James’ lost fortune: from the early days of Bitcoin mining when coins were worth pennies, to his desperate attempts to recover the drive buried deep beneath tons of toxic waste.

🔹 How James first discovered Bitcoin and mined thousands of coins
🔹 The fateful mistake that sent his fortune to the dump
🔹 His ongoing battle with the city council to dig it back up
🔹 Why experts believe the data could still survive
🔹 And what his story reveals about the risks of digital wealth

Is James the unluckiest man alive… or a visionary still holding onto hope?

fixed on the shifting mountains of

hard drive. On it, 8,000 bitcoins

billion. At the time of this video,
$94,128,000
to be precise. And the man who owns it

James Howells discovered Bitcoin early

Using free software, he began mining,
lending his computer's power to secure
transactions in exchange for coins. Back

explaining mining not so simple. Let's

Bitcoin mining uses powerful computers
to solve complex mathematical puzzles

earns a reward in newly created bitcoins
and transaction fees. This is called the
block reward. Once sold, each block of
transactions is permanently recorded in
the currency's public ledger. the
blockchain forming the backbone of the
entire system. In short, the puzzles are
there to protect Bitcoin from
manipulation and maintain trust without
banks or middlemen. Got it? Great. James
mined over 8,000 Bitcoin and stored it
in a single wallet file on a small
unremarkable hard drive. Then he moved
on. The computer was dismantled and the
hard drive put away in a classic mand
drawer.

an idea. There were no billion-dollar

away, spent it on pizzas. honestly

>> or forgot about it entirely. James was

miscommunication with his partner at the

Its storage platters weren't just plain

anti-corrosive cobalt. This combination
is far tougher than you might think.
Able to resist rust and decay even in

landfill. How cited realworld examples

text:
Amsterdam’s charm has made it one of the world’s most visited cities—but overtourism is taking its toll. From TikTok-fuelled queues and rising rents to noise and litter, locals are feeling the strain. This video explores how Amsterdam is tackling the crisis with strict Airbnb caps, Europe’s highest tourist tax, and plans to reshape its visitor economy. We also look at lessons from Venice, Barcelona, and Rome. Can cities welcome the world without losing what makes them unique?

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Brimm delivers high-grade animated explainers on business, brands, and the marketing stories shaping our world.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#Netherlands #HousingCrisis #Amsterdam #Overtourism #CheapTourism #TourismCrisis #BusinessExplained #ModernTourism #TikTokTourism #MarketingExplained #BusinessStrategy #BrandStrategy #MarketingTrends #BusinessInsights #AnimatedExplainers #BrandMarketing #BusinessGrowth #EconomyExplained

[Music]
You've lived above the same quiet
takeaway for years. Never a problem,
never a fuss. Then overnight it goes
viral on Tik Tok. Now your street is
choked with cues. The noise never ends.
And litter covers what was once a
beautiful place.
Life above isn't yours anymore. It
belongs to the tourists.
This scene is playing out daily in the
center of Amsterdam. The charm of narrow
streets and historic canals has drawn
crowds so dense that life at the city's
heart has begun to change. The dawn of
the millennium brought a milestone
moment for the city. For the first time,
more than 4 million visitors arrived in
a single year. By 2019, over 21 million
overnight stays were recorded, a figure
that revealed a city more sought after
than ever before. However, popularity
has come with a price. They should
forbid to eat on the streets, for
example. I think that's one of the
biggest annoyments that uh yeah, people
are sitting on the street eating on the
staircases. It's just not nice.
>> The complaints from Amsterdam residents
started to crop up in 2013 when tourism
had fully bounced back from a downturn
following the financial crisis of 2008.
Locals said that tourists were being
loud and disruptive in the city center,
showing disrespect toward workers in the
red light district, occupying short-term
vacation rentals that drove up housing
prices and taking over some of the
city's most beautiful historic areas.
This tension between a city's allure and
the burdens it brings raises a deeper
question. What drives such overwhelming
waves of visitors in the first place?
Over tourism is not accidental. It stems
from three interlocking causes. Low-cost
carriers reduced ticket prices to such
an extent that short urban getaways
became accessible to vast numbers of
travelers. As emerging markets grew
wealthier, tourism evolved, no longer
the preserve of the elite, but a mass
experience shared worldwide. And
crucially, apps like Instagram and Tik
Tok. These apps don't merely share
photos and hotspots. They direct tourist
traffic, funneling millions into the
same picture perfect locations.
Amsterdam's long cues once formed
outside landmarks like the Anne Frank
House or the Reichkes Museum. Timed
ticketing has ended those lines, but new
ones have appeared in the famous Nine
Street District. Crowds of young
visitors now wait outside food spots
such as the Chun Cafe or Fable Fre
turned into must- vvisit attractions by
social media.
>> Hi guys, we're in Amsterdam. We just
went to the famous Fable and Bri. It's a
basically a fries place and you can get
them topped with like anything that you
want.
>> If apps and airlines explain how mass
tourism took shape, the next question is
why cities like Amsterdam remain so
invested in it. The answer is
straightforward. Revenue. In Amsterdam,
tourism contributes around 5.7 billion
annually and sustains more than 60,000
full-time jobs. Many of these are in
hospitality, retail, cleaning, or
transport. Roles that, while often low
paid, provide flexible entry points into
the labor market for young people,
migrants, and students. And unlike
manufacturing or export industries,
tourism requires no shipping routes or
distribution networks. The product,
Amsterdam itself, simply sits and waits
to be consumed.
The same forces that once made tourism
look like a reliable engine of growth
also created imbalances in the city's
economy. And nowhere was this more
striking than in the housing market.
Platforms such as Airbnb and Booking.com
quietly transformed thousands of homes
into makeshift hotels, leaving fewer
places for residents to live. Pressured
by these changes, Amsterdam took
decisive action. In 2019, the mayor
imposed a strict cap of just 30 rental
nights per year on primary homes. The
effect was dramatic. By 2024, the number
of Airbnb listings had fallen by 54%.
However, the city's balance sheet
doesn't tell the full story. What seems
like easy money for businesses and city
coffers often comes with hidden costs
for residents. Economists have a name
for these unseen burdens. Negative
externalities. The side effects never
included in the price tag.
In Amsterdam, they show up in the form
of congestion, noise, and litter. A
cheap flight from London might cost a
traveler £40, but the real bill is paid
in the blocked bike lanes, overflowing
trash cans, and public spaces that seem
more like products to be consumed than
places to belong. The burden on
infrastructure is especially acute. The
city spends millions annually on extra
cleaning crews and police patrols to
manage weekend surges. Crowds spill over
into residential streets, straining
transport networks and eroding quality
of life. Yet, these expenses are rarely
captured in the neat statistics of GDP
contribution. That's not to say that
Amsterdam has stood idle.
Over the past decade, the city has
steadily raised its tourist tax, now the
highest in Europe, on the logic that
visitors should help cover the public
costs of their presence. A night in an
Amsterdam hotel carries a 12.5% levy,
while cruise ship passengers pay a flat
fee per day. From 2026, the city plans
to move its cruise ship terminal away
from the city center and force some
ships to dock 85 km away in Rotterdam.
The idea is simple. Make tourists share
the costs of the city they use. Other
measures go beyond taxation. For
example, in 2020, Amsterdam banned new
shops in the city center that cater
exclusively to tourists, such as tacky
souvenir and hemp shops to preserve
space for businesses serving residents.
Yet, the paradox is clear. Tourism
remains a pillar of local revenue. In
2023, spending by visitors reached
nearly€15 billion nationwide. Amsterdam
is trying to discourage the very
activity that helps fill its budget,
attempting the delicate act of cutting
dependence without toppling the economy
it's built around being visited.
And the struggle is not unique to the
Dutch capital. Venice has wrestled with
over tourism for decades and responded
by capping tour groups at 25 people,
plus introducing a 5 entry fee to its
historic center on peak days. Barcelona
has capped hotel construction and
crackdown on short-term rentals. Rome is
preparing to introduce a €2 fee to see
the Trevy Fountain. All three cities
show what happens when the tourist
economy tips into dependency. Once a
critical mass of jobs and businesses
rely on visitors, it becomes politically
and economically costly to turn the
tide. Amsterdam shares many of these
symptoms, but with a distinctive twist.
Unlike Venice, it is also a financial
hub home to multinationals like Iing,
Booking.com, and Phillips. Unlike
Barcelona and Rome, it competes globally
for talent in tech and creative
industries. This dual identity sharpens
Amsterdam's dilemma. To attract talent
and investment, it cannot slide into a
monoculture of souvenir shops and bike
rentals. Yet, the more the city bends
towards visitors, the harder it becomes
to steer back to a balanced, resilient
economy.
[Music]
The new mantra is quality over quantity.
The preference is for fewer, higher
spending visitors who engage beyond the
cliches of coffee shops and the red
light district. But unwinding the
tourist economy is hard. Once millions
of visitors shape housing, retail and
jobs, the system resists change. The
challenge for Amsterdam is not whether
tourism continues, but whether it can
pivot from selling volume to cultivating
value. The challenge is balance.
Welcoming the world without losing what
makes the city unique. After all, it's
not just a destination to visit, but a
home to preserve.

text:
Spain is a country on the up…. The past 40 years have been the countries best-ever. Democracy has been stabilized, Basque terrorism defeated and the rare transition to high-income status achieved. Public infrastructure is largely recent and therefore excellent. Life expectancy, now 84 years, is projected to be the world’s highest by 2040. 

True, the average Spaniard spends that life in a low-quality flat, often in a Soviet-looking apartment block, on a net median annual income of around 16 thousand euros. But improvement continues. With permanent contracts burgeoning, unemployment – so long the national shame – is at its lowest since 2008. 

However, Spain hides a secret at its heart: an empty, quiet expanse that few tourists ever venture to see. While bustling hubs like Madrid, Barcelona, and Seville capture the world's attention, the vast interior of Spain, known as the "Empty Spain" or "España Vacía," tells a different story—one of rural exodus, abandoned villages, and sweeping landscapes that stretch endlessly under the Iberian sun. 

This sparsely populated region, covering much of Spain's center, is a stark contrast to the lively urban centers, offering a glimpse into a forgotten side of the country where time seems to stand still.

According to Spain’s ministry for territorial policy, 90% of the country’s population – about 42 million people – is packed into one and a half thousand towns and cities that occupy 30% of the land. The other 10% - around 4.6 million people - occupy the remaining 70%, giving a population density of barely 14 inhabitants per square kilometer.

The average rural citizen must now travel 8 miles to access basic services such as ATMs, hospitals, nursery schools, supermarkets, and libraries—compared to 3 miles in Germany and Italy, and 5 miles in France.  

So, how the hell did they allow this to happen – and is there a realistic solution available?

The largest company on the planet. If
someone asked you who that is, what
would you say? Apple, Microsoft? How
about Saudi Aramco? Sometimes people are
surprised to hear that the biggest
company in the world is Walmart. That
surprise comes from the fact that most
people expect the crown to belong to a
tech titan or an oil giant and not a
chain of discount stores. In fact,
Walmart pulls in more than $1.8 billion
in sales every single day. Yet behind
these staggering numbers lies a story of
resilience and reinvention. A journey
that took Walmart from a vulnerable
position to a retail powerhouse once
again.
A decade ago, Walmart was on the ropes.
Amazon's rise had shaken the retail
world. Its endless selection and
doorstep delivery made Walmart's
sprawling superstores look like relics
of a fading era. Sales were slipping.
Profits were plunging. However, fast
forward 10 years and the tide has
turned.
Walmart now command an insane $680
billion in revenue, over 2 million
employees, and a healthy share of
America's retail and grocery spending.
The company has poured profits into
cuttingedge technology, and turned its
massive store network into a weapon,
beating Amazon at its own game. Their
secret weapon, sheer physical reach.
With 5,000 stores across America, 90% of
the population lives within 10 miles of
a Walmart store. Super centers double as
distribution hubs. Warehouses that once
served only stores now ship online
orders. And with a third party
marketplace like Amazon's, Walmart's
online shelves now hold hundreds of
millions of items. Sellers not only hand
over a cut of each sale, but they also
pay additional fees to tap into
Walmart's logistics network, adding
another 8% on average for storage,
packing, and delivery. The results are
big. In 2024, Walmart's US e-commerce
sales topped $100 billion, still far
behind Amazon's 480 billion, but growing
at roughly 20% a year, twice Amazon's
pace. And in the tricky business of
grocery delivery, where speed and
refrigeration matters, Walmart is
already in first place. But staying
ahead of rivals hasn't been about scale
alone. Walmart's resurgence rests on a
deliberate set of strategies designed to
sharpen its edge in a rapidly changing
retail landscape.
[Music]
They focus on four key improvements.
E-commerce. Walmart doubled down on its
e-commerce infrastructure, bridging the
gap between online and the customer
experience in store. For example, they
improved their Walmart Plus membership
service by adding perks with more value,
driving an increase in customer
retention.
Private label. As inflation and economic
uncertainty dominates modern life,
Walmart leaned into its strength,
offering low prices by investing more in
its in-house brands.
diversifying supply chains. The company
reduced dependence on volatile global
supply chains and began sourcing more
within the US. A pretty genius decision
given the challenges that followed.
>> If you look at that, China first row 67%
that's tariffs charged to the USA
including currency manipulation and
trade barriers.
>> And lastly, but most crucially,
technology. Behind the scenes, the
company invested heavily in automation
and digitization, essentially
overhauling its entire back-end
operations. This allowed them to cut
costs and boost agility, making
incremental gains that can be passed on
to the end customer. The latest Walmart
warehouses are vast hangers filled with
conveyor belts, computer screens, and
robotic arms that silently pick and pack
products. The company uses AI to load
pallets so items are easy to unload.
Placing fragile goods on top, urgent
products at the front, and grouping
items by aisle. One of the tasks now
handled by robots, building your
shipping box, a machine loaded with the
exact dimensions of each product, wraps
it in cardboard with a tailor-made fit.
In the old days, a worker would eyeball
it, deciding whether your item needed a
big box or a small one. Now, an
algorithm sizes it perfectly for your
order, down to the inch. These
technological upgrades didn't just
transform how Walmart serves customers.
They also reshaped how it manages its
vast workforce.
At the end of 2024, their employee count
was 2,165,465
globally. That was almost 70,000 fewer
than 5 years ago. That payroll trend
stands in huge contrast to the
competition. In the past 5 years, the
big box retailers Costco, Target, and
Home Depot each added tens of thousands
of employees. Amazon nearly doubled its
worldwide workforce to 1.6 million in
the same period. This shift in staffing
reflects more than just domestic
changes. It's part of a broader strategy
that's playing out on a global stage.
Beyond the US, Walmart has also been
reinventing how it does business around
the world. Walmart's global playbook is
simple. Trying different models in
different markets. And don't hesitate to
pull out if they don't work. In Mexico,
it's the most valuable company on the
stock exchange. In China, a Sam's Club
membership, part of Walmart's carefully
built retail empire, has become a proud
symbol of middle class ambition. And in
India, it holds a majority stake in
Flipkart, a leading online marketplace.
Since selling its businesses in
Argentina, Britain, and Japan in 2021,
Walmart's international arm has been on
fire, and it's aiming to double sales
and operating profit between 2024 and
2028
For years, Walmart studied Amazon to
learn how to survive in a world where
retail was moving online. Now, in some
areas, the roles may be reversing.
Walmart's mastery of grocery delivery,
its integration of physical and digital
assets, and its diversified global
investments show a company that has
learned how to play and win on multiple
fronts.
From a threatened brickandmortar giant
to a technology enabled global
powerhouse, Walmart's transformation
offers a lesson in adaptation. Size
alone doesn't guarantee survival, but
size paired with reinvention can
redefine the game. Soon, the company
that once scrambled to catch up may find
others scrambling to keep pace.

text:
The $2 Billion Vodka Scam: How Grey Goose Lied Its Way to the Top 🥶🍸

Imagine lying your way into becoming the most desired vodka in the world…

Grey Goose wasn’t born in Russia. It wasn’t crafted in Poland. It didn’t even come from a country that made vodka.

It came from France—with zero vodka distilleries at the time.

In this video, we uncover true story of Sidney Frank, a 76-year-old entrepreneur who defied industry norms and used psychology, storytelling, and bold pricing to launch Grey Goose into the stratosphere. From manipulating luxury perceptions to outwitting legacy brands like Absolut and Smirnoff, Frank turned a made-up backstory into a multi-billion dollar brand.

You’ll learn:

Why pricing Grey Goose twice as high as other vodkas was the best move

How "French luxury" was used as a weapon—even when it made no sense

The behind-the-scenes marketing tactics that made bartenders and trendsetters obsessed

The psychology of premium branding, and how it can rewrite consumer reality

How Sidney Frank sold Grey Goose to Bacardi for $2 billion

If you’re into marketing, business psychology, or just love a good underdog hustle — this is a story you won’t want to miss.

subtitles.plaintext:
Imagine lying your way to the top. Not
just the top of the business world, but
the top of bar and restaurant shelves
everywhere. That's exactly what one
entrepreneur did to send his vodka brand
sky high, which is fitting for a brand
named Gray Goose. But the flight to the
top wasn't without ruffling a few
feathers in what would become a $2
billion exit. First, founder Sydney
Frank would need to contend with the ice
cold Polish and Russian brands that were
dominating the vodka scene at the time.
How? With a little trickery, one massive
gamble, and an unusual decision to
nearly double the price of other premium
vodkas at the time. More on these in a
bit, but first, let's talk sales.
Within just 5 years, Grey Goose wasn't
just the number one vodka in the US, but
the number one spirit, reaching over 1.5
million cases in sales by the time
Sydney Frank sold the brand. Sales in
2025, nearly three times that. But to
understand the domination and deception
of this iconic brand, we need to rewind
the clock to 1995.
Sydney Frank was 76 years old when he
walked into Olani's Time Square pub and
ordered a glass of vodka. It was a
chilly October afternoon and while the
Yankees were playing the Mariners, all
eyes were glued to CNBC.
Microsoft had just released the first
version of Internet Explorer and Alan
Greenspan was actively defending low
interest rates and increasingly
available capital. The invention of the
worldwide web allowed anyone for the
first time in history to access a
completely untapped international
market. Companies were about to
experience whopping growth under the
influence of venture capital and rapid
succession of IPOs. The dot bubble was
forming. But Sydney Frank wasn't into
technology. He saw something completely
different. He realized that a new era of
speculative exuberance was going to
create a demand for luxury drinking and
sophisticated cocktails. At the time,
Frank was an entrepreneur best known for
securing the American importing rights
to an obscure German digestive called
Jermeister. It turned out to be an
inspired move, turning Frank and Joerger
Meister into an international success.
But he wasn't ready to rest on his
laurels.
He observed a gap in the vodka market,
which lacked a high-end option. When
Frank eventually launched Grey Goose 18
months later, the top shelf vodka was
absolute, known for its iconic bottle
and steep price tag of $15 in 1996. And
that was considered an outrageous price
at the time. To succeed, Frank knew he'd
need to capture a slice of Absolute's
premium market. So, what did he do? A
more short-sighted marketer might have
undercut absolute and charged $10 a
bottle, but Frank understood the
psychological power of pricing. So, he
just decided to sidestep all that
competition and charge an eye watering
$30 a bottle. This worked because of two
psychological principles. One, people
don't judge a product's value in a
logical way. Instead, we decide how much
something is worth based on the
situation and how it makes us feel. and
two, the price quality effect. When it
comes to certain products, people tend
to think that if something costs more,
it must be better quality than something
that's cheaper. As powerful a
psychological signal as price is, Frank
knew you couldn't rely on people to buy
something just because it was expensive.
He knew that if he wanted to charge $30
a bottle for his vodka, he'd need a
product story that was interesting,
distinct from other vodka brands, and
that screamed luxury and sophistication.
two things that vodka wasn't known for
at the time. So, Frank gathered his team
at his company's headquarters and told
them to go to the country best known for
luxury and sophistication and bring back
a vodka. That's right. City Frank sent
them to France, a country that didn't
even have a single vodka distillery at
the time. Instead, they met with Cognac
distillers whose business had slowed
down. While vodka can be sold
immediately, even the cheapest cognac
must age at least 2 years in costly
French oak casks, requiring expensive
storage and enduring a 2% annual loss
from evaporation. Despite some willing
manufacturing partners, the location
itself was still a risk.
At the time, vodka was still deeply tied
to its Russian and Eastern European
roots in the minds of consumers. The
prevailing belief was that real vodka
came from places like Russia or Poland,
regions with centuries old vodka
traditions. France, by contrast, was
associated with wine and luxury cuisine.
It should have been marketing suicide.
Instead, it became marketing
immortality. Frank understood something
profound. When you can't win on
heritage, you win on perception. He
couldn't compete with centuries of
Russian tradition. So he positioned Grey
Goose as something better. Innovative
luxury for sophisticated Americans who'd
outgrown outdated European thinking. He
was betting everything on one
fundamental truth. People don't buy
products, they buy feelings about
themselves. As advertising became
fragmented and less effective, Frank
relied on bartender relationships for
product placement and distinctive
packaging to convey quality.
Goose was shipped in wood crates just
like the best French wines. He designed
an elegant and distinctive bottle with
smoked glass and a silhouette of flying
geese taken from a painting by Sesan
whose paintings were selling for
astronomical sums at elite art auctions.
In 1998, Frank pulled off a master
stroke. He entered Grey Goose in the
beverage testing institute competition
and claimed the title world's best
tasting vodka. Frank sees the moment,
placing bottles in the hands of
trendsetters at the hottest clubs in New
York, Chicago, and Los Angeles. He
targeted the influencers who shaped
consumer taste, arming them with premium
products and a compelling story.
Oversized 1.75 L bottles, commanded
attention behind bars, hooking early
adopters, and igniting the machine. The
market responded with $3 million in
firstear profits, all of which Frank
reinvested into advertising, including
Daily Wall Street Journal placements.
The campaign proclaimed Grey Goose as
the best tasting vodka in the world,
indoctrinating distributors and over
20,000 bartenders who would then
recommend it when customers asked for
their best vodka.
By 2004, over 18 million bottles of Grey
Goose were being sold a year, and all
the major players were taking note. But
Cardi came along and made an offer of
over $2 billion. Sydney Frank took it.
The brilliance of his success lied in
how easy he made it look. Unlike his
competitors, who played by the rules and
frameworks of categories they were in,
Frank aspired to be something different
from the start, a category of one. Grey
Goose wasn't necessarily better than
Smirnoff or Absolute. It wasn't more
authentically vodka. What it was was
more strategically marketed. Frank
didn't sell vodka. He sold identity,
aspiration, and the feeling of making
sophisticated choices. Frank didn't just
build a brand. He rewrote the rules of
reality itself, one perfectly positioned
bottle at a time. And that perhaps is
the most intoxicating part of the whole
story.

the biggest reasons for the start of the

mid-200s, budget airlines like Ryionaire
and EasyJet made it cheaper and easier

Club 1830, is that the thing at the very

more subtle. People like to think
they're being spontaneous and original
in their tastes, not doing the same

of millennials, but it's notable that

demise wasn't met with outrage or
nostalgia, but with indifference. Proof
that the new generation had already
moved on. What was once a cultural
phenomenon went out not with a bang, but

report rather than making headlines. The
story of Club 1830 is more than just a
tale of a holiday company. It's a vivid
snapshot of changing British youth
culture from the late 20th to early 21st
century. What began as Vladimir Wright's

text:
This is the true story of Anthony “Fats” Pino — the Boston burglar who planned one of the most legendary heists in American history.

In 1950, the Brink’s building in Boston was considered almost impossible to rob. It held one of the most secure private cash vaults in the United States. The guards were trained. The vault was reinforced. The building had locks, procedures, and decades of confidence behind it.

Anthony Pino did not attack it with violence.

He studied it.

For 18 months, Pino and his crew secretly entered the Brink’s building again and again. They removed locks, copied keys, replaced them before morning, mapped the routines, learned the timing, and turned the most secure cash facility in America into a building they understood better than its own guards.

Then, on January 17, 1950, eleven men arrived in matching coats, matching caps, and smiling Captain Marvel Halloween masks that cost $22 total.

In 20 minutes, they walked out with $2.7 million in cash.

Adjusted for today, that is tens of millions of dollars.

No shots fired.
No raised voices.
No broken windows.

Just keys, timing, patience, and a crew that stayed silent for six years while J. Edgar Hoover and the FBI spent millions trying to find them.

This became known as the Crime of the Century — a heist so clean that the FBI created pressure, launched massive interviews, questioned criminals across New England, and still could not break the case.

In the end, the Brink’s robbers were not caught because the FBI outsmarted them.

They were caught because one of their own men was betrayed.

This is the full story of Anthony Pino, the Brink’s robbery, the $22 Halloween masks, the copied keys, the FBI investigation, the betrayal, and the missing millions still searched for in Boston’s North End.

[music] of currency in four trips from
the vault to the truck, 270 lb per man
per trip. At 7:28, the last sack reaches
[music] the truck. The rope used to bind
the employees is gathered up and removed
to leave no DNA, no fibers, [music] no
thread. At 7:30, the Ford pulls away.
Total time inside the building, [music]
20 minutes. Total cash removed,
$2,775,395.12.
[music]
In 2026,
approximately 36 million.
At 11:38 p.m., J. Edgar Hoover is woken
at his home in Washington.
12 minutes later, he is on the line to
the FBI's Boston Field Office. Hoover in
his transmitted instruction to Special
Agent in Charge Edward Powers, "This is
not ordinary crime. This is the crime of
the century. I want every leading
hoodlum in New England questioned within
72 hours." Anthony Pino had moved. In 20
minutes, without firing a single shot or
raising a single voice, the largest
single sum of cash ever removed from a
private American facility in the history
of the United States. The morning after
the heist, Pino made the second rule
that would define the operation. No
money was to be spent by anyone for any
reason. The cash in the Brinks vault had
been newly issued. The serial numbers
ran in long consecutive blocks. A single
bill spent at a Boston tobacconist
could, in the hands of any competent FBI
accountant, be traced back to the Brinks
shipment [music] within 48 hours.
The 11 men received $5,000 each in
untraceable older bills drawn from
McGinnis's bootlegging cash on hand as
expense money.
The remaining two and a half million
dollars went into hiding. It went into
the walls of Adolf Matty's wife's house
in Roxbury, into the basement of
McGinnis's liquor store,
into a concealed cavity at the back of a
mausoleum in a cemetery in the North
End,
into a forgotten boiler room beneath an
abandoned brewery in East Boston. By the
spring of 1953, much [music] of the cash
had begun to mold. Some of it, by
O'Keefe's later admission, had been
chewed by mice. The FBI's response,
under Hoover's direct supervision,
became the largest non-federal criminal
investigation in the agency's history.
$29
million [music] in budget, 5,000
interviews, every leading hoodlum in the
six New England states questioned within
72 hours,
then again at six months, then again at
12. [music] had been organized by the
communist underground, Soviet funded, an
attack on the American banking system.
The crime of the century, he believed,
could not be the work of ordinary
American criminals.
On March 14th, 1950, eight weeks after
the robbery, Hoover launched the FBI's
Top 10 Most Wanted Fugitives List,
partly as a public relations response to
the Brinks case. For the next five
years, the list produced arrest after
arrest. None of those arrests was
Anthony Pino. 11 men, six years. Not a
single one of them spoke. Not at a bar,
not to a girlfriend, not on a tapped
telephone, not in a confessional booth.
The largest cash investigation in
American FBI history, conducted at a
cost greater than the heist itself,
produced zero leads on Anthony Pino. By
the late autumn of 1955, the case was
within 60 days of closure under the
Massachusetts six-year statute of
limitations.
In June 1954, Specs O'Keefe was arrested
in central Pennsylvania for a separate
unrelated armed burglary, sentenced to 4
years. From his cell, O'Keefe began
writing letters to McGinnis. He wanted
his $100,000 share of the Brink's money
now to pay for top-shelf legal counsel.
McGinnis refused. O'Keefe, in prison by
his analysis, was a security risk who
would, if returned to the streets with
money in his pocket, eventually talk. On
June 16th, 1954, a Brooklyn-based
contract killer named Elmer "Trigger"
Burke was hired by McGinnis for $25,000.
Burke flew to Boston. He waited outside
an apartment building on Newlands Street
where O'Keefe, on furlough, was visiting
his sister. At 10:09 in the evening,
O'Keefe walked out the front door. Burke
opened fire with a Thompson submachine
gun, 30 rounds. O'Keefe was hit in the
right arm and the chest. He survived 17
days in Boston City Hospital. O'Keefe,
by his own later account in his 1971
memoir, "That was when I knew my own
crew wanted me dead, not the FBI, not
[music] the cops, my own crew." Trigger
Burke was arrested in 1955 on an
unrelated New York homicide. He was
executed in the electric chair at Sing
Sing on January 9th, 1958.
Six years of perfect silence held by 11
men through 5,000 FBI interviews, $29
million of investigation, and the
personal supervision of J. Edgar Hoover
was broken, not by the Federal Bureau of
Investigation, but by an internal
disagreement over a single $100,000
share.
On January 6th, 1956, Specs O'Keefe was
paroled 28 months early from the
Pennsylvania State Correctional
Facility. The terms of the parole had
been negotiated 3 weeks earlier between
O'Keefe's attorney and the Boston Field
Office of the Federal Bureau of
Investigation. On January 11th, 1956,
11:00 in the morning, O'Keefe walked
into that field office at 1 Court Street
and asked to speak with Special Agent in
Charge Edward Powers.
O'Keefe, as recorded in Powers'
contemporaneous case file notes, "I want
them as much as you do." The confession
ran to 60 single-spaced typewritten
pages. O'Keefe named every man on the
team. He described the routes, the keys,
the locksmith, the masks, the truck, the
rope, the cash. He named every location
where Brink's money had been hidden
across the previous 6 years. At 4:00
p.m. the following afternoon, January
12th, 1956, a federal grand jury in
Boston returned sealed indictments
against the eight surviving members of
the Pino crew. Anthony Pino was arrested
in his apartment on Mount Vernon Street
that evening. He was finishing supper.
Vivian was washing the dishes. He did
not attempt to run.
He did not, by the booking officer's
report, speak a single word during
processing.
At midnight on January 17th, 1956,
exactly 6 years to the day after the
heist, the Massachusetts statute of
limitations on the Brink's robbery
expired. The indictments had been filed
5 days too early. The federal trial
began in October 1956.
Eight defendants. Specs O'Keefe,
cooperating witness, immunity granted,
testifying against every man he had ever
robbed beside.
The verdict came in on January 9th,
1957
Guilty. All eight. Pino and McGinnis
received life sentences. The remaining
six received between 20 and [music] 40
years. Pino, at sentencing, by the
contemporaneous reporting of the Boston
Globe, nothing. He nodded once at the
judge. He did not speak. 18 months of
preparation, 20 minutes of execution,
six years of perfect silence. All of it
undone by 30 bullets fired outside a
Newland Street apartment by a man
Anthony Pino's own partner had hired.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation had
spent $29 million and six years
searching for the men who had robbed the
Brink's Company. They were brought down
in the end for $25,000
paid to the wrong hitman.
Anthony "Fats" Pino died on October
27th, 1973 at the Federal Medical Center
in Springfield, Missouri of a heart
attack at the age of 66. He had been in
federal custody for 16 years. He is
buried at Mount Auburn Cemetery in
Cambridge, Massachusetts, 50 yards from
his mother, Anna. The headstone reads,
in full, Anthony S. Pino, 1907 to 1973.
It does not mention the crime of the
century. His wife, Vivian, outlived him
by eight years. She died in 1981 in the
same Mount Vernon Street apartment they
had rented together since 1940. She had
no children. She is buried beside him.
Joseph McGinnis died of cancer at the
federal prison in Springfield in 1966.
Specs O'Keefe was released from federal
cooperation custody in 1960. He moved to
Los Angeles. For the last decade of his
life, he worked as a private chauffeur
for the American film actor Cary Grant.
He died of natural causes in San
Francisco on March 9th, 1976
at the age of 67. His ashes were
scattered in the Pacific Ocean.
In 1978, William Friedkin, director of
The French Connection and The Exorcist,
released a feature film about the heist
titled The Brinks Job. Peter Falk played
Anthony Pino. The film was shot with the
permission of the Brinks Company inside
the original Prince Street building. The
Prince Street building was demolished in
1986. A small bronze plaque installed in
2000 marks the spot. Of the $2,775,000
originally taken, only $92,000 was ever
recovered. The remaining $2.5 million
adjusted for inflation, approximately
$33 million in 2026, has never been
found. Treasure hunters still search the
basements and cemeteries of Boston's
North [music] End. He did not fire a
single shot. He did not raise his voice.
He did not break a single window. He
just walked in through the door 20 times
until the largest cash facility in the
United States opened its own vault for
him.

title: The Man Who Stole EVERY Pentagon Secrets and Sold Them to the KGB
channelDescription: Just history, told clearly and honestly.

text:
This true crime documentary tells the true story of the first cyber-spy in history — a broke freelance programmer in West Germany who broke into 400 American military computers, sold their secrets to the KGB, and was caught not by the FBI or the NSA, but by an astronomer chasing a 75-cent accounting error. The video details how a single bug in a UNIX text editor and one forgotten password opened the Pentagon, NASA, and the U.S. Air Force to a man in a one-room flat — exposing the cyber security failures that every nation-state hacker still exploits today.

Hannover, West Germany. Autumn 1986. Markus Hess is twenty-five years old. A freelance programmer with a one-room flat and a phone bill he can barely pay. He is about to invent a category of crime that doesn't yet have a name.

He won't rob a bank. He won't rob a government building. With nothing but a 1,200-baud modem, he goes after the most secure network on Earth — the United States military. Four hundred American computers. The Jet Propulsion Lab. The Pentagon. Ramstein Air Base. Naval Coastal Systems in Florida. Over two years, thousands of military files pass through the modem in his flat — and every few weeks, a man flies to East Berlin with floppy disks in his pocket and comes back with KGB cash.

The Department of Defense never notices. The NSA never notices. The FBI never opens a case.
Six thousand miles away, an astronomer named Cliff Stoll notices something else: a seventy-five-cent error in a billing system. Nine seconds of unpaid computer time charged to a user who doesn't exist. His boss tells him to forget it. He won't.
This is the full story of how one stubborn scientist, alone in a Berkeley basement, hunted an invisible intruder across ten months and thousands of pages of printouts. How Hess erased himself from the map — appearing to every American system as a defense contractor in Virginia while sitting in a German flat. How Stoll built a fake military program called SDInet to keep the intruder online long enough to trace the line across an ocean. How a letter addressed to a secretary who didn't exist turned a billing dispute into a counterintelligence case — and the first treason charge for cyber espionage in history. And how, after all of it, the man who wrote the playbook every state hacker still uses today walked away with twenty months — suspended. Not a single day in prison.
The money was never the real story.
The playbook was.
