subtitles.plaintext:
Hanover, West Germany. Autumn, 1986.
Markus Hess is 25 years old, freelance
programmer, one-room flat, a phone bill
he can barely pay. He is about to invent
a category of crime [music] that does
not yet have a name. Not robbing a bank.
Not robbing a government. Not robbing a
single ordinary person. He is going
after the most secure network on Earth.
The United States military.
400 American computers. The Jet
Propulsion [music] Lab, the Pentagon,
Anniston Army Depot, Ramstein Air Base,
Naval Coastal Systems in Florida, Air
Force installations on three continents.
Over 2 years, thousands of military
files [music] will pass through a 1,200
baud modem in his flat. NASA blueprints,
defense contractor schematics, SDI
research, one keyboard, one bug in a
Unix text editor, one forgotten
password. That's all it takes.
Every few weeks, a man flies to East
Berlin with floppy disks in his pocket.
The KGB pays him in cash. $54,000
American. The Department of Defense
never notices. The NSA never notices.
The FBI never opens a case. 6,000 miles
away, an astronomer notices a 75-cent
accounting error, 9 seconds of unpaid
computer time. He won't let it go.
Markus Hess is 25 years old. He grew up
in West Germany. He abandoned a degree
in mathematics at the FernUniversität in
Hagen and started studying informatics,
computer science.
He works at a small [music] software
firm in downtown Hanover. The work is
intermittent. The paychecks are small.
But Hess has access to something most
programmers in 1986 don't have. He has
access to the European X.25 packet
network, Datex-P.
The Bundespost's [music] commercial data
line, available from any phone in
Germany to anyone willing to pay the
connection fee.
From Datex-P, Hess can hop to Timnet.
From Timnet, he can reach almost any
academic computer in the United States.
In Hanover, there is a circle of
programmers who meet at the same bars.
Some of them are members of the Chaos
Computer Club, Germany's new generation
of hackers who treat networks as
playgrounds. In early 1986, one of them,
a former casino croupier from Berlin
named Peter Carl,
walks into the Soviet trade mission in
East Berlin. He says he has a business
proposal. The trade mission is a KGB
front. Carl returns to West Germany. He
needs a hacker.
Hess is a hacker [music] without a
buyer. Carl is a buyer without a hacker.
In September 1986, Karl Koch, another
Hanover hacker, alias Hagbard, brings
them into the same room. Hess hacks,
Carl sells. The first delivery is
scheduled for the end of the month.
To understand what Hess walks into, you
have to understand the network he walks
through.
In 1986, the United [music] States
Department of Defense operates one of
the largest computer networks in the
world. It is called ARPANET and its
successor MILNET. ARPANET connects
universities, research labs, [music] and
military bases.
MILNET, created from ARPANET in 1983, is
for active military use. The two were
officially split, but the connections
between them remained. A researcher at
Berkeley could log into a system at the
Pentagon. An academic at MIT could open
a session at a US Air Force base. There
was a reason for this. The network was
designed in the 1970s by people who
trusted each other, engineers,
researchers, graduate students. The
protocols had no encryption. The dial-up
ports had weak authentication. Most
administrators [music] left default
passwords in place. Guest, system,
field. These were not security failures.
They were the standard configuration. By
1986, [music] the network had grown to
hundreds of thousands of users. The
trust assumption was no longer valid.
The Department of Defense had not
noticed. There is a second layer.
Lawrence Berkeley Lab, LBL, is one of
the busiest gateways in the academic
network. From LBL, a user with the right
credentials can reach Stanford, MIT, the
Optimist database at the Pentagon, the
Anniston Army Depot in Alabama, the
Naval Coastal Systems [music] Center in
Florida, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory
in Pasadena,
>> [music]
>> and through specific commands'
classified files related to the
Strategic Defense Initiative, SDI,
Reagan's Star Wars program.
LBL is not a military facility, but it
is one phone call from much of the
United States military. There is one
more thing. LBL runs a Unix utility
called GNU Emacs. Inside Emacs is a
small subprogram named movemail. It
moves email files between mailboxes.
Mundane. Emacs movemail is installed
with [music] what Unix administrators
call SUID root permissions. That means
any user, any user, can run it as if
they were the system's owner. It is a
known bug. Nobody has fixed it. In late
1985, a young programmer in Hanover
learns about the bug. He sees what he
can do with it.
In late 1985, Markus Hess starts
experimenting. He begins at the
University of Bremen. The campus has an
open dial-up line. Anyone with a modem
can reach it. From Bremen, he reaches
GAYTEX-P. From GAYTEX-P, he crosses to
TIMNET
>> [music]
>> through a satellite link or
transatlantic cable, depending on the
day.
From TIMNET, he hops to a defense
contractor's computer at MITRE in
McLean, Virginia. MITRE is where Hess
does his most important reconnaissance.
MITRE's out-dial system is supposed to
let [music] employees dial any number in
the United States. It is unsecure. From
there, Hess can dial almost any research
network in the country while his
connection appears to come from inside
Virginia. He is a German hacker in a
German flat who looks to every American
system he calls like a defense
contractor [music]
in McLean. He has erased himself from
the map.
In April 1986, he reaches Lawrence
Berkeley Lab. LBL has hundreds of active
user accounts.
Hess does not need most of them. He
needs one.
He picks an account belonging to Joe
Sventek. Sventek is the lab's UNIX guru.
>> [music]
>> He has been on long-term assignment in
England for nearly a year. His account
is dormant. Hess logs in as Sventek. The
account works.
Then comes the trick. Hess runs a small
program. The program calls EMACS
movemail. Movemail writes a file to a
system scheduling directory, the part of
UNIX that runs commands at fixed
intervals as root. The system reads the
new entry. At the next scheduled minute,
it executes Hess's command as root. He
now owns the system. He installs a
password sniffer. Every login at LBL is
now copied to a hidden file. Within a
week, he has dozens of new accounts.
Within a month, he has the credentials
of Berkeley physicist, Stanford grad
students, visiting NASA contractors.
Each credential opens a new system. He
becomes a kind of librarian of access.
He keeps a notebook, handwritten in
German, with a list of every machine he
has compromised, the credentials he has
used, the files he has copied. The
notebook will later be entered into
evidence at his trial. What he is doing,
technically, is called pivoting. [music]
He treats every compromised system as a
launchpad to the next one. LBL is his
gateway, not his target. His targets sit
one or two hops further, the Optimist
database at the Pentagon, SRI
International in Menlo Park, the US
Army's 24th Infantry Division at Fort
Stewart, Georgia, the Air Force Systems
Command in El Segundo, California, even
US Army installations in Okinawa. He
reaches them all. He works at night,
Hannover time. That is daytime in
California. [music]
The systems are busy. His sessions hide
inside legitimate [music] traffic. He is
disciplined. His sessions rarely last
longer than a few minutes. If anyone is
watching, they will lose him before they
find the line. Every few weeks, Karl
flies to East Berlin. He carries floppy
disks in his suit pocket. He meets a
Soviet handler in the Karlshorst
district, the Soviet Embassy quarter of
East Berlin. The handler pays in cash,
American dollars. Karl flies back to
Hannover. He hands Hess his share. Over
the next year, in installments, the
group will receive $54,000.
Across the Atlantic, in a half-empty
office at Lawrence Berkeley Lab, an
astronomer is starting his second day in
a new role. His astronomy grant has just
expired. He has been transferred from
research to systems administration. His
supervisor has handed him an accounting
glitch, a 75-cent mismatch in the LBL
billing system, 9 seconds of unpaid
computer time. The astronomer sits down
at the printout, picks up a pen, and
starts to read.
Cliff Stoll is 36 years old.
>> [music]
>> He has a doctorate in astronomy from the
University of Arizona. He has no formal
programming background. His grant for
astronomy has just been cut. LBL has
moved him to its computer systems group
as a research associate. His desk is in
a basement office. The supervisor's note
reads, "Find the 75-cent error. Probably
someone ran a job in the billing
algorithm rounded wrong."
Stoll opens the printout. The error is
not in the algorithm. The error is a
phantom user. Someone ran a job. The
system charged for 9 seconds of CPU
time. The user account does not exist.
The bill will never be paid. Another
similar discrepancy on the same week, a
small job disappeared. He goes to his
supervisor. His supervisor tells him to
forget about it. Stoll does not forget.
Over the next 10 months, from August
19th, '86 to June 19th, '87, he runs an
investigation almost entirely by
himself. He installs a logger on every
dial-up line at LBL. 50 teleprinters
borrowed from the desks of coworkers who
left for the weekend. Every keystroke,
every command, every file the intruder
reads. Stoll prints it on paper. He
cannot disconnect the intruder. If he
disconnects, the intruder will know he
is being watched. He has to let him in,
watch him, wait. Within 2 weeks, Stoll
knows everything except who. The
intruder logs in as Joe Sventek. The
intruder is not Joe Sventek. The
intruder runs the Emacs move mail trick.
He becomes root. He copies password
files. He installs sniffers. He moves
on. Stoll calls the FBI. The FBI tells
him 75 cents. They will not open a case.
Stoll calls the NSA. The NSA tells him
the matter is not under their
jurisdiction. Stoll calls the CIA. The
CIA tells him come back when there's
[music] real evidence. He keeps the
monitor running. Within months he has
thousands of pages of printouts. He
reads them every morning over coffee. He
builds a profile. [music]
The intruder works in the late afternoon
Pacific time. He uses German keyboard
layouts. He searches for the word SDI,
Strategic Defense Initiative, Reagan's
Star Wars program. This is no longer
about 75 cents. Stoll calls a friend at
AT&T. He asks for a phone trace. AT&T
agrees. The trace will require keeping
the line open for at least an hour. The
intruder rarely stays online that long.
Stoll has a problem. He has the entire
log of an active intrusion into the
United States military. He has no way to
keep the intruder on the line long
[music] enough to catch him. He needs
bait. In the shower one morning Stoll
tells his girlfriend Martha Matthews the
intruder is searching for SDI. There is
no SDI program at LBL. If we invent one,
he will come for it. They name the
operation after the location of the
conversation, Operation Shower Head.
Over a single weekend Stoll fills a
fictional account on the LBL system,
SDINET,
with bureaucratic memos, travel expense
forms, status reports. He invents a
fictional secretary named Barbara
Sherwin who signs off on the memos. The
account is enormous, tens of thousands
of words, all gibberish, all loaded onto
a slow public directory. [music] In May
1987, the intruder finds it. He starts
reading. He reads the first memo, the
second memo, the third memo. He starts
copying files. At 1,200 baud, 150
characters per second, the download
takes hours. AT&T traces the line
through Tymnet. Tymnet routes back
through MITRE.
MITRE forwards to a satellite link that
crosses the Atlantic. The line ends at
the German Bundespost, [music] the West
German Postal and Telephone Authority.
Bundespost technicians close the trace.
The connection terminates in a flat in
Hanover. Within days, German Federal
Police pull up to a residential
building. They knock on a door. A young
programmer answers. Behind him, a 1,200
baud modem is still plugged into the
wall.
The police walk into the apartment. Hess
does not resist. He is calm. He has been
expecting this for months. The officers
take his computer. They take his floppy
disks. They take the handwritten
notebook, credentials, IP addresses,
file paths, dates. The case is in the
hands of the Bundeskriminalamt,
Germany's Federal Police. They have a
problem. In 1987, West Germany has no
specific law against computer intrusion.
Hess has not stolen money in any
conventional sense. He has not
physically broken into any building. The
floppy disks contain text files that, in
many cases, were available to any
university student in the United States.
The Bundeskriminalamt prepares a report.
They consider charging Hess under
existing fraud and unauthorized access
statutes. The expected penalty is a
short suspended sentence. It will be
enough to close the case. Then, the
letter arrives in Berkeley.
In June 1987, Cliff Stoll receives an
envelope at the LBL mailroom. It is
addressed to Barbara Sherwin. Barbara
Sherwin does not exist. Stoll opens the
letter. The letter is from a man
identifying [music] himself as Laszlo
Balogh, a self-described businessman
based in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He
has heard, he writes, about the SDINET
research program at LBL. He is
interested in obtaining related
documentation. He is willing to pay. He
provides a PO box for further [music]
correspondence. The Pittsburgh FBI
office begins surveillance of Balogh.
>> [music]
>> Balogh is an intelligence asset of an
Eastern Bloc service, operating, like
all Warsaw Pact [music] services in this
period, in close coordination with the
KGB. Balogh did not invent SDINET from
nothing. He learned about SDINET from a
source. The source could not have been
anyone except a man who downloaded
Stoll's bureaucratic gibberish, sold it
to East Berlin, and watched the KGB pass
it along its supply chain. For the first
time, an American intelligence agency
has documentary evidence that a Soviet
Bloc service is buying
classified-sounding material from a
non-state hacker. This is no longer a
billing dispute. This is no longer an
academic curiosity. This is a
counterintelligence file. The FBI and
the BND, West Germany's foreign
intelligence service, quietly take the
case from the Bundeskriminalamt.
Hess is no longer a fraud suspect. Hess
is the first cyber spy in the history of
nation-state intelligence.
In the same period, German authorities
have already been watching Peter Carl
for many months. Carl has been making
regular trips to East Berlin. He stays
in the Karlshorst district. He meets his
Soviet handler. Carl, Hess, Brzezinski,
and a fourth conspirator have been on
the BND's radar. The BND held off
arresting them. They were waiting to see
who else would appear in the network.
The Balog letter is the bell. Within
weeks, the group is in custody. In a
court file in Hanover, a single sentence
summarizes the new charge. It reads,
"Landesverrat." In English, "high
treason."
February 15th, 1990. Higher Regional
Court of Celle. Three defendants. Markus
Hess, Peter Carl, Dirk Brzezinski. A
fourth, Hans Hübner, known online as
Pingo, has taken a German espionage
amnesty. He will not stand trial. A
fifth man is missing, Karl Koch, cocaine
addict, member of the Chaos Computer
Club, the hacker who brought Hess and
Carl into the same room in 1986.
In May 1989, after agreeing to cooperate
with prosecutors, he disappears from a
routine errand. His remains are found in
a forest [music] near Celle. Just bones.
Scorched earth. Shoes missing. No
suicide note. Officially, suicide. He
was 23.
The trial proceeds without him. The
defense argues that most of what Hess
sold to the KGB was unclassified or
deliberate fiction. SDINet, the honeypot
Stoll built in his Berkeley basement.
>> [music]
>> The court does not accept this defense,
but it accepts a related point. There is
no precedent in West German law for
charging a freelance programmer with
treason for a foreign service.
No clearance. No handler. No ideology.
Just money. The verdicts. Markus Hess,
20 months suspended. Peter Carl, two
years suspended. Dirk Brzezinski, 14
months suspended. No defendant serves a
single day in prison. The $54,000
is mostly already spent. Across the
Atlantic, Cliff Stoll publishes a book,
The Cuckoo's Egg. National bestseller.
Required reading at the NSA. A founding
document of every cybersecurity unit
built in the next decade. In Geneva, an
entry is added to the Guinness Book of
World [music] Records. First documented
case of cyberespionage.
The entry names Markus Hess. Hess
returns to programming work in Germany.
No interviews. No memoir. He has never
spent a day in prison. Every
state-sponsored cyber program operating
today inherits its basic architecture
from one freelance programmer in
Hanover. Relaying through civilian
systems to mask origin. Hess. Installing
persistent password sniffers. [music]
Hess. Pivoting through one compromised
account into hundreds of targets. Hess.
The Emacs bug he used in 1986 has its
own module in Metasploit today. Anyone,
anywhere can run it as a teaching
exercise. The intelligence service he
sold to no longer exists. The Soviet
Union collapsed. The KGB was dissolved.
The contracts he stole have been
declassified. But the playbook he wrote
is open. It is in the field. It is being
run this morning by every nation-state
hacker on Earth. He invented an entire
category of crime. [music]
And then, after 20 months suspended, he
went home. The world has been louder
ever since.

text:
Charles Ponzi scheme explained — the true story of how an Italian immigrant ran the most famous financial fraud in history. In 1920, a five-foot-two immigrant sat in a small Boston office with thirty dollars' worth of postal coupons in a drawer.

Eight months later, he had collected fifteen million dollars.

He never traded a single stock. He never bought more than that first handful of coupons. He simply promised people a fifty percent return in ninety days — at a time when the best bank in America paid four percent in a year — and for eight extraordinary months, he paid every single person exactly what he promised.

His name was Charles Ponzi. Before 1920, the word meant nothing. Today it is in every dictionary in the English language.

What makes his story strange is that the loophole he discovered was real. Buried inside the international postal system was a genuine flaw — a way that a coupon bought cheaply in one country could, in theory, be redeemed for far more in another. On paper, the math worked. The opportunity was legal. It was simply impossible to do at the scale he claimed.

This is the full story of how an immigrant with two dollars and fifty cents to his name built the most famous financial scheme in history — how it grew faster than anyone could control, why a single newspaper investigation brought it down, and how the United States Congress ultimately passed a new federal law for the specific purpose of making what he did illegal.

A century later, his name is still attached to the scheme. This is how it actually happened.

subtitles.plaintext:
January, 1920, Boston. A 5 ft 2 man sits
at a wooden desk on the second floor of
27 School Street. In a drawer beside
him, about $30 worth of postal reply
coupons, a few hundred pieces of paper.
That is the entire inventory of his new
company. A grocer named Ettore Giaberti
walks in and hands him $10 in cash. This
is the first investment. The man writes
Giaberti a promissory note, 50% return
in 90 days. The best American savings
account in 1920 pays 4% a year. 90 days
later, Giaberti gets paid on schedule,
in cash. Full 50% return. He tells his
neighbors, his neighbors invest, they
get paid. They tell their neighbors. By
February, intake is $5,000.
By March, 30,000. By April, 141,000.
By June, 2 and 1/2 million dollars. By
July, he is collecting $250,000
a day, 1 million a week.
40,000 investors across three states. He
is not investing in stocks. He is not
trading commodities. He has not bought a
single additional postal coupon. He has
found a real loophole in the United
States postal system, but he has never
actually used it. In 8 months, he will
turn $30 of inventory into $15 million.
And when it is over, the United States
Congress will pass a new federal law,
specifically to make what he just did
illegal.
His name is Charles Ponzi. In 1920,
nobody in Boston has ever heard that
word.
A hundred years later, every English
dictionary will contain it. He was born
Carlo Pietro Giovanni Guglielmo Tebaldo
Ponzi, Lugo, Emilia-Romagna, March 3rd,
1882
The family was once well-off. His mother
kept the honorific Donna. There was a
little money, a little status, a little
expectation that Carlo would become
something.
He lasted 4 years at La Sapienza in
Rome.
Drank and gambled with richer students,
ran out of money, washed out. So, he got
on a ship, November 1903, the SS
Vancouver, from Naples to Boston.
He boarded with $200.
He landed with $2.50.
The rest he lost to a card shark
crossing the Atlantic. His own line,
given to a reporter 30 years later. I
landed in this country with $2.50
in cash and $1 million in hopes. For the
next 4 years, he works every bad job in
Boston. Dishwasher, waiter, store clerk.
Learns English on the job. Then, 1907,
he goes to Montreal, hired as an
assistant teller at Banco Zarossi, a
bank serving Italian immigrants.
Advertising rate, 6% on deposits, double
what any real bank paid. Ponzi notices
something. The bank isn't earning 6%
anywhere. It's paying old depositors
with new depositors' money. He is 25
years old and he is watching the machine
run from the inside. The bank collapses.
The owner runs to Mexico. The money is
gone. Ponzi goes to a cousin of one of
the bank's bonding directors and forges
a check, $423.58.
On arrest, he simply says, "I'm guilty."
3 years in Saint Vincent de Paul
Penitentiary. Inmate number 6660.
Serves 20 months. Walks out in 1910.
Gets picked up again immediately. This
time for smuggling five Italian
nationals across the Canadian border. 2
more years. Atlanta Federal
Penitentiary. Paroled July 1912, he
comes back to Boston, does odd jobs for
six more years. Marries Rose Geneco, a
grocer's daughter from the North End in
1918. He is 36 years old, twice
convicted, penniless, married to a woman
who has no idea what he did in Canada.
And he has been thinking for 13 years
about the machine he saw in Montreal.
In 1906, in Rome, representatives of 63
countries met for the Universal Postal
Union Congress. They created something
called the International Reply Coupon,
IRC. The problem it solved was small. If
you live in Boston and you want your
cousin in Naples to write you back, you
can't send him American stamps. American
stamps don't work in Italy. So, the
Postal Union invented a single global
coupon, denominated in gold centimes.
Buy one in any member country, the
recipient redeems it for local stamps in
their country. Fixed value, universal
exchange. For 13 years, this was a
boring clerical instrument. Nobody paid
attention.
Then came the First World War. The war
ended in November 1918. Europe was
destroyed and every European currency
collapsed against the dollar. The
Italian lira, before the war, traded at
roughly five to the dollar. After the
war, 15, 20, 30. But, the IRC, the
International Reply Coupon, was still
priced in gold centimes, which meant its
face value stayed the same across the
world.
This is where the gap opened. In 1919,
in Rome, you could buy an IRC for a
handful of lira, about 1.5 cents in
American money. You could walk into any
post office in the United States and
redeem that exact same coupon for 5
cents. Buy for 1.5, redeem for five.
every coupon margin per transaction,
233%.
This is arithmetic. The Universal Postal
Union is a real organization. The
coupons were real. The currency collapse
was real. The arbitrage existed. So, why
did nobody run it as an actual business?
Because of a dozen small frictions
nobody thinks about until they try to
scale. To redeem one coupon takes 30
seconds at a counter. To redeem a
thousand takes a week and requires a
post office willing to do it. Most
aren't. Postmasters in Boston started
refusing large volumes after 10 or 20
redemptions. Each coupon physically has
to be shipped across the Atlantic. At
industrial scale, the friction eats the
margin. Wikipedia's entry on
international reply coupons puts it in
one sentence. The overhead on buying and
selling large numbers of the very low
value IRCs precluded any profitability.
The gap was real. The execution was
impossible. This is the part Ponzi
understood before anybody else. He
didn't need to execute. He just needed
people to believe he was executing.
Ponzi rents the office at 27 School
Street, one desk, one chair, borrowed
furniture. He registers a company name,
the Securities Exchange Company, 15
years before the United States
government will create an agency with a
nearly identical name, the Securities
and Exchange Commission, 1934, to
regulate exactly what he is about to do.
In December 1919, no such agency exists.
Massachusetts has a blue sky law. It is
almost never enforced. His written
promise, printed on simple cards, is one
sentence. 50% return in 45 days, backed
by international arbitrage and postal
reply coupons. The average American
savings account in 1920 pays 4% a year.
He is offering more in 6 weeks than a
bank will pay in a decade, but a promise
on paper is worth nothing. He needs a
salesman.
He hires A Torre Ghiberti, a quiet
grocer from a Boston suburb, on a 10%
commission.
Ghiberti's first move is careful. He
invests $10 of his own money to test
that Ponzi will actually pay it back.
Then, he walks next door and talks to
his neighbors. This is the engine. Ponzi
does not sell to the public. His agents
sell to their neighbors. The neighbors
sell to their cousins. The cousins sell
to their co-workers at the shipyard. The
first 18 investors in January 1920 are
not strangers to each other. They are
one grocer's social circle. 90 days
later, Ghiberti gets paid on schedule,
in cash, 50% profit. He does not
withdraw it. He reinvests. This becomes
the pattern that defines the next 6
months. Investors do not take the money
back. They leave it in. They bring
friends. By April, Ponzi has 30
sub-agents on commission. By June, 150.
They work across Massachusetts, New
Hampshire, and Maine, knocking on doors,
signing up dock workers, shopkeepers,
school teachers. At the peak, a single
agent in Brockton is registering 200 new
depositors every week. The mathematics
of the scheme are brutal. For every
dollar of new money Ponzi collects, he
books a 50% liability. For every dollar
of promised return, he needs $3 of newer
cash behind it. The required inflow
doubles every 6 weeks. The actual inflow
is doubling every three. As long as new
money arrives faster than old money has
to be paid out, the machine runs
forever. By June 1920, it is collected
from 7 and 1/2 thousand investors. Not
one of them has asked for their
principal back.
By July 1920, Charles Ponzi walks into
his office every morning carrying a
gold-handled Malacca cane, a diamond
stickpin, and the largest single deposit
account at Hanover Trust Bank. He has
moved from the borrowed desk in the
Niles Building to an office suite with a
staff of 20. He has rented a 12-room
mansion in Lexington, servants,
chauffeur, a custom limousine. He is 38
years old, 5'2, and for a period of
about 4 weeks this summer, Charles Ponzi
has more liquid cash on hand than the
treasurer of the state of Massachusetts.
Then he does the thing that will begin
to end him. There is a Boston bank
called Hanover Trust. A few years
earlier, Hanover had rejected Ponzi's
application for a $2,000 personal loan.
He has not forgotten. Over 2 months, he
deposits roughly 3 million dollars at
Hanover Trust. He becomes its single
largest depositor. He uses the position
to buy approximately 1,500 shares of
bank stock spread across himself and
friends. He is given a seat on the
board. He has bought the bank that once
refused him. This is the moment in every
scheme when the operator has enough
money to quit. Ponzi will later be asked
why he didn't. His answer, given to a
reporter 30 years later, "I went looking
for trouble and I found it." On July
2nd, 1920, something strange happens.
The United States Postal Service
announces a new rule. International
reply coupons may not be redeemed in
lots greater than 10 per transaction,
effective immediately. A postal official
calls the timing coincidental. It is not
coincidental. Somewhere inside the
federal bureaucracy, a clerk has noticed
that a man in Boston is publicly
claiming to be trading millions of
dollars in coupons the United States
government has never sold in those
volumes. But, here is the strange thing.
The rule change does not hurt Ponzi
because Ponzi is not redeeming coupons.
He has never been redeeming coupons. His
entire inventory on July 2nd, 1920, is
still about $30. The USPS has pointed a
weapon at a machine that does not exist.
What the rule change does instead is
attract journalists. On July 4th, the
Boston Post prints a small notice about
a furniture dealer named Joseph Daniels
suing Ponzi for money owed on office
desks. On July 24th, the same newspaper
runs a favorable profile, "Doubles the
money within 3 months." Lines on School
Street begin to form at 5:00 in the
morning. Ponzi is so confident that he
makes the decision that will destroy
him. On July 23rd, he hires a
professional publicist. The man's name
is William McMasters. Ponzi pays him
$5,000 to manage the press. McMasters
asks for access to the books. Ponzi
gives it to him.
William McMasters is not a criminal. He
is a respected Boston publicist, a
former newspaper man. He takes the
$5,000. He opens the ledgers. He spends
10 days reading. On the 10th day, he
writes, in a memo that will later be
reprinted word for word, "The man is a
financial idiot. He does not seem to
know how to add. Liabilities are 9 to 10
million. Assets, roughly three." On July
26th, 2 days after the favorable profile
ran, the Boston Post prints a second
piece, written by Clarence Barron, owner
of Dow Jones & Company, publisher of The
Wall Street Journal. Barron does the
arithmetic in public. To cover Ponzi's
outstanding investments, the required
number of international reply coupons in
circulation would need to be roughly 160
million. The total number of IRCs in
circulation worldwide across every
country in the world is approximately
27,000.
Barron's conclusion, in print, the
volume necessary is impossible. July
27th, 1920, a Tuesday morning.
Depositors begin arriving at 27 School
Street asking for their money back. By
noon, the line stretches three blocks.
By 3:00, police are directing traffic on
School Street. Ponzi does something that
almost saves him. He walks into the
crowd personally. He brings coffee. He
brings donuts. He pays out every request
in cash, every single one. Over three
days, July 27th, 28th, 29th, he pays out
roughly $2 million.
The crowd thins. The panic eases. Some
depositors leave their money back in. It
almost works.
Then, William McMasters, the publicist
Ponzi had paid $5,000, walks across the
street to the Boston Post and sells his
memo to the editor, Richard Grozier, for
another $5,000.
August 2nd, 1920. The headline on the
front page of the Boston Post reads,
"Declares Ponzi is now hopelessly
insolvent." Grozier does one more thing.
He sends a telegram to the warden of the
Atlanta Federal Penitentiary asking
whether they have a prisoner file for a
man named Charles Ponzi.
The warden confirms by telegram. The
Post sends a reporter to Montreal, pulls
the 1908 forgery file, including the mug
shot.
On August 11th, 1920, the Boston Post
prints the mug shot on its front page.
The telegram confirming Ponzi's prison
record is still preserved today in the
National Archives, an inmate case file
number 6660.
The next morning, on August 12th,
federal agents arrest Charles Ponzi in
his office at 27 School Street. 86
counts of mail fraud. Hanover Trust, the
bank he had bought in revenge, is closed
the same day by the Massachusetts bank
commissioner, Joseph Allen. For 8
months, no federal agency in the United
States had been able to touch him. Not
the Treasury, not the Postal Service,
not a single prosecutor or regulator.
And the man who finally broke the
machine was not an investigator. It was
not a journalist. It not the law. It was
a publicist hired, briefed, and paid by
Charles Ponzi himself.
The auditor's final report is one page
long. Liabilities, $7 million.
Assets, $3 million. Total international
reply coupons found in Ponzi's
possession, roughly $30 worth. A few
hundred in a drawer. Every dollar paid
out in 8 months had come from a newer
investor's pocket. Not one trade. He had
found the gap. He had marketed it. He
had acquired a bank. He had built trust.
He had never executed the arbitrage, not
once. 5 years federal, 7 to 9 years
state.
Investors recover 30 cents on the
dollar. Deported to Italy in 1934.
Drifts to Rio de Janeiro. January 18th,
1949
A charity ward of the Federal University
Hospital in Rio. Charles Ponzi dies at
66. In his pocket, $75.
Enough, exactly, to pay for his own
burial. 15 years earlier, on the ship
out of Boston, a reporter had asked him
if he regretted it. "It was easily worth
15 million bucks to watch me put the
thing over. The loophole was real.
Nobody ever used it." 9 years after his
arrest, Congress created the Securities
and Exchange Commission. Every
investment product sold in America today
is regulated under the framework built
in response to men like him. The
arbitrage was real. He never used it.
And his name is now an English word.

title: The Homeless Who Captured a German Town Using a Trick That Cost Eighteen Marks
channelDescription: Just history, told clearly and honestly.

text:
Wilhelm Voigt Captain of Köpenick story — the true story of how a 56-year-old ex-convict cobbler in Imperial Germany used pure social engineering and a $150 used uniform to capture a Prussian town, arrest its mayor, empty its treasury, and make the Kaiser laugh. On October 16, 1906, a grey-haired man in a captain's uniform stepped off a train at Köpenick station outside Berlin. He stopped four guardsmen returning to barracks and spoke one sentence.

"Follow me. In the name of the Kaiser."

The soldiers turned around. They followed him.

The man was not a captain. He had never served in any army. He was a homeless shoemaker named Wilhelm Voigt. He was fifty-six years old. He had spent twenty-seven of those years in prison.

Over the next six hours, this one ex-convict would collect six more soldiers from a different battalion, march them three kilometres into the centre of Köpenick, arrest the mayor, arrest the chief of police, and empty the city treasury. He would do all of this without firing a single shot. He had no weapon. No accomplices. No plan to escape.

The uniform he was wearing cost eighteen marks — roughly one hundred and fifty dollars in today's money. Bought used. From four different secondhand shops.

This is the full story of how Imperial Germany — the most rigid, rank-obsessed military culture in Europe — was conquered for one afternoon by a man who simply put on the right coat. How Wilhelm Voigt spent twenty-seven years in Prussian prisons for petty theft, was released into a country whose passport laws made it illegal for him to legally exist, and discovered that the same uniform-worship culture that crushed him also contained the one trick that could break it. How the Kaiser of Germany read the police report — and laughed. How Voigt was eventually caught, pardoned by the Kaiser within two years, became a celebrity across Europe, toured theatres playing himself, and died wealthy in Luxembourg in 1922.

Bertolt Brecht wrote a play about him. Five films have been made. The story has been translated into twenty-four languages.

In a country where uniformed authority was the highest law of the land, one ex-convict in a $150 coat proved that the law was nothing more than what people agreed to believe.

subtitles.plaintext:
Berlin suburbs, October 16th, 1906.
2:00 in the afternoon. A gray-haired man
in a captain's uniform steps off the
train at Köpenick Station. He stops four
guardsmen [music] returning to barracks.
He says one sentence,
>> Follow me in the name of the Kaiser.
>> The soldiers turn around. They follow
him. The man is not a captain. He has
never served in any army. He is a
homeless shoemaker named Wilhelm Voigt.
He is 56 years old. He has spent 27 of
those years in prison. In Imperial
Prussia, a man without a passport is not
legally permitted to exist. Voigt does
not have a passport. In the next 6
hours, this man will collect six more
soldiers from a different battalion. He
will march them 3 km into the center of
Köpenick. He will arrest the mayor.
He will arrest the chief of police. He
will empty the city treasury, and he
will vanish. Within 7 days, his story
will be translated into 24 languages.
The Kaiser of Germany will read the
police report and laugh. The uniform
Voigt is wearing cost 18 marks, bought
used from four different shops. He has
no weapon, no [music] accomplices, no
plan to escape.
8 months earlier, Anklam, East Prussia,
February 1906. Wilhelm Voigt walks out
of a prison gate, 30 pfennigs and a
release certificate. The certificate
orders him to register with police
within 48 hours. To register, he needs
an address. To have an address, he needs
work. To get work, he needs a Reisepass,
an internal passport. To get a
Reisepass, he needs to be registered.
Voigt has lived inside this circle for
40 years. He buys a ticket to Berlin
with 25 of his 30 pfennigs. In
Friedrichshain, he pays for floor space
in a Troedler shop with his coat.
Morning, a shoe workshop. The owner asks
for his Reisepass. Voigt does not have
one. The owner shows him the door.
April, Berlin police arrest him for
vagrancy, no charge. They put him on a
train back to Anklam.
May, Hamburg, deported within 7 days.
June, Dresden, deported.
By August, he has been physically
expelled from every German city in which
a shoemaker could find work. Nine marks
left. He sits down on a park bench near
Konigsplatz. A Berlin police constable
walks past a group of construction
workers. The workers ignore him. Then, a
real army captain walks past the same
group. The workers stop. They straighten
their backs. They remove their caps.
Voigt watches this exchange for 2 hours.
He realizes for the first time in his
life that he has been measuring his
weakness against the wrong system. The
bug is not in the law. The bug is in the
people.
Imperial Germany in 1906 has a problem
nobody in Berlin sees as a problem. The
problem has a name, Uniformsglaub,
belief in the uniform. In Prussia, an
officer is not a man. He is the visible
body of the state. The gray wool tunic
of a guards captain carries more legal
weight than a written court order. When
a soldier on patrol encounters [music]
an officer, regulations require him to
stop, salute, and await [music] orders.
Regulations do not require him to ask
for identification. There is no
procedure for verifying an officer's
identity at a chance encounter. There is
no need for one because in 1906, the
question, is this man a real officer,
does not exist as a question. Officers
are produced by Kadettenschulen,
military academies that take noble
children at 12 and process them for 13
years. The result is a closed cast of
approximately 4,000 men in the entire
German army. They know each other by
face, family, regiment, and accent. For
an outsider to impersonate one is
considered by the general staff
technically impossible. The flaw in this
assumption is the part Voigt
understands. Real officers are not the
people standing next to fake ones. The
people standing next to officers are
enlisted soldiers, and enlisted soldiers
do not know the 4,000 faces. They know
the 4,000 uniforms. A soldier may
legally refuse an order if it is
manifestly criminal. The procedure has
been used three times entire history of
the German army by 1906. It requires an
enlisted man to publicly accuse an
officer of being a criminal. In Prussia
in 1906, this is socially
indistinguishable from suicide. Voigt
has spent 27 years inside this system at
its lowest possible position. He
understands it better than any general
on the general staff. He has watched it
from underneath for four decades. He
sees on the park bench in September 1906
that the entire Imperial army can be
operated by anyone wearing the correct
coat. He needs nine more marks. He
stands up and walks to the first of four
used clothing shops.
A complete Prussian guard's captain's
uniform has seven components:
tunic, trousers with red lampas,
regiment collar patch, captain's
shoulder boards with three stars, peaked
cap with Imperial cockade, belt, saber.
Voigt skips the saber. Carrying one
without skill would betray him in the
first hour. German law forbids the sale
of complete military uniforms to anyone
without service papers. A complete
uniform in one transaction requires the
seller to register the buyer's
identification. So, Voigt fragments the
purchase. First, Trodler,
Friedrichshain, a coat for the theater,
three marks, a guard's tunic.
Second, wedding, trousers for the
theater, four marks, red lampas.
Third, Tempelhof, a captain's cap for an
amateur show, two marks. Fourth,
Charlottenburg, shoulder boards and a
belt, nine marks, the regiment collar
patch included. Total, 18 marks.
The composition is not perfect. The
tunic is from the first foot guards
regiment. The trousers are from a
different regiment. A real officer would
notice the mismatch within 15 seconds.
Voigt is not planning to be seen by real
officers. For six weeks between August
and early October, he rents the cheapest
room in Berlin and stands on railway
platforms.
>> [music]
>> He watches captains arriving at the
general staff building on Konigsplatz.
He memorizes how they hold their gloves,
how they remove their caps in doorways,
the exact pitch of voice they use giving
orders to enlisted men, a tone Prussian
officers call kalt, cold, without
emotion, expecting no response.
He practices the voice alone in the
rented room at night. Then, he chooses
his target, Köpenick, population 16,000,
a suburb southeast of Berlin, 28 minutes
by suburban rail. Köpenick has a town
hall built in 1905.
>> [music]
>> Inside, the city treasury with the
previous month's tax receipts,
approximately 4,000 marks in cash. It
has a mayor named Georg Langerhans, a
civil servant who has never met an
active-duty captain in his career,
except at ceremonial functions where he
stood 20 m back. It has a small police
station with eight constables. None
carry firearms when off the main square.
The nearest military garrison is 3 km
outside the town. Köpenick is a place
where everyone has been trained [music]
to obey a uniform and where no one has
ever seen an officer up close. On
October 15th, Voigt counts his money, 12
marks, enough for 10 train tickets to
Kopenick at 55 pfennigs each plus three
marks for himself. He folds the uniform
into a paper parcel. He goes to bed
early. He has never planned anything
successful in his life. Tomorrow, he
will become the most famous criminal in
Europe.
The bathroom at Putlitzstrasse Station.
Voigt enters [music] the public bathroom
in civilian clothes carrying a paper
parcel. He locks the cubicle. He changes
in 7 minutes. He folds his civilian
clothes into the parcel and places it in
a station locker. He walks out as
Hauptmann Voigt of the First Foot
Guards. He does not check a mirror. He
has decided that hesitation is the only
mistake he cannot afford.
9:50, the first patrol.
He walks east along Tegeler Strasse.
Four soldiers returning to Platzensee
Barracks after morning exercises.
He stops walking. He waits for them to
come to him. When they are 6 m away, he
says in the cold register he has
practiced for 6 weeks,
>> Halt!
>> The four soldiers stop. He says,
>> Follow me.
In the name of the Kaiser, imperial
business.
>> None asks for orders in writing. None
asks his name. The senior corporal
salutes. They follow him.
10:20, reinforcement. [music]
Half a kilometer on, he stops a second
patrol. Six men returning to Naumburg
Barracks from a different exercise. Same
order. They join him. He now has 10 men,
three from one battalion, seven from
another. None of them know each other.
This is the part of the operation that
has no precedent. Voigt is using the
soldiers as social proof for each other.
The unfamiliar uniforms on the
unfamiliar men become evidence in the
mind of each individual soldier that the
operation is real.
11:15,
the train.
He marches the 10 men to Putlitzstrasse
station, buys 10 tickets to Köpenick out
of his own pocket, five marks 50, six
marks 50 [music] left. The soldiers sit
silently in the carriage.
Voigt sits at the far end facing them
expressionless. A first-class passenger
across the aisle, a Berlin lawyer named
Friedrich Bernhard, will later testify
that the captain seemed exceptionally
tired and exceptionally calm.
Exhaustion is the part Voigt is not
faking.
12:00, the town hall.
The train arrives. Voigt marches the 10
soldiers from the station through the
town square to the front steps of the
Köpenick Rathaus. He gives his first
detailed order. Two men guard the main
entrance. Two guard the rear. Two guard
the staircase. Two enter with him. Two
go directly to the treasury room on the
ground floor.
He has memorized the building's layout
from a public guidebook printed for the
1905 grand opening. He climbs the
stairs. He walks down the corridor
without asking directions because the
guidebook printed the room numbers. He
opens the door to office [music] 14.
Mayor Georg Langerhans is at his desk
reviewing [music] a budget document.
Voigt says,
>> I am here on Imperial orders. You are
under arrest.
>> Langerhans stands up. He asks the
question Voigt [music] has been waiting
40 years to answer correctly.
>> Where are your orders?
>> Voigt walks to the window.
>> [music]
>> He gestures at the soldiers on the steps
below.
>> My orders are up there.
>> Langerhans does not ask again. He puts
on his coat. He follows Voigt down the
stairs.
12:30, the treasury.
Voigt orders the city treasurer, a man
named Rosenkrantz, to open the safe and
count the cash in front of him. Two
soldiers stand behind Rosenkrantz.
Inside the safe, 4,000 marks and 37
pfennigs. Voigt confiscates the money.
He places it inside the tunic against
his chest. Then he does the thing that
no operator of military fraud in
recorded history has ever done. He asks
for a sheet of municipal stamped paper.
He sits at the treasurer's desk. He
writes a formal receipt for the funds.
He dates it. He signs it. Hauptmann von
Schmalzahn, first foot guards. He hands
the receipt to Rosenkrantz. He instructs
him to file it with the next month's
audit. This single piece of paper will,
20 months later, save Wilhelm Voigt from
the gallows because it will prove, in
the prosecutor's own files, that Voigt
never considered himself a thief.
13:30, the dispatch.
He orders Mayor Langerhans, Treasurer
Rosenkrantz, and Chief of Police
Friedrich Weigand transported to the new
guardhouse on Unter den Linden, where,
he tells them, they will be questioned
by senior officers of the general staff.
He hires three open carriages from his
own remaining money. He places the three
prisoners in the carriages with two
soldiers each as escort. The carriages
depart north toward Berlin. The
remaining four soldiers will hold the
town hall closed for 30 minutes. No one
in or out.
14:00,
the vanish.
Voigt walks alone to Köpenick station.
He buys a single ticket to Berlin,
second class, 15 pfennigs. On the train,
in the bathroom cubicle, he removes the
uniform piece by piece. He folds it into
the paper bag he has carried inside the
tunic since morning. When he steps off
at Potsdamer Straße at 3:30, he is
wearing his old civilian coat. He
carries a paper bag of clothing and
4,000 marks against his chest. He does
not run. He does not hide. He walks to a
coffee house on Friedrichstraße, orders
bread and coffee, reads the early
evening edition of the Berliner
Tageblatt. The paper does not yet
contain news from Köpenick.
By the time it does, at 6:00 that
evening, when the three carriages arrive
at the new guardhouse and a confused
general staff officer asks who exactly
is supposed to be conducting an
interrogation, Wilhelm Voigt has
dissolved into a city of 2 million
people.
The story breaks at 10:15 [music] the
next morning. Berliner Tageblatt, front
page. Dreist Hauptmann verhaftet.
Bürgermeister von Köpenick.
By noon, every newspaper in Berlin. By
the next morning, every newspaper in
Europe. The Vossische Zeitung publishes
the receipt. The fraudulent signature of
Hauptmann von Malzahn is reproduced in
facsimile within 48 hours in Paris,
London, Vienna, Rome, New York,
Stockholm,
>> [music]
>> Moscow, and Tokyo.
The story is funny. That is the part the
Prussian General Staff cannot manage. A
Le Petit Journal cartoonist draws a
column of Prussian soldiers saluting an
empty uniform. Punch prints Kaiser
Wilhelm II
reviewing a parade of mannequins. The
Russian foreign minister sends a
telegram to Berlin congratulating the
Imperial Court on the unprecedented
loyalty of Prussian enlisted men.
The Berlin police initiate the largest
manhunt in the city's history. 400
constables, 200 plainclothes [music]
detectives, every flop house and lodging
house searched, a 2,000 mark reward, the
largest civilian reward in Imperial
history.
For 10 days, they find nothing because
Voigt is doing the one thing none of
them expected. He is staying in Berlin.
A rented room in Rixdorf, 1 and 1/2 km
from Tempelhof Station. He goes out
twice a day, once for bread,
>> [music]
>> once for newspapers.
He is reading about himself. He is also
doing the one thing he has never done in
his life. He is talking.
Six months earlier, in the Anklam
prison, he had shared a cell with a
smaller time thief named Kallenberg.
They had become friends. Voigt, in the
loneliness of his last weeks before
release, had told Kallenberg about the
plan. Kallenberg was released 2 months
after [music] Voigt. He came to Berlin
looking for him. They met at a beer hall
in Schöneberg. They spent an evening
drinking. Voigt, half drunk, told
Kallenberg the operation had worked,
showed him the rented room, showed him
the paper bag still containing fragments
of the uniform.
The next morning, Kallenberg walked to
the police station. He collected 2,000
marks.
At 7:30 on the morning of October 26th,
[music]
10 days after the operation, four Berlin
detectives knock on the door of the room
in Rixdorf.
Voigt opens [music] the door. He is
sitting down to breakfast. Coffee, black
bread.
The detectives [music] ask if he is
Wilhelm Voigt. He says, "Yes.
Would you like coffee?"
Voigt is charged on three counts:
impersonation of an officer, theft,
unlawful deprivation of liberty. The
first two carry a combined maximum of 15
years. The third carries the death
penalty.
The trial opens at the Royal Prussian
District Court on December 1st, 1906.
The courtroom holds 390 people.
The press waiting list runs to 490.
Reporters arrive from London, Paris,
Vienna, New York. Harper's Weekly sends
a special correspondent. The prosecutor
reads the indictment. Voigt confirms
every fact. The uniform, the soldiers,
the receipt. Then he is asked why. His
answer takes 7 minutes. Preserved in the
court's stenographer's transcript,
[music]
still accessible today in the Prussian
Royal Archives. He says, flat voice,
[music] plain German, that he did not
want the money. He says he was looking
for blank passport documents [music] and
an official stamp in the town hall so
that he could finally produce papers and
find [music] legal work. He says, "When
I found there were no passports in
Köpenick, I took the cash. I did not
want to leave empty-handed [music] after
so much effort."
The courtroom holds 2 seconds of
silence. Then the audience applauds. The
judge calls for order. The audience
continues. The judge clears the chamber.
Reporters in the corridor describe
people weeping with laughter and
clapping at the same time.
The trial concludes on December 4th.
Conviction on the first two counts. The
third, kidnapping, dismissed. The
prosecutor's closing statement on file
in the court record.
The defendant clearly did not intend to
deprive these officials of liberty in a
meaningful sense, given his courteous
and well-documented treatment of them.
The well-documented treatment is the
signed receipt.
Sentence, four years.
The reaction in Berlin is immediate.
Within 24 hours, petitions for clemency
circulate [music] in 17 cities. By the
end of December, more than 100,000
signatures. The petitions reach the
Imperial Palace on January 4th, 1907.
Kaiser Wilhelm II reads the police
report and the trial transcript at his
desk in Potsdam. According to his
secretary's diary, published in 1929, he
laughs [music] through the entire
transcript. When he finishes, he turns
to his chief of staff. Recorded text.
>> A brilliant little fellow.
>> He does not order an immediate pardon.
He waits 20 months, long enough for the
petitions to keep arriving, long enough
for the international press cycle to
amplify the story to maximum. On August
16th, 1908, Voigt's 58th birthday,
Wilhelm II [music] personally signs a
clemency order. Voigt is released from
Tegel prison the following morning. A
crowd of 4,000 people is waiting at the
gate.
In the 18 months after his release,
Wilhelm Voigt is the highest earning
lecture performer in Europe. A wax work
in full Köpenick uniform is [music]
installed in Madame Tussaud's in London.
For a period in 1909, it is the most
photographed exhibit in the museum,
ahead of Queen Victoria.
He is paid 400 marks per appearance to
attend private dinners at the homes of
German industrialists, where he is asked
to put on the uniform and shout commands
at the guests.
The men paying include, verified in
surviving household [music] ledgers,
Karl Duisberg, chairman of the Bayer
Chemical Works, and Hugo Stinnes, the
largest single coal mining employer in
the Ruhr Valley.
The German industrial elite is paying a
homeless ex-convict to humiliate them.
In 1910, he is granted a passport by the
Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, which has no
political reason to refuse him. He
leaves Germany permanently. He tours the
United States and Canada in 1911. New
New papers describe his ticket as the
most expensive on Broadway [music] this
season. He fills Carnegie Hall. He never
returns to Prussia. He buys a small
house in Luxembourg City. He never
marries. He never speaks publicly about
his prison years.
He dies on January 3rd, 1922.
72 years old. The estate contains
approximately 70,000 current euros. The
savings of a quiet, well-funded [music]
retirement. In 1931, the playwright Carl
Zuckmayer publishes Der Hauptmann von
Köpenick. It becomes one of the most
performed plays in 20th century German
theater. Filmed seven times between 1931
and 2006.
In 1996, the borough of Köpenick, now
part of unified Berlin, installs a
bronze statue in front of the town hall.
The statue does not depict Mayor
Langerhans, who held the elected office.
It does not depict any of the soldiers
who guarded the building. It does not
depict the chief of police, the
treasurer, the prosecutor, or the
Kaiser. It depicts Wilhelm Voigt in the
captain's uniform he assembled piece by
piece from four used clothing shops in
1906 for 18 marks. The Imperial German
Army, the institution he proved did not
need to be defeated, only addressed in
the correct tone, would lose the First
World War 12 years later.
The empire that produced it would
dissolve the same year.
Wilhelm Voigt, the shoemaker who
arrested its mayor, would outlive the
empire by four years.
The system he had bypassed, the
unquestioned authority of a uniform over
the people inside the uniform, would not
be designed out of any military, any
corporation, any institution in the 20th
century. It would only be renamed.
Today, security researchers have a term
for what Wilhelm Voigt did Köpenick
Station on the afternoon of October
16th, 1906.
They call it social engineering.
He was 89 years ahead of them.

title: He Printed $500,000 Every Day With a Wedding Press Until One Tiny Scratch Exposed Him

text:
This is the true story of a Lima wedding-invitation printer who helped build one of the most advanced counterfeit dollar operations the U.S. Secret Service had ever seen.

On the surface, his shop printed wedding invitations, business cards, and posters for local restaurants. Downstairs, in a converted basement, a second-hand printing press was producing fake U.S. $100 bills so convincing that banks, cashiers, and investigators struggled to tell them apart from real money.

The secret was not hacking.
It was not a criminal supercomputer.
It was paper.

Worthless Venezuelan bolívar notes were made from the same cotton-linen blend used in American banknotes. Once that paper became nearly worthless, counterfeiters in Lima found a way to turn it into something far more dangerous: fake U.S. dollars that felt real in the hand.

By 2016, Peru had become the world capital of counterfeit American currency. The U.S. Secret Service had been chasing the network for years. But the break did not come from a confession or a security camera.

It came from a flaw so small it had to be seen under an electron microscope.

This is the full story of the wedding printer, the basement presses, the elderly women sewing security threads by hand, Operation Sunset, and the counterfeit $100 bills America could not stop.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
