subtitles.plaintext:
Lima, Peru, November 14th, 2016. A small
printing shop in the San Juan de
Lurigancho district is open for business
as usual. The sign outside reads,
"Wedding Invitations and Commercial
Printing." Inside, the smell of ink, a
few stacks of glossy invitations for an
upcoming wedding sit on the counter,
ready for pickup. A 40-something printer
is downstairs in the basement running a
second-hand offset lithography press.
The press is printing $100 US bills. By
the end of his shift, he will have
produced approximately $500,000
in counterfeit American currency. He
will do it again tomorrow. He has been
doing it for years. His shop is not the
only one. In the same Lima district,
[music] there are dozens of others.
Together, they produce roughly 60% of
all the counterfeit US dollars currently
in circulation anywhere on Earth. The
man at the center of it is not a hacker,
not a chemist, not a printing engineer.
He runs a wedding invitation business.
He does it from a converted basement. In
fewer than 16 hours, the United States
Secret Service will lead the largest
counterfeit currency raid in the
agency's history into the building above
him. And on every single one of his
bills, in a moment a Secret Service
analyst will eventually find under an
electron microscope will be a
microscopic [music] scratch beside the
left eye of Benjamin Franklin, exactly
300,000ths of a millimeter wide. It will
not stop the operation. So, how does a
wedding invitation printer from Lima
produce a $100 bill [music] that the US
Treasury, the Federal Reserve, and the
Secret Service cannot tell from the real
thing? And what is the single material,
a material everyone in the US government
had assumed was uncopyable, that he
found a way to steal from the only other
country in the world whose currency was
printed on it?
The man at the center of it has a name.
The Peruvian National Police, in their
internal files, identify him as Joel
Quispe. In the documentary footage that
will eventually surface, he refuses his
real name on camera. He goes by Raul. He
is, by every visible measure, not a
criminal. He is in his early 40s,
married, two children. He owns a
legitimate printing shop. He prints
wedding invitations, business cards,
posters for local restaurants. He pays
his taxes. He sponsors a small youth
football team in his neighborhood. The
neighborhood matters. San Juan de
Lurigancho is the largest residential
district in Peru, more than a million
residents, an enormous expanse of
self-built homes climbing the steep
hills around Lima. Many of those homes
were built by their owners, brick by
brick, over decades. [music]
Many were never finished. Many were
built without legal title. This is the
district in which an estimated 60% of
all the counterfeit US dollars currently
in circulation on Earth are physically
produced. Raul learned printing as a
teenager. Apprenticeship under an older
Lima printer in the 1990s, during the
worst years of Peru's own
hyperinflation. He learned offset
lithography on a Heidelberg press. He
learned how to mix ink. He learned the
smell of paper. By his late 20s, he was
running his own small shop. By his 30s,
he was printing wedding invitations for
almost every wedding within 10 miles of
his neighborhood. The work paid. It did
not pay enough. Around him, in the same
district, an industry was growing. Lima
was already, by the late [music] 2000s,
the world capital of counterfeit US
dollars. NPR's Planet Money would
document it in 2013. The US Secret
Service would identify Peru as the
world's leading manufacturer of fake
American currency in its first formal
report [music] on the subject in the
early 2010s.
A police investigator interviewed by
Vice News in 2016 would say it on
camera, [music]
in a single sentence, "It is more
profitable than cocaine." The
investigator was not boasting. He was
complaining. He was a man whose budget
did not match his problem.
In the late 2000s, the exact year is not
on the public record, Raul is said to
have begun experimenting in the basement
of his print shop [music] in the hours
after his apprentices went home. He is
said to have started with an old offset
press and a single batch of low-grade
rag paper. The first bills he produced,
on his own admission years later, were
terrible. A cashier at any US bank would
have caught them in a glance. The
wedding invitation business stayed open.
It continued to print wedding
invitations. It continued to file tax
returns. It continued to sponsor the
youth football team. And in the basement
beneath the press that printed
flower-bordered cards for the weddings
of mostly working-class neighbors, a
second [music] press was being
installed. A press for something else.
To understand what Raul was about to do,
you have to understand what he was
supposed to be unable to do. In 2014,
the United States $100 bill was the most
counterfeited consumer document in the
world and, according to the US Treasury,
the most counterfeit resistant. That is
not a contradiction. It is the design.
The US Bureau of Engraving and Printing
had spent more than a century building
defenses into the $100 note. By the time
Raul bought his second press, every bill
in circulation carried six layers of
protection.
>> [music]
>> One, the paper. Not paper, in fact.
Every American banknote in modern
circulation is printed on a blend of 75%
cotton and 25% linen, manufactured by a
single approved supplier, Crane Currency
in Dalton, Massachusetts. Domestic paper
does not behave the same way. Under
ultraviolet light, ordinary paper
fluoresces white. Currency paper does
not. Two, the intaglio print. Engraved
metal plates pressed into paper at 20
tons of pressure, leaving the ink raised
in microscopic ridges along Franklin's
collar, the Treasury seal, the
lettering. Run your thumb across a real
$100 and you can feel them. Three, the
watermark. Franklin's portrait ghosted
[music] inside the paper itself. Four,
the metallic security thread. A
continuous strip of foil woven into the
paper at Crane's Massachusetts mill,
carrying the words USA 100 in
microscopic letters that glow pink under
ultraviolet light.
Five, the 3D security ribbon added in
the 2013 redesign. Bells and numbers
that appear to move when you tilt the
bill.
>> [music]
>> Six, the color-shifting ink on the 100
in the lower right corner. The
Treasury's design philosophy was simple.
A forger would need to beat all six at
once. Every defense began at the same
place, the paper. If a forger could not
get the paper, nothing else mattered.
The ink would smudge, the thread would
peel, the watermark would be a printed
photograph instead of a structural
feature. For 70 years the Treasury slept
on this. The cotton-linen paper of the
US dollar was the line that no [music]
foreign counterfeiter had ever crossed.
The Treasury did not realize that
somewhere on the other side of the
world, the cotton-linen paper was also
being used to print a different
country's money, and that country's
money was about to become worthless.
In December 2013, the government of
Venezuela introduced a new series of
Bolívar banknotes. The Bolívar,
Venezuela's national currency, named
after the country's founder, had been on
a slow slide for more than a decade. By
2014, it lost 2/3 of its purchasing
[music] power. By 2015, more. By 2017, a
single American dollar would buy more
than 100,000 bolívares [music] on the
black market. Venezuelan mothers in
widely circulated photographs from those
years made origami handbags for their
daughters out of the cash. They taped
the bills into wallpaper. They burned
them for [music] heat. The bolívar was
not money anymore. It was paper.
Specifically, [music]
and this is the detail that almost no
one outside the world's counterfeiting
industry noticed, it was paper made from
75% cotton and 25% linen, the same blend
used for the US $100 bill. This was not
coincidence. For most of the late 20th
century, the world's central banks
bought their banknote paper from the
same handful of specialist [music]
mills. Crane Currency in Massachusetts,
De La Rue in the United Kingdom,
Giesecke+Devrient
in Germany. The Venezuelan Central Bank,
in the run-up to its 2007 currency
redesign, contracted out its paper to
one of the same international suppliers.
The Venezuelan bolívar and the American
dollar [music] were structurally printed
on identical paper. For 70 years, this
had not mattered because the Venezuelan
bolívar had been worth something close
to the American dollar.
>> [music]
>> By 2015, the Venezuelan bolívar was, on
the black market, worth approximately 2
10,000ths of an American cent per bill.
Stacks of real bolívares, genuine bills
issued by a [music] real central bank,
could be purchased on the streets of
Caracas in suitcases for the equivalent
of a few dollars. Each stack [music]
contained millions of pieces of
cotton-linen banknote paper manufactured
to the same specifications as the paper
used by the United States Bureau of
Engraving and Printing. Somewhere in the
early months of 2014, Raúl is said to
have been handed his first Venezuelan
bolívar bill, likely by a Lima trader
who had been to Caracas and back.
[music]
He is said to have held it up to the
light. He is said to have run his thumb
across it. Then he is said to have
folded it gently between [music] his
fingers, feeling the weight, the
crispness, the dry texture. Then he is
said to have done something no other
counterfeiter on earth had done. He took
the bolivar to the basement and held it
up beside one of his own counterfeit
American hundreds. The textures were the
same. The colors were different. The art
was different. The serial numbers were
different. The denominations were
different. The paper was identical.
[music]
A man in Lima who could find a way to
remove the Venezuelan ink without
damaging the paper and [music] to print
US ink in its place would have access to
the one material the US Treasury had
assumed for 70 years no foreigner could
obtain. The man in Lima would not need
to invent a paper mill. He would need to
invent [music] a bleach.
The chemistry took years. The first
attempt, by published documentary
accounts, ended with a sink full of gray
pulp. The bath was too aggressive. The
cotton linen fibers separated. The paper
dissolved into the water. The next
attempt was the opposite. The original
Venezuelan ink ghosted up through the
new American print like a watermark of a
different country, visible under any
decent lamp. It took Raul, by his own
later account, more than a year to find
the bath. The published reconstruction,
[music] based on the recipes the
Peruvian National Police would
eventually seize in November 2016,
describes approximately 11 minutes in
the chemical [music] bath, long enough
to lift the Venezuelan ink, short enough
that the cotton linen [music] weave
held, followed by a wash at
approximately 72° C,
>> [music]
>> followed by pressing, followed by
drying. When the process worked, the
paper that came out of it was no longer
Venezuelan. It was nothing. It was a
clean sheet of 75% cotton, 25% linen
banknote stock, 4/10,000 of an inch
thick with the same crisp dry texture as
a brand new bill from the Federal
Reserve Bank of New York. The first
printing pass was white, a solid
background. The second was black, the
engraving lines, the portraits, the
seals. The third was the green serial
numbers. By the end of an 8-hour shift,
the press was producing, on its best
days, approximately $500,000
in face value counterfeit American
currency. The bills were not yet
finished. They were flat. A real US $100
note, printed on a 20-ton intaglio
press, carries microscopic [music]
raised ridges along Franklin's collar,
the Treasury seal, the lettering.
A trained [music] cashier in the United
States, running a thumb across the bill,
will feel them without consciously
noticing. Raul's [music] bills, fresh
off the offset press, were smooth. This
is where the work moved upstairs, out of
the basement and into the kitchen of a
Lima taxi driver. The taxi driver, known
in the seized materials only by the
nickname Cristiano Ronaldo, was not a
printer. He had not finished secondary
school. He drove a cab six nights a
week. He prepared the bills during the
day at his kitchen table. The recipe he
developed by trial and error over months
was three ingredients. One part flour,
two parts wood glue, four parts water.
He mixed it. [music] He stirred it. He
let it cool. Then, with the bills laid
flat on his kitchen [music] table, he
applied the mixture to specific
positions on each bill, to Franklin's
collar, to the Treasury seal, to the
lettering, with the tip of one finger.
As the mixture dried, it contracted. It
pulled the cotton linen fibers into
microscopic ridges. A real intaglio
press produces these ridges through 20
tons of physical pressure. The taxi
driver produced them with flour, [music]
glue, water, and his right index finger.
Each bill took him approximately 30
minutes. By the published account in the
Hazel documentary, when the technique
first worked, the first time he ran his
finger over a finished bill and felt the
raised collar of Benjamin Franklin under
his fingertip, he laughed for a full
minute in his own kitchen alone at 3:00
a.m.
The bills now passed the touch test.
They still had one final defense to
defeat.
The US Treasury's metallic security
thread is woven into the cotton linen
paper at Crane Currency's Massachusetts
mill before the paper is shipped to the
Bureau of Engraving. It is woven into
the structure of the paper itself. It is
impossible to add afterwards,
unless the Lima counterfeiters
discovered you found a way to push it
in.
The bills, after Cristiano Ronaldo's
kitchen treatment, were soaked again. A
precise 4-minute bath, just enough to
soften the cotton linen fibers without
separating them. Then, they were carried
by hand to a back room in a different
building in San Juan de Lurigancho. In
that room sat several elderly women,
magnifying loops, surgical needles,
reading lamps. The recruitment of the
grandmothers was, by published [music]
account, the most carefully managed part
of the operation. They were recruited
individually [music] from the same
neighborhood. They were chosen for
steady hands and excellent close-up
vision. They were paid in cash weekly in
US dollars that the operation guaranteed
were genuine. The pay, by the
operation's later admission to
investigators, exceeded the average
Peruvian state pension by a factor of
five. In return, the women were asked to
do one thing. Each was given a thin foil
thread, the USA 100 security strip
manufactured by the operation's own
suppliers, and a softened freshly bathed
counterfeit bill. Each thread was passed
[music] through the cotton linen fibers
of the bill by hand in the precise
position specified by the Federal
Reserve's own design, 5 to 10 minutes
per bill. When the paper dried, the
thread was locked inside, fused into the
same fibrous structure as a genuine
thread inserted at Crane's mill in
Massachusetts.
A trained banker holding a finished bill
up to the light would see [music]
exactly where it should be, USA 100 in
microscopic letters glowing pink under
the bank's ultraviolet lamp.
It was, [music] by every published
account from the US Secret Service in
the years that followed,
indistinguishable from a real bill.
By the autumn of 2015, a single Lima
cell, one wedding invitation print shop,
one [music] taxi driver's kitchen, one
room of elderly women with surgical
needles could produce approximately
$500,000
in finished bills per working day. The
US Secret Service estimated that [music]
approximately 16 million counterfeit
bills of Peruvian origin were seized in
the United States that year alone. The
seized figure, by the agency's own
[music] published estimate, represented
between 5 and 10% of the total Peruvian
counterfeit currency that successfully
[music] reached American hands. The
bills moved north, by land, mostly.
Mules carried them through Colombia,
Panama, Costa Rica, and Mexico into the
United States via Tijuana. The bills
moved through the same routes the
[music] Sinaloa Cartel used for cocaine.
According to the US Drug Enforcement
Administration, at least one major
Mexican trafficking organization began
buying Peruvian counterfeit currency in
bulk [music] at approximately 20% of
face value and using the bills to pay
US-based [music]
suppliers.
The bills were laundered in the simplest
possible way. A counterfeit 100 [music]
used to buy a $6 drive-thru meal
produced 94 real dollars in change. A
single mule making 12 stops a day along
an American highway could launder up to
$10,000 in a working shift. By the end
of 2015, an estimated $80 million in
finished Peruvian counterfeit bills were
entering the United States economy every
year.
The US Treasury, [music] the Federal
Reserve, the Secret Service, and the
entire American banking industry had,
for the first time in living memory,
lost the paper war. They did not yet
know they had lost it.
The break came, as it usually does, not
from technology, but from a single human
being who could not keep his mouth shut.
In the late summer of 2016, somewhere in
the United States, a mid-level
distributor of Peruvian counterfeit
bills sat down at a bar with a man he
believed was a regular customer. The
customer had bought from him before. The
customer had paid cash. The customer had
never asked questions. The customer was
a US Secret Service agent. Over a drink,
by [music] the published documentary
account, the distributor wanted to
explain why his product was worth what
he charged. He talked about the bath. He
talked about the press. He talked about
the men in Lima. He named the city. He
used the word Raul. The agent paid for
the drinks. He went home. He wrote it
up. The US Secret Service had been
investigating Peruvian counterfeiting
for more than a decade. They had
jurisdictional [music] cooperation
arrangements with the Peruvian National
Police. What they had not had until that
night was a name. In Washington, a
Secret Service forensic analyst placed a
recently seized counterfeit $100 bill
under an electron microscope. She
magnified the area around Benjamin
Franklin's left [music] eye. She found
it almost immediately, a microscopic
scratch, 300,000ths of a millimeter
wide, a wear mark on a single cylinder
of a single [music] offset press
somewhere in Lima.
A defect so small that no human eye
could see it without 10,000 times
magnification. [music]
The scratch was on every counterfeit
bill the agency had tested from the same
family of seizures. Cross-referenced
against bills [music] found in US Drug
Enforcement Administration interdictions
of northbound Mexican shipments, the
same scratch. Miami, New York, [music]
Los Angeles, every bill, the same press.
In Lima, the Peruvian National Police
had been quietly building a parallel
file for months. By autumn 2016, the two
investigations met. [music] The
coordinated raid was set for the early
morning of November 15th, 2016.
The US Secret Service's Lima Station
coordinated with the Peruvian National
Police's specialized counterfeit unit.
The operation was code-named [music]
Sunset.
At 4:00 in the morning, 1,500 Peruvian
National Police officers moved in
coordinated columns to 54 addresses
across the city.
In a basement in San Juan de Lurigancho,
one of the 54, Raul, was woken by his
wife. He did not run. By later accounts
of officers present, he was already
dressed when they reached the basement
door. He had finished a glass of water.
He had set the empty glass on the desk
beside the press. He let them in. In the
basement, the police found $30 million
in stacked counterfeit currency. Floor
to ceiling.
The Heidelberg press [music] was still
warm. In a back room of a different
building, by the press footage from the
morning of the raid, a Peruvian officer
pushed open a door and found one of the
elderly grandmothers still at her
worktable, a surgical needle in her
hand, mid-stitch through a freshly
bathed bill. She did not stand up. She
finished the stitch. In a kitchen drawer
of a third location, the police [music]
found a children's school notebook,
written in colored pencil, containing
every recipe in the operation. Every
bath time, every temperature, every
flower to glue ratio, every dimension of
the security thread. By the end of the
day, 48 people had been arrested, eight
presses had been seized, six [music]
factories had been raided, more than
1,600
printing plates and negatives were in
evidence. It was, by the US Secret
Service's own published statement,
[music] the largest counterfeit currency
seizure in the history of the agency.
The scratch was the thread that pulled
the [music] entire system down. For
about 3 months,
the legal proceedings began in early
2017. Raul pleaded guilty. He
cooperated. He provided the names of his
suppliers, his distributors, the
grandmothers who had stitched the
threads, the taxi driver who had
perfected the kitchen glue recipe. His
sentence was approximately 3 and 1/2
years. He served most of it at a
low-security facility outside Lima.
After his release, he returned to the
same district. He did [music] not return
to printing. He bought, with money the
police never traced, a small plot of
land on the outskirts of the city. He
planted mango trees. He gave one filmed
interview after his release. The
producer asked [music] him whether he
ever thought about the Americans who had
unknowingly handed his counterfeit $100
bills to cashiers at coffee shops, gas
stations, drive-thrus across the United
States. He thought about the question
for a long time. Then he answered, in
Spanish, in a single sentence that has,
in the years since, become the
unofficial motto of the Peruvian
counterfeit industry.
Money has no face.
In February 2017, approximately 3 months
after Operation Sunset, bills bearing
the same microscopic scratch beside
Benjamin Franklin's left eye began
appearing in Miami, New York, and Los
Angeles.
The children's notebook the Peruvian
National Police had seized in November
had been a copy. [music]
The original recipes were in other
hands. The presses had been replaced.
The grandmothers had moved to new back
rooms in different buildings [music]
with new needles. The bath times were
unchanged. The flower to glue ratio was
unchanged. The US Secret Service ran a
second large-scale operation in Lima in
May 2020, another in subsequent years.
Each operation has seized tens of
millions [music] of dollars in finished
counterfeit currency. Each has
dismantled multiple factories. Each has
resulted in dozens of arrests. After
each operation, production has resumed.
By 2026, the US Secret Service's
official estimate of Peru's share of the
global counterfeit US dollar market is
unchanged from 2015, approximately 60%.
The wedding invitation print [music]
shops are still open. The grandmothers
are still sewing. The taxi driver's
kitchen recipe is still being mixed
[music] somewhere in the hills of Lima
every morning before dawn. And the
cotton linen paper, stripped from
worthless Venezuelan bolivares, is still
being shipped by suitcase, by truck, by
occasional cargo container to the
basements of San Juan de Lurigancho. The
US Treasury has not, in the 10 years
since, found a way to replace the cotton
linen paper of the American
hundred-dollar bill. The system Raul
[music] found in 2013 still works.
In 2026, Joel Quispe, known to the world
as Raul, is in his early 50s. He grows
mangos outside Lima. The US [music]
Treasury still prints its money on
cotton and linen. Venezuela has cotton
linen bolivares that nobody wants. And
every morning in a Lima district built
brick by brick on the hills above the
Pacific, the presses start running
again. Money, as Raul said, has no face.
It has only paper. And the paper is the
same.

title: He Stole Most Secret Jet to Escape North Korea

text:
No Kum-sok defection story — the true story of how a 21-year-old North Korean fighter pilot stole the Soviet Union's most secret jet, the MiG-15, and defected to the West in seventeen minutes, accidentally collecting the largest secret bounty of the Cold War. On September 21, 1953, eight MiG-15 fighters lifted off from Sunan Airfield in North Korea for routine morning training. Seven minutes in, one of them broke formation, dropped to two hundred feet, and turned south.

The pilot's name was No Kum-sok. He was twenty-one years old. He had been lying to every officer he had ever met, for seven years.

The jet beneath him was the Soviet Union's most closely guarded weapon — the MiG-15 fighter that had been outflying American Sabres over Korea for two years. The CIA had been trying to capture one since 1951. The U.S. Air Force had dropped one million leaflets across the north under a classified program called Operation Moolah, offering one hundred thousand dollars to any pilot who would deliver a MiG-15 to United Nations forces.

No Kum-sok had never read a single leaflet. He had never heard the radio broadcasts. He was flying south for free.

Seventeen minutes after breaking formation, he landed at Kimpo Air Base in South Korea — and handed the United States its most-wanted intelligence prize of the Cold War.

This is the full story of how a thirteen-year-old boy watched the Soviet Army take everything his family owned in 1945, decided he would one day escape — and spent the next seven years quietly becoming the model communist citizen the regime would never suspect. How he memorized Party doctrine, gave speeches denouncing American imperialism, flew over a hundred combat missions while deliberately missing every target that mattered, and rose to senior lieutenant in the North Korean Air Force without anyone — not his commanders, not his fellow pilots, not even his own mother — ever knowing his real beliefs. How he picked the morning of September 21, 1953 for one reason: routine training meant a fueled jet, an unsupervised flight path, and a window of exactly seventeen minutes before the air defense net would react. And how the United States quietly disassembled his MiG-15 in Okinawa, studied it for months, and used what they learned to redesign every Western fighter that followed.

The bounty was never claimed — until two years later, when the U.S. Air Force tracked No Kum-sok down in Delaware and handed him a hundred-thousand-dollar check he had never asked for.

He had not been flying for the money. He had been flying away from a system that took his childhood, his father, his country, and his name.

subtitles.plaintext:
Sunan Airfield, North Korea, September
21st, 1953.
Eight MiG-15 fighters lift off for
routine training. Seven minutes in, one
of them breaks formation. It dives,
drops to 200 ft, turns south. The
pilot's name is No Kum-sok, a senior
lieutenant in the North Korean Air
Force, 21 years old. He has been lying
to every officer he has ever [music] met
for seven years. The jet beneath him is
the Soviet Union's most secret weapon.
The CIA has been trying to capture one
for two years. The US Air Force has
dropped a million leaflets over the
north
offering $100,000
to any pilot who delivers one. No
Kum-sok has not read a single leaflet.
He has not heard the radio [music]
broadcast. He is flying south for free.
In 17 minutes, he will land at Kimpo Air
Base and accidentally collect the
largest secret bounty of the Cold War.
To understand what No Kum-sok did on
that morning, you have to understand the
seven years that came before it.
He was born on January 10th, 1932 in a
small town on the northeast coast of
Korea.
His father owned a small factory. His
mother ran the household. A normal
middle-class family.
Then, in August 1945, the Soviet army
crossed into northern Korea.
No Kum-sok was 13 years old. He watched
the new authorities take his father's
factory, then his savings, then the
family's standing in the town. All of it
relabeled in a single afternoon as
bourgeois property.
His father died of illness shortly
after.
By the time he was 14, No Kum-sok had
made a decision he would not share with
anyone for the next seven years.
He decided he would leave.
But the system he was born into did not
allow people to leave. There was no
exit, no application, no travel. The
border was sealed. The radios were
jammed. Letters were read. So, he made a
second decision. If he wanted to escape
this system, he would [music] first have
to become its model citizen.
He joined the Communist Youth League. He
memorized the party doctrine. He
volunteered for political education
classes. He gave a speech denouncing
American imperialism with a smile his
classmates believed.
He kept his real opinions in his head
and only in his head.
His grades were perfect. His ideological
reports were perfect. His loyalty rating
in the new songbun classification system
the regime was assembling was placed in
the highest category.
In 1949 at 17, he was selected for the
elite Naval Academy in Wonsan.
A year later, he transferred to the
Korean People's Air Force. He learned to
fly trainers in Manchuria at airfields
ringed with anti-aircraft batteries 10
miles from the Soviet border.
Then jets under the personal supervision
of Soviet instructors who never gave
their real names.
By 1951, he was flying MiG-15s in combat
against the Americans.
He flew over 100 missions. He never
fired in a way that hit anything
important. He aimed wide. He aimed late.
He claimed mechanical issues.
On one mission, he watched a stricken
B-29 try to limp home and deliberately
broke off the kill reporting that his
cannons had jammed. No one ever caught
him. His own mother did not know.
He understood [music] very young that to
escape a totalitarian system, you do not
fight it. You become indistinguishable
from it and you wait.
To understand why no pilot had ever
delivered a MiG-15 to the West before
September 1953,
you have to understand what the Soviet
Aerospace program had built around
[music] it. The MiG-15 was not just an
airplane. It was the most closely
[music] guarded piece of military
technology in the Eastern Bloc. It was
lighter than the American F-86 Sabre. It
climbed faster. It flew higher. It
carried two 23-mm cannons and one 37-mm
designed to bring down American B-29
bombers in a single pass.
When it appeared in Korean skies in
November 1950, [music]
it changed the war overnight. The US Air
Force, which had owned the air for 5
years, suddenly could not own it
anymore. American pilots gave the
corridor along the Yalu River its own
name.
They called it MiG Alley.
Two American pilots had been seen
ejecting over it. Neither was ever
found.
In the rooms where American planners
worked, the MiG-15 became an obsession.
They needed one. Not a wreck, not a
photograph, not a debriefed prisoner, a
flying example with manuals, with the
engine intact, with the pilot alive
enough to explain it. For 2 years, they
had nothing. The Soviet system around
the jet was built like a vault. Most of
the pilots flying MiG-15s out of Antung
were not Korean or Chinese. They were
Russian officers of the Soviet 64th
Fighter Aviation Corps.
>> [music]
>> They wore Chinese or North Korean
uniforms. They were forbidden to speak
Russian on the radio. They were
forbidden to fly south of Pyongyang, so
that if they were ever shot down, no
Soviet body would fall into American
hands.
Officially, the Soviet Union was not at
[music] war. Every MiG-15 in North Korea
was tracked by ground control from the
moment it started its engines.
Pilots flew in groups, always in
formation, never solo. Fuel was rationed
to the exact distance of the planned
mission. Defection was treated not as a
crime against the state, but as a crime
against the entire family of the pilot.
If a pilot landed in the South, his
parents would be executed. His siblings
would be sent to the camps. His name
would be erased from records. His
village punished. His neighbors
interrogated. The system did not need to
physically stop a pilot from flying
South. It only needed to make him
imagine the cost. There was, on top of
all of this, a deeper problem. To
deliver a MiG-15, a pilot would have to
fly low, fly fast, and land at an enemy
airfield without being shot down by the
Americans first.
The F-86 Sabres on those airfields were
trained to kill MiG-15s on sight. A
MiG-15 approaching a UN base from the
wrong direction, in formation with no
one, would be considered [music]
hostile. By 1953, after 2 years of
trying, the Americans had concluded the
same thing the Soviets had. No pilot was
going to deliver this jet. Then, in
April 1953, the Americans tried one more
idea.
On April 26th, 1953, B-29
Superfortresses of the 581st Air
Resupply and Communications Wing flew at
altitude over the territory north of the
38th parallel and began releasing paper.
Nearly 1 million leaflets came down in a
single morning. They drifted across
Sinuiju, across Wiju, across the city of
Antung on the Chinese side of the Yalu,
where the Soviet pilots were based. The
leaflets were printed in three
languages: Korean, Chinese, and Russian.
They carried photographs of American
$100 bills. The text was direct. [music]
To any pilot of any nation who flew a
fully operational MiG-15 to a
UN-controlled airfield. $50,000 in cash.
An additional 50,000 for the first
pilot. $100,000 total. Permanent
political asylum. Relocation. A new
identity. Total confidentiality.
The program had a name, Operation
Moolah.
The man behind the idea was a US Air
Force psychological warfare officer
named Allen Abner. The plan was approved
at the theater level by General Mark
Clark, commander of UN forces. At the
Washington level, it was signed by
President Eisenhower himself. The drop
was followed by a second weapon, radio.
The Voice of the United Nations Command
began transmitting the offer in Korean,
Chinese, and Russian on shortwave and
medium wave every day.
The Soviet response was immediate.
Anyone caught with a leaflet was
arrested. Possession was treated as
treason. Radios capable of receiving
shortwave were confiscated, jammed, or
destroyed.
Ground crews who fueled and armed the
MiGs were rotated daily so that no
individual could speak with a pilot in
private. Political officers were
assigned [music] to every flight. The
leaflets were collected and burned
within hours of landing.
Around the same time, the Russian pilots
flying out of Antung began quietly
rotating home. Historians have argued
about the cause for 70 years. Some
attribute the withdrawal to Operation
Moolah. Others to the death of Stalin on
March 5th, 1953.
Others to the simple fact that the war
was ending.
The result was the same. By June, the
experienced Soviet pilots who had fought
the F-86s for 2 years were gone. By
August, the Americans counted the
results of Operation Moolah. 5 months.
Roughly 1 and 1/2 million leaflets.
Daily broadcasts in three languages,
zero MiG-15s delivered. The North Korean
pilot who would eventually deliver one
was at that moment flying training
missions out of Sunan and going home
every evening to a small apartment in
Pyongyang.
He had not seen a leaflet. He had not
heard a broadcast. [music] He had no
idea that the United States had put a
price on his airplane. His own plan was
older than Operation Moolah. He had been
waiting since 1951 for the right combat
mission. A flight that would let him
peel off, push south, and disappear into
UN airspace before the Americans could
shoot him down. Then, on July 27th,
1953, the war ended. The armistice was
signed. Combat flights stopped. The
borders went quiet. And every flight he
had been waiting for, every [music]
chance to slip away in the middle of an
air engagement, was gone.
For 2 months, he kept flying training
missions. He kept smiling at his
political officer. He kept performing.
And on the evening of September 20th,
1953,
he saw the schedule for the next
morning. A four-aircraft training
pattern. Then, a second four-aircraft
pattern stacked above it. Eight jets in
the air at the same time.
He understood immediately that this was
the window. It would not come again.
The morning of September 21st, 1953,
No Kum-Sok arrives at Sunan before
sunrise. The sky over the airfield is
clear and cold. He preflights his MiG-15
with the careful, mechanical attention
of a man who has done this a thousand
times. He checks the fuel. Full. He
checks the canopy seal. He smiles at the
ground crew. [music] He does not say
goodbye. At 9:00, eight MiG-15s lift off
into a clear morning sky. They climb out
together, form into pairs, and begin a
routine [music] training pattern. 7
minutes in, No Kum-Sok's jet falls
behind the formation. He waits 1 [music]
second, 2, then he pushes the stick
forward, drops the nose, and dives. He
levels off at 200 ft above the ground.
The MiG-15 is doing roughly 600 mph. He
turns due south. Below him, rice paddies
blur into a single gray green line. The
mountains around Pyongyang fall away
behind his left wing. There is no radio
traffic. There is no warning. On the
ground, North Korean radar operators
watch the eighth jet vanish from their
screens. They assume mechanical failure.
They begin the standard search pattern
looking for crash debris.
Above him, in the formation, no one
notices for nearly a minute. By the time
they do, he is 10 miles south of where
he should be and dropping below the
horizon line. He does not climb. He does
not slow. He does not signal. He flies
on his own dead reckoning toward a place
he has never seen. The Imjin River
passes beneath him in a silver flash.
The DMZ slides under his nose at 630
mph. The terrain begins to change.
Paddys turn into airfields, then a
ridge, then a city.
He has been flying for 16 minutes. His
fuel gauge is at half. Then he sees it.
A long concrete runway running roughly
east to [music] west. American buildings
around it. American jets parked along
the apron.
He knows it is Kimpo, K-14, the largest
UN airbase in South Korea. He has never
approached it before. He drops his
landing gear. He banks onto final, and
he turns the wrong way. He is now lined
up to land on the runway from the east.
Coming the other direction, west to
east, is an American F-86 Sabre on its
own approach.
The two jets are now on the same strip
of concrete at a closing speed of
roughly 900 mph. Neither pilot has seen
the other yet. Kimpo's radar is off this
morning. The system is undergoing
scheduled maintenance. No one in [music]
the tower has been watching. The first
person to see the MiG-15 with North
Korean markings gear down, lined up
backwards on the runway, is the F-86
pilot.
The F-86 pilot pulls up. He banks hard
right, throws the throttle forward, and
clears the threshold of the runway by
less than 100 ft. No Kum-Sok lands. He
rolls out, taxies to a stop near the
apron, and shuts off the engine. For a
moment, the airfield is silent. Then,
the canopy opens. A young man in a North
[music] Korean flight suit climbs out
with both hands raised above his head.
He is 21 [music]
years old. He has just flown the Soviet
Union's most secret weapon across enemy
lines. The first ground crew to reach
him does not yet know who he is. A jeep
arrives, then a second jeep, then
security with weapons drawn.
He keeps his hands raised. A
Korean-speaking officer is brought
[music] in. He explains, quietly and in
his own language, that he is a senior
lieutenant of the North Korean Air
Force. He explains that he wishes to
defect. He explains that he has brought
the airplane. He is taken to a
debriefing room on the base. He is
searched. He is given water.
He is asked repeatedly why he has done
this.
He tells them, "For freedom, not for
money." The American officer in the room
pauses, then asks, "Do you know what
Operation Moolah is?" No Kum-Sok does
not. The officer slides a leaflet across
the table. The leaflet is in Korean. It
describes a program that has been
running for 5 months. It describes a
reward of $100,000.
No Kum Sok reads it for the first time.
He has just earned, by accident, more
money than he has ever seen. More money
than his father ever earned. More money
than anyone in his hometown had ever
earned. He had not flown south for it.
He had not known it existed. He would
later write in his memoir that the
moment he read the leaflet was stranger
than the flight itself. The officer asks
him if he understands. He says yes.
Then he asked the officer if his mother
is alive. She is. She had been evacuated
from the port of Hungnam with 100,000
other civilians in December of 1950,
almost 3 years earlier. She had been
living in South Korea the entire time he
had been a pilot in the north. He had
not known.
Within 48 hours, the MiG-15 was
disassembled. It was flown to Kadena Air
Base on Okinawa and reassembled inside a
hangar guarded by armed Marines. On
September 29th, 1953, Captain Tom
Collins became the first American pilot
to fly it. A few weeks later, Major
Chuck Yeager, the man who had broken the
sound barrier 6 years earlier, flew the
same airplane. Yeager later [music]
wrote that the MiG-15 was a fast climber
and a vicious gun platform. But a flying
booby trap at high speed. It pitched up
violently when pushed past Mach 0.86.
It snap rolled without warning. The
hydraulics buckled in tight turns. The
gun sight was inferior to the one on the
F-86. Within months, the US [music] Air
Force had rewritten its dog fighting
doctrine. F-86 pilots were taught to
drag a MiG-15 into a high speed turn it
could not survive. The advantage that
had reshaped the Korean air war was
quietly neutralized. The Soviet Union
refused for years to publicly
acknowledge that its newest fighter was
sitting in an American hangar. No
Kum-Sok was flown to the United States.
He was granted political asylum. He was
given a new name, Kenneth Hill Rowe. In
1954, the US Treasury cut him a check
for $100,000. [music]
At first, he refused. He had not flown
south for it. The officers explained
that the offer had been made publicly in
three languages on more than a million
pieces of paper. The government had to
honor it. Otherwise, no future program
could ever promise anything to anyone.
He took the check. He spent it on a
degree in mechanical engineering at the
University of Delaware. He went on to
design American jet aircraft, [music]
the same kinds of jets in many cases
that had been designed to fight his old
MiG-15. After his retirement, he taught
aeronautical engineering at Embry-Riddle
University in Florida. He published his
memoir, A MiG-15 to [music] Freedom, in
1996
The MiG itself sits today in a glass
hangar at the National Museum of the
United States Air Force in Dayton, Ohio.
The North Korean star [music] on its
tail has not been repainted. The board
number on its nose, 2057,
has not been wiped off. It is the most
studied piece of [music] foreign
military equipment of the Cold War.
Kenneth Hill Rowe died on December 26th,
2022 [music]
in Daytona Beach, Florida. He was 90
years old. He had outlived the Soviet
Union by 31 years. He had been 21 when
he flew south. He had been pretending to
be a communist for seven. He had not
seen a single leaflet. In 17 minutes, he
had ended the most expensive
intelligence search of the Cold War. Not
for the money.

text:
This is the true story of George C. Parker — the Brooklyn conman who sold the Brooklyn Bridge, the Statue of Liberty, Madison Square Garden, Grant’s Tomb, and some of New York’s most famous landmarks without owning a single inch of them.

For more than 40 years, Parker built one of the most unbelievable scams in American history.

He created a fake government office near the immigrant arrival points of New York. He hired actors to play city clerks, officials, and engineers. He forged deeds, used fake seals, staged official-looking meetings, and convinced newcomers that they could buy pieces of the city itself.

His best-selling property was the Brooklyn Bridge.

According to later accounts, Parker sold it again and again — hundreds of times, possibly more than 1,000 — to people who believed they had just bought one of the most famous bridges in the world.

Some buyers even showed up the next morning with tools, signs, and toll booths, ready to take control of their new property.

The scam became so common that the NYPD had to assign patrols to stop Parker’s victims from trying to claim the bridge.

But Parker did not stop there.

He sold the Statue of Liberty.
He sold Madison Square Garden.
He sold Grant’s Tomb.
He sold New York landmark by landmark — using nothing but paper, performance, and the dreams of people who had just arrived in America.

This is the full story of George C. Parker, the Brooklyn Bridge scam, the fake city office, the police patrols, the courtroom legend, and the conman who helped create one of the most famous sayings in American culture:

“If you believe that, I have a bridge to sell you.”

subtitles.plaintext:
Brooklyn Bridge, Manhattan side, April
14th, 1909.
>> [music]
>> An NYPD officer walks the East Tower
foot patrol, a job no department in any
other American city has needed to
assign.
A horse-drawn cart approaches the bridge
from the Lower East Side. The two men in
it are unloading toll booths. They are
not city employees. They have a
notarized deed in their pocket. The deed
says they own the bridge. They paid $800
for it three days ago. They are not the
first. They are not the last.
Between the bridge's opening in 1883 and
the morning a Manhattan court sentenced
a Brooklyn con man named George C.
Parker to life in Sing Sing, Parker sold
the Brooklyn Bridge approximately 1,000
separate times. He also sold the Statue
of Liberty, the Metropolitan [music]
Museum, Madison Square Garden. He sold
Ulysses S. Grant's Tomb to a delegation
of Alabama Baptists who arrived [music]
the next morning to install a hymn
board. Two questions decide the next 45
years. [music] How does a Brooklyn-born
grade school dropout sell the most
famous bridge in the world a thousand
times without owning a single nail of
it? And why did the NYPD maintain a
permanent foot patrol on the East Tower
of the Brooklyn Bridge for 23 years just
to stop his buyers?
The man who would sell the Brooklyn
Bridge for the next 45 years was born in
1860, approximately 1 mile from where
the bridge would eventually stand.
George C. Parker, Brooklyn, second of
four children of Irish immigrants from
the post-famine wave of 1851. His father
worked the docks. His mother took in
washing. They lived in a tenement on
Hick Street. George Parker finished four
years of grammar school. He did not, in
1872, continue. For the next 10 years,
he worked the small fraud economy of
late 19th century New York, patent
medicine on Coney Island, shell games on
the Brooklyn ferry, fake mining bonds at
Bowery saloons. He learned three things:
a confidence operation could not be
improvised, it had to be staged, the
most reliable victim was not the rich
[music] man with experience, it was the
new arrival with savings, and watching
three of his partners go to prison in
the same year that the moment a victim
could prove what he had paid for, the
operation collapsed. [music] The
solution to all three was the same.
Paper.
On May 24th, 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge
opened to the public. George Parker was
23 years old. He walked across the
bridge on the second day it was open. He
walked back to Brooklyn that evening. By
the end of the week, he had drafted his
first deed.
In the winter of 1883, Parker rented a
small ground floor office at 38 Pearl
Street, three blocks from the Castle
Garden immigrant arrival point. Over the
door, in painted gold lettering, New
York City Department of Public Works,
Bureau of Asset Disposition. There was
no such bureau in the New York City
government. Inside, a printing press,
three official-looking city seals
purchased without questions from a small
stamp maker on Mott Street. A drawer of
notarial signatures Parker had spent
[music] six months practicing, a file
cabinet of approximately 300 forged
documents, each prepared for a specific
landmark.
Behind the operation worked [music]
Parker's standing staff, a senior clerk
in a green visor who would emerge from
the back room to corroborate any
document Parker presented, a Tammany
Hall liaison who would arrive, by
apparent coincidence, at the moment the
customer began to hesitate, a retired
city engineer who would, when asked,
swear on his late wife that the deed
Parker was selling was the same one he
had personally drawn up. They were not
clerks. They were not liaisons. They
were not engineers. They were three
Irish-American actors Parker had hired
in the spring of 1884 at $5 a day plus a
percentage. Their previous credit, a
touring production of The Octoroon that
had closed after 11 performances. In
[music] the 44 years that followed, none
of them ever broke character in the
presence of a customer. From the
customer's point of view, the operation
was indistinguishable from a small
bureau of the city government. By 1886,
it was generating approximately $1,200 a
month. In 1886, that was the income of a
senior bank vice president.
The customer was found, almost always,
the same [music] way. Every immigrant
ship between 1883 and 1924 docked at
Castle Garden or, after 1892, Ellis
Island. Approximately 15,000 arrivals
walked through processing each week.
Parker maintained, on his Pearl Street
books, a single line item entry every
Wednesday. $10, Mr. D. Mr. D was a clerk
at the Ellis Island cash deposit window.
For $10 a week, he sent [music] Parker,
every Tuesday evening, a list of
arrivals who had declared cash holdings
[music] over $500.
The list, by 1895, ran to 40 names a
week. Parker would meet the arrival on
the second or third day at a hotel, a
saloon, the reading room of the Astor
Library. Always by what looked like
coincidence.
He would introduce himself by one of his
seven aliases. He would explain that
[music] his family had owned the bridge,
the museum, the tomb, whatever the
target, for two generations.
He would explain that recent city
expenses had bankrupted him.
He would explain [music] that he was
selling privately before the city took
it for whatever the buyer could pay.
He would never name a price first. The
customer, who could not believe his good
fortune, would offer whatever he could
afford. Parker, looking pained, would
accept. He would take the customer to
the Pearl Street office where the three
actors would corroborate the
transaction. He would prepare the deed.
He would notarize it. He would shake the
customer's hand. He would walk the
customer back to the hotel. He would
tell the customer at the door that he
would be unable to attend any handover
the following day owing to a personal
matter requiring travel to Boston. By
the time the customer reached the
landmark the next morning with tools,
Parker was already at his office
preparing the next deed.
The Brooklyn Bridge was Parker's best
seller, approximately a thousand
transactions over 45 years. Twice a week
at the peak in the 1890s. Prices from
$50 for an Italian widow with three
children to 50,000 for a Hamburg textile
heir. But it was not the most lucrative
single sale. That distinction belongs to
Madison Square Garden, sold in 1903 to a
Hoboken brewer for $25,000.
The brewer had been told the arena was
being demolished to make way for a
German beer garden. He arrived the next
morning with three demolition
contractors. Three NYPD officers held
him back from the entrance while a
fourth ran for a German interpreter.
Grant's tomb was sold approximately 50
times between 1897 and 1926.
Parker's approach was to identify
himself as Ulysses S. Grant's grandson,
carry a small photograph of himself next
to the gravestone, and offer the tomb at
a price reflecting his urgent need to
relocate to Europe. In the summer of
1907, the buyers were a delegation of
Alabama Baptists in town for the
Northern Baptist Convention. They
arrived at the tomb the following
morning with a hymn board, a brass
plaque commemorating their congregation,
and a freshly purchased pew bench. The
hymn board, engraved at a Tuscaloosa
carpenter shop the previous month, read,
"In memory of General Grant from the
saints of Tuscaloosa." The NYPD officer
on duty turned them away. The Baptists
left the hymn board on the steps. By the
following morning, it was gone. What
happened to it has never been
determined. The Statue of Liberty was
sold approximately 100 times. Parker's
pitch by 1908
was that the statue was being relocated
to Cuba, and he had been authorized to
sell the pedestal as scrap. Trinity
Church, 12 times. The Metropolitan
Museum, eight.
The Astor Library, 15. Across 45 years
and 2,000 transactions, Parker generated
between 1 and 3 million dollars, between
50 and 100 million in current value.
He never owned real estate worth more
than the rental on his Pearl Street
office. The NYPD's response to Parker,
in retrospect, looks bewildered. The
first complaint reached a precinct in
1888, a second in 1891, a third in 1894.
By 1900, the department was receiving
approximately one fraud complaint per
month directly related to Parker. It did
not arrest him for any of them. The
victims, almost without exception, did
not file formal complaints.
They were immigrants. They did not speak
English. They were, in many cases, in
the country without complete
documentation.
Walking into a New York precinct in 1900
to report a fraud was more frightening
for the average immigrant than the loss
of the money.
By a 1932 Brooklyn Bar Association
study, fewer than 3% of Parker's victims
appear to have filed. The remaining 97%
disappeared into the city.
Parker's confederates were positioned
[music] to corroborate any deed. When a
victim did walk into a precinct, the
desk officer's first call was usually to
the Department of Public Works. Parker's
people by 1895 had bribed two clerks
inside the real department to confirm
for the duration of any single phone
call that the office in question was
real.
One Manhattan detective, in his
resignation letter to the NYPD in 1907,
described his last 11 years on the case
as the professional [music] pursuit of a
man whose office I have walked past more
than 700 times. He resigned without
making the arrest. In June 1911, the
NYPD attempted what would later be
referred to as the Pearl Street
operation. A coordinated raid intended
to seize the office and arrest Parker
mid-transaction.
12 officers in plainclothes converged on
the address at 9:40 in the morning. The
office was empty. The printing press had
been moved, the seals were gone, the
wooden file cabinet had been emptied of
every document. Parker had been tipped
off approximately 6 hours earlier. The
route was never determined. He reopened
the office in the same room on a
different door on the 11th of July. The
NYPD's response by 1909 was not to
arrest Parker. [music] It was to assign
permanent foot patrols to the most sold
landmarks: Brooklyn Bridge, Grant's
Tomb, Madison Square Garden, the Statue
of Liberty after 1912. The patrols were
instructed to stop anyone arriving with
tools. Parker, in his 1928 [music]
court testimony, called this the most
expensive municipal compliment [music]
ever paid to a private citizen.
Parker was, in fact, arrested four
times. [music]
The first arrest came in 1908, 25 years
into his career. The complainant was a
Boston pharmaceutical heir who had
purchased the Brooklyn Bridge for $800
and, unlike most of Parker's victims,
had a lawyer.
What happened between Parker's arrest at
the office and his arrival at the
Battery Precinct 17 blocks later is
recorded in the arresting officer's
report. During the walk, Parker
attempted to sell the arresting officer
the Brooklyn Bridge. He had offered it
at $40 and the officer's [music]
silence. The officer declined. He filed
the offer as an addendum to the original
charge. Parker was sentenced to 1 year.
He served 8 months. He returned to Pearl
Street the same week he was released. He
raised his prices 15%.
The second arrest, 1916, ended in a
4-year sentence. Parker served two and
escaped from Auburn State Prison through
a tunnel that, according to the guard
who later confessed, had been excavated
by another prisoner who had taken a
kitchen job because Mr. Parker had
purchased him the position.
The third arrest, 1923, resulted in a
6-year sentence at Sing Sing.
Parker escaped during a routine
transfer, [music] walking out of a train
car wearing what was described in the
departmental review as items of clothing
not originally his.
He rode a regional rail line into
Canada. He returned voluntarily 18
months later, having found Toronto, in
his own description, too quiet for an
Irishman of feeling.
He resumed the operation immediately. By
1927, Parker was 67. The Pearl Street
office had been operating for 44 years.
Two of his three original actors [music]
were dead. The third, by then in his
80s, was still arriving every morning in
a green visor. Two years earlier, the
New York State Legislature had passed
the habitual offender act. The act
required automatic life imprisonment for
any fourth felony conviction. The fourth
arrest came on April 16th, 1928.
A Manhattan assistant district attorney
had spent the previous 14 months
building the case. He had located three
immigrant victims, now naturalized
[music]
citizens with English fluency and
lawyers. He had identified by a former
public works employee turned witness,
the two clerks who had been
corroborating Parker's calls for 20
years. The arrest team entered the Pearl
Street office at 11:40 in the morning.
Parker was at his desk. The third actor,
the engineer in the green visor, now 83,
was at the back counter. Parker was in
the middle of preparing a deed. The
customer across from him was a New
Jersey school teacher who had inherited
$11,000 [music]
and had decided to invest the entire sum
in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. She
had not yet signed. When the officers
identified themselves, Parker turned to
her, apologized for the interruption,
and told her the transaction would be
completed within the week by [music] a
colleague at a different address. He
then asked the arresting officer if he
could finish writing the deed. The
officer declined. [music]
The school teacher was not arrested. She
received her $11,000 back in cash from
the desk drawer. The trial opened in the
Manhattan Court of General Sessions on
December 11th. The courtroom held 320
people. The press section was full. The
public gallery by the second day
contained approximately 50 individuals
whom court reporters identified [music]
as former victims attending out of
curiosity.
Parker conducted his own defense. His
opening statement, preserved in the
trial transcript, [music]
was a single paragraph. Your Honor, the
prosecution will argue that I have, for
45 years, sold property that does not
belong to me.
I will not contest this point. I will
simply ask [music] the court to consider
how much joy I have given to a city of
strangers.
How many stories I have furnished for
the children of the people who paid me?
And how many of the gentlemen in this
room would prefer the New York of 1928
to a New York in which no man like me
had ever lived?
>> The courtroom was, by the New York Times
coverage the following morning, silent
for approximately [music]
7 seconds.
The presiding judge sentenced George C.
Parker on December 17th, 1928 to life
imprisonment at Sing Sing. Parker
laughed. The transcript [music] records
the next exchange. The judge asked him,
for the record, if he wished to make a
final statement.
>> Your Honor, I would, but I have already
sold the courtroom.
>> Parker served 8 years at Sing Sing. He
was, by every account from prison staff
who later spoke to journalists, the most
popular prisoner in the institution. He
was given the job of running the prison
library. He spent his evenings
instructing other prisoners, for free,
on the elements of a properly [music]
constructed forged document.
He told them, in a phrase the Sing Sing
warden later quoted to a 1934 Saturday
Evening Post profile, that the only
honest thing a man can produce in this
country is a confession.
The Sing Sing chaplain, in a 1935 letter
to a seminary classmate, wrote [music]
that Parker's classes were better
attended than Sunday services. 24 of his
known students went on, after release,
to careers the New York Times would
track, in a 1948 retrospective, across
nine American cities. Parker did not
produce a confession. He maintained that
everything he had done had been a public
service.
His logic, articulated in a 1932
interview with the New York Sun,
>> "I have given more entertainment to the
American people than any actor on
Broadway.
The bridge was the cheapest theater in
this country.
For $500,
a man could come from Hamburg to New
York, buy the most famous bridge in the
world,
find out from the New York Police
Department that he had been cheated, and
have a story he could tell at his own
wedding."
>> He died at Sing Sing on June 25th, 1936,
at the age of 76. The cause of death was
congestive heart failure. He was reading
on his hospital cot a Brooklyn Eagle
article about himself published the
previous Sunday. It was the 78th feature
about him to have been published during
his lifetime. The obituary that ran the
following Tuesday contained one sentence
that would be quoted in every subsequent
account.
The man who sold America's most famous
bridge died as he lived, owing rent. His
funeral was held in Brooklyn on June
28th, 1936.
Approximately [music] 1,200 mourners,
among them, by the Brooklyn Eagle
photographer's count, four Sing Sing
guards in civilian dress, a delegation
from the Tony Pastor Vaudeville Alumni
Association, one elderly woman who had
purchased the Brooklyn Bridge in 1894
and brought a small framed copy of her
deed, and six men who had been Parker's
victims and had paid for the burial
expenses out of their own pockets. The
journalist asked them why. One of the
six, an Italian-born tailor who had
purchased the Statue of Liberty from
Parker in 1911 for $200, said one
sentence, "Because we are the only proof
he ever existed." The Brooklyn Bridge,
purchased [music] an estimated thousand
times in the previous half century,
remained on the morning of his funeral
the property of the city of New York.
The American English idiom, if you
believe that I have a bridge to sell
you, first documented in print in 1908,
20 years before Parker's final
conviction, has not in the 90 years
since his death gone out of common use.
It has in the same 90 years never been
credibly traced to any other man.

title: The Female Spy Who Stole the Soviet Union's Most Secret Jet
channelDescription: Just history, told clearly and honestly.

text:
Operation Diamond story — the true true story of how a single female Mossad operative, whose real name remains classified sixty years later, stole the Soviet Union's most secret fighter jet without ever touching it — by spending eleven months befriending the wife of an Iraqi pilot. Baghdad, spring 1965. A European woman in her late twenties sits in a small bar in the Hindiyya district, reading a Greek travel magazine. She does not look at the Iraqi Air Force officer at the next table — one of only five pilots in Iraq qualified to fly the MiG-21.

Her cover name was Lisa Brat. Her real name has never been released by any government on Earth. The Israeli archives remain sealed to this day.

She was not the first operative sent to steal a MiG-21. She was the sixth. The five before her had failed — and five people were dead.

This is the full story of Operation Diamond: the most audacious intelligence operation of the Cold War, and the one that handed Israel the aircraft that would help win the Six-Day War. In the early 1960s, the MiG-21 was the most secret fighter jet outside the Soviet Union. Israel had none. The CIA, after seven years of trying, had never seen one up close. The Mossad director, Meir Amit, gave the operation an unlimited budget and a single objective: get one intact.

The first five attempts ended in catastrophe. An agent hanged in Cairo. A pilot killed in São Paulo. A pilot shot in a Texas bar. A pilot killed in Baghdad after refusing to defect. A pilot thrown from a moving train in West Germany after trying to renegotiate his fee. Five attempts. Five bodies. No aircraft.

So Meir Amit authorized a sixth approach that used none of these methods. One woman, working alone, with no operational contact for six months — building a relationship not with a pilot, but with a pilot's wife.

Her target was Captain Munir Redfa: a Chaldean Catholic, restricted by his commanders because of his religion, ordered to fly napalm runs over Kurdish villages in the north of Iraq. A man with every reason to feel betrayed by the country he served. This is how she found him. How she spent eleven months never mentioning Israel, the jet, or money. What she said to him on a beach in Greece that the three operatives before her could not. How, on August 16, 1966, Munir Redfa flew his MiG-21 across three borders and landed it in Israel. And how the jet he delivered was studied, flown against, and used to rewrite Israeli air combat doctrine — eleven months before the Six-Day War.

Munir Redfa lived the rest of his life under an assumed name. The woman who recruited him was never publicly identified. Sixty years later, her file is still sealed.

We may never know her real name. We only know what she did.

When Munir Redfa was on duty at

sometimes four,
>> [music]
>> the two women dined together.

In June 1966,

>> I went to Greece every August.
>> I was thinking about taking Betty and

>> In late July 1966, the Redfa family flew
from Baghdad to Athens.
Lisa Bratt was at the airport to meet
them.
They went to Mykonos. Three days of

The brother-in-law was named Stanislaw.
He was 45. He spoke Polish-accented
English. He was, by Lisa's earlier

Munir answered. The questions were

answer. He asked, eventually, who was

Lisa Bratt.
And two other people in Tel Aviv.
How do you get my family out of Iraq?

Iraq for 11 years. His name is on no
list.
He has, by our account, 17 members of
your extended family willing to travel.
He can put them in trucks within 96
hours of your signal. The Kurdish
leadership in the north has agreed to
escort them to the Iranian border. Munir
did not answer immediately. He looked at
Lisa. Lisa Bratt reached into her
handbag. She removed an Israeli
passport. She placed it on the table
face up. The photograph in the passport
was Munir's. The name on it was Moshe
Mizrahi. The date of issue was eight
months earlier. The implication was
specific. The Mossad had been preparing
Munir's defection for eight months
before this conversation. He had been
their target the moment Lisa Bratt sat
down next to Betty in the Greek
ambassador's salon. [music]
The three operatives before Lisa had
died because they had asked their pilots
to make a a decision in a single
conversation. [music] Lisa had asked
Munir instead to make 80 conversations
with his wife and to find at the end of
the 80th that the decision had already
been made for him. Munir picked up the
passport. He looked at the photograph.
He looked at the date. He said one
sentence.
>> You knew?
>> Lisa Bratz did not deny it. What
happened in the next 90 days has been
reconstructed from three Mossad
operational files declassified between
2008 and 2017.
Munir Redfa returned to Baghdad alone on
August 6th, 1966.
Betty Redfa did not return. She remained
in Greece with the children under the
impression that the family was extending
the vacation.
In Iraq, the operative named Ezra Zelka,
born in Mosul, a Jew, fled to Israel in
1951, returned to Iraq in 1955 under a
forged Sunni identity, was running the
family extraction.
Zelka had spent four months building a
list. 17 Redfa relatives, brothers,
sisters, parents, in-laws, three
cousins, a great-aunt, [music]
two nephews.
Each had been quietly told by a relative
they trusted that an emergency was
coming and that they would need to move
quickly when the signal arrived. On the
morning of August 12th, 1966,
Zelka began calling the relatives in
sequence. Each was given the same
instruction. Pack one suitcase, bring
the children, drive north toward
Kurdistan within 12 hours. Do not return
for forgotten items.
16 of the 17 left within 48 hours.
One, Munir's eldest cousin, a colonel in
the Iraqi Army's logistics branch,
refused. He was, in subsequent Mossad
communications, listed as compromised
but not [music] active. The remaining 16
reached the Kurdish stronghold of Mount
Hamrin by August 14th. Mustafa Barzani's
Peshmerga forces escorted them across
the Iranian border on the morning of
August 15th.
In Paris, on the morning of August 16th,
the day of the flight, Lisa Bratt sat
down with Betty Redfa in a Mossad safe
house [music] in the 7th arrondissement.
She told Betty what was happening.
Betty's reaction is recorded in the
Mossad debrief. She tried to leave. She
said she would go to the Iraqi embassy.
She said her husband had been kidnapped.
She said her children were in danger.
Lisa Bratt told her three things. That
Munir had flown to Israel that morning
of his own choice.
That Betty's parents, two brothers,
three sisters, and most of her in-laws
had crossed the Iranian border the day
before.
That if Betty walked into the Iraqi
embassy, her husband would be killed by
Iraqi intelligence within 72 hours.
Betty did not go to the embassy.
She did not, by the same debrief, speak
to Lisa Bratt again for the next 3 days.
What happened in the air on August 16th,
1966?
The 70 minutes between Habbaniyah and
Hatzor is documented in the operational
records of the Israeli Air Force.
Lisa Bratt is not in those records. Her
work, by the morning of August 16th, had
been finished for 11 days. Munir Redfa
lifted off from Habbaniyah at 11:00 a.m.
Iraqi time on a routine training sortie.
He climbed to 15,000 ft and turned west.
Jordan's air defense system detected the
unexpected westward heading at 11:23
a.m. The Jordanian command contacted
Syrian air defense. Syria, not aware of
the situation, replied, "Do not worry.

Jordanians scrambled two Hawker Hunters
anyway. They could not catch a MiG-21
climbing at 9,000 m.
At 11:58 a.m., Munir Redfa crossed the
Israeli border.
Two Israeli Air Force Mirage IIIs were
waiting for him. On the agreed radio
frequency, an Arabic song played,
"Marhaban, Marhaban, welcome."
At 12:11 p.m., the MiG-21 landed at
Hatzor Airbase. The aircraft had
approximately 40 seconds of fuel
remaining when it touched down. The tail
number painted on the aircraft by the
Israeli Air Force technical crew two
weeks later was 007.
The actor Sean Connery, visiting Israel
six months after the operation, was
photographed standing in front of the
aircraft. The fighter the CIA had been
trying to capture for seven years was
sitting in a hangar in central Israel by
the afternoon of August 16th, 1966.
Lisa Bratt, [music] that afternoon, was
in Paris.
By the end of August, she had returned
to her cover identity in Athens. By
February 1967,
she had been withdrawn from Mossad
operational service entirely. She does
not appear in any photograph from the
operation. She does not appear in any
debrief that the Mossad has so far
chosen to release.
She had spent 486 days in Baghdad as a
Greek textile dealer. She had attended
80 meetings with Betty [music] Redfa.
She had introduced her once on a beach
in Greece to the man who would conclude
the operation. She had not, in 11
months, told a single lie that could not
be defended as an inconsistency in her
cover.
In January 1968,
16 months after the landing at Hatzor,
the Israeli Air Force shipped the MiG-21
to the United States. The aircraft was
flown for 4 months at a US Air Force
test facility in Nevada that was, in
1968, not publicly acknowledged to
exist. The American code name for the
program was Have
>> [music]
>> Donut. The aircraft was given the
designation YF-110.
US test pilots discovered three critical
flaws in the MiG-21: a massive blind
spot directly behind the pilot seat, a
14-second engine spool-up time from idle
to maximum thrust, a visible fuel vapor
signature from the afterburner that
betrayed the aircraft's position at
night.
The findings became the foundation of
two new American programs. The first,
established at Naval Air Station
Miramar, California, in 1969, was named
the Navy Fighter Weapons School.
The pilots called it Top Gun.
The second, established at Nellis Air
Force Base in 1975,
was named Red Flag. In return for access
to the MiG-21, the United States lifted
its long-standing embargo on advanced
weapon sales to Israel. The first sale
[music] in 1968 was the F-4 Phantom, 25
aircraft, then 40, then more than 100
over the next decade. Eight months
before the Six-Day War of June 1967,
using only the months of analysis that
the Israeli Air Force had been able to
conduct between August 1966 and the war,
Israeli pilots flying Mirage IIIs shot
down six Syrian MiG-21s over the Golan
Heights without losing a single
aircraft. The score was 6 to 0. It was
the first major air engagement after the
operation. It set the pattern for the
entire 1967 War. Iraq, in the wake of
the defection, banned all Christians
from the Iraqi Air Force. The ban
remained in place for 37 years. It was
lifted in 2003.
Munir Redfa lived in Israel for
approximately six years. In 1973, he and
Betty changed their names a second time
and were relocated by joint arrangement
of the Mossad and the West German
intelligence service to a small European
country where they ran a gas station for
the rest of his working life. They never
spoke publicly about the operation.
Munir Redfa died of a heart attack in
approximately 1998.
He was 64 years old. His grave is, by
the family's request, unmarked. His
children continue to live under assumed
names. The MiG-21 with tail number 007
was returned to Israel in 1972.
It sits today in the Israeli Air Force
Museum at Hatzerim in the Negev.
Children climb on it.
Ezra Zelka, the operative who built the
17-person extraction list and shepherded
16 relatives across the Iranian border,
returned to Israel in 1968 after his
Iraqi cover became unsustainable. He
died in Tel Aviv in 1999.
Zev Liran, the head of Israeli Air Force
intelligence who had played the retired
Polish pilot in the Mykonos bar, lived
until 2014.
He gave a single on-record interview to
the Yedioth Ahronoth daily in 2008. He
referred to Lisa Bratt in the interview
only as the operative. Lisa Bratt does
not appear in any Israeli, American,
Arab, or European newspaper or
documentary [music] released in the 60
years since the operation. The Israeli
State Archives in 2009, 2014,
2019, and 2024
have all declined to release any
document that names her.
Two journalists, Yossi Melman in 1988
and Ronen Bergman in 2014, [music]
have published independent claims that
they have learned her real name through
unofficial channels. Both have declined
to print it. Bergman, in his 2018 book
on the Mossad, wrote one sentence on the
subject. "I know who she is. She has
asked, in writing, that I not say."
The most successful single agent
operation in the history of the Israeli
intelligence service was conducted by a
person whose name has not been published
in any language on Earth. A European
woman in her late 20s, with no recorded
accent and no [music] recorded
biography, who spent 486 days becoming a
friend of one Iraqi woman in a Baghdad
salon, and walked away at the end of it
with the most secret fighter jet of the
Cold War. She never appears by name in
any of the histories. She is the most
consequential Mossad operative whose
existence the Israeli state has chosen,
for 60 years, not to confirm.

text:
Joseph Jagger Monte Carlo story — the true story of how a Yorkshire mill mechanic with four years of schooling found a hidden flaw in the world's biggest casino's roulette wheels and legally won the equivalent of seven million dollars in 1881. In the summer of 1881, a fifty-year-old factory mechanic from Halifax named Joseph Jagger walked into the Casino de Monte-Carlo with an empty leather notebook in his pocket.

He had never gambled in his life. He had never crossed the English Channel. He had spent twenty-five years repairing spinning wheels inside a wool mill.

But Joseph Jagger understood one thing that the casino's mathematicians never had: no spinning machine is ever perfectly balanced. Every wheel — every single one — has a microscopic imperfection. A worn bearing. An off-center axle. A flaw too small to see, but not too small to measure.

He sent six clerks to record every number that came up on every wheel, for weeks. Then he read the data. And on one specific wheel, in one specific room, nine numbers were coming up far more often than chance allowed.

The wheel was biased. The casino had no idea.

This is the full story of how a working-class engineer from West Yorkshire quietly beat the most profitable building in Europe — the casino that funded an entire country, that employed more people than Monaco had citizens, that was believed to be mathematically unbeatable. How he turned twenty-five years of listening to factory machines into a system no gambler had ever tried. How the casino finally caught on and secretly moved every wheel in the building overnight to stop him. And why, for the next hundred years, no casino on Earth ever left a roulette wheel unwatched again.

He walked in with an empty notebook. He walked out with two million francs.
