subtitles.plaintext:
Monte Carlo, the summer of 1881.
A gray-haired Yorkshireman walks into
the Casino de Monte Carlo. His name is
Joseph Jagger. He's 50 years old. He's a
mill mechanic from Halifax. In his
pocket, a small leather notebook, empty.
Jagger isn't a gambler. He's a mechanic.
A man who has spent 25 years repairing
spinning wheels in a wool mill, carding
frames, roving spindles, looms running
14 hours a day. But in 2 weeks, he's
going to walk out of the largest casino
in Europe with 2 million francs.
Casino de Monte Carlo, owned by the
Blanc family, guaranteed reserve in
every table, backup vault under the
building, the most profitable building
in continental Europe, [music] backed by
the Principality of Monaco itself. Every
croupier on the floor knows this casino
could not lose. It has never been beaten
by an engineer. Never. By the second
week, croupiers at one table will be
losing money to one quiet Englishman
every day. By the end of the month, the
casino will be moving every roulette
wheel in the room at night after
closing. And for the next 100 years, no
European casino will leave a wheel
unwatched again. Because Joseph Jagger
heard something in those wheels the
casino's mathematicians never could.
To understand what happened in that
casino, you have to understand the man
who walked through the door. Joseph
Hobson Jagger, born September 2nd, 1830.
Cockhill Shelf, a small village outside
Halifax in West Yorkshire. His father
raised cattle. His mother kept the
house. Jagger had 4 years of parish
school. That was the end of his formal
education. At 14, he started working in
a wool mill. Halifax in the mid-1800s
was the wool capital of the world.
Smoke, steam, spindles spinning at 5,000
revolutions [music]
per minute, carding wheels, roving
frames, looms shaking the floorboards.
Jagger's job was to keep the machines
running. By his 20s, he was a foreman
mechanic. By his 30s, he was the man the
mill called when no one else could fix
something. By his 40s, he had spent more
time inside textile machinery than most
engineers spend inside any single object
in their lives. There is one detail that
matters above all the others. A man who
fixes spinning wheels for a living
develops an ear for them. He can tell,
from sound alone, when a spindle is out
of balance. No instruments, just 25
years of memory. He knew, the way few
people in the world knew, that no
machine is ever truly perfectly
balanced. Every spinning thing has
microscopic imperfections, wear in the
wood, a bearing slightly off center, a
bracket that loosened [music] over time.
To the eye, the machine looks identical
to the day it was installed. To the ear,
it sounds slightly different. In the
late 1870s, sitting in a smoke-filled
room in Halifax, Jagger started turning
the question around. If a spinning wheel
can be off balance, what about a
roulette wheel? He had never gambled in
his life. He had never crossed the
English Channel. He had a quiet life, a
family, modest savings. He had a theory
that no engineer had ever tested. He
took two people with him, his son
Alfred, his nephew Oates Jagger. Three
men, three notebooks, and a one-way
train to the South Coast.
To understand why no one had tested
Jagger's theory before him, you have to
understand what the Casino de Monte
Carlo was in 1880. The casino had opened
in 1863.
By the time Jagger walked through its
doors 20 years later, it was the most
profitable single building in Europe. It
was owned by the Blanc family. François
Blanc had run the casino at Bad Homburg
in Germany for 30 years.
When Bismarck banned gambling across
Germany in 1872, Blanc moved his
operation south. There, he found a
desperate man, Charles III, Prince of
Monaco. Monaco was bankrupt. The royal
family had run out of land to sell and
tax to collect. Charles signed Blanc an
exclusive 50-year gambling concession.
The deal saved Monaco from extinction.
The casino became the principality.
Without it, there was no army, no roads,
no treasury. Every croupier and cleaner
on the floor knew this. The casino could
not lose.
Roulette in 1880 worked the way it had
since the 1790s.
A wheel of 37 numbered pockets, a small
ivory ball. The croupier spins the wheel
one direction, the ball the other. A
player who bets on a single number gets
paid 35 to 1.
The true odds are 36 to 1 because of the
zero.
That 2.7% gap [music] is the house edge.
Played indefinitely, the house wins,
always.
This is why every casino mathematician
in Europe agreed on a single principle.
A balanced roulette wheel cannot be
beaten.
The Blanc family took this principle
seriously. The wheels were inspected
monthly, disassembled, cleaned,
rebalanced by professional mechanics.
Tolerances measured to fractions of a
millimeter.
The casino had a phrase the croupiers
said quietly to each other on slow
nights. The wheel doesn't lie.
But here is what every mathematician at
the Casino de Monte Carlo missed. A
balanced roulette wheel cannot be
beaten. A wheel that is not perfectly
balanced can be.
Microscopic mechanical defects creep
into any rotating machine over time. The
wood frame warps a fraction of a
millimeter in the dry Mediterranean air.
A bearing wears unevenly. A bracket
loosens by a thread of a turn. The
result is that some sections of the
wheel, some clusters of pockets, collect
the ball slightly more often than
others. To the eye, the wheel looks
perfect. To the mathematics, it should
be perfect. To the engineering, it
isn't.
But in 1880, the casino was not staffed
by engineers. It was staffed by
mathematicians and accountants and
trained croupiers. The mechanics who
serviced the wheels were craftsmen, not
theorists. Nobody had ever connected the
two worlds. To find a biased wheel, you
had to think like a man who had spent
his career listening to wool spindles.
You had to think like Joseph Jagger. And
in the early 1880s, three Englishmen
walked into the casino and didn't place
a single bet.
Jagger arrived in Monte Carlo with a
plan that had two phases. The first
phase was observation. He took cheap
accommodation outside the principality
where strangers attracted less
attention.
Each morning, he and Alfred and Oates
paid the modest entrance fee, took their
seats at the roulette tables, and
ordered nothing.
The casino's main rooms held six wheels.
Jagger's instructions to his companions
were precise. Sit at one wheel for as
long as the body allows. Watch every
spin. Record every number. Do not place
bets. Do not speak. Do not look at each
other across the room. By the end of the
first week, they had thousands of
numbers logged in pocket notebooks. By
the end of the second, far more. Each
evening, Jagger walked back to the
lodging with all three notebooks under
his coat. He laid them out on a small
table. He found a pencil and paper. He
started counting. [music]
If a roulette wheel is perfectly
balanced, each of the 37 numbers should
land roughly the same percentage of the
time. Statistical noise, no pattern over
thousands of spins.
Jagger went through the data [music]
wheel by wheel. Five of the six behaved
as a balanced wheel should. The sixth
was different. A cluster of numbers in
one section of that wheel was landing
significantly more often than the rest.
>> [music]
>> Not dramatically. Not in a way any pit
boss would notice. Just enough to break
the assumption that the casino was built
on. The wheel was [music] biased.
Jagger sat with his pencil and his data
and a cup of cooling coffee and he
understood what he was looking at. A
microscopic mechanical defect. The kind
of thing he had been seeing in textile
machinery his entire working life.
Probably a slight warp in the frame.
Probably wear on one side of the
bearing. Something the casino's monthly
inspection had missed because the
inspection was looking for visible
damage, not statistical drift. In
Halifax, this would have been a problem
to fix. He would have [music] walked
into the mill manager's office and
ordered the machine rebuilt. In Monte
Carlo, he didn't say a word. He folded
the notebooks. He blew out the candle.
He went to sleep. The next morning, the
second phase began. Jagger walked into
the casino alone. He went straight to
the sixth wheel and sat down. He took
out a small purse of francs. He placed
his first bet on one of the cluster of
biased numbers. The croupier spun the
wheel. The ball landed inside the
cluster. 35 to 1. He bet again. The next
spin landed outside. Lost. Bet again.
Inside. Bet again. Inside. This is how
the second phase began. Not with a
single dramatic strike, with slow,
steady accumulation. Bet after bet, hour
after hour. Some won, some lost. The
bias did not guarantee that any
individual spin would land in the
cluster, only that over hundreds of
spins the cluster would land slightly
more often than chance would predict.
That slight edge applied for hours was
enough. By the end of the first day,
Jagger was significantly ahead. By the
end of the third day, he was up by an
amount that would have funded a small
mill in Halifax for a year. By the end
of the first week, the casino noticed.
The Casino de Monte Carlo had seen every
kind of gambler. System players, men
with notebooks of their own betting
according to martingales and
progressions. The casino loved them. The
math was never on their side. Streak
runners, men who got hot, won 20,000
[music] francs in a night, then chased
it back across the table empty-handed.
Cheats, loaded chips, magnetic [music]
balls, dealers paid off. The casino had
detectives whose entire job was watching
[music] for these. They were good at it.
They had never seen a man like Joseph
Jagger.
Jagger sat at the same wheel every day.
He bet only on the same small cluster of
numbers. He did not signal. He did not
switch tables. He did not get angry when
he lost or excited when he won. He just
sat and he won. Not on every spin, not
even on most spins, but over the course
of a day, over hundreds of spins, he won
more than he lost by an amount small
enough that no croupier could call it
suspicious, but large enough that the
casino's daily ledger started to bend.
The pit bosses watched him. They saw
nothing. The casino's standard
countermeasures all assumed an active
cheat, a confederate, a device, a
system. Jagger had none of these. He
just sat and counted his chips.
By the second week, the daily reports
were showing a consistent loss
attributable to a single Englishman at a
single wheel. This was not a casino that
tolerated consistent losses. [music]
The Blanc family's management considered
the options. They could ban Jagger, but
on what grounds? He was a paying
customer. He had broken no rules. To
eject him would be to admit the casino
had a problem it did not understand, and
word travels. They could close the wheel
for maintenance, but this would tell
every observer in the room that
something was wrong with that specific
wheel. The casino's mathematical aura,
the [music] wheel doesn't lie, would
crack. So, they did something they had
never done before. Quietly, at night,
after the casino closed, they sent for
the maintenance crew. They had the crew
remove the roulette wheels from their
tables, and they had the wheels swapped,
placed back on different tables in
different positions in the room. The
wood and felt tables stayed in their
fixed positions. The croupiers came in
the next morning to the same stations.
Nothing about the room looked different,
but the wheels themselves had been
rotated. The biased wheel was no longer
at the table where Jagger had been
sitting. It was somewhere else in the
room.
Jagger walked into the casino the next
morning. He went to the same table where
he had been winning all week. He sat in
the same chair. He took out his francs.
He placed his first bet on one of the
cluster. The ball landed somewhere else.
He bet again, lost, bet again, lost. By
the end of the third hour, he was down
significantly. By the end of the day, he
had given back a meaningful fraction of
what he had won the week before. He sat
at the table as the casino lights
dimmed. He looked at the empty chips in
front of him. He did not know yet what
had happened. He only knew that the
wheel he was sitting at was no longer
the wheel he had been winning at.
Jagger walked out of the casino that
evening and sat at the bar of his
lodging across the border. He took his
notebooks out of his coat. He laid them
on the wooden counter. He turned to the
page where he had recorded the bias data
from the original observation week. The
pattern was on the page. One cluster.
One specific section of one specific
wheel. He had not been wrong. The bias
had been real.
He had won for a week on the strength of
it.
What had changed?
This is the part of the story where the
engineer's mind matters more than any
gambler's intuition.
Jagger had spent 25 years inside textile
machinery, knowing that machinery is not
magic.
Mechanical objects are physical things.
They can be moved, swapped, replaced,
repaired, and rebuilt in ways that look
invisible if you are not paying
attention.
He thought about the room. He thought
about the wheels. He thought about who
in the casino had the access and the
motivation to do something about a
single profitable Englishman. And he
understood. The table he had been
sitting at, the felt, the chairs, the
fixed location in the room, was the
same. But the actual wheel mounted into
the table had been changed. The biased
wheel was still in the room. It just
wasn't in front of him anymore.
Jagger walked back into the casino the
following morning. He did not sit at his
usual table. He walked the floor,
slowly.
He looked at each of the six wheels. He
was looking for a marker, a scratch on
the wood, a worn pattern, a maker's
stamp, something physical that
distinguished the biased wheel from its
five neighbors.
He found it.
He sat down at the table where the
biased wheel had been moved. He placed
his first bet on the cluster.
The ball landed inside. He won. He bet
again. Inside. Bet again. Inside.
By the end of that day, Jagger had
recovered most of what he had lost the
day before. The casino now understood
what they were dealing with. The Blanc
family had attempted a quiet, invisible
countermeasure, and the Englishman had
simply walked the room and found the
wheel they had hidden from him.
Whatever method he was using, it was
tied not to the table or the chair, but
to a specific physical wheel that he
could identify by sight alone.
The casino now had a different problem
to solve. They could no longer just move
the wheel. They had to fix it.
They sent the maintenance crew back in.
This time, the work took longer. Each of
the six wheels was disassembled, the
frames inspected, the bearings checked.
Anything worn or warped was replaced.
Each wheel was rebalanced to fresh
tolerance. The bias was gone.
When Jagger walked back into the casino
the next morning, his marked wheel was
still in the room. He could still find
it. He sat down at it. He placed his
first bet on the cluster. The ball
landed somewhere else. Bet again. Lost.
Bet again. Lost. The bias had been real.
The wheel had been physical. The casino
had been fooled, briefly, by a man who
understood machinery better than any of
their mathematicians.
But the casino, given enough time, could
fix any machine.
Jagger played small for a few more
hours. He broke roughly even. He stood
up. He paid his cashier slip. He counted
his stack of banknotes. He had won an
amount that no English engineer had ever
seen. It was time to go home.
Approximately 2 million [music] francs,
roughly 80,000 pounds, 10 million in
today's money. Jagger packed it into
banknotes, boarded a train north. Alfred
and Oats went with him. The casino never
publicly admitted what had happened.
They paid him out in full and let him
walk through the front door. But
quietly, they changed their procedures.
Within a few years, every casino in
Europe was rotating its wheels between
tables on a regular schedule. The biased
wheel exploit was killed by the man who
invented it. Jagger came home in the
summer of 1881. He did not return to the
wool mill. He did not start a business.
He did not invest in shipping or
railroads. He bought houses. Records in
the Calderdale Council archives show the
family acquired several modest homes in
Little Horton, Bradford. Tradesmen's
houses,
>> [music]
>> quiet streets.
He gave no interviews. He published no
method. He never returned to Monte
Carlo. He simply went home.
Joseph Hobson Jagger died on April 25th,
1892
Diabetes. In his own bed in West
Yorkshire. 61 years old. He left a will.
He left an estate. He did not leave a
method.
10 years after his win, Charles Wells
walked into the same casino and broke
the bank 11 times in 11 hours. Wells was
[music] arrested for fraud the following
year. He died in poverty in 1922.
Jagger had died 30 years earlier, free,
in his own house, on his own terms. He
is the only known gambler to have beaten
the Casino de Monte Carlo at scale and
walked away clean.
A century later in Madrid, the Garcia
Pelayo family used the same method to
win over a million euros at Casino Gran
Madrid. Spanish courts ruled it legal.
>> [music]
>> Observation is not cheating.
Asked how a musician beat the casinos,
Garcia Pelayo said, "Engineers don't
believe in luck."
Joseph Jagger, a man who fixed wool
spinning wheels for 25 years, walked
into the largest casino in Europe,
counted thousands of spins, walked out
with 2 million francs, and went home.

text:
How a Vietnamese Rice Farmer DESTROYED the US Air Force

On December 2nd, 1967, American F-4 Phantom II fighter jets, the most advanced aircraft of their time, clashed with Soviet MiG-21s in the skies above Hanoi during the Vietnam War. Despite the technological disparity, Vietnamese pilots, with a fraction of the training, were winning engagements. This video highlights the intense dogfight encounters and the surprising outcomes.

In 1967, the US Air Force brought the most advanced fighter jet in the world to the skies of Vietnam—the $2.5 million F-4 Phantom. Armed with cutting-edge radar and beyond-visual-range missiles, it was supposed to be invincible. But the Pentagon was about to learn a brutal lesson from an unlikely enemy.

Meet Nguyen Van Coc, a 23-year-old son of a rice farmer with just 120 hours of flight training. Piloting a cheaper, outdated Soviet MiG-21, he executed a brilliant "guerrilla air warfare" tactic to ambush American formations, shoot down nine US aircraft, and become the most successful fighter ace of the entire Vietnam War.

From Robin Olds' legendary Operation Bolo to the exact 60-second hit-and-run tactic that paralyzed American commanders and ultimately forced the creation of the TOP GUN program, this is the unbelievable true story of the ultimate David vs. Goliath aerial battle.

If you enjoyed this deep dive into military history, please LIKE the video and SUBSCRIBE to the channel for more incredible true stories!

December 2nd, 1967.
The sky above Hanoi.
American F-4 Phantoms, the most advanced
fighters in the world. Two and a half
million dollars each. Cutting edge
radar, six air-to-air missiles. Against
them, outdated Soviet MiG-21s, 1/8 the
price. Basic radar, two missiles, pilots
with a fraction of the training. On
paper, it's not even a fair fight, but
the Americans are losing. Vietnamese
pilots are shooting down Phantoms using
tactics the Pentagon can't understand.
Hit and run. Ambush from below.
Disappear into the clouds before the
Americans can react. And at the center
of it all, one man, Nguyen Van Coc, a
rice farmer's son, 23 years old. By the
end of 1967, he will have shot down nine
American aircraft, making him the most
successful fighter ace of the entire
Vietnam War. How did a pilot in an
outdated aircraft defeat the most
powerful air force in history? What
tactics did the Vietnamese discover that
the Americans couldn't counter? And how
did the lessons from these dogfights
change aerial combat forever? [music]
Let's dive in.
Nguyen Van Coc was born in 1944 in Nam
Dinh province, 90 km southeast of Hanoi.
His father grew rice. His mother raised
chickens. The family had never seen an
airplane up close.
In 1963, North Vietnam began recruiting
for the air force. Coc was 19. He
volunteered. Not because he was
patriotic, because he wanted to fly. Out
of 500 applicants, only 30 were chosen.
Coc made the cut.
>> [music]
>> In 1964, he was sent to the Soviet
Union, a secret training facility near
Krasnodar. This is where North
Vietnamese pilots learn to fly MiG-21s.
[music]
The training was brutal. The MiG 21 was
fast, agile, and unforgiving. Maximum
speed 2,100 km/h.
Combat radius 480 km. In a dogfight, you
had 15 minutes of fuel before you had to
return to base or die. The Soviets
taught them a simple doctrine. You
cannot win a prolonged fight with
American aircraft. They have better
radar, better missiles, more fuel. So,
strike fast, disappear faster. By late
1965, returned to North Vietnam.
Total flight time 120 hours. American
pilots arriving in Vietnam had over 500
hours. didn't care. He had a tactic
and he was about to test it against the
most powerful Air Force [music] in the
world.
The F-4 Phantom II was a monster.
Designed by McDonnell Douglas in the
late 1950s, it was built to do one
thing, destroy Soviet bombers before
they could reach American cities. It
could fly at twice the speed of sound.
It could climb to 18,000 m in under 2
minutes. It cost $2.4 million per
aircraft, roughly $23 million in today's
money.
It was equipped with the AN/APQ-72
radar system capable of tracking targets
up to 45 km away. It carried six AIM-7
Sparrow missiles designed to lock on to
enemy aircraft from beyond visual range
and destroy them before the pilot even
knew he was being hunted. But, it had
one critical flaw. It had no gun.
The designers believed the era of
dogfighting was over. Future air combat
would happen at long range. Missiles
would do all the work. Close quarters
combat was obsolete. They were wrong.
When the F-4 Phantom arrived in Vietnam
in 1965,
American commanders were confident. The
North Vietnamese Air Force had maybe 40
aircraft total, mostly obsolete [music]
MiG-17 and a handful of new MiG-21s.
The US had hundreds of Phantoms, plus
the best trained pilots in the world.
Air superiority was supposed to be
guaranteed within [music] months.
But the war in Vietnam wasn't fought at
45 km. It was fought in the clouds at
low altitude in close-range ambushes
where radar didn't work and missiles
couldn't lock on. And in that kind of
fight, the [music] F-4 Phantom wasn't
invincible. It was vulnerable.
The Americans called it hit and run. The
Vietnamese called it guerrilla air
warfare.
Here's how it was supposed to work.
American bombing missions over North
Vietnam followed predictable patterns.
Formations of F-105 Thunderchiefs,
heavily loaded attack aircraft, would
fly north from bases in Thailand.
They'd be escorted by F-4 Phantoms
flying cover above and behind.
The Americans had one major advantage,
airborne radar. Their radar could detect
enemy aircraft up to 45 km away, giving
them plenty of time to maneuver and
engage. But radar had a weakness. It
struggled to detect targets flying low,
close to the ground, where the signal
would be drowned out by ground clutter.
And it couldn't see through clouds. The
North Vietnamese planned to exploit
both. Ground control was the key.
The North Vietnamese built a network of
early warning radar stations across the
country, guided by Soviet advisers.
These stations would track American
formations from the moment they [music]
crossed into North Vietnamese airspace.
The information would be relayed to a
central command post in Hanoi,
code-named Bison. Bison would control
everything, [music]
when to launch the MiGs, what altitude
to fly, what direction [music] to
approach from. The MiG pilots wouldn't
make decisions. They would follow
orders. The plan was this. MiG-21s
[music] would take off and immediately
dive to low altitude, 500 m above the
ground, sometimes lower. Radars off.
Silent. Invisible to American detection.
The MiG-21 was small. On American radar,
flying low, it looked like ground
clutter. Bison would guide the MiGs into
position using ground radar. The MiGs
would hide in clouds or behind hills,
waiting. The Americans would fly
overhead, confident their radar was
clear.
>> the formation locked. Then Bison would
give the order. Climb and attack. The
MiGs would pull up vertically,
afterburners screaming. They'd emerge
from the clouds directly beneath the
American formation, the F-4's radar
blind spot. At close range, American
AIM-7 Sparrow missiles were useless.
They needed time to lock on. In a sudden
ambush, there was no time. The MiG-21's
Atoll missile had an effective range of
just 3 km, but a lock-on time of only 2
seconds.
Fire. Dive back into the clouds.
Disappear before the Americans could
react. Total engagement time, 60 to 90
seconds.
On paper, it was brilliant. But would it
actually work in combat? [music]
Could a farmer's son with 120 hours of
flight time execute this tactic against
the best-trained pilots [music] in the
world?
November 28th, 1966,
2:14 p.m. Gia Lam Airfield, Hanoi.
When Van has been a combat pilot
for 18 months. He's flown 47 sorties.
He's fired his weapons in anger exactly
three times. He's never hit anything.
Today, he will witness the tactic work
for the first time. The alarm sounds.
American strike package inbound. 12
F-105 Thunderchiefs escorted by four F-4
Phantoms
heading north toward the Paul Doumer
Bridge, a critical supply route the
Americans have been trying to destroy
for weeks. runs to his MiG-21, but
today he's not the primary shooter. His
flight leader is Win Nac Do, a senior
pilot with 3 years of combat experience.
is the wingman. His job, stay on
Do's wing, watch for threats, learn.
Pre-flight checks are fast. Fuel, full.
Missiles, two K-13 Atolls loaded.
Cannon, 60 rounds. Radio, working. He
straps in. Engine start. The Tumansky
R-11 turbojet roars to life. Ground
control, Bison, comes through his
headset.
Four aircraft, take off immediately. Fly
heading 180. Altitude, 500 m. Radar off.
doesn't question it. He never does.
The ground controllers see the whole
picture. He sees only what's in front of
his canopy. They take off. Do leads.
follows 2 seconds behind. They stay
low, skimming over rice paddies and
villages. American radar is looking for
targets at medium and high altitude.
Down here, they're invisible. Bison's
voice again. American formation bearing
045, distance 40 km, altitude 6,000 m.
Maintain current heading.
checks his fuel. He has maybe 12
minutes before he has to turn back. The
MiG-21 wasn't designed for long
missions. According to declassified
Soviet technical manuals, the aircraft's
internal fuel capacity gave it roughly
45 minutes of flight time under normal
conditions. In combat, with afterburner
use, that dropped to 15 minutes or less.
American pilots knew this. If they could
keep a MiG engaged for more than 10
minutes, it would run out of fuel and
have to disengage or crash. But, the
Vietnamese weren't planning to stay
engaged for 10 minutes. Target 20 km.
Begin climb. Afterburner.
Do pulls the throttle to full first.
follows. The afterburner kicks in.
The MiG-21 accelerates vertically at
over 200 m per second. The G-forces slam
them back into their seats. Vision
narrows. Breathing becomes difficult. 5
seconds later, they break through the
cloud layer at 5,500 m. And there they
are. Four F-4 Phantoms, 800 m ahead,
slightly above them. Flying in a loose
formation, scanning for threats. But,
they're looking forward and up, not
below. Do's targeting system locks on to
the nearest Phantom. A steady tone in
his headset. The pilot still hasn't seen
them. According to a 1984 US Air Force
study on Vietnam air combat, American
pilots reported that in 68% of MiG
ambush encounters, they had no radar
warning before the attack. The MiGs were
simply too close, too low, and moving
too fast for the F-4's radar to detect
them in time. Do doesn't hesitate. He
fires. The K-13 Atoll missile drops from
the rail, ignites, and streaks toward
the F-4. White smoke trail. The American
pilot sees it. Too late. He tries to
break left, but [music] the missile is
already there. The F-4 explodes.
watches it happen. The fireball. The
debris spinning through the air. The
other three Phantoms scattering, trying
to locate the threat. But, Do is already
diving. Throttle cut. Rolling inverted.
Disappearing back into the clouds.
follows, staying tight on his wing. The
other three Phantoms are already turning
toward where the MiGs had been. But by
the time they acquire a lock, there's
nothing there. Total time above the
clouds, 12 seconds. They level out at
500 [music] m, heading south, fuel gauge
blinking red, 4 minutes left. Gia Lam
Airfield is 35 km away. They make it
back with 90 seconds of fuel to spare.
When they land, the ground crew is
waiting. They've already heard the radio
chatter. One kill confirmed. An F-4
Phantom down. When Ngoc Do climbs out of
his cockpit, calm, professional. He's
done this before. climbs out of his
aircraft. His hands are shaking. His
flight suit is soaked with sweat. Not
from fear, from adrenaline, from the
realization that the tactic actually
works. He didn't fire a shot. He was
just the wingman, watching, learning.
But he knew soon it would be his turn.
That night Radio Hanoi announces the
shootdown. They don't mention names, but
in the Pentagon, analysts are trying to
figure out what the hell just happened.
According to declassified US military
records, between September and December
1966, American forces lost 43 aircraft
over North Vietnam. Of those, eight were
confirmed MiG kills. The loss rate was
climbing, and it was getting worse. The
North Vietnamese MiG tactics were
working, and Van had just seen
exactly how.
The Americans weren't going to just
accept defeat. After witnessing MiG-21s
successfully ambush their formations in
November and December 1966,
US military analysts began studying the
pattern.
The MiGs would attack when F-4 Phantoms
were escorting bombers, distracted,
protecting the slower F-105
Thunderchiefs. But they avoided engaging
pure F-4 fighter sweeps with no other
mission. Colonel Robin Olds saw an
opportunity. Olds was a World War II ace
with 13 confirmed kills against German
fighters. He was 44 years old,
aggressive, and frustrated. He'd been
leading fighter sweeps over North
Vietnam for months. The MiGs refused to
engage him. So, he decided to make them
engage. Operation Bolo. The plan was
deceptively simple. F-4 Phantoms would
disguise themselves as F-105 bombers.
Same flight paths, same altitudes, same
radio frequencies, same electronic
signatures. The North Vietnamese ground
controllers would see what looked like a
routine bombing raid, a vulnerable
target. But, when the MiGs attacked,
they'd find the best fighter pilots in
the US Air Force waiting for them.
January 2nd, 1967,
2:45 p.m. Olds leads a formation of 28
F-4 Phantoms toward Hanoi. They fly at
4,500 m, standard altitude for F-105
strike packages. They use F-105 call
signs. They follow the exact routes the
bombers normally take. On the ground,
North Vietnamese radar operators track
the formation. To them, it looks like
another American bombing run. Standard
response, scramble the MiGs. 16 MiG-21s
take off from Phúc Yên and Gia Lâm
airfields. Among them, some of North
Vietnam's best pilots. They climb to
intercept altitude expecting to find
slow, heavily loaded bombers with
distracted fighter escorts. Instead,
they find Robin Olds and 28 F-4s with
one mission, kill MiGs. The Vietnamese
realize their mistake within seconds,
but it's too late. Olds already has
altitude, speed, and position. The MiGs
try to execute their hit and run tactic,
climb, fire, dive away. But there's
nowhere to run. The sky is full of
Phantoms.
What happens next last exactly 12
minutes. Olds fires first. His AIM-7
Sparrow missile tracks a MiG-21 and
destroys it at medium range. His wingman
gets another, then another. The
Vietnamese pilots scatter trying to
escape into the clouds, but the
Americans are everywhere. Seven MiG-21s
are shot down. Zero American losses.
According to declassified US Air Force
after action reports, Operation Bolo
destroyed nearly half of North Vietnam's
operational MiG-21 fleet in a single
engagement. It remains the most
successful air-to-air operation of the
entire Vietnam War. It was a devastating
blow to the North Vietnamese Air Force,
but not a fatal one because Nguyen Van
Coc wasn't there.
He was scheduled to fly that day. His
MiG-21 was fueled, armed, and ready on
the tarmac at Gia Lam. But minutes
before takeoff, ground control
reassigned him to a different patrol
sector. Some historians believe it was
luck. Others argue the Vietnamese
controllers suspected something. The
American formation was too perfect, too
coordinated. Whatever the reason, Coc
stayed on the ground, and he survived.
Operation Bolo forced the North
Vietnamese to adapt. They became more
cautious. They stopped launching large
formations against obvious targets. They
waited for perfect opportunities,
moments when American defenses were
stretched thin or distracted. The tactic
didn't change, but the execution became
more selective, more patient. The 921st
Fighter Regiment was grounded for 3
months, retraining, recovering. The
Pentagon declared Operation Bolo a
decisive victory. The MiG threat was
neutralized, but was it really over? Or
had the Vietnamese just learned to be
more careful? And what would happen when
they returned to the sky? On April 30th,
1967,
the Americans would find out.
April 30th, 1967,
2:14 p.m., Gia Lam Airfield, Hanoi.
3 months after Operation Bolo, the 921st
Fighter Regiment is back.
The alarm sounds. American strike
package inbound.
Nguyen Van Coc runs to his MiG 21, but
this time, [music] he's not the wingman.
Today, he's number two in a
four-aircraft formation, his own target,
his own kill.
They take off, low altitude, clouds
waiting. Ground control guides them into
position.
Target 20 km, begin climb, afterburner.
Coc pulls up, breaks through the clouds
at 5,500 m. Four F-4 Phantoms ahead. He
locks on to the second aircraft. He
fires. The F-4 explodes. He dives back
into the clouds. Total time above, 12
seconds. When he lands, the ground crew
is waiting. Two kills confirmed. Nguyen
Ngoc Do got the other, but this time,
Coc is the one who pulled the trigger.
That night, Radio Hanoi announces his
name, the farmer's son from Nam Dinh,
his first kill.
Between April and December 1967,
Nguyen Van Coc flew 23 more combat
missions. October 3rd, kill number two,
an F-4D.
October 7th, kill number three, an
F-105.
November 18th, kills four and five, two
F-105s in a single mission, ace status.
His photograph appeared on propaganda
posters. Radio broadcasts called him
"Defender of the Sky."
Schoolchildren learned his name, but the
Americans were learning it, too.
According to declassified CIA reports,
US analysts began tracking individual
North Vietnamese pilots. Cock's call
sign, Red 3107, [music]
appeared repeatedly in after-action
reports. He was now a priority target.
American pilots were briefed, "If you
see a MiG-21 climbing vertically from
clouds, firing at close range,
disappearing immediately, it's probably
Kill him first."
But was careful. He never stayed
engaged longer than 60 seconds. He never
flew predictable patterns. He never
fought when the odds weren't in his
favor.
December 1967,
kills six and seven. December 28th,
1967, kills eight and nine. Double ace.
Nine confirmed kills. The most
successful fighter pilot of the entire
Vietnam War. He was 25 years old.
Nguyen Van never flew combat again
after 1969.
The North Vietnamese pulled him from
frontline service to train the [music]
next generation of pilots.
He survived the war.
Retired in 2002 as Chief Inspector of
the Vietnamese Air Force.
But his impact lasted far beyond
Vietnam.
Operation Bolo and the MiG ambush
tactics led directly to the creation of
the US Navy Fighter Weapons School in
1969,
better known as Top Gun. The dog fight
wasn't obsolete after all.
And a farmer's son with an outdated
aircraft had proven it.
If you enjoyed this, please subscribe
and leave [music] a like. It really
helps us out.

text:
On February 13, 2017, in front of two hundred security cameras at Kuala Lumpur International Airport, two women rubbed something on a man's face — and walked away laughing.

Twenty minutes later, that man was dead.

His name was Kim Jong-nam — the older brother of North Korea's Supreme Leader Kim Jong-Un. The substance on his face was VX nerve agent, one of the most lethal chemical weapons ever developed.

But here's what makes this assassination unlike any other in modern history: the two women who killed him had absolutely no idea what they were doing.

They thought they were filming a Japanese prank show.

This is the story of how the North Korean Ministry of State Security spent months psychologically engineering two innocent women into committing the most public political assassination of the 21st century — and how they walked away from the scene completely free.

It is also the most chilling answer ever given to one simple question: how do you make someone commit murder without them knowing?

>> [music]
>> North Korean agent Ri Ji U had flown out

desperate, it was calculated. The North

diplomats from leaving Pyongyang.

In May 2019, Do-won pleaded guilty to a
lesser charge and walked free. 2 years
and 3 months behind bars for something
they didn't know they were doing. So,
the most terrifying thing this case
leaves behind isn't how did they do it,
it's how many times have they done it
already?
How many times has something like this
already happened and simply didn't leave
200 cameras worth of footage behind?
How many people right now think they're

text:
In 1943, Klaus Barbie tortured and executed French Resistance leader Jean Moulin in a Lyon hotel basement. Two French courts sentenced him to death. The CIA gave him a new identity, a Red Cross passport, and a boat ticket to Bolivia instead. For the next 33 years, this single Nazi war criminal outwitted the CIA, West German intelligence, the French government, and two Bolivian dictatorships — while building a cocaine empire with Pablo Escobar and orchestrating the world's first narco-state coup in 1980.

This is the true story of how Klaus Barbie, the Butcher of Lyon, became one of the most protected war criminals in history. Recruited by the US Army Counter Intelligence Corps in 1947. Smuggled out through the Vatican ratlines. Hired as Bolivia's top counterinsurgency advisor. Paid simultaneously by the CIA and the BND under the codename "Adler." Security chief for cocaine kingpin Roberto Suárez. Architect of the 1980 Cocaine Coup that made Bolivia the world's first narco-state.

code name he chose himself. In July
1980, those Austrian tanks rolled
through La Paz at 3:00 in the morning.
Cocaine money purchased an entire
government. Bolivia became the world's
first narco state, designed by a man who
had perfected his methods in occupied
France. The question is not what Klaus
Barbie did. It's who watched him do it
and for how long. But before the cocaine
and the coups, there was a hotel in Lyon
where it all began. And the first person
who tried to stop him would not survive
the attempt.
November 1942.
The Hotel Terminus sits near Lyon's
Perrache station like any other grand
hotel. What makes it different lies two
stories below the marble lobby, where
Barbie has mapped hell by function. Room
three receives guests who still have
names. The basement handles those who no
longer matter as people. Above, waiters
serve wine and the [music] orchestra
plays Chopin. Below, screams echo
against stone walls that have learned to
swallow sound. The hotel maintains
perfect cover while the real business
operates where daylight cannot reach.
Barbie is 29 and has been SS since 22,
starting with assignments in Amsterdam
where he shut down Freemason lodges and
cataloged Jewish residents for
deportation. Lyon requires something
more sophisticated. The French
Resistance is growing stronger every
month, and it has a weapon Barbie has
not encountered before. One man who has
unified every faction into a single
command. Barbie does not know this man's
name yet. He will learn it in the worst
possible way.
Charles de Gaulle, broadcasting from
London, had given Jean Moulin an
impossible task: bring [music] three
competing underground movements under
one command. Moulin was a former prefect
who drew political cartoons under a
pseudonym and served as the youngest
prefect in France at 38. In June 1940,
German soldiers beat him so severely
that he cut his own throat with a shard
of glass rather than sign a false
declaration blaming Senegalese troops
for atrocities committed by the German
army. He survived, and the scar across
his throat led to the scarf he wore for
the rest of his life. A scarf that would
become the most recognized symbol of
French defiance. But the man wearing it
was walking into a trap he could not
see. By May 1943,
>> [music]
>> Moulin had unified three movements under
one council, making him the most
important figure in the French
underground. Success had made him
visible. Someone inside the Resistance
was about to hand him over. June 21st,
1943
Caluire, a suburb north of Lyon.
Barbie's men surround the building while
Moulin sits inside. What follows last 3
[music] weeks in the Hotel Terminus
basement, where Barbie interrogates him
personally. Moulin reveals nothing. Not
one operative, not one safe house, not
one radio frequency. He falls into a
coma during transport near Metz at 44.
Andre Malraux would call him "poor
tortured king of the shadows." His
remains now rest in the Pantheon. For
this capture, Barbie received the Iron
Cross First Class from Hitler. The
recognition opened doors that would lead
him towards something involving children
who had no idea there was a war at their
doorstep.
April 6th, 1944.
Maundy Thursday. A stone farmhouse in
Izieu, east of Lyon, hiding Jewish
children aged 4 to 17.
That morning, the table was set for
breakfast with hot chocolate still warm.
Three vehicles drove up the lane. A
witness who escaped through a window
would testify, "They threw the children
into the trucks like sacks of potatoes.
Most of them were crying, terrorized."
From Izieu to Drancy transit camp. From
Drancy to Auschwitz. Not one came back.
That afternoon, Barbie typed a telex to
Berlin. Operational language, no names,
no ages. A shipping manifest in every
way [music] but format. He filed it and
moved on, unaware this document would
survive the war, three decades of
silence, and an ocean crossing to become
the most damning piece of evidence at a
trial not yet imagined. Four months
later, the Allies liberated Lyon and
found the Hotel Terminus basement empty.
Barbie was gone. French investigators
searched for years. What they did not
know was that the people who should have
been helping them had already their
target a new job.
1947
The US Army Counter Intelligence Corps
offers Klaus Barbie not an arrest
warrant, but an employment contract, a
salary, a handler, a room in Memmingen,
Germany.
The Cold War has rewritten every
calculation. Former enemies become
assets. [music] War crimes files become
bureaucratic inconveniences.
The Americans need operatives who know
how to penetrate underground networks.
Barbie spent 3 years doing that in Lyon.
His skill set transfers seamlessly to
the new enemy. His war crimes file
[music] apparently does not. The
arrangement holds until France discovers
the Americans have him and demands his
[music] return. A man sentenced twice.
The request reaches John McCloy, US High
Commissioner for Germany, whose answer
will define the next 33 years. McCloy
refuses. Decades later, a Justice
Department investigator named Allen Ryan
will write the explanation into public
record. The protection was as much to
avoid the embarrassment of having
recruited him in the first place. They
could not hand over a man whose
employment they could not acknowledge.
So, they did something worse.
1951
The CIC activates the rat lines, escape
routes originally built by fleeing
Nazis.
Catholic clergy now maintain these
pathways alongside Red Cross
administrators and Western intelligence
officers who find them useful for moving
assets beyond the reach of inconvenient
prosecutors.
A Croatian priest named Krunoslav
Draganović runs the critical junction
from a seminary in Rome, processing
travel documents that will carry up to
9,000 war [music] criminals to new lives
across the ocean. Eichmann to Argentina.
Mengele to Brazil.
Barbie receives a Red Cross document
[music]
under the name Klaus Altmann and boards
a ship in Genoa with his wife and two
children. Destination, Bolivia. 6,000
miles from the nearest French
prosecutor, with a military government
that does not ask German immigrants
about their past. Klaus Barbie ceases to
exist on paper. Klaus Altmann [music] is
born. For 13 years, Altmann is nobody
special, just another German managing a
sawmill in the Bolivian Amazon until it
gets sold, then opening a carpentry
workshop making wooden boxes for canned
goods. He buys a small timber business,
becomes a Bolivian citizen, speaks
Spanish with a thick accent that draws
no attention in a country full of German
immigrants seeking fresh starts. He
joins the German Club in La Paz and
keeps no stories about his past. 6,000
miles away, French prosecutors continue
searching for a man sitting at this very
table. They will not find him. Not
because he is hiding well, but because
the people who hid him did it so that no
one would ever look. Then a military
coup makes the carpenter's old resume
the most valuable document in Bolivia.
1964
General Barrientos seizes power and
needs advisers who understand
counterinsurgency.
The German carpenter from the La Paz
Social Club receives a Bolivian
diplomatic passport and begins training
paramilitaries using methods he
perfected in Lyon. The continent has
changed, the rooms have not. West German
intelligence recruits him, too. Code
name Adler, eagle. Two agencies on
opposite sides of the same war, paying
the same man, and neither knows about
the other. When the BND asks him to come
to Germany, he refuses. He cannot set
foot in Europe. They grow suspicious.
The relationship ends. The Bolivian
arrangement does not.
1966,
Castro sends Che Guevara to Bolivia.
Overnight, Barbie's anti-partisan
expertise becomes the most sought-after
skill in the country. He advises the
interior ministry, and later claims he
designed the strategy that led to
Guevara's capture. Through arms dealing,
he arranges delivery of Austrian [music]
Steyr armored vehicles that go into
storage for 14 years. What emerges from
those warehouses will reshape an entire
country. By the mid-1970s, Barbie
[music] has offices in inside the
Ministry of Interior, and his compound
in Santa Cruz is designed in the shape
of a swastika. Nazi flags hang from its
walls, in Bolivia, in the 1970s.
CIA cables from 1974 flag his
involvement in the drug trade. Both the
army and CIA knew where he was. They
chose to do nothing, because the man
they had smuggled out of Europe was
about to meet someone who would make all
his previous work look like rehearsal.
Roberto Suárez Gómez descends from
Bolivia's rubber barons, old money that
built cattle ranches and opened doors
across the Beni region for generations.
By 1978, he controls the largest cocaine
production operation on Earth, through a
fleet of Cessna 206s and Douglas DC-3
cargo planes shuttling product from the
Bolivian Amazon to Colombia.
1,500 private soldiers and
Libyan-trained bodyguards patrol his
estates. He builds churches, hospitals,
and roads for communities who call him
Robin Hood, and Hollywood will base the
character Alejandro Sosa in Scarface on
his operation.
He once wrote Ronald Reagan offering to
pay Bolivia's entire $3 [music] billion
foreign debt in exchange for amnesty,
which gives some indication of the scale
involved. Suárez does not need another
bodyguard. He needs a systems architect
who understands military intelligence
and surveillance networks. One man in
Bolivia has that background.
Gary Suárez, Roberto's son, told Der
Spiegel he had extensive knowledge of
security,
military strategy, and intelligence
work.
He never spoke about his past, and no
one cared, because he was [music]
helping turn Bolivia into a cocaine
empire.
Barbie organizes the entire security
apparatus. Through Suárez, he meets
Pablo Escobar and the Medellín Cartel.
>> [music]
>> The arrangement is simple. Barbie
secures the coca supply chain from
Bolivian fields to Colombian labs.
Escobar funds anti-communist [music]
operations.
Two of the most notorious figures of the
20th century at the same table, running
the same product. There is one fact that
has never appeared in any documentary
about Klaus Barbie. Suárez's wife is Ida
Levy, a woman with Jewish roots whose
aunt lived in Lyon during the
occupation. In 1944, her aunt was taken
by the Gestapo, the same office Klaus
[music] Barbie ran. The man eating
dinner at her table, running her
husband's security, sleeping under her
roof, is the same person responsible for
her family members' deportation.
Ida Levy had no idea who Klaus Altmann
really was.
By 1980, Suárez wants a government. He
has $100 million to spend. Bolivia
cycles through nine presidents in four
years, creating the chaos that makes
coups look stabilizing. General García
Meza provides military muscle. His
cousin, Arce Gómez, will serve as
interior minister. Arce Gómez is also
Suárez's cousin. Three families
connected by blood and cocaine money,
building something that has never
existed, a government purchased entirely
with drug revenue. Barbie provides the
operational blueprint,
>> [music]
>> a 3,000-man paramilitary force. The
Steyr vehicles he imported 14 years
earlier roll out of storage. Stefano
Delle Chiaie, Italy's most-wanted
neo-fascist,
>> [music]
>> co-plans the operation. They call
themselves Los Novios de la Muerte, the
bridegrooms of death. July 17th, 1980,
3:45 in the morning. Steel treads grind
against cobblestone as the armored
vehicles Barbie imported from Austria
move through empty streets. Columns of
trucks follow, each carrying 300 men
armed with automatic weapons, their
faces hidden behind black masks. They
move through the sleeping city like a
steel river flowing toward three
destinations that will determine
Bolivia's future. The presidential
palace grows larger through their
windshields. Radio towers pierce the
darkness ahead. Union headquarters waits
in silence, unaware that history is
about to break down [music] its doors.
The interim president, Lidia Gueiler, is
García Meza's own cousin. She is removed
before sunrise. At the union hall,
Congressman Quiroga Santa Cruz has been
building a corruption case that could
imprison generals. Paramilitaries drag
him from the building. His body is never
recovered. By noon, every political
party is banned, every newspaper shut
down. Arce Gómez announces on radio, All
Bolivians who oppose the new order
should walk around with their written
will under their arms. Barbie receives
the rank of honorary lieutenant colonel
with full immunity. Cocaine production
becomes official state policy. DEA agent
Michael Levine, working undercover,
completes the largest covert narcotics
purchase in history while documenting
active CIA obstruction. The cartel puts
a $200,000 bounty on his head, calling
him El Judio Trigueño, the dark Jew.
For 13 months, Bolivia operates as the
world's first narco-state,
>> [music]
>> with political parties banned, press
silenced, and professional interrogators
imported from Argentina's military
junta. International condemnation builds
until even the Reagan administration
distances itself. The Council on
Hemispheric Affairs names Bolivia's
regime the worst human rights violator
in Latin America, after Guatemala and El
Salvador. In August 1981, García Meza is
forced to resign under pressure from his
own military. The regime falls. The drug
lord remains free. The Italian
neo-fascist returns to Europe, and Klaus
Barbie stays in Bolivia, still
protected, still untouchable for two
more years, until a woman with no badge,
no warrant, and no army decides she has
waited long enough.
Beate Klarsfeld was born in Berlin in
1939
She married Serge Klarsfeld, whose
father was deported from Nice to
Auschwitz and never returned.
In 1968, Beate slapped German Chancellor
Kiesinger across the face on camera
because he had been a Nazi Party member.
In 1971, the Klarsfelds linked the name
Klaus Altmann to Klaus Barbie and traced
him to Bolivia.
January 1972,
La Paz. French journalist Ladislas de
Hoyos interviews Klaus Altmann while a
cameraman films. The conversation is in
Spanish until de Hoyos switches to
French and asks if Altmann has ever
visited Lyon. Klaus Altmann, the man who
speaks only German and Spanish, answers
no in German. Automatic, instinctive, a
language reflex that erased 30 years of
cover in two seconds.
Fingerprints confirm the rest.
In France, Simone Lagrange recognizes
him on the broadcast. He had tortured
her in 1944.
Bolivia's dictator refuses extradition.
Beate returns to La Paz and chains
herself to a public bench. Two mothers
from Izieu stand beside her holding
photographs of children who were four
and six and 11 years old, faces that
never aged.
A year passes, then five, [music]
then 10. During those years, Barbie
builds the cocaine empire, helps topple
a government, attends parties with
Escobar.
Every year, Beate files another
extradition request. Every year, a
different general stamps it rejected.
She has a filing cabinet, a telephone,
and 10 years of the word no. She does
not stop.
February 1983,
Bolivia's new president has Barbie
arrested for commercial fraud, a
meaningless charge everyone understands.
Days later, Klaus Altmann is on a plane
to Lyon.
May 1987,
the first trial for crimes against
humanity in French history, 41 counts.
His defense attorney is Jacques Vergès,
who fought in the French Resistance
during the same war Barbie waged against
it, was friends with Pol Pot since their
student days in Paris, and titled his
autobiography The Brilliant Bastard.
Vergès does not argue innocence. He
argues France has no right to judge.
Barbie has been promoted to the rank of
an expiatory victim, a scapegoat, so
that France can shed [music] its own
responsibility.
When brought back to face his accusers,
Barbie offers two words. "Nothing to
say."
Sabine Zlatin stands. She founded the
children's home at Izieu.
Then the telex is entered into evidence.
Barbie's own words, his own typing,
April 6th, 1944.
A record that treats the removal of
children like warehouse inventory. The
document that sat in an archive for 43
years and would not disappear.
July 4th, 1987.
Guilty on all 41 counts. Life
imprisonment with no mitigating
circumstances. Robert Badinter watches
from the gallery. French Minister of
Justice, whose own father was deported
from Lyon during Barbie's command and
sent to Sobibor. Badinter is also the
man who abolished capital punishment in
France in 1981.
The sentence two courts issued in the
1940s can no longer be carried out. The
man who ended execution in France
ensured that the butcher of Lyon would
spend his remaining years in a cell
instead.
September 1991. Saint Joseph Prison,
Lyon. Leukemia. 77 years old. The same
city where he [music] played Chopin at
dinner parties while people screamed two
floors below.
Garcia Meza extradited from Brazil in
1995
>> [music]
>> 30-year sentence.
Suarez arrested in 1988. Served seven of
15 years. His final interview. The worst
mistake [music] I ever made
was getting involved in cocaine
trafficking.
Dalla Chiesa arrested, extradited,
acquitted, walked free.
In 1983, Allan Ryan's investigation
concluded. Officers of the United States
government were directly responsible for
protecting a person wanted by the
government of France on criminal charges
and in arranging his escape from the
law.
The apology arrived 33 years late.
>> [music]
>> At the farmhouse in Izieu, 44 names are
carved into a memorial you can visit
today. None of them grew old enough to
pour wine [music] for guest, or laugh at
anyone's jokes, or play Chopin.
But it was war, and war is over. Thank
you for that.
C'est fini.
Merci.

text:
The CIA Spy Who Outsmarted Iran Using a Fake Hollywood Movie

In January 1980, six Americans walked through the most dangerous airport on Earth carrying business cards from a Hollywood studio that didn't exist.

They weren't soldiers. They weren't spies. They were diplomats who had been hiding in Tehran for 86 days while the Revolutionary Guard hunted them street by street.

The man who got them out wasn't a commando. He was a painter from a Nevada mining town of 400 people — and his plan was so strange the White House was certain it would fail.

He built a fake science-fiction movie. Real ads in Variety. Real offices on Sunset Boulevard. A real script with concept art by the man who co-created Captain America. Steven Spielberg mailed in a screenplay — never knowing he was writing to the CIA.

This is the story of how fiction became the most powerful weapon in the room — and how one man used a movie that was never made to outsmart an entire security apparatus.

Forty-six years later, the same trick is being used again. This time, the question is who's better at it.

ABOUT THE CHANNEL

Lume tells the true stories of ordinary people who outsmarted impossible systems — using nothing but intelligence, patience, and the parts of the world everyone else ignored.

If you like documentaries that don't waste your time, you'll feel at home here. Subscribe for a new story every week.

subtitles.plaintext:
Mehrabad Airport, Tehran.
January 28th, 1980.
5:00 a.m.
An armed revolutionary guard is studying
an American's passport. He looks at the
photograph, looks up at the face, looks
back at the photograph. The passport is
Canadian. The name is fake. The business
cards in the man's jacket pocket are
from a Hollywood studio that does not
exist.
Behind him, five more Americans. Same
forged names, same fake story. Hunted by
the revolutionary guard across Tehran
for 86 days. Not a tunnel, not forged
escape papers, not a midnight
exfiltration. A fake science-fiction
movie called Argo. Real ads in Variety
magazine, real offices on Sunset
Boulevard. Steven Spielberg himself
mailed in a script, never knowing he was
writing to the CIA.
One man built all of it in four days. A
quiet painter from a Nevada mining town
of 400 people. $10,000.
A fake company called Studio Six
Productions, and a plan the White House
was certain would fail.
The guard handed the passport back.
Every one of them boarded the plane. 46
years later, Iran is flooding the
internet with AI war films, nuclear
strikes, deep fakes, millions of views.
They've just rediscovered what one man
knew in 1979.
Fiction is the most powerful weapon ever
built. The only question left is who's
better at using it.
1979
Iran is burning.
For 26 years, the United States had
propped up the Shah, Mohammad Reza
Pahlavi. American money, American
weapons, a secret police force the CIA
helped build from the ground up. Iran
gave the oil, America gave the
stability. The Iranian people got a
dictator who answered to Washington. By
the late 1970s, the anger had been
building for a generation. In early
1979,
it broke.
February 1st, 1979.
Ayatollah Khomeini returned to Tehran
after years of exile. A crowd of
millions met him at the airport. The
Shah had fled 10 days earlier, dying of
cancer, admitted to a New York hospital
for treatment. That single decision
would cost 66 Americans their freedom.
November 4th, 1979.
A group of Iranian students, calling
themselves the Muslim Student Followers
of the Imam's Line, stormed the walls of
the United States Embassy in Tehran.
Within hours, they had seized the
compound. 66 American diplomats taken
hostage. Khomeini's demand was simple:
return the Shah. Until then, nobody goes
home.
Washington went into crisis mode. But,
in the minutes before the gates were
overrun, six people slipped out. Robert
Anders, consular officer, 54.
Mark Lijek, consular, 29. His wife,
Cora, 25.
Henry Schatz, agricultural attaché, 31.
Joe Stafford, consular officer, 29. His
wife, Kathleen, 28. They were in a
separate building when the crowds poured
over the walls. They didn't run. They
walked out a side door. Then, they had
no idea what to do. For 12 days, they
moved between locations, staying with
contacts, trying not to be seen, trying
not to panic. The British Embassy
sheltered them briefly. So did the New
Zealand
Then, on November 16th, Canadian
Ambassador Ken Taylor made a decision
that was either extraordinarily brave or
extraordinarily reckless. Probably both.
He took all six in. Taylor and Canadian
Consul General John Sheardown split the
group between their private residences.
Joe and Kathleen Stafford stayed with
Taylor. The other four with the
Sheardowns. And then, they waited. For
nearly 3 months, they cooked, they read,
they played Scrabble. They could not go
outside, could not call their families,
could not tell anyone where they were.
The Revolutionary Guard was actively
hunting them. Every day without
discovery was a miracle. Every knock at
the door a potential catastrophe.
In Washington, the question was no
longer if someone would find them. The
question was how fast.
The State Department knew about the six
almost immediately. Almost immediately.
They started generating ideas to get
them out. The ideas were, to put it
charitably, not good. Proposal one.
Disguise them as English language
teachers. Drive them through Turkey.
They didn't speak Turkish. The roads
were monitored, and nobody had ever
heard of an English teacher driving
through a revolution for fun.
Proposal two. Agricultural specialist
heading to a regional conference. Schatz
was actually an agricultural attaché.
His face was likely on Iranian watch
list already.
Proposal three.
Bicycle the group across the Zagros
Mountains into Turkey. In January. In
winter. In a mountain range that kills
experienced climbers in summer. That
plan lasted approximately 4 minutes. The
problem was structural, and it was
brutal. Iran in early 1980 was not a
country you could move through quietly.
Every checkpoint manned. Every foreigner
suspicious by definition. Every exit,
airports, land borders, seaports,
revolutionary guard presence. You needed
a cover story, not just a passport, a
reason to be there that made complete
instinctive sense to an armed
22-year-old revolutionary who hated
Americans and was looking for a reason
to prove it. That is where Tony Mendez
came in. Antonio Joseph Mendez, born
1940, Eureka, Nevada, a mining town of
400 people, no money, dropped out of
university, worked as a draftsman
drawing missile components for the
defense contractor Martin Marietta. One
afternoon, he saw a blind classified ad
in the newspaper. Artist needed for work
overseas. He applied. The ad was the
CIA. For 25 years, Mendez worked in the
agency's Office of Technical Service,
the division responsible for disguises,
forged documents, false identities, and
what the CIA politely called
exfiltration,
getting people out of places that don't
want to let them go.
He had disguised a black CIA officer and
an Asian diplomat as two white
businessmen in Vietnam. He had built
fake identities so convincing that
subjects passed through hostile
intelligence screenings without a second
look. By the time Iran became a crisis,
he was the agency's chief of disguise,
and he thought every plan on the table
was going to get six people arrested or
worse.
The breakthrough came on a Tuesday night
in December 1979.
Mendez was at home. His son was watching
television. On the screen, Battle for
the Planet of the Apes. Something
clicked. If you needed to move a group
of foreigners through a hostile country
with checkpoints, with guards, with
paranoid authorities scanning every face
for an American, you needed a reason
bigger than the suspicion, a reason so
strange, so specific, so Hollywood that
it was its own proof. Because who else
in their right mind would travel to
revolutionary Iran in January 1980? A
film crew scouting locations for a
science fiction movie.
>> Everyone knows that people from
Hollywood go where they want to go.
Never mind the time in history.
>> Mendez called John Chambers the next
morning. Chambers was not a CIA officer.
He was a Hollywood makeup artist and one
of the most respected in the industry.
He won a special Academy Award for his
work on Planet of the Apes. He created
Spock's ears for the original Star Trek.
He built the alien prosthetics that
defined a generation of science fiction.
He also had a long, quiet relationship
with the CIA helping the agency build
disguises for officers in the field.
Mendez trusted him completely. The
conversation was short. Mendez told
Chambers he needed help making a fake
movie.
>> You came to the right place.
>> 24 hours later, they had a plan. Four
days later, they had a company, Studio
Six Productions. The name was a tribute.
Six for the six Americans hiding in
Tehran. $10,000 of CIA money rented them
office space on the old Columbia Studios
lot on Sunset Boulevard. Sunset Gower
Studios. The same offices Michael
Douglas had used months earlier while
filming The China Syndrome. They brought
in a third man, Bob Sidell, a veteran
Hollywood makeup artist with credits on
The Waltons and later E.T. Sidell didn't
know about the CIA when Mendez first
approached him. He knew something was
unusual the moment Mendez asked him to
sign a secrecy agreement.
>> At first, I was floored.
Then we got down to business.
>> In four days, three men built a
functioning Hollywood production company
from nothing. Business cards printed,
letterhead designed, production phone
line installed with two regular lines
and one secret CIA channel. They needed
one more thing, a script, a real script
because if an Iranian border officer
asked to see the screenplay, a blank
page would not work. Mendez needed a
story that was visually spectacular,
required exotic locations that could
plausibly be in Iran, and was science
fiction because science fiction
justified everything strange about the
setting. John Chambers knew exactly
where to look. A few years earlier, a
producer named Barry Geller had optioned
the rights to a 1967 science fiction
novel by Roger Zelazny, Lord of Light.
The project had collapsed spectacularly.
Geller's business partner had stolen
$50,000.
The FBI got involved. Geller ended up
under arrest for securities fraud. But
before the project imploded, Geller had
commissioned concept art for the film
from Jack Kirby. Jack Kirby, co-creator
of Captain America, the Fantastic Four,
the X-Men, Thor, the Incredible Hulk,
the greatest visual storyteller in the
history of American comics.
His artwork for Lord of Light was
extraordinary. Massive alien landscapes,
futuristic cities, epic battles across
desert terrain. Terrain that looked, if
you squinted, exactly like the Iranian
Plateau. Mendez took the script, changed
the cover page, renamed the project
Argo, after the ship sailed by Jason and
the Argonauts in their quest for the
Golden Fleece. The parallel was
intentional. Jason sailed into hostile
waters to bring something precious home.
So would Mendez. Now they needed to make
the movie real, at least real enough to
survive a phone call from a suspicious
Iranian official. Chambers enlisted his
industry contacts. A casting
announcement was prepared. Ads ran in
Variety magazine and The Hollywood
Reporter, two of the most read
publications in the industry, announcing
Studio 6 Productions was in
pre-production on a science fiction epic
called Argo. Principal photography
scheduled for March 1980. Hollywood
noticed. Within days, the phones at
Studio 6 would not stop ringing. Writers
calling to pitch, agents calling to
submit clients, directors calling to
express interest. Bob Sedell's wife,
Andy, answered every call. One
afternoon, a script arrived in the mail.
The return address read, "Steven
Spielberg." The project was called Night
Skies, an early version of what would
eventually become E.T. the
Extra-Terrestrial.
The most successful director in
Hollywood had just submitted a
screenplay to a CIA front company. He
had no idea. By the time Studio 6 closed
its doors, it had received 26 genuine
screenplays. 26 real Hollywood writers
submitting real projects to a fake
studio run by the CIA to rescue six
people from a country that wanted them
dead. None of them ever knew.
The fake movie was only half the
operation. For the cover story to work,
the six Americans needed documents. Not
fake documents, real ones, issued by a
real government. Real stamps, real
security features, real visa pages that
could survive detailed inspection by
someone who knew what to look for. The
only way to get real documents was to
ask Canada to break its own law. Prime
Minister Joe Clark and Foreign Affairs
Minister Flora MacDonald faced a
decision with no good options. Issue
fraudulent Canadian passports, real
passports with false identities, and
they would be violating Canadian law at
the highest possible level. Don't issue
them and six people might not make it
out of Iran alive. They issued the
passports. Through a secret order in
council, a cabinet-level government
decree that bypassed normal legal
procedure, Canada produced six genuine
Canadian passports bearing the names and
photographs of six Americans who did not
exist. This had never been done before
in Canadian history. The passports were
sent to Tehran the only way that
couldn't be searched or intercepted, the
Canadian diplomatic pouch. The same
pouch used for classified government
correspondence. Diplomatic immunity
protecting six American lives disguised
as Canadian paperwork.
While the CIA was building Studio Six in
Los Angeles, Tehran was tightening. The
Revolutionary Guard had not forgotten
that six Americans were missing. Signals
intelligence picked up increased
activity near the Canadian Embassy.
Suspicious phone calls, unusual
surveillance patterns in the
neighborhood. There were indications,
not confirmed but real enough to be
alarming, that the six might already be
compromised. Every day of delay raised
the probability. Somebody talked.
Somebody remembered. Somebody connected
the dots. In Washington, President Jimmy
Carter personally approved the
operation. The cable back to Tehran from
CIA headquarters ended with two words,
"Good luck."
Tony Mendez and his CIA partner,
referred to only as Julio in
declassified documents, landed at
Mehrabad International Airport in Tehran
at 5:00 a.m. on January 25th, 1980.
They carried Argo production materials,
alias documentation, and Canadian
passports identifying them as film
producers on a location scouting trip.
At the Canadian Embassy, they met the
six Americans for the first time.
Three months of hiding had taken a toll.
The six were anxious, exhausted, and
they had exactly 48 hours to transform
from American diplomats into Hollywood
film professionals.
Mendez distributed the new identities.
Each person received a complete persona,
a Canadian name, a backstory, a specific
role on the fictional Argo production
team. Robert Anders became Robert Baker,
production manager. Mark Lijek was now
Mark Leland, a writer. Cora Lijek became
Cora Leland, production assistant. Henry
Schatz was Joseph Harris, cameraman.
Joe and Kathleen Stafford became Joseph
and Kathleen Stafford Cain, a director
and his wife, traveling as script
consultants. Mendez himself was Kevin
Harkins, an Irish-Canadian film
producer.
Then Mendez did something that made the
diplomats deeply uncomfortable. He told
them to stop being diplomatic.
>> If anyone stops you, don't be polite.
Don't be cooperative. Don't be helpful.
You are the most important people in the
room.
This border officer is wasting your
time.
You have a film to make. Act like it.
>> Diplomats spend their careers learning
to be deferential, careful, precise.
Mendez was asking them to become
arrogant, impatient, flamboyant. Silk
shirts, gold chains, sunglasses indoors.
48 hours to learn how to be Hollywood.
The night before departure, Canadian
diplomat Roger Lucy, who spoke fluent
Farsi, volunteered for one final
preparation. He changed into military
fatigues, put on jackboots, took a cane
as a swagger stick, put on sunglasses.
He spent two hours interrogating each of
the six Americans in Farsi at full
intensity, playing the role of a
revolutionary guard officer who
suspected everything. He asked about the
movie, the studio, the budget, who
authorized the location scout, why Iran,
why now, why not somewhere safer. After
those 2 hours, the six Americans were as
ready as they were ever going to be.
Monday, January 28th, 1980, 4:30 a.m.
Eight people loaded into cars and drove
through the dark streets of Tehran
toward Mehrabad International Airport.
Mendez had chosen the 7:30 a.m. Swiss
Air flight to Zurich deliberately.
>> If we arrived at the airport at 5:00
a.m., the chances were the airport would
be less chaotic.
Also, the officials manning the controls
might still be sleepy.
And most of the revolutionary guards
would still be in their beds.
>> It was the coldest calculation
imaginable, and it was almost certainly
correct. Mehrabad Airport in January
1980 was not a place that forgave
mistakes. Revolutionary guard units
stationed at multiple checkpoints,
passport control officers specifically
briefed to watch for American faces,
every foreigner a potential spy, every
exit a potential crime scene. The eight
walked in together, eight members of a
Canadian film crew scouting locations
for a science fiction movie called Argo.
First checkpoint, departure tickets,
travel documentation, passed. Second
checkpoint, passport control. The
officer took Robert Anders' passport,
Robert Baker, Canadian citizen,
production manager, and studied it. He
looked at the photo, at Anders' face, at
the photo again. He handed it back. They
reached the airline check-in desk. They
stopped. The Swiss Air agent could not
find their reservation in the system.
Iran's telecommunications infrastructure
in January 1980 was not functioning
normally. The revolution had disrupted
everything. Phone lines, computer
systems, international booking networks.
The reservation existed, it had been
made, the confirmation wasn't showing.
Mendez stood at the counter and did not
move. Did not reach for the documents
again. Did not raise his voice. Did not
explain or justify or apologize. He
waited. 10 minutes passed. The
confirmation came through. They cleared
the final security gate, walked onto the
tarmac, boarded the aircraft. The
Swissair flight lifted off from Mehrabad
Airport at 7:58 a.m. on January 28th,
1980. Below them, Tehran. The
Revolutionary Guard, the checkpoints,
the surveillance operations grew small,
then disappeared. Nobody had stopped
them. Nobody had looked twice. Nobody
had connected the Canadian film crew on
the morning flight to the six missing
Americans the entire Iranian security
apparatus had been hunting for 86 days.
The plane landed in Zurich. The six
Americans were met by State Department
officials and driven to Ramstein Air
Base in West Germany.
Two days later, January 30th, 1980, they
arrived home in the United States.
Then the American government did
something remarkable. It told the world
Canada had done it alone. The reason was
not ingratitude. 52 Americans were still
held hostage inside the embassy in
Tehran. If Iran discovered that the CIA
had run a covert exfiltration using a
fake Hollywood film, Canadian government
passports, and a functioning front
company in Los Angeles, the fury
directed at the remaining hostages could
have been catastrophic. So, the CIA's
role was buried. Canada took the credit.
Ken Taylor became a national hero across
America. Maple leaf flags flew in cities
from Boston to San Diego. Billboards
went up. Thank you, Canada.
Tony Mendez received the Intelligence
Star, the CIA's highest honor for valor,
in a ceremony with no audience, no
press, no public record. He locked the
medal in a drawer.
The CIA's role in the Canadian Caper
stayed classified for 17 years. In 1997,
President Bill Clinton declassified the
operation. Mendez could finally talk. In
2012, Argo, a film based on the
operation, won the Academy Award for
Best Picture. The fake movie that never
existed inspired a real movie that won
Hollywood's highest honor.
Studio Six Productions was quietly
dissolved, its files sealed. 26
screenwriters, including Steven
Spielberg, never received a response.
Tony Mendez retired, became a painter.
When people asked how he would describe
himself, he always gave the same answer.
>> I've always considered myself an artist
first.
And for 25 years,
I was a pretty good spy.
>> He died in 2019. He was 78.
Here's what Iran doesn't want you to
remember. The Revolutionary Guard that
hunted six Americans for 86 days, that
ran checkpoints, surveillance posts,
interrogation cells, was defeated not by
helicopters, not by commandos, not by
satellite intelligence, by fake business
cards, a script for a movie nobody was
going to make, and one CIA officer who
believed art was the most powerful
weapon you could carry.
Now, in 2026, Iran is back. AI-generated
war films, LEGO animations, nuclear
strike simulations, millions of views,
banned, re-uploaded, viral again.
They've rediscovered what Mendez knew in
1979
Fiction is the most efficient weapon
ever invented. The only question is,
who's better at using it? In 1980, the
answer was a quiet painter from Nevada
with a drawer full of fake passports and
a plan nobody in Washington believed
would work. Somewhere in a sealed CIA
archive, there are 26 screenplays
submitted to a studio that never
existed. One of them became ET. The rest
never got a response.

text:
The American Spy With a Wooden Leg Who Humiliated the ENTIRE Nazi War Machine

She had one leg. The Gestapo had thousands of agents, informants, and 
torturers. They couldn't catch her for three years.

Virginia Hall was rejected by the U.S. State Department because she had 
a wooden leg. So she went to France, walked into occupied territory, 
and built the most effective spy network the Allies had in Europe. She 
ran agents from a brothel in Lyon. She organized a prison break that 
freed 12 captured operatives in 12 minutes. She crossed the Pyrenees 
on foot — in November, on a wooden leg, through snow. And when she 
came back, she did it all over again disguised as an old milkmaid 
selling cheese to the Nazis who were hunting her.

Klaus Barbie, the most feared torturer in France, called her "the most 
dangerous Allied spy" and put her face on every train station in the 
south. He never found her.

This is the story the country she saved spent 70 years trying to forget.

CHAPTERS:
00:00 - The Hook
00:27 - The Origin
06:18 - The Heckler Network  
07:42 - Near Miss / Revelation
