Mission complete. I was not detected.
Baltimore, Maryland, 1906.
Virginia Hall is born into the kind of
family where ambition is expected. Her
father is a banker. Her mother belongs
to Baltimore society. They have a farm
in Parkton.
Virginia grows up climbing fences,
training horses, shooting rifles with
the farm hands. She is the kind of girl
who refuses to sit still in church. Her
school yearbook will describe her as the
most original student in our class. She
takes that as a compliment. She is not
interested in what Baltimore women are
supposed to want. She studies at
Radcliffe, then Barnard, then the
Consular Academy in Vienna. She speaks
French, German, and Italian by the time
she is 25. She lives in Paris during the
Annee Folle, the crazy years, when the
city belongs to artists and exiles and
women who smoke in public. She watches
fascism rising in Germany and Italy and
feels something shift in her that she
cannot name. A cold, certain fury.
She applies to [music] the US Foreign
Service. She is turned down.
She takes a clerk position in the Warsaw
Embassy hoping to prove herself from the
inside. Then Istanbul. Then Izmir. Then
Turkey, 1933.
She is 27 years old. She is hunting
woodcock in the hills above Izmir. She
slips.
The gun goes off.
She shoots herself in the left foot. The
infection begins that night. By morning
it is spreading. There is no surgeon
close enough.
By the time they get her to a hospital,
there is only one decision left to make.
They amputate [music] her left leg below
the knee. She wakes up to a world that
has changed completely.
The prosthetic they give her is wooden.
Thick leather straps, heavy enough to
feel like a punishment. No articulated
ankle, just a rigid peg that forces her
into a rocking walk. Every step a
negotiation with gravity. The skin on
her stump opens and bleeds when she
overdoes it. She names the prosthetic
Cuthbert.
She goes back to work. She serves in
Venice, then Tallinn, Estonia. She
learns to navigate stairs, cobblestones,
train platforms, muddy roads. She
adapts. She does not discuss this
adaptation. She does not discuss it with
anyone. In 1937, she applies [music] for
a promotion to full Foreign Service
Officer. Washington sends back the
rejection in writing. The rule is clear.
No person with an amputated limb may
serve as a Foreign Service [music]
Officer. It is policy. It has nothing to
do with her record, her languages, her
judgment. Virginia Hall appeals directly
to the President of the United States.
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who governs
the most powerful country on Earth from
a wheelchair, does not respond. [music]
She resigns in March 1939.
She has no plan. She has a wooden leg,
four languages, and a fury that has been
building for 6 years.
In September 1939, Germany invades
Poland.
France declares war. Virginia Hall is in
Paris.
She does not go home. She enlists in the
French Army as a private, first class,
ambulance corps. She drives wounded
soldiers out of the upper Loire Valley
>> [music]
>> under Stuka bombardment. She does this
for 9 months until the French Army
collapses and there is nothing left to
drive the wounded to. Then France falls.
Germany occupies the north. A puppet
government takes the south. Virginia
Hall makes it to London in a series of
trains and boats [music] that take 3
weeks and should not have been possible.
In London, she has nothing, no
connections, no rank, no credentials. A
former clerk with one leg and no future
in the government that rejected her. She
attends a dinner party. Across the table
is a British intelligence officer named
Nicholas Bodington. He watches her argue
in flawless French about the geography
of the Rhone Valley. He watches her
explain with precise tactical detail
which roads out of Lyon are worth
knowing and which are traps. He excuses
himself. He makes a phone call. In a
building near Baker Street, a different
kind of organization is recruiting. They
are called the Special Operations
Executive, SOE. Winston Churchill has
given them one instruction, set Europe
ablaze. They are not the gentlemen's
club of MI6. MI6 watches bridges and
counts soldiers. SOE blows up the bridge
while the soldiers are on it. Their
founders understand something that
conventional military thinking has never
grasped. The most dangerous operative in
occupied territory is not the one who
looks dangerous. It is the one the enemy
cannot see. A woman in wartime Europe
can move through checkpoints that stop
men cold. A woman with a disability is
invisible in a way that no able-bodied
man ever could be. The Nazi security
apparatus has been built on a set of
assumptions about what a spy looks like.
Virginia Hall does not match a single
one of them. SOE recruits her in April
1941
They train her in demolitions, weapons,
hand-to-hand combat, the dirty kind,
knees and thumbs in the throat. Radio
operation. Cipher codes. She learns how
to survive a Gestapo interrogation. She
learns how to withstand pain long enough
to give false answers. In August 1941,
SOE sends Virginia Hall to France. She
is the first woman deployed on an
extended mission. She arrives in Lyon.
Lyon is the right city, France's third
largest, a medieval city built at the
junction of two rivers. It is also, in
1941, the unofficial capital of the
French Resistance. Dozens of networks
operate here, overlapping, suspicious of
each other, constantly on the edge of
collapse. What they lack is [music] a
center. Someone to coordinate the money,
the weapons drops, the escape routes.
Virginia Hall becomes that center. Her
cover is immaculate. The United States
is still neutral. Pearl Harbor is 3
months away. She presents herself as a
stringer for the New York Post, an
American journalist in unoccupied
France. The name she files her articles
under is Brigitte Lecomte. The articles
are real. She writes them. Inside the
prose, woven into descriptions of
markets and weather, are intelligence
reports encrypted for Allied [music]
planners in London. She dresses like
someone who does not want to be noticed.
She changes her hair, her makeup, her
posture. She is always someone slightly
different from the person who was just
here. She builds the network she calls
Heckler.
The first person she recruits is Dr.
Jean Rousset, a local physician. He
treats wounded agents who cannot go to a
hospital. He runs safe houses. He is her
right hand. The second is Germaine
Guerin. Germaine Guerin owns the finest
brothel [music] in Lyon. Her clients
include German officers, Vichy
officials, Gestapo informants.
>> [music]
>> They arrive nervous and leave relaxed.
In between, they talk. Virginia Hall
understands immediately what this means.
She approaches Guerin. She lays out the
proposition with characteristic
directness. Guerin agrees. What follows
is one of the most effective
intelligence operations in occupied
France. The women who work in Guerin's
establishment [music] begin to listen.
Conversations about troop movements,
transfer orders, inspection schedules,
documents left in coat pockets. Within
weeks, a stream of military intelligence
is flowing from a Lyon brothel to a
radio in a Lyon apartment to a desk in
London. It does not stop there. Guerin's
women begin to target [music] specific
officers. Men who are healthy when they
arrive leave infected with syphilis.
German military units across [music] the
region begin losing operational
capacity. The Gestapo investigates. They
cannot find the source. Virginia Hall
also establishes a channel through the
American Consulate. A sympathetic
diplomat lets her use the diplomatic
pouch, letters carried by official
couriers immune to search. Downed Allied
pilots who make it to Lyon are told
[music] to ask at the consulate for a
contact named Olivier. Olivier is
Virginia Hall. She also learns to refuse
orders she considers dangerous. SOE
sends her a commanding officer, a
Frenchman named Duboudon. She
investigates him. She decides he is
reckless. She cuts contact. London
protests. She sends back a single word
response.
The word is not printable. Her instincts
save the network. She is invited to a
large [music] meeting of resistance
leaders in Marseille. In autumn 1941,
dozens of key figures in one room. She
declines. The logic is simple.
Aggregating that many targets in one
place is not an operation. It is a gift
to the Gestapo. The Gestapo raids the
meeting. 12 key agents are arrested.
Among them, George Bégué, SOE's most
valuable radio operator in France.
Virginia Hall is now the only SOE
operative in southern France with a
working radio and a direct line to
London. The entire network runs through
her.
She begins planning the operation that
will become legend. The 12 arrested
agents are moved to Mauzac prison near
Bergerac, a facility for dangerous
prisoners. They're waiting for a trial
that will almost certainly end in
execution.
Virginia Hall is 200 miles away in Lyon.
She cannot go near the prison. Her face
is already circulating in Gestapo files.
She designs the escape anyway, from a
distance, piece by piece, like
assembling a machine she will never see
operate. She recruits Gabby Block. Gabby
is the wife of one of the prisoners.
Gabby visits the prison regularly with
packages of food and clothing. Inside
tins of sardines, soldered shut with
professional precision, are tiny notes,
tools, instructions. One note reaches
George Bégué. Bégué is a radio engineer.
Inside his cell, using components
smuggled piece by piece inside tins and
shoe heels and a Catholic priest's
vestments, he builds a [music] working
radio transmitter from inside a Gestapo
prison.
He establishes direct contact with
London. He also makes a key, a copy
fashioned from a stolen impression of
the door to the prison barracks.
Outside, Virginia Hall assembles the
rest. Transport, safe houses along the
escape route, false papers, two stolen
French police [music] uniforms. She
coordinates the timing with London. July
15th, 1942.
A Catholic priest working inside the
prison on pastoral duties cuts the power
to a guard tower at a prearranged
signal. 12 men walk out of Mauzac
prison.
The active phase of the escape takes 12
minutes. Not one man is captured. Not
one is shot. All 12 are moved through a
series of safe houses across the
Pyrenees into Spain and eventually back
to London, where most of them will
volunteer to return to France and build
new networks. When word of the escape
reaches Adolf Hitler, he delivers a
furious public rebuke to the French
police. He orders a surge of Gestapo
operatives into southern France. He does
not know who organized it. He will find
out.
Klaus Barbie opens a new file. [music]
He calls it Artemis.
It is her new Gestapo code name,
Artemis, goddess of the hunt. But
[music] his officers, and then the
French themselves, use a different name,
a simpler one, La Dame qui boite,
[music] the limping lady.
Wanted posters go up across southern
France. Her face,
>> [music]
>> reconstructed from informant
descriptions, from sightings, from the
memory of people who saw her once across
a cafe and did not realize until later
who they had been watching.
High cheekbones, [music]
wide eyes, a noticeable limp.
Barbie becomes obsessed.
He believes she is Canadian. Her accent
is perfect in French,
>> [music]
>> and whatever American inflection she
has, she has buried completely.
He believes [music] she is the logistics
hub of the entire resistance in the
south. He is correct on the second
count. [music] He presses informants. He
applies pressure to prisoners. Virginia
Hall receives the intelligence from
Guérin's network, [music] from the
consulate, from a priest who overhears a
Gestapo briefing. She begins changing
apartments every 48 hours. She trims her
network [music] to its most trusted
nodes. She destroys documents the moment
they are transmitted.
November 7th, 1942.
The American consulate delivers a
message. Allied forces have landed in
North Africa. Operation Torch is
underway. Germany's response is certain.
Within hours, Wehrmacht troops will
cross into the free zone and occupy all
of France. Every border will close.
Every checkpoint will be reinforced. She
has maybe one day.
She sends a radio message to London.
Then, she closes the apartment. She
walks out into the Lyon [music] morning
with a single suitcase.
Dr. Rousset is arrested the next day.
Two of her network's safe houses are
raided by nightfall. She is already on a
train to Perpignan. The Pyrenees begin
just beyond the city.
There is no legal way out of France now.
One route remains, a smuggler's path
through the mountains into Spain.
The Spanish guide charges what he knows
is an extortionate fee.
Virginia pays it.
The group is small.
Herself,
two Frenchmen,
a Belgian officer,
a Spaniard who says he knows every path.
The route climbs to 7,500
ft.
It is November, snow on the upper
passes,
temperature below freezing.
The path is loose rock and ice, and a
darkness so total that you navigate by
feel.
For a person with two working legs, this
crossing takes three to four days.
Virginia Hall has Cuthbert.
The wooden leg has no articulated ankle.
Each downhill step is a controlled fall.
The leather straps that hold the
prosthetic in place cut into the stump
of her knee. The skin there has been raw
for years. In the cold, in the dark, on
the ice, it opens.
She does not stop.
She does not say anything to the men
ahead of her.
Somewhere on the second day, she pauses
to send a coded radio message to London.
The message reads,
She means the leg.
She is telling her handlers that the
crossing is hard but survivable. London
does not know Cuthbert is the leg.
London's response arrives [music] within
the hour. If Cuthbert is causing
problems, eliminate him.
She reads this.
She keeps climbing.
She will later describe the Pyrenees
crossing to her niece as the most
terrifying thing I have ever done.
From a woman who has done most of what
this story contains, the statement
deserves attention.
They descend into Spain.
Spanish border guards arrest them
immediately. Illegal entry. She is taken
to a jail in San Juan de las Abadesas.
Her papers are confiscated. She has no
way to contact London.
In the cell, she befriends a woman who
will be released before her. She gives
this woman a note and a single
instruction, find the American consulate
in Barcelona.
The note reaches the consulate.
Diplomats secure her release.
July 19th, '43. Virginia Hall returns to
London. The British award her the Member
of the Order of the British Empire in
secret because she is still officially a
journalist and because she is already
planning her return. SOE refuses to send
her back. She is too well known, they
say. Her description is on every Gestapo
wanted list in France. Sending her back
is sending her to her death. Virginia
Hall resigns from SOE.
She walks across the street.
The American OSS, the Office of
Strategic Services, forerunner to the
CIA, has offices in London.
She knocks on the door.
She tells them who she is and what she
can do.
General William Donovan, who built OSS
from nothing, understands immediately.
She gets a new code name, Saint.
She gets a new mission, the Haute-Loire,
the agricultural highlands of central
France. She gets a specific task.
With the Allied invasion approaching,
the resistance must be transformed from
a collection of networks into a fighting
force capable of disrupting the
Wehrmacht's ability to respond.
There is one problem. She cannot
parachute into France.
A one-legged woman landing in a field at
night has a meaningful probability of
landing wrong and a meaningful
probability of dying before the mission
starts.
Instead, in March 1944, 3 months before
D-Day, a British torpedo boat runs dark
off the coast of Brittany at 2:00 in the
morning.
Virginia Hall goes over the side. She
swims to the beach. She has a new
identity,
Marcelle Montagne, a French milkmaid
from the countryside, an old woman,
nobody's idea of a threat. She is 38
years old. She spends several evenings
in London before her departure, making
herself into Marcelle.
She asks a dentist, not politely, to
grind down her teeth. Her real teeth are
American, straight, white,
well-maintained. A French peasant woman
who has lived through the depression and
the occupation would not have those
teeth.
The dentist refuses. She explains the
situation. He grinds the teeth.
She dyes her hair from dark brown to
iron gray. She puts on three layers of
rough wool. She practices a walk, not
her own careful, compensated stride, but
the rounded shuffle of an old woman
whose knees hurt more than her pride.
She acquires [music] a herd of goats.
In the villages of the Haute-Loire,
Marcelle Montagne is known as a reliable
local supplier of fresh cheese.
She walks the roads with a cart, the
goats behind her, the cheese in wicker
baskets.
German patrol officers stop her
regularly. She speaks to them in the
thick regional accent of a woman born
[music] 30 km from where she stands.
Twice, SS officers who stop her cart
[music] buy her cheese.
Underneath the cart, wrapped in
oilcloth, is her radio. She transmits to
London from barns, from cellars, from
haystacks. She transmits in code, in
Morse, on a type 111 MK2 radio, powered
by a car battery that is charged by an
arrangement she designed herself, a
bicycle frame stripped of everything
unnecessary, its chain linked to a
generator. Edmond Le Brat pedals.
Virginia transmits. She orders supply
drops using coded poetry phrases
broadcast [music] on BBC French
services. The phrase "Les marguerites
fleuriront ce soir." "The daisies will
bloom tonight." means that a field in
the Haute-Loire should be cleared and
marked by midnight. The response is
three aircraft loaded with rifles,
explosives, and folded currency.
The local maquis, the French guerrillas,
young men hiding in the hills to avoid
forced labor in Germany, do not want to
take orders from a milkmaid.
Virginia Hall does not argue.
She has a monopoly on something they
cannot get anywhere else. Radio contact
with London. Supply drops.
Money. She makes the terms clear.
Coordinate with her on her terms or
receive nothing. The maquis leader
refuses.
She waits.
He calls back within a week.
She calls the units she builds the Diane
Irregulars. By the summer of 1944, she
commands three full battalions of the
French Forces of the Interior, roughly
1,500 fighters. She has trained them
personally in the tactics she has spent
3 years learning. Ambushes on convoys,
precision attacks on rail lines, timed
destructions of communication
infrastructure. She does not do this
from a distance. [music]
She is in the field with them. In August
1944, an OSS Jedburgh team, three Allied
officers, drops in to reinforce her. The
officers expect to take command. They
meet a milkmaid who has been running a
war for 4 [music] months and hands them
their assignments. The Diane Irregulars
destroy rail lines, telephone exchanges,
fuel dumps. German troop movements
across the Haute-Loire [music] slow,
then stop, then reverse. Bridge after
bridge goes down. When elements of the
US Third Army reach the Haute-Loire in
September 1944, they find a region
already liberated. German garrisons
gone.
Local officials already in Allied hands.
The maquis standing in the roads waving.
The American officers are confused. They
ask who did this. Nobody seems to know.
Donovan pins the Distinguished Service
Cross to her lapel, second highest
military honor in the United States,
only civilian woman to receive it in the
entire war. Truman wants a public
ceremony, the White House lawn, cameras.
She refuses. She's not done yet.
The OSS becomes the CIA. She joins in
1951, builds sources, runs agents. She
is extraordinary at this. The CIA does
not care. Internal evaluations describe
women as emotional, vain, talkative. The
woman who crossed the Pyrenees in
November on a wooden leg continues to do
her job. She is passed over for
promotion, then again,
then again.
She retires in 1966,
mandatory age 60. She moves to a farm in
Maryland, grows vegetables, keeps
animals. Her neighbors don't know what
she did. She doesn't tell them. She dies
in 1982.
The New York Times runs four paragraphs.
The Gestapo that hunted her collapsed in
1945. Klaus Barbie died in prison in
1991
The CIA men who called her too emotional
to serve are long dead. Their arguments
are now studied as the pathology of a
broken system. Virginia Hall outlasted
all of them. The country she saved spent
most of her lifetime trying to forget
she existed. In 2016, the CIA put up a
statue in her honor at Langley. She
never saw it.

Paris, March 18th, 1314. You're watching
a 70-year-old man climb the steps of a
scaffold in front of all of Paris. He
can barely walk. Seven years of torture
do that to a man. His name is Jacques de
Molay, and today is the easiest day of
his life. All he asked to do is read a
piece of paper, a confession he already
signed. Admit his sins in public, bow
his head, and disappear into a prison
cell [music] for whatever years he has
left. The King of France has scripted
every second of this moment. The crowd,
the clergy, the guards, the paper in de
Molay's shaking hands. Everything is
controlled. Everything is perfect.
Except one thing. The old man looks at
the paper. Then, he looks at the crowd.
Then, he puts the paper down. Not from
fear, not from madness. [music]
He had already decided how this ends.
Philip the Fourth spent seven years
destroying Jacques de Molay. Jacques de
Molay needed 30 seconds. This is how.
Paris, 1300, seven years earlier.
Philip the Fourth of France is the most
powerful man in Europe. He controls
armies. He controls courts. He controls
the Catholic Church itself, or close
enough that it doesn't matter. Kings
across the continent watch what he does
and adjust accordingly. He is also
completely, catastrophically broke. And
today, he has to do something that no
one in France would believe if they saw
it. He has to go ask for money. Not send
a messenger, not dispatch a minister.
Him, personally. Because the people he
needs money from are the only ones in
Europe who can say no to a king and mean
it. He walks into a room and sits across
a table from a man in a white robe with
a red cross on his chest. The man
doesn't stand up when Philip enters. He
doesn't bow. He opens a ledger, writes a
number, and slides it across the table.
Philip sighs. He has been signing their
ledgers for years. So has his father. So
has every king in Europe. This is the
Knights Templar. Not just warriors, not
just Crusaders, the first international
bank in human history. 200 years before
anyone else thought to try it, the
Templars built a financial network that
ran from London to Jerusalem. Kings
borrowed from them. Popes needed them.
Entire wars were financed through their
system. And they had one rule that made
them untouchable. They answered to no
one. Not to kings, not to courts, only
to the Pope himself. And even that was
negotiable. For two centuries this had
worked perfectly until Philip did the
math. The number on the ledger is
impossible. Not difficult, not
uncomfortable, impossible. Philip will
never repay what he owes the Templars.
Not in his lifetime, not in his
children's lifetime. The debt is so
large that even saying it out loud feels
like a confession. He sits with this
number for three days. On the fourth
day, he makes a decision that will echo
for 700 years. He doesn't find a way to
pay. He picks up a pen and starts
writing a different kind of document.
Paris, 1307.
3 months before the arrests. What Philip
the fourth is about to do has never been
done before. Not the violence. Medieval
kings were good at violence. Not the
betrayal. Betrayal was practically a job
requirement. What had never been done
was the scale. The Knights Templar
[music]
are everywhere. France, England, Spain,
Italy, Germany. Thousands of men,
hundreds of properties, castles, farms,
banks, ports, a private army spread
across an entire continent with its own
laws, its own courts, its own chain of
command. You can't arrest an
organization like that unless you arrest
all of it simultaneously before anyone
has time to react, before a single
messenger can ride to warn the others.
Philip sits with his advisers for
months. The math is brutal. France alone
has over 2,000 Templars. They are
trained soldiers. They are armed. And if
even one of them escapes with the
treasury, the gold, the documents, the
ledgers, everything falls apart. The
plan has to be perfect and it has to be
secret. Philip starts with the Pope,
Clement V, a weak man in a difficult
position.
Philip had essentially installed him,
moved the entire papacy from Rome to
Avignon, a city in southern France, so
the Pope would be easier to control.
Clement knew what Philip [music] wanted
from him. He had always known.
Philip tells him what he has planned.
Clement V signs. Now Philip has God on
[music] his side, or at least the man
who speaks for God. Next, the charges.
[music]
You can't arrest the most powerful
military order in the world without a
reason. You need something that makes
the public not just accept the arrest,
but cheer them. Philip's lawyers spend
weeks on this. The final list of charges
against the Knights Templar is
extraordinary.
Heresy, devil worship, spitting on the
cross, obscene initiation rituals,
sodomy, worshipping a demonic idol
called Baphomet. None of it is true. All
of it is perfect because now this isn't
a king destroying his creditors. This is
a holy war against servants of Satan.
The public will demand justice. The
church will provide cover, and Philip
will get everything he needs. The gold,
the land, the property, all of it.
Clean, legal, God approved. The orders
go out in secret. Every sheriff, every
royal guard, every local magistrate
across France receives a sealed letter.
Do not open until October 13th. Do not
speak of this to anyone. On Friday, the
13th of October, 1307, at exactly 4:00
in the morning, you will open this
letter and follow every instruction
precisely.
France, October 13th, 1307,
3:59 a.m. 2,000 soldiers are standing in
the dark, each one outside a different
door, each one with the same sealed
orders now open in their hands. Each one
waiting for the same moment. None of
them know the others exist. At exactly
4:00 a.m., they knock. In the next 6
hours, every knight Templar in France is
arrested simultaneously. No one escapes.
No one is warned. The most powerful
private army in the medieval world is
taken down without a single battle. Not
by a stronger enemy, by a knock at the
door. Philip the Fourth reads the
reports as they come in. City by city,
castle by castle, name by name. He picks
up his wine. He has won. There is one
problem. The Grand Master of the Knights
Templar, Jacques de Molay, is not broken
yet. And Philip needs him broken. Paris,
1307,
the first day. Jacques de Molay has been
inside worse places than this. He
survived the fall of Acre, the last
Christian city in the Holy Land. He
watched everything the Templars had
built in two centuries collapse into the
sea in a single afternoon. He carried
wounded men out of a burning city while
arrows came from every direction. He is
not afraid of a cell. Not yet. Philip's
men come every day, not to ask
questions, not at first. First, they
just talk. They explain the situation
calmly and professionally. The charges,
the evidence, the signed testimonies of
other Templars who have already
confessed, the papal authority behind
the arrest, the absolute certainty of
what comes next if DeMolay refuses to
cooperate. They are very reasonable men.
DeMolay listens, says nothing, waits for
them to leave. This goes on for weeks.
Then the questions start. Did you
participate in the initiation rituals?
[music]
Did you spit on the cross? Did you
worship the idol Baphomet? DeMolay says
no every time to every question. The men
write something in their ledgers, thank
him for his time, leave.
The next day they come back. Same
questions, same answers, same ledgers.
This goes on for months. Then the
methods change. We don't have clean
words for what happens next. The
medieval justice system had developed
very precise techniques for extracting
confessions from people who refuse to
give them. Techniques that had been
refined over centuries. Techniques
designed not to kill because a dead man
cannot confess, but to make a living man
wish he were dead.
Philip's interrogators are
professionals. They are very good at
their job. [music]
1308,
the second year. DeMolay is still saying
no. His body is not what it was. He
moves differently now, holds himself
differently. There are things he cannot
do anymore that he could do before.
But every morning when they come with
their questions, he says no. Philip
reads the reports, increases the
pressure.
1310,
the third year. Other Templars are
breaking. 54 of them confess and then
recant, [music]
take back their confessions, say they
were forced. Philip burns them alive in
a field outside Paris, all 54 in a
single afternoon. DeMolay watches the
smoke from his window. He says nothing.
1312, the fifth year. The Pope
officially dissolves the Knights
Templar. [music]
The order that had existed for 200
years, that had fought crusades, built
cathedrals, invented international
banking, ceases to exist on paper.
DeMolay is still in his cell, still
saying no.
1314,
the seventh year. Something has changed.
Not in the cell, not in the questions,
not in the methods, [music]
in DeMolay. He is 70 years old. He has
been in this cell for seven years. His
body [music] has been through things
that bodies are not designed to survive.
And somewhere in those seven years, in
some specific moment that no historian
has ever been able to identify,
something breaks. He picks up the pen.
He signs the confession. Philip reads it
and feels something he hasn't felt
[music] in seven years, relief.
The Grand Master of the Knights Templar,
the last leader of the most powerful
organization in medieval history, has
admitted to everything, heresy, devil
worship, every charge on the list. It's
over. Philip schedules the final public
ceremony for March 18th, 1314.
DeMolay will read his confession in
front of all of Paris. The case will
close. The world will move on.
There is only one thing Philip doesn't
know. In the seven years he spent
breaking Jacques DeMolay, DeMolay had
been doing something, too.
Deciding.
Paris, March 17th, 1314.
The night before.
The man who comes to DeMolay's cell that
evening is not a stranger. DeMolay knows
his face, knows his hands, [music] knows
exactly what those hands are capable of.
For 7 years, this man has been Philip's
instrument, his professional, the person
the king sent when questions needed
answers and answers weren't coming fast
enough. He sits down across from
DeMolay. He doesn't have any tools with
him tonight, just two [music] cups of
wine. He explains the situation simply.
Tomorrow is the last day. The ceremony
is arranged. The crowd will be there.
The clergy will be there. The king will
be watching from a distance. All DeMolay
has to do is stand on the scaffold, read
the confession out loud, and it ends.
Prison, yes, for the rest of his life.
But life, food, a bed, no more of this.
He slides one of the cups across the
floor toward DeMolay. DeMolay looks at
it, doesn't touch it. The man tries
again.
He has done this before, sat across from
broken men the night before their last
day. Sometimes they rage, sometimes
[music] they weep, sometimes they just
stare at the wall and say nothing.
DeMolay does none of these things. He
looks at the man across from him, the
man [music] who has spent 7 years taking
things from him, and he asks one
question.
>> Do you know why they arrested us on a
Friday?
>> The man doesn't answer.
>> In the time of the Crusades,
>> DeMolay continues,
>> Friday was the day Christ died, the day
the world went dark. Philip chose it
deliberately. [music] He wanted us to
feel like we were already dead.
>> He pauses.
>> He was right. We were.
>> The man shifts in his seat. This is not
how these conversations usually go.
>> Tomorrow,
>> DeMolay says,
>> I'm going to do something, and I need
you to understand that nothing you say
tonight will change it. Not more wine,
not more threats, not more of whatever
comes after threats.
>> The man leans forward. What are you
going to do?
>> DeMolay looks at him for a long moment.
>> I am going to tell the truth.
>> The man leaves before midnight. He walks
directly to Philip's residence, requests
an urgent audience, is told the king is
asleep and cannot be disturbed. He
insists. He is told again the king is
asleep. He writes a note, hands it to
the guard, watches the guard disappear
[music] behind a closed door. The note
is never delivered. Philip sleeps
through the night. March 18th, 1314.
Dawn. DeMolay watches the sun come up
through the small window in his cell. He
has not slept. He is not afraid. He has
spent seven years in this cell being
turned into something Philip could use.
A broken man. A signed confession. A
public admission of guilt that would
make the destruction of the Templars not
just legal, but righteous. Philip got
the signature. He didn't get the man.
They come for him at 9:00 in the
morning. He stands up slowly. His body
does what it always does now. Protests.
Remembers. [music] Reminds him of seven
years of reasons to sit back down. He
stands anyway. They lead him out of the
cell and into the light. For the first
time in seven years, Jacques DeMolay is
outside. He looks up at the sky. Then he
follows them toward the scaffold. He
already knows exactly what he is going
to say.
Paris, March 18th, 1314. Midday. The
scaffold is exactly as Philip designed
it. Center of the city. Maximum
visibility. Thousands [music] of people
pressed together in the square.
Merchants, clergy, nobles, commoners.
Everyone who matters in Paris is here.
Everyone who doesn't matter is here,
too. Philip watches from a distance, not
on the scaffold, not in the crowd, from
a window, clean, separate, the way
powerful men watch things they've
arranged. He has been waiting 7 years
for this moment. He allows himself to
[music] feel it. De Molay climbs the
steps, slowly, the way he does
everything now. His body has its own
calendar, one that marks every year
since 1307 in ways that don't heal. The
crowd goes quiet. This is the man they
were told worshipped demons, spat on the
cross, led an order of heretics and
perverts. He doesn't look like any of
those things. He looks like a very old
man who has been through something no
one in this crowd can imagine. A clerk
steps forward, hands him the confession.
De Molay takes it, looks at it. This is
the moment. 7 years of planning, [music]
54 burned alive, an entire order
dissolved by papal decree, the most
sophisticated political operation in
medieval history. All of it building
toward one old man reading one piece of
paper in front of one crowd. Philip
watches from his window.
>> [music]
>> The clerk nods at De Molay. De Molay
looks at the paper one more time. Then,
he looks [music] up. He doesn't read it.
Instead, he does something no one on
that scaffold, no one in that square,
[music] no one watching from any window
in Paris is prepared for. He speaks, not
the words on the paper, his own words,
in a voice that should not be as strong
as it is, in a voice that carries across
the entire square and into the streets
beyond. He says the confession is a lie.
He says it was extracted by torture.
[music]
He says the Knights Templar were
innocent. Every single charge, every
carefully constructed accusation
Philip's lawyers [music] spent months
building, he dismantles in front of the
entire city, one
>> [music]
>> by one, clearly, without hesitation. The
clerk tries to [music] interrupt.
DeMolay keeps speaking. Guards move
toward the scaffold. DeMolay keeps
speaking. Philip's hands tighten on the
windowsill.
>> [music]
>> It takes less than 30 seconds. When
DeMolay finishes, the square is
completely [music] silent. Philip
doesn't move. He understands immediately
what has [music] happened. The
confession is worthless now, recanted
publicly, in front of thousands of
witnesses, in front of the clergy, in
front of everyone who matters and
everyone who doesn't. Seven years of
work gone in 30 [music] seconds. The
guards seize DeMolay immediately. There
is no deliberation, no second trial, no
appeal. Philip gives the order before
the echo of DeMolay's [music] last word
has left the square. Death tonight by
fire. Paris, March 18th, 1314,
evening.
They burn him on a small island in the
Seine River, Île des Juifs, the island
of the Jews, a place reserved for
executions. The fire is lit at dusk.
DeMolay does not [music] scream, does
not beg, does not say anything for a
long time. Then, from inside the fire,
[music]
he speaks one last time. He calls out
two names, Pope Clement V, King Philip
IV of France.
He summons them before God. Before the
year is out to answer for what they have
done. The crowd hears it. Everyone hears
it. Philip hears it from his window.
[music]
He doesn't move. The fire burns until
there is nothing left.
Paris, April 20th, 1314, 33 days later,
Pope Clement V is dying. He has been
sick since the execution. The doctors
have different explanations. Bad air,
bad food, bad fortune. None of them say
what everyone in Paris is already
[music] whispering. He was the first
name called from the fire. He dies on
April 20th, 1314.
33 days after Jacques de Molay burned.
Philip receives the news at breakfast.
He sets down his cup. He doesn't say
anything for a long time. Then, he calls
[music] for his advisers and spends the
rest of the day on other matters.
Treaties, taxes, the business of running
the most powerful kingdom [music] in
Europe. He is not superstitious. He is a
king. Kings don't believe in curses.
Summer, 1314.
Philip goes hunting. He does this often.
The forest outside Paris. Good horses,
good weather.
>> [music]
>> The kind of morning that makes a man
feel like the world is exactly the right
size. He is 46 years old. Strong,
healthy, no reason to think about death.
November 29th, 1314.
His horse throws him. It happens fast,
the way these things always happen. One
second, everything is fine, and then it
isn't. Philip hits the ground hard. His
men reach him within seconds. He never
fully recovers.
Eight months after Jacques de Molay
burned, Philip IV of France is dead. The
second name called from the fire. Paris
goes quiet with it. Not publicly, not
officially. Kings don't die from curses.
There are proper explanations. The fall,
the injuries, the fever that followed.
But in the streets, in the taverns, in
the churches where people speak quietly
after the sermon ends, [music] everyone
knows what DeMolay said. Everyone is
counting the months.
Here is what history records. Pope
Clement V dead, 33 days after the
execution. Philip IV dead, eight months
after the execution. Both men called by
name from the fire. Both dead before the
year was out, exactly as DeMolay said.
Here is what history [music] cannot
record. Whether it was God, whether it
was poison slipped into a cup by a
surviving Templar who had nothing left
to lose, whether it was coincidence so
precise it stopped feeling like
coincidence [music]
centuries ago.
No one knows. No one has ever known.
What history does record is this. The
Knights Templar were destroyed. Their
gold was taken. Their land was seized.
Their name was erased from official
record. Philip IV got everything he
wanted and died eight months later with
the echo of a dead man's voice still in
the air. Jacques DeMolay had nothing. No
army, no order, no gold, no allies, no
future.
He had one morning on a scaffold and 30
seconds and a voice that carried across
a square. He used all three. The last
thing he did on this earth was refuse to
let Philip write the ending. So he wrote
it himself
from the fire.

He Stole a Military Ship to Escape the Soviet Union

In 1961, a Soviet naval commander did the unthinkable: he stole his own ship to escape the USSR. And he did it using only a pocket compass. Jonas Pleskys was a brilliant Soviet officer who orchestrated one of the most daring and unbelievable defections of the Cold War. Trapped in a totalitarian system and facing the end of his naval career, he devised a deadly and flawless plan. Under the cover of a massive storm in the Baltic Sea, he destroyed the ship's navigation charts, smashed the main compass, and hijacked his own vessel with nine crew members on board who had absolutely no idea they were leaving the Soviet Union forever.

This is the incredible true story of the man who outsmarted the Soviet Fleet, triggered a 30-year KGB manhunt, and became the real-life inspiration for the legendary blockbuster "The Hunt for Red October".

00:00 - THE STORM
01:19 - THE MAN
02:48 - THE TRAP

Baltic Sea, April 6th, 1961,
2:00 a.m.
Nine Soviet sailors are holding on for
their lives.
The storm came out of nowhere, waves
crashing over the deck, the ship rolling
hard left, then hard right. Men grabbing
anything bolted to the wall just to stay
standing.
Their commander is calm. Lieutenant
Jonas Pleshkov stands at the helm, eyes
forward, hands steady. He's giving
orders. Adjust course. Push through.
We'll be fine. The crew trusts him
completely. He's their commander. He
knows these waters. He's navigated
worse. What they don't know is that he
destroyed the compass 2 hours ago. What
they don't know is that the navigation
charts are gone.
All of them, burned. What they don't
know is that they stopped heading to
their Soviet port a long time ago.
While they're fighting the storm, he's
using it. Every wave that forces the
crew below deck buys him another minute.
Every minute buys him another mile west.
Nine men think their commander is saving
them. He's stealing them.
And the Soviet Union had no idea it just
lost a ship.
The man at that helm didn't [music] wake
up one morning and decide to steal a
ship. This started 20 years earlier
>> [music]
>> on a train to Siberia.
1948
Soviet secret police came for his family
in the middle of the night.
His stepmother [music]
had owned land before the war, 40 acres.
In Stalin's Soviet Union, that was
enough to be labeled an enemy of the
[music] people. They loaded the entire
family into a cattle car heading east.
Siberia, labor [music] camps. A death
sentence with extra steps. His father
made one decision on that train. He
pushed Jonas and his siblings out of the
moving car into the dark. Jonas was 13
years old. He hit the ground, watched
the train disappear into the night, and
never saw his father again. That moment
doesn't just [music] explain who Jonas
Pleshkov is. It explains everything that
happens on that ship in the Baltic Sea
20 years later. He grew up, kept his
head down, joined the military. The same
system that destroyed his family handed
him an officer's education in Leningrad.
Trained him as a submarine navigator,
one of the most elite positions in the
Soviet Navy. Then they offered him a
real submarine. He said no. Instead,
[music] he asked for a barge, an old
unglamorous vessel that spent its days
dumping toxic military waste into the
Baltic Sea. Nobody understood [music]
why. Nobody asked. But he had his
reasons.
Klaipeda, Lithuania, early 1961.
For 4 years he waited for the right
moment. The right moment never came.
>> [music]
>> So, life made the decision for him. It
started with a woman in Latvia. Her name
was Paula. He proposed to her during one
of his leaves. She said no. Nobody knows
why. So, he moved on, found another
woman in Lithuania. And because the
Soviet military expected its officers to
be married, stable, respectable, he
proposed after just a few weeks. She
said yes. The wedding happened in early
1961
Fast, uncomfortable. His own family
thought something was off. They were
right. A few weeks after the wedding, he
found out Paula was pregnant with his
child. He told both women the truth.
Then he told his family. Within days
everyone knew. In the Soviet Navy, this
wasn't [music] just a personal problem.
It was a career death sentence. An
officer with an illegitimate child faced
a military honor tribunal. Demotion,
expulsion, public humiliation. And
demotion meant one thing, [music] no
more command, no more ship, no more
access to open water.
Klaipeda naval base, April 5th, 1961.
The order was routine. Take the barge
out, dump the toxic waste into the
Baltic, then proceed to Tallinn. Same
mission he had done dozens of times
before. Same crew, same ship, same cold
Baltic water. He read the order, signed
it, handed it back. Nobody noticed
anything unusual. Why would they? He was
a model officer, calm, professional,
reliable. But here's what nobody knew.
He had been studying this exact mission
for 4 years. Every detail, every
checkpoint, every patrol route, every
window where the Baltic Fleet's
attention was somewhere else. And this
mission had something the others didn't.
A storm coming in from the northwest,
big enough to force the crew below deck,
big enough to kill visibility for miles
in every direction. He had waited 4
years for this combination. The right
mission, the right weather, the right
moment. It was now or never. That night
he went back to the ship alone. Think
about what he's about to do. He's a
Soviet naval officer about to destroy
military property, steal a government
vessel, and betray every man on his
crew. If anyone catches him in the next
10 minutes, it's over. Not
He took the navigation charts first,
every single one. Spread them on the
floor of his cabin. Then he burned them.
Not one or two, all of them. Every chart
that showed where they were, where they
were going, and how to [music] get back.
Now the crew is blind, but so is he.
Unless he has something else. He did. A
small handheld compass, the kind [music]
any sailor might carry in his pocket,
barely bigger than a watch, the kind of
thing nobody would ever think twice
about. [music]
With that compass, he had spent weeks
memorizing one single route. Not to
Tallinn, west across the Baltic toward
the Swedish island of Gotland, 200 miles
of open hostile water through Soviet
patrol zones. One man, one pocket
compass, nine men who had no idea. Then
he turned to the main ship compass, the
one bolted to the helm, the one the
entire crew relied on. He destroyed it.
Not damaged, not malfunctioned,
destroyed. Beyond any repair, beyond any
question. Now ask yourself something.
You're a Soviet sailor. You wake up the
next morning. Your commander tells you
there's a storm coming. He tells you the
compass malfunctioned overnight. He
tells you not to worry. He's navigated
these waters a hundred times. Do you
question him? Of course you don't. He's
your commander. By morning, the barge
had everything it needed for a routine
mission, a full crew, assigned order, a
destination. Except it had no charts, no
working compass, and a commander who had
already decided where they were really
going. One question. How do you hide 200
miles of open ocean from nine people
standing on the same ship?
Baltic Sea, April 6th, 1961,
3:00 a.m.
The storm is getting worse. Waves
hitting the deck hard enough to knock a
man off his feet. Wind so loud you can't
hear the person standing next to you.
Visibility, almost zero.
For the crew, this is a nightmare.
For Jonas Pleshkov, this is perfect.
Every sailor on that barge is below deck
right now. Holding on. Praying. Waiting
for the storm to pass.
Nobody is watching the horizon. Nobody
is checking their position. Nobody is
asking questions.
He's alone at the helm. And he's flying.
Not toward Tallinn. Not toward any
Soviet port.
West. Directly west. Toward Sweden.
Toward freedom. Toward a life that
doesn't end in a military tribunal or a
Siberian labor camp.
He checks the handheld compass. Adjusts
course slightly. Checks again.
This is the part that should be
impossible. He's navigating a Soviet
military vessel through a Baltic storm
at night with no charts, no working
compass, and nine men below deck who
think they're on a routine mission.
Most trained navigators wouldn't attempt
this in daylight with full equipment.
He's doing it alone in the dark with a
compass the size of his palm.
But here's what the Soviet Navy never
understood about Jonas Pleshkov. They
trained him too well.
4 years on submarines. 4 years learning
to navigate by instruments, by stars, by
instinct. 4 years memorizing Baltic Sea
patrol routes, water depths, coastline
shapes. They built the perfect
navigator.
Then they gave him a reason to use those
skills against them.
4:00 a.m. The storm is still raging.
One of the crew members comes up to the
helm. Seasick. Confused. He looks at the
commander standing calm at the wheel and
asks the one question Pleshkov has been
dreading.
Where are we? Think about that moment.
Everything depends on the next 5
seconds. One wrong answer and it's over.
The sailor might not know navigation,
but he knows what direction Tallinn is.
He knows how long this mission is
supposed to take. Pleshkov doesn't
blink. We got pushed off course by the
storm. I'm correcting now.
Go back below. The sailor nods, goes
back below deck. Just like that.
That's it. That's all it took. One
sentence and the Soviet Union lost a
ship. 5:00 a.m. The storm starts
breaking and that's when he sees it. A
dark shape on the horizon, barely
visible through the clearing fog.
Land. Not Soviet land. Swedish land.
He's made it across. 200 miles of
hostile water, through a storm, at
night, with a pocket compass and nine
men who had no idea they just left the
Soviet Union forever.
But now comes the part nobody talks
about. He's arrived, but he can't just
walk off the ship. He needs a reason to
go ashore. A reason the crew will
believe. A reason that doesn't end with
eight Soviet sailors overpowering their
commander and turning the ship around.
What he does next is either brilliant or
completely insane.
Probably both.
Swedish coastline, April 6th, 1961,
5:30 a.m.
The fog is clearing. Through the windows
of the barge, the crew can see land.
Close land. Too close. They start asking
questions. This doesn't look like
Tallinn. The coastline is wrong. The
lights are wrong. Everything is wrong.
Pleskis doesn't give them time to think.
He gives an order. Fire the signal
flares. The crew looks at him. Signal
flares are for emergencies, for distress
calls, for when your ship is in danger
and you need help. He tells them the
storm pushed them [music] off course. He
tells them he has no idea whose
coastline that is. He tells them they
need help. It's the third lie he's told
in the last 6 hours. It works perfectly.
One by one, flares shoot into the
morning sky, bright red, visible for
miles. A Soviet military barge sitting
in Swedish territorial waters screaming
for help to anyone who will listen.
Swedish Coast Guard responds within
minutes. Now Pleskis has one more
problem. Eight Soviet sailors are
standing on this ship. Eight men who are
about to realize what just happened.
Eight men who have families back in
Lithuania, Latvia, Russia. Eight men
whose lives are about to be destroyed by
what their commander did last night. He
can't take them with him. He can't leave
them without explanation and he can't
let them stop him. So he does something
nobody expects. He tells the crew to
stay on the ship. He tells them he needs
to go ashore to figure out where they
are. He tells them he'll be back. He
takes one man with him, the only other
Lithuanian on board, a 24-year-old
sailor named Jurgis Krizciunas.
They lower a small rescue boat into the
water. Two men, 1 km of cold Baltic
water between them and the Swedish
shore. They row in silence. Here's
what's going through Krizciunas's head
right now. He's 24 years old. He has a
family in Lithuania. He has no idea what
his commander is about to do. He thinks
they're going ashore to ask for
directions. He has no idea he's rowing
toward the biggest decision of his life.
They reach the shore. Swedish Coast
Guard officers are waiting. Police are
waiting. Everyone wants to know the same
thing. What is a Soviet military vessel
doing in Swedish territorial waters?
Pleskis steps forward and then he says
it. Three words that will trigger a
30-year manhunt, a Soviet military
tribunal and one of the most famous Cold
War novels ever written. [music]
I request asylum.
The Swedish officers look at each other.
Then they look at Krizciunas.
>> [music]
>> Pleskis turns to his sailor, tells him
this is his chance. Stay. Start a new
life. The Soviets will never know where
you are. Krizciunas goes quiet. He
thinks about his mother in Kaunas, his
brothers, [music] his friends. He knows
exactly what happens to families of
defectors in the Soviet Union.
Interrogations, labor camps, destroyed
lives. He shakes his head. He gets back
in the boat. He rows back to the ship
alone. That decision will haunt him for
the next 35 years. He returns to
Lithuania, leaves the Navy, works as a
construction worker in Kaunas and tells
nobody what he saw that morning. Not a
single person. For 35 years. [music]
Because in the Soviet Union, being a
witness to treason is almost as
dangerous as committing it. But Pleskis
doesn't watch him go. He's already
talking to the Swedish authorities and
in Moscow, nobody knows yet. They're
about to find out.
It took Moscow 6 hours to realize they
just lost a ship. By noon, they did.
The reaction is immediate and it is not
calm.
A Soviet naval vessel just sailed into
neutral [music] waters and its commander
asked for political asylum in the middle
of the Cold War, 6 weeks before Yuri
Gagarin makes the Soviet Union look
invincible to the entire world. The
timing could not be worse.
Three Soviet warships are dispatched
immediately. [music]
They escort the barge to the port of
Slite on the island of Gotland. A Soviet
military attache flies [music] in from
Stockholm. His real job is not
diplomacy. His real job is damage
control. The crew is brought together
and for the first time they are told the
truth. Their commander destroyed the
compass deliberately. He burned the
navigation charts. He steered them to
Sweden on purpose.
Everything they thought was happening
last night,
>> [music]
>> the storm, the malfunction, the
confusion, was a lie.
Eight men stand in silence processing
the fact that [music] they were stolen.
The Soviets want the ship back. Sweden
hands it over. On April 8th, the barge
leaves Swedish waters under a new
captain. In international waters, the
entire crew is arrested and replaced.
[music]
Every single man who was on that ship is
taken in for questioning. Most of them
lose everything. [music]
Jurgis Krizciunas, the sailor who rode
back alone, returns [music] to Kaunas.
Others are not so lucky.
Two key crew members die shortly after
the incident under mysterious
circumstances at Soviet naval bases.
>> [music]
>> The KGB calls it natural causes.
Historians call it [music] cleanup.
And Jonas Pleskis? On August 29th, 1961,
the military tribunal of the [music]
Baltic Fleet finds him guilty of high
treason in absentia.
The sentence is death. [music]
And somewhere in Sweden, Jonas Pleskis
reads about his own execution and he
starts running.
The CIA got to him first. They flew him
to Guatemala, then to Seattle. New
passport, new name. Jonas [music]
Pleskis officially ceased to exist. The
man who stole a Soviet ship was now
Jonas Plaskus, an ordinary American
citizen. He worked [music] on submarine
repair docks in Seattle, taught computer
programming at the University of
Washington,
>> [music]
>> lived quietly, told nobody.
But the KGB never forgot. For the next
30 years he moved constantly, changed
routines, trusted nobody. A death
sentence doesn't expire in the Soviet
Union. Then in 1984, an insurance agent
from Maryland published a novel about a
Lithuanian [music] submarine commander
who defected to the West. Tom Clancy
called his character Marko Ramius, the
Vilnius Skipper. Ronald Reagan read it
in one sitting and called it the perfect
Cold War novel.
Hollywood made it into a blockbuster
[music]
with Sean Connery. The real Vilnius
Skipper was stocking shelves in Oakland,
California under a name that wasn't his,
unable to tell a single person that the
most famous Cold War story ever told was
actually his.

title: The Electrician Who Smuggled His Family Over Europe's Most Guarded Border in a Homemade Balloon
channelDescription: Just history, told clearly and honestly.

text:
On a September night in 1979, an East German electrician and his family climbed into a hot air balloon stitched together from curtains, taffeta, and umbrella silk. They flew over the most fortified border in Europe — built in his attic over 18 months, while the Stasi were closing in.

His name was Peter Strelzyk. He had no engineering background, no blueprints, no help from anyone outside his family and one neighbor — a bricklayer named Günter Wetzel. What they did would become one of the most audacious escapes in Cold War history.

Two families. Eight people. Twenty-eight minutes in the freezing dark at 2,500 meters. A border with 1,400 kilometers of barbed wire, landmines, and standing orders to shoot. And one decision the Stasi made that accidentally bought them the time they needed.

This is the story of the Ballonflucht — the balloon escape of 1979.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

CHAPTERS

01:21 — A Country That Watches Everyone
05:21 — A Newspaper from the West

24:52 — Operation Pear
