subtitles.plaintext:
You're watching two men standing in a
dark forest about to do the most insane
thing anyone has ever attempted at this
border. Not a tunnel, not forged
documents, not hiding in the back of a
truck. They're going to fly. Two
families, four children, a balloon
hand-stitched from scraps of fabric.
Built in secret inside a house the Stasi
was already watching. 28 minutes from
now, they're either in the west or Stasi
agents are pulling their children out of
a field. But, here's what you don't know
yet. By the time they lifted off, the
Stasi already knew about them. The
circle was closing, days away from
knocking on their door. Here's the
question that won't let you go. How did
two ordinary men, an electrician and a
bricklayer, slip through the most
paranoid border regime in European
history where your neighbor could be a
paid informant, where buying too much
fabric could end your life as you knew
it, where the guards had standing orders
to shoot? And why was this escape only
possible because the Stasi made one
specific decision and accidentally
bought these families the time they
needed?
The Strelzyk family and the Wetzel
family are at a picnic with another
couple, the Kellers. Kids running
around, food on the table, the kind of
afternoon that feels completely normal
until it isn't. Then, the Stasi agents
arrive. They explain calmly and
professionally that the Kellers' teenage
son, Lucas, is gone. He tried to cross
the border in a bulldozer, of all
things. The guards got him before he
reached the fence. The Keller family is
told right there, in the middle of their
picnic, and then immediately taken away
by the police. Peter Strelzyk and Günter
Wetzel watch this happen. They don't say
anything. They go home, but both of them
walk away from that picnic understanding
the same thing. In this country, the
wrong move doesn't just cost you. It
costs everyone around you. Your wife,
your children, the people who had no
idea what you were planning. That moment
doesn't leave them. And it's important
to understand exactly what kind of
country they were living in. Because
without that context, what they built in
the next 18 months sounds like a
reckless adventure. By the late 1970s,
the German Democratic Republic was one
of the most comprehensively monitored
societies in modern history. The
Ministry for State Security, the Stasi,
ran a surveillance network that reached
into every corner of daily life. Over
90,000 full-time officers supported by
an estimated 200,000 civilian
informants, neighbors, co-workers,
friends, sometimes family. A careless
remark at dinner, a complaint about food
shortages said too loudly, recorded,
filed away, sometimes kept for years.
Travel to the West was forbidden.
Attempting to leave Republikflucht was a
criminal offense. Relatives of those who
ran could lose their jobs, their
housing, their children.
The border itself stretched roughly
1,400 km. Barbed wire, signal fences,
patrol roads, floodlights, watchtowers,
guard dogs, land mines, armed soldiers.
The inner strip was raked smooth every
morning so footprints would show.
Watchtowers every 250 m. Guards
operating under unambiguous orders.
Don't hesitate to use your firearm, not
even when the border is breached in the
company of women and children.
Between 1961 and 1989, at least 140
people were confirmed killed at the
Berlin Wall alone. Across the full
inner-German border, estimates reached
650
The youngest victim was 1 year old.
Every single one of them tried to cross
at ground level. Not one had tried to go
over all of it at once, from above, in
something they built themselves.
Strelzyk was an electrician, former Air
Force mechanic. Wetzel was a bricklayer
who could build or fix almost anything.
They met at a local plastics factory,
became close friends, and for years had
the same private conversation. How do
you leave a country designed to stop you
leaving? They considered walking across,
hiding in vehicles, a helicopter,
quickly ruled out. No engine. Then, one
afternoon, Wetzel's sister-in-law
visited from the West and left behind a
newspaper. Inside, a feature on a hot
air balloon festival in Albuquerque, New
Mexico. They looked at the photographs
for a long time. Neither had ever built
a balloon. Neither knew exactly how
large one needed to be, or what
materials it required. What they knew
was this. If they could build one in
secret, and if the wind was right, they
could fly over everything. The fences,
the mines, the watchtowers. On March
7th, 1978, they made a decision. They
were going to build a balloon.
March 7th, 1978.
Two men shake hands in a small town in
Thuringia and agree to do something
never done before at the inner-German
border. No blueprints, no engineering
background, no instructions.
Just a newspaper photograph and the
understanding that every other option
was worse.
First question. How big does a balloon
need to be to carry eight people? They
had no idea. Nobody they could safely
ask would know. So, they studied
magazine photographs, estimated
proportions, worked backward from the
weight of eight people. They settled on
1,800 cubic meters.
Whether that number was right, they had
no way of knowing. They told their
wives, and this matters because Doris
Strelzyk and Petra Wetzel didn't just
accept the plan. They became part of it.
The first problem was fabric. A hot air
balloon requires enormous amounts.
Lightweight, airtight, heat-resistant.
None of that was easy to find in East
Germany. And buying 900 square meters in
one purchase would attract exactly the
wrong attention. Their cover story, they
were making tents for a camping club.
Using that explanation, they sourced
around 900 square meters of leather
lining material in small quantities from
different locations. Cost, 2,400 marks.
Petra Wetzel began sewing panels
together on a 40-year-old manual sewing
machine, working behind drawn curtains.
While she sewed, Strelzyk built the
burner, entirely improvised. Two 11-kg
propane cylinders, salvaged rubber
hoses, water pipe sections, a modified
nozzle, a piece of stove pipe. Nothing
purchased specifically for this purpose.
The gondola, an iron frame, sheet metal
floor, clothesline rope for sides.
Functional, ugly, exactly what it needed
to be.
By April 1978, they had something
resembling a balloon. They found a
secluded forest clearing near
Ziegenrueck, 10 km from the border.
They laid out the envelope, connected
the burner, and tried to inflate it.
Nothing happened. The burner lit, but
the balloon just sat on the ground. The
problem, you can't heat air inside a
collapsed envelope lying flat. There's
nowhere for warm air to go. You need to
fill it with ambient air first, then
heat from inside. They built a blower, a
14 horsepower motorcycle engine from
Wetzel's old MZ, connected to 1 meter
fan blades, silenced with a Trabant
muffler, started with a car battery.
Back to the clearing. The envelope
lifted and took shape. Then the second
problem, the fabric was too porous. Warm
air leaked out faster than the burner
could replace it. The balloon would
never generate enough lift. 2,400 marks,
weeks of Petra's work, all of it
unusable. They went home and started
again. This time they drove 160 km to a
department store in Leipzig. New cover
story, a sailing club needing material
for sales. The quantity had to be
specially ordered, which meant coming
back the next day and an entire night of
wondering whether the sales person had
quietly called the Stasi. They came back
the next morning. The fabric was
waiting. No police, no questions. 800
meters of new material, 4,800 marks. On
the way home, they bought an electric
motor for the sewing machine. Petra had
been driving the pedal by foot for
weeks. Wetzel sewed a new envelope, 15
meters wide, 20 meters long. But the
burner still wasn't powerful enough.
They returned to the clearing again and
again, doubling propane tanks, adjusting
fuel mixtures, running variations of the
same experiment, getting closer, never
quite there. Then something nobody who
tells this story sees coming. Wetzel
quit. He stepped back entirely, began
pursuing a small aircraft instead. The
partnership, the handshake from March
1978,
over. Strelzyk kept going alone. In June
1979,
14 months after that handshake, he found
it. If you inverted a propane cylinder
completely upside down, internal
pressure caused the liquid propane to
evaporate differently, faster, more
completely. The result, a flame 12 m
long. He modified the gondola to mount
the tanks upside down, went back to the
clearing, lit the burner. The flame hit
the air inside the envelope like a wall
of heat. For the first time, it was
actually going to work.
June 1979,
Strelzyk calls Wetzel. They haven't
worked together in months. Wetzel had
walked away, convinced it was going
nowhere. He'd been drawing glider
sketches, thinking about engines,
looking for a different way out.
Strelzyk shows him the inverted propane
configuration, the test results, the
flame. Wetzel looks at it for a long
time, then he comes back. But now they
face a direct problem. The gondola is
too small. It can carry the Strelzyk
family, four people, not eight. And both
men had understood from the beginning
that this was either all of them or none
of them. You don't escape and leave your
partner's wife and children behind in a
country that punishes the relatives of
people who run. They needed more time to
build a larger gondola, time they didn't
have. The weather window was closing.
The wind patterns were becoming less
predictable as summer moved toward
autumn. The longer they waited, the
greater the chance something went wrong
before they even lifted off. So, they
made a decision that would nearly end
everything. The Strelzyk family would go
first, alone. What they didn't know was
that this decision was about to hand the
Stasi exactly what it needed. July 3rd,
1979,
1:30 in the morning, the forest clearing
near Heinersdorf. The envelope inflated
in roughly 5 minutes. The shape rose
above the tree line. The flame held.
Peter Strelzyk, his wife Doris, and
their two sons, Frank, 15, and Andreas,
11, climbed into the gondola. They
lifted off 4 m per second. Within
minutes, they were above the trees.
Strelzyk watched the altimeter he'd
built from a modified barometer. 500 m,
1,000, 1,500,
2,000. A light wind pushing them
southwest toward the border, toward West
Germany. For a few minutes, everything
worked exactly as it was supposed to.
Then, the balloon entered a cloud.
Atmospheric moisture condensed on the
outer fabric, invisible, distributed,
impossible to counteract. The altimeter
needle stopped climbing, then reversed.
They were going down. Strelzyk hit the
burner. The flame roared. It wasn't
enough. The balloon kept descending, the
dark ground rising up through the cloud.
They hit the earth at the edge of a
heavily mined border zone. Everyone was
unhurt. Strelzyk climbed out into total
darkness. No landmarks, no idea which
side of the border they were on. He
walked into the dark alone to find out.
He found a bread bag from a bakery in
Wernigerode. Wernigerode was an East
German town. They had come down 180 m
short of the border, less than two
football fields from West Germany. They
left everything behind, the gondola, the
envelope, the burner, and walked 8 miles
back through the dark to their car. But
here is the detail that changes
everything. In that field, 180 m from
the border, they had just left behind
the most dangerous thing imaginable. Not
the balloon, the evidence. On July 20th,
17 days later, a hunter found it. Within
hours, the Stasi had a full
investigation team at the site. They
analyzed everything, the fabric, its
composition, weave, likely source, the
stitching technique, thread type,
machine marks. Every piece of physical
evidence cataloged, cross-referenced,
sent to specialists. On August 14th,
they went public, partially. A bulletin
distributed across East Germany appealed
for information about a serious criminal
offense. It listed every recovered item
in precise detail. Unusual fabric
purchases, propane equipment, sewing
materials. But, they made one specific
decision. They did not say what the
crime was. The reasoning was logical.
Republikflucht had too many
sympathizers. If ordinary citizens
understood that someone had tried to fly
over the border, some might warn the
suspects instead of reporting them. That
decision accidentally gave the two
families the time they needed. This is
the moment the Stasi lost the race. They
just didn't know it yet. Strelzyk read
the bulletin the morning it was
published. He recognized every item on
the list. He understood that the Stasi
had his equipment and was looking for
him, but hadn't found him yet. The
investigation was still moving outward
from the evidence rather than inward
toward a name. He destroyed everything
that could connect him to the site, sold
his car, told Wetzel. Then he said
something that was either the most
rational thing a man in his position
could say or the most extraordinary act
of controlled desperation in this entire
story. We need to build another one.
Bigger. And we need to go before they
find us. Wetzel didn't argue. They had
weeks, maybe less. The Stasi was already
circling. The only question now was
whether they could finish a second
balloon, larger, better, capable of
carrying all eight of them before the
knock came at the door.
August 1979.
The Stasi is looking for them. They have
no way of knowing exactly how much time
they have. The only thing they know for
certain is that sitting still and
waiting to be found is not a strategy.
So, they get to work. They calculate the
new target volume, 4,000 cubic meters,
more than double the previous balloon.
The envelope alone will require 1,250
square meters of fabric. That number
creates an immediate problem. Buying
1,250
square meters of fabric anywhere in East
Germany is the kind of purchase that
gets noticed. The Stasi bulletin had
specifically asked about unusual fabric
purchases, which meant that every fabric
counter in the country was now a
potential trap. So, they do something
that is simple in concept and exhausting
in practice. They buy small amounts
everywhere, different cities, different
shops, different days, different cover
stories for each purchase. Taffeta in
one town, umbrella silk in another, tent
nylon somewhere else, different colors,
different patterns. Whatever is
available in whatever quantity won't
raise an eyebrow. Wetzel goes to his
doctor. He tells him he's been having
stomach trouble. The doctor signs off on
5 weeks of sick leave. 5 weeks during
which Wetzel does not rest.
The sewing happens mostly at night
behind closed curtains. The electric
motor they had added to the old sewing
machine makes the work faster than
before. But, 1,250
square meters of fabric sewn into a
functioning balloon envelope is still an
almost incomprehensible amount of labor.
Every joint has to hold under heat,
under pressure, under the weight of
eight people's lives depending on it not
failing at 2,500 meters in the dark.
When visitors come, everything
disappears. The fabric bundled away, the
machine covered, normal life
reconstructed in seconds. Then the door
closes and the work continues. And while
they sew, the Stasi keeps moving.
Investigators have found a potential
witness near the July landing site. They
are mapping the likely launch zone based
on wind patterns and flight trajectory.
They are cross-referencing fabric
purchases in the region around Possneck.
Two separate timelines are running
simultaneously and only one of them
knows the other exists. Through all of
this, Strelzyk focuses on the mechanics.
The new gondola is bigger and better
than the last one. A platform 140 by 140
cm. Four corner posts 80 cm high.
Clothesline rope forming the walls. Four
propane cylinders in the center. Built
to carry eight people and nothing more
than that. And then something happened
that accelerated everything. A store
manager in a nearby town quietly
contacted the authorities after a man
came in asking to purchase taffeta,
claiming it was for a group of young
pioneers. The claim didn't quite add up.
The manager made a note, filed it.
Strelzyk found out. The net was no
longer closing around East Germany
generally. It was closing around
Possneck, around their street, around
them specifically. They were not weeks
away from being found. They were days
away.
He told Wetzel there was no discussion
about whether to continue. That
conversation had already happened months
ago in a forest clearing when they shook
hands and agreed that this was the only
way out. The only question now was
speed.
September 14th, 1979.
Wetzel is in his attic hunched over the
sewing machine. It is late. Most of
Possneck is asleep. He is almost done.
The envelope is nearly complete. And
outside, for the The time in weeks, the
wind has shifted. North. Strong and
steady from the north. A northerly wind
at this time of year blowing across
their position would carry a balloon
southwest, directly toward West Germany.
This is the exact wind they have been
waiting for.
The balloon is not tested. They have had
no opportunity to test it. They don't
know with certainty that the new
envelope holds air, that the new gondola
handles the weight, that the new burner
configuration performs at altitude the
way it did on the ground. What they know
is that the wind is right tonight, and
that tomorrow the Stasi might know their
names. The window they have been waiting
18 months for is open right now, and may
not open again.
Wetzels finishes the last seam. He picks
up the phone and calls Strelzyk.
>> Tonight.
>> September 15th, 1979.
Late evening. It's time. Both families
pack only what they can carry without
looking strange. They load the equipment
into their cars quietly, in the dark.
Drive to the launch site separately. The
meadow near Heinersdorf is dark and
quiet. They unload fast and move into
the tree line. Strelzyk and Wetzels set
up the blower while the women keep the
children still and silent. The envelope
goes out, all 1,250
square meters of it, spread across the
clearing. The blower starts. The
envelope begins to fill. Immediately,
something goes wrong. A tether line
doesn't release cleanly. The balloon
tilts sideways, and the burner flame
swings directly toward the fabric. In a
balloon made of nylon and taffeta, that
ends the flight before it begins.
Strelzyk had thought about this. He
packed a fire extinguisher specifically
because he had thought about this. He
grabs it, hits the flame, it goes out.
The envelope writes itself. They keep
going. By 2:26 a.m., the balloon is
fully inflated, straining against its
tethers, pulling upward. Eight people
climb into a gondola the size of a large
dining table. Four propane cylinders in
the center, clothesline rope for walls.
Strelzyk releases the last tether. They
rise. The ascent is fast. Pößneck
becomes a dark shape below them, then
just darkness. The children are silent.
The adults are silent. The burner roars.
1,000 m. 1,500.
2,000. The cold reaches through clothing
and settles into bones. The gondola
sways. The northerly wind pushes them
southwest, toward the border, toward
Bavaria, toward West Germany. Then, at
roughly 2,500 m, the envelope tears. Not
a small tear, a seam separating,
bleeding hot air into the cold night
sky. They have no idea how bad this gets
before it gets better. They are 2,500 m
above a border where the standing order
is to shoot. Wetzl grabs the burner
igniter. The tear loses heat faster than
the burner can replace it. Every time
the flame dies, they drop. Every time it
roars back, the rush of hot air makes
the tearing worse. He lights it,
stabilizes. The tear widens. He lights
it again, striking matches at 2,500 m,
in the dark, in freezing air, in a
gondola swaying under a balloon coming
apart. He keeps lighting it. Below them,
things are happening the families know
nothing about. West German radar has
picked up an unidentified object moving
toward the border. On the East German
side, a border commander has noticed
something against the sky. He gets on
the phone to Berlin, requests permission
to open fire." Berlin gives the order.
Searchlights sweep the border zone,
scanning the sky. The order is live. The
balloon is already gone. The wind
carried them past the border zone faster
than the searchlights could find them.
They are over West German territory,
though from inside a dark gondola at
2,500 m with a tearing envelope and a
burner that keeps dying, there is no way
to know that.
At 3:00 a.m., the propane runs out. All
four cylinders empty. The burner dies.
The balloon descends, not gradually,
quickly. The tear has been growing the
entire flight, and now, with no flame to
compensate, the gondola drops hard. They
hit the ground in an open field. Nobody
moves. The envelope collapses around
them in a heap of mismatched fabric. One
child is crying. Then, all of them are.
Then, they hear it. A car engine.
Headlights sweep across the field,
moving slowly, methodically, the way a
vehicle moves when it's looking for
something. Strelzyk and Wetzel watch the
lights get closer. Everything they spent
18 months building comes down to whose
car this is. The vehicle stops. Two men
get out in uniforms. Strelzyk steps
forward. He asks the only question that
matters.
>> Are we in the West?
>> The officers look at each other, then at
him, then at the collapsed balloon, then
at six people climbing out of a gondola
made of scrap iron and clothesline rope.
>> Yes.
You're in Bavaria,
district of Hof.
>> Peter Strelzyk turns back to his family.
For the first time in 18 months, he has
nothing left to plan.
By morning, newspapers across Europe
have the photographs. But in Pößneck,
things are moving very differently. The
Stasi knows within hours. Peter
Strelzyk's brother is arrested before
sunrise. His sister, Maria, and her
husband shortly after. None of them knew
anything. Both receive sentences of 2
and 1/2 years. And then the Stasi
launches Operation Peach, a coordinated
effort to destroy the family's new life
from the inside. One of Strelzyk's
closest friends takes a job in his shop
in Bad Kissingen. He is a Stasi
informant. The friendship between the
two families doesn't survive the
attention, the money, the pressure of
suddenly being symbols. By 1985, the
Strelzyks move to Switzerland. They
return after the wall falls. Peter
Strelzyk dies in Pößneck in 2017. The
balloon envelope ends up behind glass in
the Museum of Bavarian History in
Regensburg. A physical object that
somehow survived everything, which is
more than can be said for the border it
flew over.

text:
The video depicts scenes of warfare, showing soldiers in trenches and forests, with some engaging in combat and others lying on the ground, offering a glimpse into the grim realities of war. It also features a historical photograph of two military figures shaking hands, suggesting a narrative that spans different eras of conflict and resolution, highlighting significant moments in military history. This true story provides a raw and unflinching look at the human cost of world war 2, making it a compelling piece for those interested in war films and real history.

On October 8, 1918, a Tennessee farmer with shaking hands walked out of a French forest followed by 132 German soldiers who chose — without being forced — to follow him home. He had filed twice for conscientious objector status. He had begged not to fight. He was afraid not of dying, but of coming home someone his mother wouldn't recognize. And on that Tuesday morning in the Argonne Forest, Alvin York became the most decorated American soldier of World War I using a skill he learned before dawn in the mountains of Tennessee — hunting wild turkeys. 🔴

This is the story nobody fully tells. Not the headlines. Not the movie. The real story — of a pacifist who made a deal with God on a troop ship, of a patrol with a map written in French that nobody could read, of six men dead in under ten seconds, and of one farmer who understood something about turkeys that no military training manual had ever written down. ⚡

Alvin York WWI, Sergeant York Medal of Honor, Battle of Argonne Forest 1918, Meuse-Argonne offensive, conscientious objector WWI, WWI true story, greatest WWI battle, American hero World War One, 132 German prisoners, turkey hunting tactics war, WWI history documentary, Medal of Honor stories — if you've ever wanted to understand what actually happened on that hillside, why 132 trained German soldiers surrendered to one man, and what York did with the fame and money that followed — this is that story. 🎖️

He never shot the front bird first. He worked from the back. Quietly. Methodically. The same rhythm he had used a thousand times before sunrise in Fentress County. Except this time the targets were shooting back. And the man who was afraid of becoming someone different stood completely still and kept firing — not because the fear disappeared, but because the fear of doing nothing became larger than the fear of dying. 👀

He was promoted to sergeant on the spot. Every newspaper in America wanted the story. Hollywood offered him more money than he would see in ten lifetimes of farming. He said no. He went back to Tennessee. And when he finally accepted — he took everything they paid him and built a school for kids who grew up the way he did. Poor. Isolated. More talent than opportunity. 🏫

The general asked him if he'd captured the whole German army. York thought about it for a second. "No sir," he said quietly. "Just a few of them." 👻

subtitles.plaintext:
France, October 8th, 1918.
One man is walking through the forest.
Behind him, 132 German soldiers.
Armed, trained, alive, following a
Tennessee farmer they just tried to
kill. Nobody ordered them to follow him.
They chose to. His hands are still
shaking. He left home a pacifist. He is
about to go home a legend, but not for
the reason you think. Because this story
isn't about how one man defeated 132
soldiers. It's about why 132 soldiers
decided one man was worth surrendering
to.
But first, who is this man?
Alvin York grew up with one rule: if you
miss, the family doesn't eat. 11
children, one rifle, mountains of
Tennessee.
By the time York was 12, he was the best
shot in Fentress County. Not because
[music] he practiced, because he had no
choice. He could hit a moving turkey at
200 yards.
>> [music]
>> He never missed twice.
But 2 years before the draft letter
came, [music] York walked into a revival
meeting. He walked in one man, he walked
out someone different. The Bible was
clear: thou shalt not kill. Not [music]
unless your country asks. Not unless
it's wartime. Just
>> [music]
>> thou shalt not kill.
York believed this the way he believed
in gravity. So, when the draft [music]
letter came in 1917, York did something
almost nobody in his county did. He
said, [music] "No." Filed for
conscientious objector status, denied,
filed again, denied again. The third
letter wasn't a request. York folded it,
put it in his pocket, walked out to the
field behind his house. He stood there
for a long time looking at the
mountains. He wasn't afraid of dying. He
was afraid of coming home different, of
sitting at his mother's table, looking
at his hands, knowing what they had
done. He reported for duty anyway.
Somewhere between Tennessee and France,
he made a deal with God. He just wasn't
sure God was listening.
France, October 8th, 1918, before dawn.
17 men move through the forest in
silence. York is one of them. Not the
leader, just a corporal following
orders, doing his job, trying not to
think about Tennessee. They have one
mission, capture the Decauville
Railroad, cut German supply lines.
Simple on paper. They also have a map.
The map is in French. Nobody in the
patrol reads French. They move anyway,
deeper into the forest, further from
their lines, further from everything
familiar. The trees get thicker, the
light gets darker, the sounds of their
own artillery fade behind them. Then,
they hear voices, German voices, close,
too close. They have walked directly
into the middle of a German camp. For 1
second, nobody moves. The Americans open
fire first. Germans scatter. The patrol
captures a group of prisoners instantly,
more than they expected. For 1 second,
it feels like a victory. Then, the
hillside explodes. Machine guns above
them, hidden in the trees, firing down
into the valley where York's patrol is
standing with their prisoners in the
open. There is nowhere to run,
>> [music]
>> nowhere to hide. In the first burst of
fire, six Americans go down, dead before
they hit the ground. Three more [music]
wounded. Nine men out of 17 in under 10
seconds. York looks around for someone
[music] to give an order. The sergeant
is dead. The other sergeant is dead. The
corporal is down. Every man above
[music] York in the chain of command is
either dead or bleeding. There is nobody
left. The machine guns are still firing,
[music]
and Alvin York, the pacifist farmer from
Tennessee who begged not to be here, is
now [music] in command.
The man who didn't want to kill anyone
is now the only man left standing. York
doesn't freeze. He doesn't pray. He
doesn't think about Tennessee or God or
the deal he made on the ship. There is
no time for any of that. There is only
the hillside above him and the sound of
machine guns and eight men still alive
who are looking at him waiting for
someone to tell them what to do. He
takes command the only way he knows how,
not with orders, not with a plan, with
instinct. He tells the surviving men to
hold the prisoners and stay down. Then
he turns toward the hill, toward the
machine guns, toward the thing that just
killed six of his friends in under
[music] 10 seconds. And he starts moving
forward. Not charging, not running.
Moving the way a hunter moves through
the Tennessee mountains before dawn when
the animals don't know he's there. Low,
slow, deliberate, using every tree,
every shadow, every fold in the ground.
His body doing something his mind has
never had to think about because he has
done this 10,000 times [music] before.
Not in France, in Fentress County.
Before sunrise when the family needed
food and missing meant [music] going
hungry. The Germans on the hill are not
looking for him. They are watching the
Americans below waiting for the patrol
to break [music] and run. That's what
happens when machine guns open up at
close range. People panic, scatter,
>> [music]
>> retreat. It's not cowardice, it's
biology. Every military unit in every
war in history has broken under
unexpected machine gun fire from an
elevated position. York's patrol doesn't
break because York doesn't let them. He
keeps moving up the hill. Now, here is
the detail that most people don't know.
And it's the detail that explains
everything. York grew up hunting wild
turkeys, and turkeys are not stupid
animals. They are fast, alert, and they
communicate with each other. If you're
hunting a flock and you shoot the bird
at the front, the rest scatter
instantly. You get one bird, maybe two
if you're fast. Then the whole flock is
gone and you walk home with nothing. So,
you never shoot the front bird first.
You shoot from the back. Take the last
bird in the line. It drops quietly.
[music]
The birds in front don't see it, don't
hear it, don't know anything has
changed. Then you take the next one from
the back, and the next. You work your
way forward slowly and methodically, and
by the time the birds at the front
realize something is wrong, there are no
birds [music] left behind them to warn
them. York had been doing this since he
was 8 years old. He applied the exact
same logic to the German machine gun
position. He positioned himself at an
angle where he could see the line of
gunners, but they couldn't easily see
him through the trees. Then he started
from the back. One shot. The last gunner
in the line goes down. The gunners in
front don't notice. The noise of battle
covers everything, and nobody looks
behind them when they're under attack.
Then the next one from the back, then
the next. Clean, methodical, precise.
The same rhythm he had used a thousand
times in the Tennessee mountains, except
the targets were shooting back. The
German fire is coming at him from every
direction. Bullets hitting the trees
around him, hitting the ground next to
him. He can hear them. He can feel the
air move when they pass close. And York,
the man who begged not to be here, who
filed twice for conscientious objector
status, who was afraid not of dying, but
of becoming someone different, stands
completely still and keeps shooting. Not
because he stopped being afraid, but
because somewhere in the noise, in the
smoke, in the bodies of his friends on
the ground below him, the fear of dying
became smaller than the fear of doing
nothing. He fires 28 times. 28 times he
hits exactly what he aimed at. The
machine gun position that had killed six
Americans in 10 seconds goes quiet. And
then something happens that nobody, not
York, not his patrol, not anyone on that
hillside expected. A German officer
stands up.
His name is Major Paul Vollmer, and he
has just watched York kill every gunner
on his hill. Now, he is coming down
himself.
Vollmer is not a coward. He is not
inexperienced. He is a decorated German
officer who has been fighting on the
Western Front for 4 years. He has seen
things that would break most men. He has
survived artillery barrages, gas
attacks, infantry charges across open
ground. [music] He knows what war looks
like from every angle. What he is
watching right now doesn't make sense.
One man standing in the open under
direct fire from an entire machine gun
battalion, not moving, not retreating,
just shooting. Calmly and methodically
working through his position like he has
all the time in the world and nowhere
else to be.
Vollmer watches his gunners go down one
by one.
>> [music]
>> He counts. He does the math. He looks at
the angle of fire and tries to
understand what he is dealing with. He
can't figure it out. So, he decides to
end it himself. Vollmer stands up, draws
his pistol, takes six of his best men,
and leads them directly down the hill
toward York in a bayonet charge. It is a
brave thing to do. It is also the
logical thing to do. One man with a
rifle cannot stop seven soldiers
charging at close range. By the time he
reloads, they will be on top of him.
This is how you stop a sniper. You
charge him before he can react. York
sees them coming. He puts down his
rifle.
>> [music]
>> He draws his pistol. What happens next
has a very simple explanation that
nobody talks about. Back in Tennessee,
York didn't just hunt turkeys. He
competed in shooting matches across
Fentress County. The most important
skill in a shooting match isn't
accuracy. It's speed. How can you
acquire a target, fire, and move to the
next one? How fast can your hands work
while your mind stays calm? York had
spent years training his hands to move
faster than his brain. Vollmer's men are
charging downhill, seven of them,
closing fast. Most soldiers in this
situation would panic. Too many targets
moving too fast at too close a range.
Most soldiers would fire wildly and
hope. York doesn't panic. He starts from
the back. The last man in Vollmer's
charge goes down. Then the next from the
back. Then the next. York works his way
forward through the charging soldiers
the same way he worked through the
machine gunners, methodically, from back
to front, giving the men ahead no time
to understand what is happening behind
them. Six shots, six men down in the
time it takes [music] most soldiers to
fire twice. Vollmer stops. He is now
alone on the hillside. His pistol is
empty. Six of his men are behind him on
the ground. In front of him is a single
American soldier with a pistol pointed
directly at his chest who has just done
something that Vollmer's entire military
training tells him is not possible.
Vollmer does something that surprises
even York. He offers to surrender.
>> [music]
>> Not just himself, everyone. The entire
position. Every German soldier on that
hill. York looks at him for a moment,
then he responds in the only German he
knows, a phrase he learned from a fellow
soldier on the way to France, because
someone told him it might be useful.
Kamerad. He says.
Surrender. Volmer turns to his men and
gives the order. One by one, the Germans
stand up, come out from their positions,
put down their weapons, line up in the
valley below. York counts them as they
come. 10, 20, 50, 100. He keeps
counting. 132.
Here is what York said about this moment
years later when people asked him how he
felt. He said he felt grateful, not
proud, not powerful, not like the hero
every newspaper in America was about to
tell him he was. Grateful, because every
single one of those 132 men was alive,
because Volmer made the decision he
made, because nobody else had to die
that morning. The man who was afraid of
what killing would do to him had just
survived the most violent 20 minutes of
the entire war, and his first feeling

not in the way he expected.

132
German soldiers, [music]
seven surviving Americans, and 7 km of
enemy territory between them and the
American line.
York does the math. The prisoners
outnumber his patrol 20 to 1.

are. They know exactly how many
Americans are guarding them. If they

both ways.
The same chain of command that sent them
up that hill is now keeping them in line
behind a Tennessee farmer with a rifle.
York understands this instinctively. Not
from military training, from hunting.
You control the lead animal, the rest
follow. So, he controls Vollmer, and
Vollmer controls everyone else.
They move through the forest in silence.
7 km through terrain that York has never
seen before, using a map that is in
French, navigating by instinct and by
watching [music] Vollmer's face for any
sign that something is wrong.
Twice they pass close [music] to other
German positions.
York feels Vollmer tense up next to him.
Both times, he presses the rifle
slightly [music] into Vollmer's back.

keep walking.

perimeter when he sees them through the

starts counting. He counts again. He

When York reaches him, Buxton looks at

second. No, sir. Just a few of them.

Within days, the story is everywhere.
Every newspaper in America, every radio
broadcast, every conversation in every
diner and barber shop from Tennessee to
California.
One man, one morning, 132 prisoners.
America has its hero, and Alvin York has
a problem he never anticipated. Everyone
wants a piece of him.
America wanted a hero. York just wanted
to go home.
The newspapers found him before the ship
docked. Reporters, photographers,
everyone with a pen and a camera [music]
and a story to sell. One man, 132
prisoners. The kind of story that writes
itself. York answered their questions
politely, said what needed to be said,
then went back to Tennessee. His

quiet for a moment.
>> [music]
>> I wasn't alone. He said. Nobody was sure

[music]
the story, his face on posters across

text:
In 1962, three Israeli intelligence agents walked into a Nazi's living room — and offered him a job. 🔴

Hitler's most dangerous commando. The man who rescued Mussolini from a mountain prison. The man who paralysed Eisenhower with a single rumour. A committed Nazi who kept a portrait of the Führer on his wall until the day he died.

And by the end of that conversation — he was working for the Jewish state.
This is the true story of Otto Skorzeny — the most decorated SS officer of World War II, the most wanted commando in Europe, and the most unlikely intelligence asset in Mossad history. A story about impossible choices when survival becomes the only principle left. About a spy agency willing to shake hands with a man who helped murder millions — because the alternative was worse. And about one Nazi who spent his final useful years systematically destroying everything his former comrades had built. ⚡

By 1962, Egypt was months away from fielding missiles capable of hitting Tel Aviv. Former Nazi scientists — the same men who built Hitler's V-2 rockets — were working in the Egyptian desert at a facility called Factory 333. The Mossad was running out of options.

So Isser Harel — the man who kidnapped Adolf Eichmann from a Buenos Aires street corner — made the most morally impossible decision of his career. Don't kill Skorzeny. Recruit him. ⚖️

What followed was one of the most extraordinary double lives in the history of espionage. Mondays: dinner with former SS colonels at the Madrid villa, toasting fallen comrades. Tuesdays: dead drops in a Madrid park, passing intelligence to handlers he never met face to face. One wrong word at either table — and he was a dead man. 👀

The German missile programme never produced a weapon capable of reaching Israel. Factory 333 went silent. The scientists went home. Millions of civilians never knew how close it came.

Skorzeny died in his bed in Madrid in 1975. Former SS officers raised their arms in salute beside his coffin. They were saluting a man who had spent his final years dismantling everything they believed in.
They never knew. They never found out. 👻

No one in this story gets a clean conscience. Only one side needed it.

text:
What if America woke up tomorrow… communist?
The big corporations vanish, the stock market stops, and every job, farm, and factory becomes state‑run.

Supermarkets go from 40 types of cereal to one. Careers get assigned. Innovation slows. Life becomes more predictable — and a lot less exciting.

Healthcare becomes free, inequality shrinks, and essentials are guaranteed… but choice, variety, and economic dynamism take a hit.

America would still function — just not the America we know.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

subtitles.plaintext:
This is North Korea. A country of 26
million people
where the state owns nearly every
factory, every farm, and every shop. The
government decides what gets made, what
it costs, and who works [music] where.
Now, picture the United States.
349 million people, the largest consumer
economy on Earth, waking up tomorrow
under the same rules.
No more Apple, no more Walmart, no more
Wall Street.
One employer, one landlord, one
provider.
It sounds extreme, and in many [music]
ways it is.
But before we get into how daily life
would feel under that setup, it's worth
breaking down what we're actually
talking about.
Capitalism, the system America runs on
today, is built [music] on private
ownership. People and companies own the
businesses, the land, and the factories.
[music]
Prices are set by supply and demand, and
profit is the engine that pushes
everything forward.
Build a better computer, and you get
rich. Run a bad restaurant, and it
closes.
In capitalism, the market decides. Under
communism, that entire decision-making
process is reversed. Instead, the state
owns the major industries, central
planners set the prices, [music] and the
government directs labor. Profit as a
motivator disappears.
The idea in theory is that resources get
shared more equally, and no one falls
through the cracks.
However, whether that works in practice
is a very different question.
So, let's leave politics aside and look
at what would actually change in your
supermarket, your job, your hospital,
and your [music] bank account.
The first shift would be ownership.
Overnight, the largest 500 or so
companies, think Amazon, ExxonMobil, or
JP Morgan, would no longer belong to
shareholders. They'd be nationalized
[music] and belong to the state.
What happens to Wall Street depends on
which version of communism America
adopts. [music] In a strict Soviet-style
command economy, the New York Stock
Exchange, which currently trades over
1.5 trillion dollars in shares every
month, would simply [music] stop. It's
worth noting that not every communist
country goes that far. China and
Vietnam, [music]
both run by communist parties, actually
operate stock exchanges of their own.
The Shanghai Stock Exchange is one of
the largest in the world. And Vietnam's
Ho Chi Minh exchange has hundreds of
listed companies. But in these systems,
the authorities still control the big
industries,
>> [music]
>> decides which firms can list, and steers
credit toward its own priorities.
Now, let's walk into a supermarket.
A typical American grocery store carries
between 30,000 and 50,000 different
products. There are 14 kinds of ketchup,
40 types of cereal, [music] and an
entire aisle dedicated to flavored
sparkling water. That variety exists
because hundreds of companies are
competing to win [music] your dollar.
Under central planning, that competition
disappears.
Instead of Heinz, Hunt's, and a dozen
private labels fighting for shelf space,
there'd just be ketchup. One kind, made
in one factory, distributed by one
agency.
The upside [music] is that prices stay
stable and basic goods are guaranteed.
The downside is that when that plan gets
it wrong, you get shortages.
The Soviet Union wrestled with this
problem for decades. In the 1950s,
reports described ordinary people
waiting more than 6 hours just to buy
bread.
By the late 1980s, queues had become
such a normal part of life that when the
first McDonald's opened in Moscow in
1990, [music] an estimated 30,000 people
showed up on day one.
>> The store had to stay open several hours
past its posted [music] closing time
because there were so many people still
in line. And the store set a McDonald's
record for most people served on an
opening day, 30,000.
>> Agriculture would face the same kind of
upheaval. American farms today are
astonishingly productive. [music] Barely
1.5% of the population works the land,
yet they feed the entire country and
still export more than $175 billion
worth of food every single year.
Under a communist system, those farms
wouldn't operate independently. They'd
be nationalized or folded into larger
collectives with production targets
handed down from above.
Instead of a farmer in Iowa planting
corn because the market price looks
good, a government office would instruct
[music] him to plant corn because the
five-year plan says so.
If Uncle Sam is directing what gets
grown and what [music] gets built, the
next thing he inevitably controls are
the workforce.
Today, you choose your career, negotiate
your salary, and switch jobs when
something better comes along.
Under communism, if the country needs
more nurses in Ohio or more factory
workers in Texas, there's a good chance
you'll get sent there. And you'll likely
get paid the bare minimum for the
pleasure.
In the Soviet Union, a senior engineer
earned only two or three times what an
unskilled laborer made.
In the US today, that gap can stretch to
10 or even 20 times. [music]
Your job would be more stable, protected
from layoffs or AI automation, but
security comes at the cost of career
progression.
You're unlikely to be fired, but you're
also unlikely to get rich. When workers
are tightly controlled and
entrepreneurship is smothered,
you have to ask, what happens to
innovation?
America's tech sector exists [music]
because someone with an idea can raise
millions, build a company, and [music]
if they're lucky, walk away with
billions of dollars.
But if you take profit out of the
equation, the incentive kind of
collapses. [music]
Why would anyone spend 10 years trying
to build the next Tesla [music] if the
reward is the same paycheck as the guy
working a routine admin job down the
hall?
That doesn't mean no innovation. After
all, the Soviets launched the first
satellite, [music] built the first
nuclear power plant, and produced some
of the world's greatest mathematicians.
But progress tends to follow central
priorities: defense, heavy industry,
infrastructure, rather than consumer
products. You'd still get [music]
rockets. You probably wouldn't get the
iPhone.
But it's not all downside. As a nation,
we might actually end up a little
healthier.
The US spends over 5.3 trillion dollars
a year on health care.
>> [music]
>> That's roughly $15,500
per person, more than any other country
on Earth. And yet millions of people are
uninsured or buried in medical debt.
Under a state-run system, [music]
health care would be free at the point
of use. Hospitals would be publicly
owned. Doctors would be on the public
payroll. [music] And prescriptions would
come without a bill attached. Wait times
for non-urgent treatments would get
longer, and the most expensive
treatments could be rationed according
to medical need rather [music] than the
ability to pay. Energy and
infrastructure would also fall under
government control.
>> [music]
>> In theory, that creates room for
long-term planning: expanding renewable
power, modernizing the grid, and keeping
prices stable.
In practice, large state-run energy
companies often drift toward
inefficiency and slow adaptation.
Venezuela is the starkest [music] modern
example.
In 1998, it produced 3.4 million barrels
of oil per day. After years of
nationalization and chronic
underinvestment, output collapsed to
roughly 1 million barrels, despite the
country holding the largest proven oil
reserves on the planet.
So, would a communist America actually
work?
The honest answer is that it would solve
some problems and create many others.
Inequality would shrink, healthcare and
housing would be guaranteed, and the
markets boom and bust cycles would
soften. But the cost would be paid in
variety, innovation, personal choice,
[music]
and economic dynamism. The supermarket
would have ketchup, but only one kind.
>> [music]
>> The hospital would be free, but the wait
would be longer. The job would be
secure, but the ceiling would be low.
And we'd probably all be a little bit
bored. America, in short, would still
function. It just wouldn't resemble the
America [music] we know today.

text:
Israel produces more start-ups per capita than any country on Earth — but the reasons behind this are far more surprising than most people realise. In this video, we explore the forces that shaped one of the world’s most influential tech ecosystems, and how a small nation became a global innovation heavyweight.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Welcome to BRIMM.

subtitles.plaintext:
This is Israel. It is home to more than
24,000 startups, [music]
the highest concentration per capita
anywhere in the world. 42 of those
companies have grown into unicorns,
meaning they're valued at over a billion
dollars.
>> [music]
>> And despite its small size, Israel ranks
fourth globally for the number of
[music] companies listed on the NASDAQ,
behind only the United States, Canada,
and China.
Nvidia already has 6,000 [music]
employees here and is planning a new
base with 10,000 more. Western
governments [music] are buying more
weapons. Germany signed a 3 billion euro
contract [music] for Arrow 3 batteries.
Finland became the first foreign buyer
of the David Sling system, and the
Czechs have integrated Israeli radars
into NATO networks.
Given the wider context, it's important
to be clear. This video is about the
country's business ecosystem, not its
politics. We're not promoting any
government, and we don't support war in
any part of the world.
Whatever your views on the region, the
growth of its tech and startup scene is
a genuinely fascinating story worth
understanding.
This is a country where more than half
the land is desert, and [music] water
scarcity was a chronic constraint until
recently. Yet, it produces more startups
than India, [music]
Japan, Korea, or the UK.
Bloomberg ranks Israel fifth on its
global innovation index, and first in
the world [music] for research and
development. Add to that the pressure of
international boycotts and recurring
conflict, and the picture becomes even
more surprising.
How did this wave of innovation emerge?
Were things always like this?
The answer is most definitely
>> [music]
>> not.
From 1948 through the early 1990s, the
country's economic performance was far
from [music] impressive.
For much of the late 20th century,
Israel's economy looked more like a
volatile Latin American state than the
wealthy country people recognize today.
Between 1974 and 1986, inflation stayed
above 30% every year, and by 1984, it
hit nearly 400%.
At its peak, Israel's hyperinflation
actually surpassed what Venezuela
experienced [music] during its 2015
crisis.
The turning point came in the mid-1980s.
In 1985, the US helped design a
stabilization plan that finally brought
inflation under control and created an
environment where people were willing to
stay, work, and invest. By the early
1990s, Israel entered a period of
stability, [music] and the foundations
of today's economy began to take shape.
This shift sparked the first generation
of homegrown startups. [music]
Many natives returned from the US to
launch companies, open R&D centers for
their American employers, or invest in
the emerging tech [music] scene, setting
the stage for the boom that followed.
A wave of immigration during that same
decade brought more than 900,000 people
to Israel. Many of them engineers,
professors, and scientists from the
former Soviet Union.
For a country with a population of only
about 4.8 million at the time, it
[music] amounted to a 20% surge almost
overnight, and it arrived at exactly the
moment the country needed an infusion of
talent.
They injected Israel's young tech sector
[music] with exactly the kind of
expertise it lacked.
Around the same time, the government
launched the now-famous Yozma program.
It put $20 million on the table on a 1.5
to 1 [music] matching basis. The state
would take a 40% equity stake, but
allowed partners to buy out that share
cheaply after 5 years.
In practice, the government absorbed
much of the risk while [music] investors
got all the reward. Startups began
appearing across the country. Venture
funds multiplied, and the [music] tech
ecosystem quickly became a magnet for
global capital.
No exploration of Israel's business
culture is complete without recognizing
the influence of its army.
The long history of regional conflict
has produced a culture of constant
military readiness. As a result, [music]
all citizens over 18 are required to
serve, roughly 24 months for women and
32 months for men.
The system was built to protect [music]
the country, but it has evolved into an
unexpected talent development engine.
Recruits are sorted early into fields
where they show promise, physics,
material science, engineering, or
leadership, creating a pipeline that
cultivates technical skill and sound
judgment years before most people enter
the workforce.
During service, young Israelis work with
advanced military technologies that
often spark ideas for research and
commercial products. This is where Unit
8200 stands out, where they are asked
with intercepting and decoding signals,
calls, emails, and other communications,
and it attracts some of the brightest
minds in [music] the country. The unit
has extraordinary latitude in
recruitment. It can select anyone it
[music] wants, and in some cases begins
identifying talent years before
conscription.
One of its feeders, Mog Shamim, is an
after-school [music]
program designed for exceptional high
school technologists and hackers. Its
alumni are impressive. Look at Uri
Levine. After leaving the army, he and
several partners founded Waze in 2008.
[music]
Five years later, Google acquired the
app, now the world's most widely used
navigation tool, for over $1 billion,
>> [music]
>> the largest acquisition in Google's
history.
Unit 8200 is only one pillar of Israel's
military-driven innovation model.
Talpiot is an elite [music] academy
built to recruit the country's strongest
scientific minds and train them to come
up with innovative ideas to help the
army.
Its outcomes are extraordinary. Around a
quarter of graduates become
entrepreneurs, and one in three of those
founders have built a company worth over
100 million dollars. In practice, that
means one in eight Talpiot entrepreneurs
creates a unicorn.
Roughly 10% of all Israeli unicorns, and
about 30% of its deca unicorns,
companies worth over 10 billion dollars,
trace back to this single program.
Graduates have spawned a string of super
interesting companies, like Takadu, who
develop smart water infrastructure
monitoring systems that [music] detect
leaks in real time anywhere in the
world. One of its major clients is
Britain's Thames Water. So, when a pipe
bursts [music] in London, the first
alert often comes from a computer in Tel
Aviv, which is pretty remarkable.
And finally, but crucially, Israel
benefits from an unusually close link
between academia and industry. [music]
Universities function almost like
conveyor belts, pushing research out of
the lab and into commercial use.
This proximity matters because
researchers aren't typically
entrepreneurs. They generate patents,
but turning those patents into products
requires business expertise. The
Institute of Technology publishes The
Book of Good Ideas, a catalog of patents
companies can license. It's a simple
system, but it keeps promising
technologies from gathering dust and
helps them move directly into the
market.
Put all these pieces together, and you
get a country that operates nothing like
its scale. Israel is smaller than every
major Middle Eastern nation, with only
Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, and Lebanon
coming in below it.
In a region dominated by vast land
masses like Saudi Arabia and Iran, it's
geographically tiny. Yet, it produces
more startups, more unicorns, and more
cutting-edge tech than almost all of
them.
And whatever you make of Israel,
especially after years of difficult
headlines, its rise from a small,
resource-strained state to a global
innovation heavyweight is, at the very
least, a fascinating story. [music]

title: He Survived 62 Hours Inside a Sunken Ship 100 Feet Underwater
channelDescription: Just history, told clearly and honestly.

text:
This is the true story of Harrison Okene — the Nigerian ship cook who survived for 62 hours inside a sunken tugboat, 100 feet underwater, while everyone above the surface believed the entire crew was gone.

In May 2013, the tugboat Jascon-4 capsized off the coast of Nigeria during a violent storm. Twelve men were on board. Eleven did not make it out.

Okene was trapped inside the wreck in total darkness, wearing only boxer shorts, sitting in a tiny air pocket while the ship lay upside down on the ocean floor.

He had no training.
No diving gear.
No light.
Almost no food or water.

For more than two days, he stayed still, prayed, listened to the metal around him creak under pressure, and waited in the dark while his wife hundreds of miles away began preparing his funeral.

When commercial divers finally reached the wreck, they were not searching for survivors.

They were sent to recover bodies.

Then, inside the flooded engineer’s cabin, a diver felt a hand grab his wrist.

The man was still alive.

This is the full story of Harrison Okene, the Jascon-4 sinking, the storm, the air pocket, the physics that kept him breathing, the rescue divers, the dangerous decompression process, and the phone call that made his wife stop the casket.

just after sunset.
A South African diver named Nico van
Heerden
>> [music]
>> swims through the flooded engineer's

the ocean floor.

crew.
A hand reaches out of the dark [music]

The hand belongs to the ship's cook. His

>> [music]
>> He is 29 years old. He has been alone
inside the sunken tugboat for 62 [music]
hours.
The other 11 members of his crew are
dead. The contract is a body recovery
mission. Nobody is supposed to be alive
down here.
The wreck is 100 ft underwater. The air
pocket Okene has been breathing is 1 and
1/2 m wide. He is wearing boxer shorts.
400 km away in Lagos, his wife, [music]
who has not heard from him in 3 days, is
finalizing the seating chart for his
funeral.
How does a ship's cook
>> [music]
>> in his underwear stay alive for 62 hours
at the bottom of the Atlantic when every
physiology textbook says the air should
have run out after 15? And what does
Nico [music] van Heerden tell his
support team on the surface in the next
4 seconds when he realizes the hand he
is holding is not the hand of a corpse?
Harrison Ojeba Okene, born March 1984,
Warri, Nigeria. His father drove a
truck. His mother sold fabric at the
central market. Harrison finished
secondary school in 2003. He did not go
to university. In 2011, he was hired
[music] at 27 as a steward and cook on a
tugboat operated by West African
Ventures, a marine services contractor
working for Chevron and Shell on the
offshore platforms [music] of the Niger
Delta, the tugboat was the Jascon 4. The
job paid $1,200 a month. For a married
man from Warri with no university
degree, it was a transforming amount of
money. Okene had married a year earlier.
His wife was named Akpevwe [music]
Okene. They had no children yet. He was
a cook, not a sailor. His job on the
boat was three meals a day for the
12-man crew. He had never been more than
12 nautical miles from shore. On the
morning of May 22nd, 2013, his wife
drove him to the bus station in Warri.
He kissed her on both cheeks. He told
her he would call when the tugboat
docked off Bayelsa. He did not call. On
the night of May 25th, he served the
evening meal at 6:00, washed the
kitchen, and went to bed. The cabin
door, by company protocol, was locked
from inside. In the Niger Delta in 2013,
the protocol existed because of piracy.
It was the reason Harrison Okene was
alive 48 hours later. It was also the
reason 11 other men were not.
4:15 in the morning on May 26th, an
Atlantic squall arrived. The wind
shifted 30°. The sea state went from
moderate to severe within 12 minutes. A
6-m rogue wave hit the Jascon 4 from the

Harrison Okene was in the bathroom
adjacent to his cabin. He had gotten up
at 4:20 because he had drunk too much
water before bed.
He was, at the moment of capsizing,
sitting on the toilet. The boat rolled.
The water came up through the floor
drain. Within 4 seconds, the bathroom
was upside down and full of water.
O'Kini was thrown against what had been
the ceiling, which was now the floor.
He hit something solid in the dark. He
grabbed it.
For the first half [music] second, he
thought it was the body of one of his
colleagues. It was a door frame. He
pulled himself through.
>> [music]
>> He was screaming his wife's name. For
the next 12 hours, the world above the
surface would believe that the Jascon 4
had sunk with all 12 men on board. For
the next 62 hours, exactly one of them
would still be inside it. The bathroom
O'Kini was thrown into had not
completely filled with water.
A column of air, approximately 1 and 1/2
m high, 2 m long, had been trapped
against what was now the ceiling.
O'Kini moved through the dark on his
hands and knees, his head above the
waterline, into the engineer's cabin.
The water was up to his sternum.
The air pocket above was slightly
larger.
He found the metal bunk frame.
He climbed onto it.
He sat with his head 1 in from the
ceiling.
The tugboat had been upside down for 10
minutes.
He was wearing only boxer shorts.
The water temperature was 22° C,
7° below his body's core temperature.
His body began to lose heat at 25 times
the rate it would have lost in air.
In the dark, he began to shake.
Within an hour, the shaking stopped.
The body, when it has been cold long
enough, stops trying to warm [music]
itself.
He felt around in the dark.
His hand encountered something soft and
floating.
A foam mattress.
He pulled it under him.
He folded it in half.
He climbed onto it.
By the end of the first day, his feet
had no feeling.
He found a Coca-Cola bottle on a shelf.
He made it last 18 hours.
In the dark, he began to pray. He prayed
the 23rd [music] Psalm. He spoke aloud
in pidgin English.
The Lord is my shepherd. I shall not
want.
He prayed it 27 times in a row before he
stopped to listen for sounds.
The sounds were the worst part.
He could hear through the metal
the structural noises of a ship being
crushed by water [music] pressure at 30
m.
The walls creaked.
The floor, which was the ceiling, popped
at irregular intervals.
He could also hear something else.
In the cabins on the other side of the
bulkhead, where 11 of his colleagues had
been trapped behind locked doors when
the water came in, the marine [music]
life of the Niger Delta had already

He understood, after the third hour of

He pressed his hands against his ears.
The sound continued inside his head.
It did not stop for the next 2 days.
He thought, on the second night, about
his wife.
He did not know whether she had been

He hoped that, if she had been told, she

On the morning of the third day, the

this was the worst news he had heard
yet.
He did not stop praying.
By every calculation the engineers
performed after the recovery, Harrison
Okene should not have been alive.
A human at rest consumes half a liter of
oxygen per minute. An air pocket [music]
the size Okene was breathing contains,
at the surface, approximately 14 hours

Three things saved him. The first

It functioned as a chemical scrubber,

The third was O'Keeffe himself.

prayed in a whisper. His oxygen
consumption was approximately [music]
40% of normal resting metabolism.
Pressure multiplied his oxygen. The
water removed his carbon dioxide. His
stillness reduced what he needed. He did
not know any of this. He was certain by

going to die.
He had begun to dictate in the dark his

the air in the direction he thought
Warie was.

The contract to recover the Jascon-4 had
been awarded to DCN Diving on May 27th,
approximately 20 hours after the boat
went down.
The contract was specific. Recover the

if not.
12 bodies were expected.
The DCN team arrived at the wreck site
at 4:00 in the morning on May 28th. The
lead diver was Nico van Heerden, 32
years old, 11 years of commercial
diving. He had recovered 17 bodies in 5

title: How Napoleon Pulled Off the Greatest Escape From Exile
channelDescription: Just history, told clearly and honestly.

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: Just history, told clearly and honestly.

text:
In April 1814, the most powerful man in the world, Napoleon Bonaparte, stepped off a boat, marking a pivotal moment in world history. This video brings to life military scenes with large armies and cavalry charges, showcasing the grandeur and conflict of Napoleon's empire. We explore this epic history, from the battlefields of France to the carriages of power, providing a glimpse into a monumental era.

In 1814, the kings of Europe thought they had finally defeated Napoleon Bonaparte. They stripped him of his empire and locked him away on Elba—a tiny island they thought he would die on. They were wrong. Just 292 days later, Napoleon engineered the most audacious psychological operation and military comeback in human history.

This is the unbelievable true story of a bloodless invasion, an army that switched sides in 30 seconds, a king who ran from his own palace in the middle of the night, and the fatal mistake in the mud at Waterloo that cost Napoleon everything.

If you enjoyed this story, make sure to subscribe to the channel!

00:00 - The Greatest Heist in History 
00:52 - THE ISLAND

23:51 - THE END

collapse, becomes every man for himself
[music] running through the Belgian mud
while Prussian cavalry cuts them down
from behind.
Napoleon stands on a hill watching his
army [music] dissolve.
His marshals surround him urging him to
flee. He doesn't move for a long time,
just watches. Then he turns his horse
and rides. The battle lasted 8 hours.
The French army that took 19 days to
build without firing a shot is gone in
one afternoon. In the 100 days that
began on a beach in southern France with
700 soldiers end here in a field in
Belgium in the rain with everything
lost. [music]
June 22nd, 1815. Napoleon abdicates for
the second time, 4 days after Waterloo.
This time [music] there is no Elba, no
small Mediterranean island with 12,000
people and a view of the sea. The
British sent him somewhere he can't
escape from, Saint Helena, a volcanic
rock in the middle of the South Atlantic
Ocean, 2,000 km from the nearest
coastline,
>> [music]
>> population 4,000. Napoleon spends the
last 6 years of his life there. No
campaigns, no armies, no maps to study,
just ocean in every direction and a
house on a hill where he dictates his
memoirs to whoever will listen.
If you enjoyed this story, subscribe.
[music]
That helps the channel grow. Thank you.

title: The Man Who Destroyed the Nazi Nuclear Factory and Saved the World
channelDescription: Just history, told clearly and honestly.

text:
On February 28th, 1943, deep within a Norwegian hydroelectric plant, five men stood before cylinders producing heavy water, an ingredient vital for Germany's nuclear weapon program. This historical account details the daring operation against a heavily guarded German military fortress. Learn about Operation Gunnerside, a critical mission during World War 2 to thwart Nazi atomic ambitions.

If the German nuclear project had succeeded, the course of the war — and possibly the entire world — could have changed forever.
In this documentary, we uncover the true story behind Operation Gunnerside, the mission that infiltrated one of the most heavily guarded industrial sites in Nazi-occupied Europe. Led by Joachim Rønneberg and supported by the Norwegian resistance and the British Special Operations Executive (SOE), the team skied across the frozen Hardangervidda plateau, descended a 200-meter gorge in the dark, and planted explosives inside the Vemork plant.

Against impossible odds, they destroyed Germany’s heavy water production and dealt a devastating blow to Hitler’s atomic ambitions.
This is the story of the men who risked everything to stop the Nazi nuclear program — and carried out what many historians call the most successful sabotage operation of World War II.
