subtitles.plaintext:
February 28th, 1943, 2:30 a.m. The
basement of a Norwegian hydroelectric
plant.
Five men are standing in front of 18
metal cylinders. Each cylinder produces
a single substance, heavy water, the
ingredient Germany needs for a nuclear
bomb. Outside this room, 100 German
soldiers. Above them, a fortress the
Wehrmacht considers impregnable. Around
them, mountains, minefields, and a
garrison on high alert. None of the
Germans know these five men are here.
One of them kneels by the nearest
cylinder, places a shaped charge against
the casing, 2 kg of plastic explosive
positioned exactly where the metal is
thinnest. He learned the weak point from
blueprints drawn by the man who built
this room. 18 cylinders, 18 charges.
Fuses cut to 30 seconds.
>> [music]
>> A Norwegian night watchman lies face
down on the floor. He saw their faces,
heard them speak Norwegian, decided not
to shout.
>> [music]
>> The leader strikes a match. Nothing. The
head crumbles against the box. For 1
second, he is 23 years old in a basement
full of explosives holding a dead match,
and the only thought in his head is, "I
should have brought more matches."
He strikes the second. The fuse catches.
30 seconds.
Get out. Now. Run.
They don't run. Running makes noise.
They walk. Fast, silent, controlled.
Back through a broken window, through a
corridor, into a cable tunnel the width
of a man's shoulders.
20 seconds. Crawling through the narrow
passage, emerging into freezing air. 10
seconds. They're still inside the
perimeter when the explosion hits. A
muffled thud. No fireball, no collapsing
walls, just the sound of liquid hitting
concrete. 500 kg of heavy water pouring
across the basement floor. Months of
production gone in seconds. The most
strategically important sabotage of the
Second World War [music] sounds like a
door slamming three floors down.
But to understand how five men got into
a basement the German army didn't know
could be reached, you have to go back
four [music] months to a room in London
where a man is staring at photographs of
the factory he built and planning how to
destroy it.
London, late 1942.
A room inside the Special Operations
Executive Headquarters. On the table,
aerial photographs of a hydroelectric
plant built into the side of a Norwegian
mountain. Around the table, men who
haven't slept in days. The plant is
called Vemork. From the air, it looks
like an ordinary power station, pipes,
concrete, steam, nothing you'd look at
twice. But in the basement, 18
electrolysis cells run day and night,
each one producing heavy water,
deuterium oxide, the ingredient Germany
needs for a nuclear reactor. Without it,
no chain reaction. [music] Without a
chain reaction, no bomb. Vemork is the
only plant in occupied Europe making it,
and it's been shipping to Berlin for
months. Hundreds of kilograms already
delivered. Germany's program needs
several tons. Every month the factory
keeps running, that number gets closer.
The men in this room know the
arithmetic. If Vemork keeps [music]
producing, Germany gets a reactor. If
Germany gets a reactor, Germany gets a
bomb. If Germany gets a bomb, London,
Moscow, [music] New York. A single
flash, a city gone. They also know the
cost. Three four British commandos have
already tried to reach this factory,
Operation Freshman. Gliders crashed in a
blizzard, men captured, every one of
them executed under Hitler's commando
order. The factory is still running. The
logical next step? Bombers. Level the
valley. Flatten Vemork from 30,000 ft.
One man stops them. Leif Tronstad. 41
years old, wire-rimmed glasses, a
professor's posture, and an operative's
patience. Before the war, he designed
Vemork's electrolysis system, the
layout, the pipework, the exact position
of every machine in the basement. He
escaped occupied Norway with the
blueprints in his coat. Now, he sits in
this room arguing against the simplest
option on the table. Bombing won't work.
The electrolysis chambers sit below
ground level, reinforced concrete built
into the mountain itself. You'd have to
level half of Rjukan to reach them and
kill hundreds of Norwegian civilians in
the process. He proposes something else.
Not bombers, not another British
assault. A small team of Norwegians, men
who grew up in those mountains, who can
ski through a blizzard blindfolded, who
speak the language, understand the
terrain, and can vanish into the
wilderness when everything [music] goes
wrong. But there's a problem. Vemork is
a fortress, guarded bridge, minefields,
100 Wehrmacht soldiers. Before they can
send anyone to blow up the factory, they
need to know if there's a way in at all.
There are already four men on the ground
who might [music] have the answer, a
reconnaissance team dropped onto the
Telemark plateau months ago, Operation
[music] Grouse. They were supposed to
guide the Freshman assault in. Instead,
they watched the gliders crash [music]
and spent the winter alone in an
abandoned cabin. London hasn't heard
from them in weeks, but if they're still
alive, they're the only people on Earth
who can tell Tronstad what he needs to
know. Is there a route into Vemork that
the Germans aren't guarding?
Rewind four months, October 1942.
Four Norwegians drop from a plane onto
the Hardangervidda plateau, the largest
high-altitude wilderness in northern
Europe. Frozen tundra, endless white,
wind that cuts through wool like it
isn't there.
Code name, Operation Grouse. They set up
in an abandoned hunting cabin. Radio
contact with London, everything on
schedule. Then, November 19th, the
gliders crash. Freshman is wiped out.
And now four men are stranded on a
frozen plateau with no extraction, no
backup, and German ski patrols hunting
anyone connected to the failed raid.
London's message, "Stay in position.
Find a way into Vemork. Wait for a
second team."
So they wait. November, December,
January. The cabin runs out of food.
Temperatures drop to minus 30. They eat
reindeer moss, lichen scraped from
rocks, anything that keeps a body
moving. No fires during the day. Smoke
is visible for kilometers. German
patrols sweep the plateau on skis. One
man's weight drops from 80 kilos to 55.
You could count his ribs from across the
cabin.
Four men, four months, starving, but
they have a job to do. In January, Claus
Helberg puts on his skis and heads
toward Vemork alone. One question, is
there a way in? The main bridge,
obvious, soldiers, checkpoints,
searchlights, minefields on both sides.
Suicide. But below the factory, a gorge
200 m deep. Frozen cliffs dropping
straight into a river. The German
military assessment is categorical,
impassable for military purposes.
Helberg climbs down anyway. No rope, no
partner, just a man on a cliff in the
dark. He reaches the bottom, crosses the
frozen Mana River, climbs the other
side, finds a railway track cut into the
rock, a service route leading directly
into the plant's lower levels,
unguarded, unmined, forgotten. He skis
back to the cabin, reports what he
found. The four men look at each other.
The route Helberg just mapped requires
every man to descend a frozen gorge in
the dark without a rope. They radio
London anyway. The message, "We have a
way in. Send the team." What they don't
know, the team London is about to send
aren't professional soldiers. They're
skiers, teachers, fishermen, men who've
never seen combat, and they'll be
carrying enough explosive to change the
course of the war.
Kompani Linge,
a Norwegian special operations unit
trained by the British, made up of men
who had fled Norway to fight from exile.
Fishermen, teachers, athletes, [music]
students, all of them waiting for a
chance to hit back.
The man chosen to lead the assault is 23
years old, Joachim Rønneberg, ski
instructor from the mountains above
Bergen. Quiet face, calm hands, the kind
of person who thinks three moves ahead
and never raises his voice. SOE gives
him one order, "Pick your team." He
finds five. Knut Haugland, Birger
Strømsheim, Fredrik Kayser, Kasper
Idland, Hans Storhaug. For weeks they
train in the Scottish Highlands,
explosives, silent movement, night
navigation. How to neutralize a sentry
without a sound. How to place a charge
that will destroy a machine but not
collapse a building. How to survive if
everything goes wrong. And how to die if
survival isn't an option.
Before they leave, each man is given a
small glass capsule, cyanide. If
captured, bite down. Do not let the
Germans take you alive.
Rønneberg puts his capsule in his breast
pocket. [music] He will carry it for the
next 3 weeks. In 3 weeks, he'll be
standing at the edge of a gorge [music]
that killed no one only because no one
was ever stupid enough to try.
February 16th, 1943.
Somewhere over the North Sea. Six men
sit in the belly of a Halifax bomber. No
lights, no heat. The roar of four Merlin
engines and the smell of aviation fuel.
Rønneberg checks his equipment one more
time.
>> [music]
>> Explosives,
detonators, fuses cut to specific
lengths. Everything where it should be.
Four hours later, they jump. White silk
against black sky. Six parachutes
opening over the Hardangervidda plateau.
Six men dropping into occupied Norway.
They land in a blizzard. Visibility,
zero. Temperature, minus 30. Wind that
knocks a man off his feet. They spend
the first night digging snow caves with
their hands just to survive until
morning.
The next 5 days are a search. Somewhere
on this plateau, four men are waiting.
No modern navigation, no instant
communication. A rough map [music] and a
radio frequency that hasn't responded in
48 hours. On February 22nd, they find
[music] them. The Grouse team is barely
recognizable. Hollow cheeks, sunken
eyes. Four months on the plateau carved
into their faces, but alive and carrying
intelligence that changes everything.
Rønneberg spreads Helberg's hand-drawn
map on the table. One look at the
bridge, one look at the gorge. The
decision takes less than [music] a
minute. Rønneberg gives one instruction.
If anyone falls, the mission continues.
No one stops. No one goes back.
February 27th, 1943.
11:15 p.m. 11 men stand at the edge.
Skis left behind in the snow. From here,
on foot. Below, 200 m of ice and
darkness. Ahead, a fortress with 100
Germans between them and the basement.
Behind, 34 dead British commandos who
tried this [music] 8 weeks ago and never
came home. Rønneberg looks at his team.
Nobody speaks. Then, he steps over the
edge.
The descent begins. No ropes, no
climbing gear. Hands, boots, and
whatever the mountain gives them.
Rønneberg goes first, testing each rock
before putting his weight on it. Finding
foot holds in the dark by touch. Behind
him, 10 men in single file, 3 m apart.
Close enough to see the shape ahead. Far
enough that one falling body won't take
the next. Minus 15. Every surface coated
in ice. The rules. No talking, no
lights, no noise of any kind. Sound
carries in a gorge. A kicked stone
echoes off both walls. A snapped branch
rings like a rifle shot. The German post
on the bridge above are close enough to
hear a man scream. Nobody screams.
They climb down using trees, roots,
frozen bushes, anything that holds. Some
sections are nearly vertical. Fingers
dug into cracks in the rock. Feet
searching for ledges they can't see. The
full depth of the gorge below them.
Total darkness. Explosives on their
backs. One man slips, catches a branch,
hangs for 3 seconds, legs over nothing,
fingers burning on frozen wood. Pulls
himself up. Keeps moving. Nobody stops
to help. Those are the orders.
Halfway down, a boot catches a loose
stone. It breaks free. Falls. Hits the
wall 10 m below. A crack that [music]
rings through the gorge like a gunshot.
11 men freeze against the rock. Eyes up.
>> [music]
>> The bridge. The German post. 5 seconds.
10. No shout, no searchlight. The stone
settles somewhere in the darkness below.
They keep moving.
At the bottom, the river Måna. Not fully
frozen. Black water moving between
shelves of [music] ice. And here's what
matters. If your boots get wet, you have
maybe 30 minutes before frostbite sets
in. Numb feet mean you can't climb,
can't run, can't escape. Wet boots on
this mission means you die on the
mountain or you die in a German
interrogation room. They find the
narrowest point. Stones just visible
above the waterline. One by one, jumping
rock to rock in the dark. Everyone makes
it across. Now, the second climb. Back
up the other side. Steeper, looser rock,
ice on everything. But they're warmer
now. Blood moving. Adrenaline doing what
adrenaline does. At 2:30 a.m., 11 men
emerge onto a narrow railway track cut
into the mountainside. They're inside
the perimeter. No alarms, no shots, no
Germans. The factory sits just ahead.
Dark windows. Steam rising from the
pipes. A single guard near the main
entrance, pacing slowly. Breath visible
in the cold. He doesn't look toward the
gorge. Why would he? Nobody comes from
that direction. The Germans built a
fortress, guarded every bridge, mined
every road, posted a full garrison
around the clock, and left the back door
wide open. Now, 11 men are standing
inside that door, and five of them are
carrying enough explosive to end
Germany's nuclear program tonight. They
have Tronstad's blueprints memorized
down to the last pipe. Fuses cut to 30
seconds. Barely enough time to get out
before the charges blow. But first, they
have to get inside. And between them and
the electrolysis hall, there's a locked
door. A cable tunnel the width of a
man's shoulders. And one Norwegian night
watchman who will decide in 5 seconds
whether this mission ends in silence or
gunfire.
Rønneberg splits the team. Five men stay
outside. Cover squad. Haukelid in
command. Their job, watch the
approaches, guard the escape route, and
engage German soldiers only if the
demolition team gets discovered.
Haukelid positions his men in the
shadows near the gorge. Five men
watching the darkness, waiting for
either silence or gunfire. This is the
worst job in the operation. The
demolition team acts. The cover squad
listens. If everything goes right,
Haukelid does nothing. If everything
goes wrong, he has 60 seconds to hold
off a garrison and then die. He's the
kind of man who'd rather be inside
planting charges. Instead, he stands in
the cold and trusts someone else to
finish the job. In exactly 11 months, he
won't have that luxury. The next bomb
will be his, and the target won't be a
machine.
The other five move toward the building.
Demolition team. Rønneberg leading. They
find the cable tunnel Tronstad marked on
his blueprints. A narrow passage where
pipes and electrical wires enter the
basement level. Big enough for one man
to squeeze through if he doesn't breathe
too deeply. One by one, they crawl
inside. The tunnel leads exactly where
it should. Basement level. The hum of
machinery vibrating through the walls.
The chemical smell of electrolysis.
Sharp. Metallic. Like a taste at the
back of your throat. The electrolysis
hall is ahead. The heart of the heavy
water production. Rønneberg tries the
door. Locked. They find a window. Kaiser
wraps his elbow in cloth, strikes the
glass. It shatters. The sound echoes
through the basement corridor like a
bottle thrown in a cathedral. They
freeze.
Five men pressed against a concrete
wall, listening. Footsteps somewhere
above them. A floor up, maybe two. Boot
heels on concrete. Getting closer.
Five men, five weapons. Nobody breathes.
The footsteps stop. A pause. Then, they
move away down a corridor. A door closes
somewhere in the building.
A night patrol walking his route. He
didn't hear the glass, or he heard it
and didn't care. They climb through the
broken window. Inside, 18 electrolysis
cells. Metal cylinders lined up in rows.
Each one producing heavy water molecule
by molecule. Months of accumulation
sitting in these tanks. The liquid
Germany's nuclear program is waiting
for. Then, a voice from the corner.
Who's there?
A Norwegian night watchman sitting at a
small desk, staring at five armed men
who just came through a broken window.
This is the moment where the operation
lives or dies. One shout and the
garrison comes running. Rønneberg walks
toward him. Speaks in Norwegian. Quiet.
Controlled.
We're soldiers. We're here to destroy
the German equipment. Stay quiet and you
won't be harmed.
The watchman looks at the guns. Looks at
the faces. Norwegian faces. He's
Norwegian. He knows what side he's on.
I'll be quiet. Rønneberg nods. Tells him
to lie on the floor. Face down. Hands
where they can see them.
Now, you're back where this story
started. The demolition team places
their charges. One per cell. 18 cells.
Each positioned exactly where Tronstad's
blueprints said the casing is thinnest.
Rupture the machines, not collapse the
building. No excuse for German reprisals
against the local population. On the
14th cell, [music] a detonator won't
seat. The thread catches, slips, catches
again. Rønneberg's gloved fingers are
too thick for the housing. He pulls off
his right glove. Bare skin on metal at
minus 15. The detonator clicks into
place. He puts the glove back on. His
fingers are already stiff. The fuses are
cut short. 30 seconds, maybe less.
Rønneberg checks every [music]
connection, every detonator. If one cell
survives, the Germans can restart
production within weeks. Everything must
[music] go. He strikes the match. The
fuse catches. 30 seconds. They already
know the way out. In 30 seconds, 100
German soldiers will pour out of the
barracks. They'll search every road,
every bridge, every checkpoint. They'll
mobilize 3,000 men across Telemark. They
won't check the gorge. They still don't
believe anyone came that [music] way.
The sirens hit the valley like a wall of
sound. German soldiers pour from the
barracks, officers screaming orders.
Searchlights sweep the bridge, the main
gate, every road leading [music] away
from the factory. They find nothing. No
enemy. No tracks in the snow around the
guarded perimeter. No sign that anyone
came through the checkpoints. Nothing.
Because the 11 men who just destroyed
their nuclear program are already back
in the gorge, down the cliff, across the
river, up the other side. Halfway up, a
searchlight beam swings off the bridge
and slides down the gorge wall. White
light on black rock.
>> [music]
>> 5 m from the last man in the line. He
presses flat against the cliff. The beam
passes, drifts back toward the road. The
guard on the bridge stares into the
darkness below for a long moment, then
turns away. Why would anyone be down
there? By the time the first German
patrol reaches the basement, the
saboteurs are strapping on their skis 2
km away. Rønneberg gives the order,
"Split up." Five men ski east, 400 km to
the Swedish border, [music]
moving only at night, sleeping in snow
caves during the day. Behind them,
tracks in the snow, clear as a
signature. If the Germans find them
before morning, it's over. By dawn, it's
snowing. By noon, the tracks are gone.
The others disappear into the local
resistance. New identities, safe houses.
Behind them, chaos. 3,000 German
soldiers mobilize. Ski patrols, search
parties combing every valley, every
cabin within 50 km. They search for
weeks, find nothing. The Germans never
figure out how anyone got inside. Their
first theory, inside sabotage. They
interrogate dozens of Norwegian workers,
arrest some, find no answers. The gorge
isn't even considered. It's impassable.
After 2 weeks on the move, Rønneberg and
four others cross the Swedish border,
exhausted, frostbitten, 20 kg lighter
than when [music] they left Scotland.
Not a single shot fired during the
entire operation. Not a single man lost.
Not a single Norwegian civilian harmed.
Not even the night watchman. The Germans
interrogated him the next morning. He
was the only person who saw the
saboteurs up close. Five faces,
Norwegian voices. He could have
described every one of them. He
shrugged, said he saw nothing, heard
nothing, just an explosion, [music] and
then he ran. He just chose his side
twice, once with a gun [music] in his
face, and once without. The Germans
rebuilt the electrolysis cells within
months, but the clock was already
broken. In November 1943, American
bombers hit the rebuilt facility so hard
that Germany abandoned Vemork entirely.
They decided to ship the remaining heavy
water to Berlin, [music]
loaded onto a train, then a ferry across
Lake Tinnsjø. That ferry was called SF
[music] Hydro. On February 20th, 1944, a
bomb in the hull split it open at the
deepest point of the lake. The man who
planted the charge, Knut Haugland, the
same man who held the gorge during
Gunnerside 1 year earlier. 14 Norwegian
civilians died on that ferry. The moral
price Haugland [music] paid for what
Rønneberg had accomplished without a
single casualty. The barrels pulled up
from the lake decades later contained
barely 1% concentration. Germany never
got enough heavy water to build a
working reactor. After the war, a
journalist asked Rønneberg what would
have happened if Gunnerside had failed.
He thought for a [music] moment. London
might have looked like Hiroshima.

title: Why the Most Trusted Doctor in Hitler's Reich Got Him Hooked on Drugs

text:
This is the true story of Theodor Morell — Hitler's personal physician, the Berlin skin doctor every real surgeon in Nazi Germany called a quack, who spent nine years injecting the Führer with methamphetamine, opioids, cocaine, and strychnine while keeping an 885-page secret diary of every single dose.

Berlin, 1936. A failed ship's doctor from Kurfürstendamm treats wealthy actors and bankers with "golden injections." Then one patient changes everything: the official photographer of the Nazi Party. Within months, Theodor Morell is sitting across from Adolf Hitler — and promising the one thing no real doctor in the Reich would offer.
It starts with a genuine cure. It ends with more than 800 injections in a single year.

Every honest physician in the Reich tried to stop him. Karl Brandt, Hitler's own surgeon, found the strychnine pills and filed a report proving the head of state was being slowly poisoned. Hans Karl von Hasselbach warned that Morell was a danger to Germany. Hermann Goering mocked him as the "Reichsspritzenmeister" — the Imperial Master of Injections. Even Himmler had suspicions.

And Morell defeated them all — using nothing but a syringe and the addiction he had created.
As the war collapsed, Hitler refused every retreat order, euphoric on Eukodal and cocaine, "no longer in our world," while his personal physician wrote down every drug, every reaction, every failed attempt to find a usable vein.

Then, on April 21, 1945, three floors beneath Berlin, Hitler screamed at the one man he had trusted with his body for nine years — and threw him out of the bunker.

Morell escaped on one of the last planes out of Berlin, carrying a single suitcase and the 885-page diary that would be seized by the US Army and locked away for 36 years.

The surgeon who tried to save Hitler was hanged at Nuremberg. The quack who poisoned him walked free — and died peacefully, by a lake.
This is the full story of Theodor Morell, Patient A, the secret diary, the drugs that kept Hitler standing, the war of the doctors, and the man who outlasted every real physician in the Third Reich.

subtitles.plaintext:
April 21st, 1945. Three floors beneath
Berlin. Adolf Hitler, shaking,
sleepless, half-blind, screams at the
one man he has trusted with his body for
nine straight years. "You wanted to drug
me with morphine. You wanted to hand me
to the Russians as a sleeping prisoner."
And throws his personal physician out of
the bunker. The man being thrown out is
not a real doctor. He is a Berlin skin
specialist from Kurfürstendamm, a man

title: The Nazi Who Saved Millions from Hitler's Last Order

text:
This is the true story of Albert Speer — Hitler's personal architect and Minister of Armaments — who spent the final 30 days of World War II secretly sabotaging Hitler's order to destroy all of Germany, then flew into the Führerbunker through Soviet anti-aircraft fire to confess treason to Hitler in person, and walked out alive.

March 1945. The war is lost, and Hitler knows it. Rather than let Germany survive defeat, he signs the Nero Decree — an order to demolish every factory, bridge, power station, water main, and food warehouse on German soil. By Speer's own estimate, carrying it out would have killed five to ten million German civilians by starvation in the eighteen months after the war.

Speer decided not to obey. But he didn't refuse openly. He did something far more dangerous: he asked Hitler for exclusive authority to carry out the decree — and used that authority to do the exact opposite. He telegrammed factory directors to disable machines instead of destroying them. He cut the demolition units' explosives by ninety percent. He drove 1,400 kilometers across a collapsing country, convincing generals and field marshals to let their industry stand — including the Ruhr, with its 1,250 factories, saved when Field Marshal Model quietly refused to blow it up, then took his own life.

By April 22, 1945, ninety-five percent of German industry was still standing. That day, Speer climbed into a tiny reconnaissance plane, flew low over contested airspace, and walked into Hitler's bunker to admit what he had done — days after Hitler had executed old associates for far less. Hitler listened. He didn't shout. He didn't order an arrest. Speer walked back out into the night and flew home.

But this is not a story with a hero. The same man who saved millions was the Minister whose signature sat on the labor orders for the Auschwitz-Buna factory — who used five million forced laborers, who spent the next forty years building a myth of the "good Nazi" who knew nothing about the camps. A myth that held up through Nuremberg, through a five-million-copy memoir, through his death — until a single letter surfaced in a Swedish archive in 2007 and destroyed the lie he had guarded for thirty-six years.

This is the full story of Albert Speer, the Nero Decree, the counter-operation that saved Germany, the confession in the bunker, and the letter that finally told the truth.

Berlin, April 22nd, 1945,
just before noon. A small German army
aircraft lands on a section of
Charlottenburger Chaussee that has been
cleared of debris 4 hours earlier.
A man in a dark gray civilian suit steps
out. His name is Albert Speer. He is the
Minister of Armaments of the Third
Reich. He has flown from Hamburg through
Soviet anti-aircraft fire to reach this
street. He is walking into Adolf
Hitler's bunker to tell Hitler to his
face that he has spent the previous 30
days secretly sabotaging Hitler's final
order.
The order, issued 1 month earlier, would
have killed, by Speer's own later
estimate, between 5 and 10 million
German civilians by starvation in the 18
months after the war.
Speer chose not to carry it out. Soviet
forward units are 800 m from the bunker
entrance. In the previous week, Hitler
has ordered the execution of two of his
oldest associates for less.
Speer is about to confess treason in
person to a dictator with nothing left
to lose.
Two questions decide what happens next.
How does the Minister of Armaments of
Nazi Germany, a man who knew exactly
[music] what was happening in the camps,
talk his way out of being shot by Hitler
at the end of his life? And how does he,
in the four decades that follow, build
himself a posthumous reputation as a
good Nazi that will not be definitively
destroyed until a single letter is found
in a Stockholm archive in 2007?
To understand who Albert Speer was when
he landed on the Charlottenburger
Chaussee in April 1945,
you have to go back 15 years.
Mannheim, Germany, March 19th, 1905.
Albert Speer is born to Hermann Speer, a
wealthy architect, and Louise Hommel,
the daughter of a Mannheim
industrialist. The family is upper
middle class, politically conservative,
and not, in 1905, anti-Semitic in any
documented way.
Speer studied architecture at the
Technical University of Berlin,
graduating in 1927.
In December 1930, he attended a National
Socialist rally in Berlin. He heard
Adolf Hitler speak for the first time.
He joined the Nazi Party on March 1st,
1931
He was 25 years old.
He was not, by any of his subsequent
statements, an anti-Semite. He joined,
by his own 1969 memoir, because Hitler
had given a speech about restoring
Germany's national dignity that had
moved him.
That is what he said. The historian
Magnus Brechtken, in his 2017 biography,
would establish that Speer's
correspondence from 1931 to 1933 already
contained the standard Nazi vocabulary
about Jewish influence in German
cultural life.
His first commission for the Nazi Party
came in May 1933,
the staging of the Tempelhof Field
Rally. Hitler attended. Hitler liked
what he saw. By August 1934, Albert
Speer was the official Nazi Party
architect. By 1939, he had designed the
new Reich Chancellery, the building
beneath whose garden, 6 years later,
Adolf Hitler would shoot himself. On
February 8th, 1942, the Minister of
Armaments, Fritz Todt, died in a plane
crash.
Hitler appointed Speer to replace him on
the same afternoon. Speer was 36 years
old. Over the next 3 years, his ministry
would expand from a staff of 2,000 to a
workforce of approximately 14 million
people. Approximately 5 million of those
14 million were forced laborers brought
to Germany from occupied territories.
Approximately 1 and 1/2 million were
inmates of concentration camps
transferred to munitions factories under
the SS labor rental program. The man who
would, on April 22nd, 1945,
fly through Soviet anti-aircraft fire to
confess treason to Adolf Hitler, was the
same man whose signature appeared on the
labor requisition orders for the
Auschwitz Buna factory. Both things were
true at the same time.
This is not a story with a hero.
By the second week of March 1945, the
war was over, and Albert Speer knew it.
The Red Army was on the Oder River, 80
km from Berlin.
American forces had crossed the Rhine at
Remagen on March 7th.
The German army had, in 3 months, lost
the entire industrial belt between
Aachen and Frankfurt. German oil
production was at 3% of its 1940 peak.
Speer wrote a memorandum. It was 22
pages long. He delivered it personally
to Hitler at the Reich Chancellery on
the afternoon of March 18th, 1945.
The memorandum was, by the standards of
Nazi internal communications,
extraordinary. It stated explicitly that
the German war effort would collapse
within 4 to 8 weeks.
It stated that the only remaining duty
of the German state was to preserve
enough infrastructure to keep the
civilian population alive after the
inevitable defeat. It listed, in three
columns, what needed to be protected.
Water systems, electrical grids, food
storage, rail bridges, coal mines,
the basic machinery of survival.
Hitler read the memorandum. He set it
down on the desk. He did not raise his
voice. Speer's account of Hitler's
response, preserved in the 1946
Nuremberg testimony of Speer's
secretary, Annemarie Kemper, who had
heard him repeat the conversation that
evening, has been corroborated by two
other witnesses.
Hitler said, "If the war is lost, the
nation will also perish. There is no
need to consider the basis of even a
most primitive existence for the German
people. On the contrary, it is better to
destroy these things ourselves. The
nation has proved itself the weaker. The
future belongs solely to the stronger
Eastern nation. What remains after this
war will, in any case, be inferior
because the best have fallen."
The next day, March 19th, 1945, Hitler
signed a decree. It was officially
titled "Befehl betreffend
Zerstörungsmaßnahmen
im Reichs-
Dekret concerning demolitions on Reich
territory." It became known to history
as the Nero Decree.
It ordered the destruction, before any
Allied advance, of every industrial
facility, every railway, every bridge,
every water main, every power station,
every food warehouse on German soil.
It was signed on Albert Speer's 40th
birthday.
What Albert Speer decided to do in the
11 days between the Nero Decree's
signing on March 19th and his next
meeting with Hitler on March 30th has
been reconstructed from his post-war
testimony, his surviving ministerial
directives, and the diary of Joseph
Goebbels.
He decided he would not carry out the
order.
He decided he would not refuse it
openly. He would, instead, lie.
clusive authority to coordinate the
implementation of the decree.
His argument in the Reich Chancellery
study was technical.
>> Mein Führer,
if we detonate the factories now, we
deprive our own forces of the weapons
they need for the final defensive
battle.
Allow me to determine the moment of
demolition for each facility.
>> Hitler agreed. He signed the
supplementary order within the week.
Speer was now, on paper, the sole
official responsible for executing the
destruction of every industrial facility
in Germany.
He used the authority to do the
opposite. He sent telegrams over his
ministerial signature in his personal
cipher to the directors of every major
industrial plant in the Reich.
The telegrams instructed them not to
detonate their facilities.
They were to temporarily disable the
machinery by hiding critical components,
draining oil from engines, removing
electrical cables.
On paper, the directors could report
that the factories had been rendered
useless to the enemy.
In practice, every disabled factory
could be restored to production within
72 hours of liberation.
On March 31st, Speer convened a meeting
at Krupp's Essen headquarters with the
senior executives of the four largest
German industrial combines: Krupp,
Thyssen, Siemens, and I.G. Farben.
The meeting was held without the
knowledge of any party representative.
Speer told them what he was doing.
He asked for their cooperation.
By the end of the meeting, all four
companies had agreed. The next move was
to block the explosives.
Speer's ministry controlled the wartime
distribution of industrial demolition
charges. Beginning the first week of
April, he issued internal orders
reducing the allocation of explosives to
Gauleiter-controlled demolition units by
approximately 90%.
The justification submitted in writing
was that explosives were needed for the
front. The fascist regional commanders
charged with implementing the Nero
Decree by mid-April 1945 had nothing to
detonate with.
In late March 1945, Joseph Goebbels
recorded in his personal diary that
Speer had become soft and was not
implementing the destruction demanded by
the Führer.
Goebbels did not yet have the evidence
to act on it.
The hardest part of the operation was
the army.
The Wehrmacht, by April 1945, a
fragmented force of approximately 2
million troops, was nominally still
under the command of the Reich
Chancellery.
Several of its generals were ideological
fascists who would carry out the Nero
Decree without hesitation.
Speer decided to visit them personally.
Between April 3rd and April 21st, Albert
Speer drove approximately 1,400 km
across what remained of unoccupied
Germany. He went to the headquarters of
every army group commander whose forces
still controlled industrial regions.
He went to Heinrici on the Vistula
Front. He went to Schultze at the Saar.
He went to Kesselring in Bavaria.
His pitch, by the post-war testimony of
three of the generals he visited, was
the same.
>> If you destroy the bridges, you will
destroy your own supply lines.
If you flood the mines, your own
families will starve.
The war is lost.
The question is whether Germany will
have a country left when it is over.
>> Most of the generals, by then exhausted,
sick of Nazi Party officials, and
increasingly aware that their families
were the same civilians the Nero Decree
would kill, agreed. The most
consequential agreement came from Field
Marshal Walter Model. Model commanded
Army Group B, holding the Ruhr
Industrial Basin, the single largest
concentration of German industry,
containing approximately 1,250
functional factories and the steel works
of Krupp. Speer met Model on April 3rd
at his headquarters near Dortmund. Their
conversation lasted 9 hours. Model
refused, formally, to disobey the
decree. But when Speer left, Model did
not issue the demolition orders to his
subordinate commanders.
On April 18th, Model formally dissolved
Army Group B.
325,000
German soldiers surrendered to the US
Ninth Army, the largest single
capitulation in German military history.
The Ruhr factories were intact. On April
21st, Walter Model walked into a wooded
area near Lintorf, between Düsseldorf
and Duisburg, and shot himself. His
adjutant found him the same day.
In conversations with his staff during
the previous week, Model had repeatedly
stated that he was not a traitor, and
that he had done what was possible for
Germany, but that he had not done what
had been demanded of him.
A field marshal, in his own words, did
not surrender.
By April 22nd, when Albert Speer climbed
into a small German Army aircraft and
flew toward Berlin, approximately 95% of
German industrial infrastructure was
still standing. It would still be
standing on May 8th.
The Fieseler Storch, a single-engine
reconnaissance aircraft with a top speed
of 175 km/h, left Hamburg at 10:00 in
the morning on April 22nd, 1945.
It flew low, below Soviet radar, across
120 km of contested airspace.
It landed on Charlottenburger Chaussee
at 11:45.
Albert Speer was met by an SS officer in
an open staff car.
He was driven the 3 km to the Reich
Chancellery.
He entered the bunker through the garden
entrance at 12:20.
He waited in the upper level conference
room for approximately 6 hours. Hitler
received him at 2300 hours.
The conversation that followed in the
small private apartment at the end of
the lower bunker corridor has been
described in three places. Speer's own
1969 memoir, the post-war testimony of
Hitler's secretary Traudl Junge, and a
single conversation Speer had in 1971
with the journalist Gitta Sereny, who
recorded it in shorthand. The accounts
agree on the structure. They disagree on
the specifics.
What is documented the conversation
lasted approximately 4 hours until 3:00
in the morning on April 23rd. Speer
raised the subject of the Nero Decree.
He told Hitler that the order had not
been fully carried out. He told Hitler
that he, personally, had made decisions
that had preserved German infrastructure
against the orders' explicit
requirements.
Hitler did not raise his voice. He did
not order Speer's arrest. He did not, by
any of the three accounts, ask Speer to
provide details of the sabotage. He
listened.
According to Speer's memoir, Hitler
ended the conversation by saying,
"If it has happened, it has happened.
You are tired. Go."
Whether this is what Hitler said or what
Speer wished he had said 24 years later,
historians still dispute. What is
certain is what happened at 3:00 in the
morning on April 23rd, 1945.
Albert Speer walked out of the
Führerbunker. He climbed into a waiting
staff car. He was driven back to the
airfield on Charlottenburger Chaussee.
He flew back to Hamburg. He was, by the
standards of the regime he had served
for 14 years, a man who had walked into
the bunker as a confessed traitor and
walked out alive.
>> [music]
>> It was, in his own subsequent
assessment, the only conversation of his
life he would never fully understand.
Albert Speer was arrested on May 23rd,
1945, in Flensburg by British forces who
had located the rump German government
attempting to operate as the successor
to Hitler. He was transported to the IMT
detention facility at Nuremberg in
October 1945.
The International Military Tribunal
opened on November 20th. 24 senior Nazi
officials were charged. Speer was
charged on four counts: conspiracy to
wage aggressive war,
crimes against peace, war crimes, and
crimes against humanity. The strongest
single piece of evidence against him was
the documented use of approximately 5
million forced laborers by his ministry,
including approximately 1 and 1/2
million concentration camp inmates whose
conditions his own subordinates
testified he was familiar with.
Speer's defense strategy, developed with
his attorney Hans Flächsner, had three
components.
First, he had not been a member of the
SS or the security apparatus. He was a
technocrat who had administered
industrial production.
Second, he took responsibility in his
testimony for the use of forced labor in
a way none of the other defendants had.
He stated,
>> I cannot evade responsibility for what
was done in my ministry.
>> Third, he had, in the final weeks of the
war, defied Hitler's Nero Decree and
saved German civilians from a death by
starvation that would have killed
millions.
The third claim was, in its broad
outline, true. The first claim was
technically true, but elided his role in
the slave labor system. The second
claim, taking responsibility, was a
calculated rhetorical move that
distinguished him from the other
defendants and probably saved his life.
The tribunal delivered its verdict on
October 1st, 1946.
Of the 22 defendants brought to verdict,
12 were sentenced to death by hanging.
Three received life imprisonment. Four
received fixed-term sentences. Three
were acquitted. Albert Speer was
sentenced to 20 years. His deputy at the
Ministry of Armaments, Fritz Sauckel,
the official responsible for the
procurement and transport of the forced
laborers, was sentenced to death and
hanged on October 16th, 1946.
Speer was transferred to Spandau Prison
in West Berlin in July, 1947.
He served the next 20 years in a
facility built for 700 inmates that, by
the late 1950s, held seven. He was one
of them. He was released at midnight on
October 1st, 1966,
20 years, day for day. He was 61 years
old. He had spent the entire sentence
preparing to be remembered as the wrong
kind of Nazi.
In 1969,
3 years after his release from Spandau,
Albert Speer published Erinnerungen,
Memoirs.
The English edition appeared the
following year under the title Inside
the Third Reich.
The book sold approximately 5 million
copies in 15 languages.
It became the most widely read
first-person account of the Nazi regime
ever published by a senior participant.
It told a specific story.
Speer, the technocrat, had been seduced
by Hitler's charisma into joining a
movement whose moral content he had not,
at the time, fully understood.
Speer, the architect had risen on
talent. Speer the minister had
administered production without engaging
with the security apparatus.
Speer in March 1945 had recognized the
catastrophe and at risk of his own life
saved Germany from total destruction.
Speer had not known by his own account
in the book about the specific
operations of the death camps.
The book was published to almost
universal critical acclaim.
The historian Hugh Trevor-Roper in his
review for the New York Times called
Speer the only Nazi to have written
intelligently about what he had done.
For the next 38 years, Inside the Third
Reich defined the international
understanding of Albert Speer.
He gave interviews. He appeared on West
German television. He corresponded with
historians.
The persona he had constructed at
Nuremberg, the apolitical technocrat who
had used his skills to save lives,
became the dominant image.
He died in London on September 1st, 1981
of a cerebral hemorrhage.
He had been recording a BBC television
interview that morning.
He was 76 years old.
The story he had constructed survived
him.
It survived until 2007.
In that year, a researcher working in a
Swedish archive located a letter Albert
Speer had written in the early 1970s to
a Belgian Holocaust survivor named
Hélène Jeanty Raven.
The letter had never been published.
Speer had not realized when he wrote it
that the recipient would deposit it with
the archive on her death.
The letter contained a single complete
sentence that destroyed the structure
Albert Speer had spent 40 years
building.
I was present at the speech Himmler gave
in Posen on October 6th, 1943,
where he spoke explicitly about the
extermination of the Jews.
Speerhead, at every previous opportunity
in his life, denied attending that
speech. He had denied knowing what was
happening in the camps. He had lied for
36 years.
In 2017,
the German historian Magnus Brechtken
published a 900-page demolition of every
remaining claim in Speer's memoir.
The book established, by means of an
exhaustive review of internal Nazi
documents, that Speer had not been a
technocrat. He had been a perpetrator
who had known what he was perpetrating.
The single thing Brechtken could not
deny was that the sabotage of the Nero
Decree had happened.
A man who knew exactly what was
happening in the camps, who facilitated
it through his ministry's labor
requisitions, who attended Himmler's
October 1943 speech, who lived for 40
years lying about both, had also, in the
final 30 days of the war, used his
authority to save the country in which
those camps had operated from physical
destruction.
Both things were true.
Albert Speer is buried in Heidelberg.
His grave is unmarked by request of his
family.
At Nuremberg in 1946, in the closing
statement of his defense, Albert Speer
had told the tribunal,
>> I cannot understand how I could have
been so blind.
>> He repeated the sentence in interviews
for the next 35 years.
After 2007, no historian believed him.
The factories remained. The lie did not.

title: He Smuggled Forged Passports in His Bike to Save 800 Jews
channelDescription: Just history, told clearly and honestly.

text:
This is the true story of Gino Bartali — winner of the Tour de France and three-time Giro d'Italia champion — who spent eighteen months under Nazi occupation riding forged identity papers through Gestapo checkpoints inside the hollow frame of his racing bicycle, and never told a single person about it, including his own wife, for the rest of his life.

Spring 1944, on the road outside Florence. A Gestapo patrol stops a man in a yellow jersey with BARTALI stitched across the chest. The commander recognises him instantly — he watched Bartali win the 1938 Tour de France with his father — and asks for an autograph. While the officer writes, twelve forged Italian identity cards and seven baptismal certificates for Jewish children are rolled up inside the seat-post of the bicycle he is leaning on.

It began in September 1943, in the chancery of Cardinal Elia Dalla Costa, the Archbishop of Florence. German forces had just occupied northern Italy. The SS had begun deportations. An underground Catholic-Jewish network was forging documents in a Franciscan monastery in Assisi, 185 kilometres away — and needed a courier who could not be searched.

The perfect cover had already been written by the Germans themselves. Bartali was classified a "cyclist of national importance" and granted unrestricted travel papers on the condition that he keep training for postwar international races. So the most famous athlete in Italy simply rode — 185 km to Assisi, 85 to Lucca, 240 to Genoa — roughly once a week, for eighteen months.

He crossed around 160 checkpoints. He was stopped at nine out of ten. And every time, he repeated the same sentence: do not touch the bicycle, every component is adjusted to my exact body — move one screw and my training is ruined for weeks. In eighteen months, not a single German or Italian soldier ever took the bike apart.

In May 1944 the fascist secret police arrested him and interrogated him for three days inside Villa Triste — the House of Sorrow. Their commander had a signed Bartali photograph in his desk drawer. On the third day, he let him walk out. Bartali collected the next batch of documents the following morning.

Around 800 Jewish lives were saved through the network he served. Four years later, at 34 and written off as too old, he won the 1948 Tour de France — while Italy stood hours from civil war after an assassination attempt in Rome, and the country stopped to listen to the radio instead.

And then he said nothing. Not to journalists, not to his children, not to his wife. When his son finally pressed him in 1989, Bartali said only that if you do good, you don't talk about it. The full story emerged only after his death — and in 2013 Yad Vashem named him Righteous Among the Nations, the only Tour de France champion ever to receive it.

text:
This historical documentary tells the incredible true story of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian resistance leader who fought against both Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union during and after World War II. For years, Soviet intelligence agencies including the NKVD and later the KGB launched one of the longest manhunts in Soviet history to capture him.

From underground bunkers hidden in the forests of Ukraine to secret resistance networks operating across the region, Shukhevych built and commanded the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) while evading thousands of Soviet soldiers and intelligence agents. For seven years the Soviet Union dedicated massive resources, informants, and military operations to track him down.

This documentary explores the complex and controversial life of Roman Shukhevych: a pianist, businessman, underground operative, guerrilla commander, and one of the most wanted men in the USSR. His story reveals the brutal reality of Eastern Europe during the Second World War and the early Cold War — a time when Ukraine found itself trapped between Hitler’s Nazi regime and Stalin’s Soviet empire.

You will learn how Shukhevych survived one of the largest manhunts ever conducted by the Soviet secret police, how the Ukrainian resistance operated underground, and why Stalin reportedly ordered that his body be burned so no grave could become a symbol of resistance.
This is the story of the man who fought two empires and became one of the Soviet Union’s greatest enemies.

>> [music]
>> part for business development, part for
the Ukrainian underground. Weapons, safe
houses, forged documents, communications
equipment, bribes, medical supplies,
everything a resistance movement needs.
And it gets better.
Every Fama advertising representative
traveling from town to town is also an
intelligence agent. They're visiting
businesses, talking to locals, taking
notes, all things a normal salesman
does.
But they're also noting police
movements, identifying sympathizers,
scouting safe houses, carrying coded
messages hidden in advertising samples.
Weekly sales reports contain encrypted
intelligence. The code looks like normal
business [music] jargon. Sales
projections, market analysis, competitor
activity.
Only someone with the key understands
what it really means.
Shukhevych hires people with wolf
tickets, former political prisoners whom
no one else will employ. He gives them
salaries and dignity. They give him
loyalty and a willingness to do whatever
needs to be done.
In intelligence terms, this is called
commercial cover. A legitimate business
that provides perfect camouflage for
covert operations.
The CIA wouldn't formalize this concept
until decades later. Shukhevych figured
it out in 1937.
For 2 years, Fama operates in plain
sight.
Polish police investigate repeatedly.
They suspect something. Everyone
suspects something about Shukhevych, but
they find nothing. The books are clean,
the employees are working, the clients
are satisfied.
How do you prove that the most
innovative advertising agency in the
region is secretly the financial hub of
a nationalist insurgency?
You can't. Then, in September 1939,
everything changes.
Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union sign a
secret pact to divide Poland.
Hitler takes the west, Stalin takes the
east, including Lviv.
Within weeks, the NKVD begins mass
[music] arrests.
Fama is shut down. Its employees
scatter. Shukhevych goes underground.
He doesn't know it yet, but he'll spend
the rest of his life there.
Here's where the story gets really
complicated and really dark.
For Americans, the simplest comparison
is this. Imagine if during World War II,
Texas had been occupied first by Nazi
Germany, then by Imperial Japan, and
both of them were trying to exterminate
the entire Texan population while also
fighting each other. And Texans were
trying to fight both of them
simultaneously with whatever weapons
they could find.
That's roughly what happened to Ukraine.
1939 to 1941.
The Soviets occupy Western Ukraine. The
NKVD, Stalin's secret police, works
around the clock. Mass arrests,
deportations to Siberia, executions
without trial. The numbers are hard to
grasp. In less than two years of Soviet
occupation, somewhere between 300,000
and 500,000 Western Ukrainians are
arrested, deported, or killed.
That's more people than died in the
American Civil War from a region smaller
than West Virginia.
Shukhevych's brother, Yuri, is arrested
and thrown into Lonsky prison in Lviv.
In June 1941, just days before Germany
attacks the USSR, [music]
the NKVD receives an order. Liquidate
all political prisoners. There's no time
for evacuation.
The solution? Mass execution.
In Lonsky prison alone, they murder
[music] thousands of people over three
days. Guards go cell to cell,
eliminating prisoners. When they run out
of time, they resort [music] to mass
methods.
Shukhevych's brother [music] dies there.
When the Germans arrive and the prison
is opened, the scene is so horrific that
it sparks violence against [music] local
Jews, whom Nazi propaganda falsely
blamed for Soviet atrocities. One horror
fuels another.
Then comes the German occupation, and
for [music] a brief moment, some
Ukrainian nationalists think, "Maybe the
enemy of my enemy is my friend. Maybe
Germany will help Ukraine gain
independence from the Soviets."
They're catastrophically [music]
wrong. The Nazis don't see Ukrainians as
allies. They see them [music] as
Untermenschen, subhumans, useful as
slave labor, but not as partners.
The Nazi [music] plan for Ukraine is
called Generalplan Ost. It calls for the
eventual elimination or deportation of
up to 65% [music] of Ukrainians, with
the rest being kept as a slave labor
force for German colonists.
Ukrainian [music] leaders who tried to
declare independence are thrown into
concentration camps.
Stepan Bandera, whose name you might
recognize, [music]
spends most of the war in Sachsenhausen.
Other leaders are simply shot. The
Holocaust begins. The Nazis and their
collaborators kill approximately 1.5
[music]
million Ukrainian Jews, along with Roma,
the disabled, and anyone else deemed
unworthy of life.
The tragedy at Babi Yar, outside Kyiv,
[music] kills over 33,000 Jews in just 2
days.
This is the situation Shukhevych finds
himself in by 1942.
His brother was murdered by the Soviets.
The Nazis are conducting genocide. Both
empires want to destroy Ukraine as a
nation. Both are killing civilians by
the thousands.
What do you do when you're caught
between Hitler and Stalin? [music]
Most people keep their heads down and
try to survive. There's no shame in
that. Survival under occupation is its
own kind of resistance.
Some people collaborate with whichever
power currently occupies their
territory. You can judge them harshly,
but [music] remember they're often
trying to protect their families from
worse fates. Some people fight.
Shukhevych's answer: Build an army that
can fight both.
In 1943, he takes command of the
Ukrainian Insurgent Army,
>> [music]
>> the UPA.
This is a guerrilla force that will
fight simultaneously against Nazi
Germany and the Soviet Union.
Think about how insane that sounds. The
two largest military machines in human
history, the armies that are destroying
each other in the biggest war ever
fought, and a few tens of thousands of
poorly armed partisans [music]
are going to fight both of them?
But Shukhevych understands something
important. He can't defeat either
empire. That's not the point. The point
is to survive, to maintain an armed
Ukrainian presence, to ensure that when
these empires [music] eventually
collapse, as all empires eventually do,
someone will still be fighting for
Ukraine.
His strategy borrows from guerrilla wars
throughout history. The American
Revolution, the Spanish resistance
against Napoleon, the Irish against the
British.
You don't fight battles you can't win.
You hit and run. You ambush and
disappear. You control nothing, but
threaten everything. You make occupation
so costly that eventually the occupiers
give up.
He develops a system of underground
bunkers called kryivky that are so well
hidden you could stand directly on top
of one and never know it exists.
Tunnels connecting bunker to bunker,
Hidden hospitals, weapon caches, supply
lines. You could hide entire units
underground for months.
And he creates a command structure based
on what intelligence agencies now call
cell networks.
Each unit operates independently. Each
knows only what it needs to know. Even
if the enemy captures one cell, the
others keep functioning.
The UPA won't defeat either empire, but
it will survive both.
I want to tell you a story that shows
you who Shukhevych really was. Because
Russian propaganda has spent decades
painting him as a Nazi collaborator and
anti-Semite.
The truth is more complicated and more
interesting.
1939
After the failed attempt to establish an
independent state in Carpathian Ukraine,
Shukhevych finds himself on hostile
territory. Hungarian soldiers are
hunting anyone connected to the
Ukrainian independence movement. He's
caught at a checkpoint. They're checking
documents, separating people by
nationality. Ukrainians get sent to
internment camps or worse.
Shukhevych's real papers would be a
death sentence. But he notices
something. There are Jews serving in the
Hungarian military. In 1939, Hungary
hasn't yet aligned completely with Nazi
racial policies. Jews still have some
rights there, [music] some protection.
Shukhevych makes an insane decision. He
claims he's Jewish. The Hungarian
gendarmes don't believe him. He doesn't
look particularly Jewish. His papers say
otherwise. They take him to the local
rabbi for verification.
Think about this [music] situation. A
Ukrainian nationalist, a member of an
organization that will later be accused
of anti-Semitism is about to be tested
by a rabbi on Jewish religious
knowledge. If he fails, [music]
he's probably dead. If he passes, he has
to convince an actual Jewish community
that he's one of them.
The rabbi starts asking questions.
>> [music]
>> The Torah, the Talmud, the traditions,
the holidays, the prayers, the dietary
laws, the Sabbath observance,
the kinds of things you would only know
if you'd grown up Jewish or studied
Judaism seriously.
Shukhevych answers every question
correctly. The rabbi pronounces him
Jewish.
How did he know all this? [music]
Probably from years of living in a
diverse city.
Lviv before World War II was a
multicultural place. Ukrainians, Poles,
Jews, Armenians, Germans, all living
together.
Shukhevych studied at the Lviv
Polytechnic and the Music Institute. He
had Jewish classmates, Jewish friends,
Jewish teachers.
Unlike the caricature that propaganda
paints, real people in real places know
their neighbors.
They attend each others events. They
learn about each others cultures.
Shukhevych wasn't pretending to be
Jewish out of disrespect. He was using
knowledge born from actual
relationships.
The rabbi believed him.
Shukhevych hid with the Jewish community
until he found a way to escape.
Now here's another story, and this one
is documented beyond any doubt.
1942
The Nazi occupation is in full swing.
The Holocaust is happening. [music]
Jews across Ukraine are being murdered
by the tens of thousands.
A 7-year-old Jewish girl named Irena
Reichenberg needs a place to hide. Her
parents were killed in the violence.
Neighbors who knew the Shukhevych
family, who knew that Roman's wife
Natalia was a decent person, bring the
child to their door.
Think about the risk involved.
Shukhevych is already wanted by the
Nazis. His house could be searched at
any moment. The punishment for hiding
Jews is death. Not just for the person
hiding them, but for their entire
family, their neighbors, sometimes their
entire village. And Shukhevych isn't
just any person. He's a leader of the
Ukrainian underground. If the Nazis find
him hiding a Jewish child, they'll use
it for propaganda. They'll kill everyone
connected to him.
But Natalia Shukhevych, Roman's wife,
[music] agrees without hesitation. Irena
lives with the Shukhevych family for
almost a year. They feed her. They
protect her.
>> [music]
>> They treat her like one of their own
children.
When the situation becomes too
dangerous, they transfer her to a Greek
Catholic [music] monastery where the
nuns continue to hide her.
Irena Reichenberg [music] survived the
war. She lived in Ukraine until 2007,
and she always remembered the Shukhevych
family with gratitude.
This is documented. It's not propaganda.
[music]
It's not legend. It's what actually
happened.
Now,
>> [music]
>> does this mean Shukhevych was a saint?
No. The organization he [music] led, the
OUN, and its military wing, the UPA, did
terrible things. There were acts of
violence. There were ethnic [music]
conflicts. There were atrocities
committed against Poles, against Jews,
against other groups caught in the chaos
of war.
History is not a movie where everyone is
either a hero or a villain. Real people
are complicated. Real wars are messy.
Real resistance movements include both
courage and cruelty, sometimes in the
same people.
But here's what we can say for certain.
A Nazi doesn't pass a rabbinical
examination on Jewish religious law.
An anti-Semite doesn't risk his family's
lives to save a Jewish child.
Shukhevych did both.
The truth about him, like the truth
about most historical figures, resists
simple narratives.
He fought against genuine evil. He also
led an organization that committed evil
acts. Both things are true.
For Americans, this might be familiar.
The founding fathers fought for liberty
while owning slaves. Abraham Lincoln
freed the slaves while expressing views
on race that would be unacceptable
today.
FDR led the fight against fascism while
interning Japanese Americans.
We don't excuse these contradictions,
but we also don't pretend they make
everything else meaningless.
History is complicated. People are
complicated. If that's uncomfortable,
good. It should be.
Comfort is not what history owes us.
1944
The Soviet Army pushes the Nazis out of
Ukraine.
For most people, World War II is ending.
For Shukhevych, a new war is just
beginning.
The NKVD opens a case file code-named
Wolf.
The target, Roman Shukhevych.
The order, find and liquidate. No
alternatives.
What follows is one of the longest and
most frustrating manhunts in Soviet
history.
55 officers are assigned full-time to
finding one man. Not part of their
regular duties, their only job. For
years.
Thousands of informants are recruited
across the region. The Soviets are
experts at this. They pressure people
with threats to their families. They
offer rewards. They exploit personal
grudges.
They promise leniency to prisoners who
provide information.
Eventually, almost every village has at
least one person reporting to the NKVD.
Regular sweeps [music] involve hundreds,
sometimes thousands of soldiers. They
comb through forests methodically,
checking every bush, every depression in
the ground, every suspicious spot.
Sometimes they find empty bunkers,
evidence that Shukhevych was there days
ago, weeks ago, never today.
The pressure is systematic. Soviet
interrogators have generations of
experience in breaking people.
Physical force, food denial, sleep
deprivation, exhausting positions,
bodily harm, and the most effective
technique of all, detaining family
members and threatening them.
You won't talk? Fine. Let's see if your
wife will talk after we've had her for a
week. Still nothing? Your children are
in the next room. Can you hear them
crying?
>> [crying]
>> Year after year, tens of thousands of
man-hours, unlimited resources, the full
power of one of history's largest police
states,
and still nothing.
Shukhevych evades them all.
How does one man evade the most
effective secret police in history for
seven years?
The answer lies in those six identities
we talked about at the beginning.
Shukhevych is never one person. He's 10
different people living 10 different
lives.
One day, he's the UPA commander, holding
meetings in an underground bunker,
issuing orders that affect thousands of
fighters. He wears a uniform, speaks
with authority, commands respect. The
next day, he's a gray-haired musician
giving piano lessons in someone's home,
gentle, artistic, discussing Chopin with
his host.
No one suspects this quiet man with the
artist's hands is a wanted terrorist.
A week later, he's a peasant farmer in
dirty clothes complaining about the
harvest. His accent changes. His posture
changes. He becomes someone you'd never
look twice at.
Then a merchant at the market [music]
haggling over prices. Then a traveling
tradesman.
Then a railway worker.
Each identity has its own documents, its
own backstory, its own way of walking,
talking, even its own handwriting.
His bodyguard, meeting him for the first
time in 1946, later recalled,
>> "He looked like an ordinary worker,
unshaven, dirty boots. I didn't even
realize I was looking at the
commander-in-chief."
>> This wasn't just changing clothes.
Shukhevych became these people. He
thought like them. He reacted like them.
If someone bumped into his peasant
persona at the market, the peasant would
respond with a peasant's irritation, not
a soldier's instincts.
The NKVD gets close several times,
very close.
1944,
a raid on a safe house. Intelligence
says Shukhevych is inside. 200 soldiers
surround the building. They move in at
dawn. They find warm tea, beds that were
slept in hours [music] ago, documents
hastily hidden, but no Shukhevych.
He left through the back door minutes
before they arrived, maybe seconds.
Someone saw the troops gathering. A
signal was sent. A warning reached
[music] him just in time.
So close, but not close enough.
1946,
an ambush on a forest road. The NKVD
know Shukhevych uses this route. They
wait in the trees with machine guns. A
perfect killing zone.
A man approaches, fits the description,
the right height, the right build. Then
the man stops. He's seen something. A
glint of metal, a footprint that
shouldn't be there. Something.
He throws himself sideways into the
forest before the trap springs. Bullets
shred the air where he was standing. But
he's already gone, running in zigzags,
using every tree for cover.
>> [music]
>> By nightfall, he's vanished.
1947, the NKVD reports Shukhevych
killed. The news goes all the way to
Moscow. Stalin himself is [music]
informed. Celebrations begin.
Except weeks later, intelligence
confirms he's alive. They killed someone
else. Mistaken identification.
The celebrations turn to recriminations.
Officers are punished. But Shukhevych is
still out there.
But the cost of this life is
devastating. In 1944, Shukhevych
officially divorces his wife, [music]
Natalia. Not because he stops loving
her, because as long as she's legally
his wife, she's a target. They'll use
her to find him. The divorce gives her
one layer of protection.
He keeps secretly contacting her through
the courier network. Brief meetings
every few months. A few minutes
together, then months of separation.
They go after her anyway. First the
Gestapo during the German occupation,
then the NKVD after the Soviets return.
She never breaks. She never gives him
up.
In 1945, the NKVD arrests his entire
family. His wife, his parents, his
sister, his two children. His father
dies in a Siberian labor camp in 1948.
He never sees his son again.
The children are sent to a special
orphanage for children of enemies of the
people. The goal, break them. Turn them
against their father's memory.
And then something remarkable happens.
In 1947, 14-year-old Yuri escapes from
the orphanage. He crosses the entire
country, thousands of kilometers,
without documents, without money, hiding
in freight cars, sleeping in fields,
stealing food when he has to. He wants
to find his father.
Against all odds, he does.
Imagine that meeting. A boy who spent
[music] two years in Soviet custody, a
father who lives as a ghost. They
haven't seen each other since Yuri was
12
>> Father, I want to stay with you.
I want to fight.
>> Shukhevych looks at his son. He sees his
own fire reflected [music] back. He has
to choose. Take the boy into a war he'll
likely die in, or send him away. He
chooses a third option.
>> If you stay with me, you'll be dead
within a year.
The movement doesn't need another
martyr. It needs people who will survive
to tell our story.
Here are forged documents.
Go back and then rescue your sister from
that orphanage. She needs you.
And then live. Whatever happens to me,
preserve our memory.
Someday Ukraine will be free. When that
day comes, someone needs to be alive to
see it.
>> Yuri returns. He's trying to rescue his
sister when an officer [music]
recognizes him. He's 14 years old. He
receives a sentence. In total, [music]
Yuriy Shukhevych will spend 31 years in
Soviet labor camps.
>> [music]
>> Every time there's an amnesty, they
check his file and send him back. He's
released in the late 1980s, blind,
>> [music]
>> ill,
but unbroken. In independent Ukraine, he
becomes a member of parliament, and he
introduces a law recognizing UPA
soldiers as fighters for independence.
[music]
The law passes. The son completes his
father's mission. 40 years late, but he
completes it.
March 5th, 1950.
4:00 in the morning. The village of Bila
Hora near Lviv.
A cold pre-dawn darkness. Snow on the
ground. Breath visible in the air.
700 soldiers silently surround a small
house. They move through the trees,
taking positions behind walls and
fences, cutting off every escape route.
According to intelligence, Roman
Shukhevych is inside. After 7 years,
they're finally certain.
The operation is commanded by General
Pavel Sudoplatov. If you know Soviet
intelligence history, you know that
name.
Sudoplatov organized the assassination
of Leon Trotsky in Mexico City. He's run
operations across three continents. He
speaks six languages. He's survived
Stalin's purges that killed most of his
colleagues.
For Sudoplatov, this is personal. Seven
years of failures. Seven years of
humiliation.
His career depends on catching this one
man.
Inside the house, Shukhevych has been
working through the night with his
liaison officer, Halyna Dydyk. The
underground never stops. [music]
There are always orders to write,
reports to read, plans to make. He's
exhausted. He's been moving constantly
for weeks, never staying in one place
[music] more than a few days.
The net is tightening. He can feel it.
But the work continues. The resistance
continues.
A knock at the door. Not aggressive,
almost polite. Halyna opens it. Armed
men, submachine guns. The moment she's
been dreading.
>> Where is Shukhevych?
>> She doesn't answer. They push past her
into the house.
Shukhevych hears the commotion. He's in
a hidden compartment, a space built into
the wall that's invisible [music]
unless you know exactly where to look.
He has seconds to decide. He could stay
hidden. Maybe they won't find the
compartment. Maybe he survives another
day.
But he hears them questioning Halyna. He
knows what's coming for her.
Interrogation, suffering, because of
him. And he knows what happens if they
take him alive. [music]
Show trials, forced confessions on
camera, propaganda films of him
denouncing everything he believed in.
They'll break him one way or another.
Everyone breaks eventually. And his
breaking will demoralize everyone who
ever followed him. He makes his choice.
He bursts from hiding with his Walther
pistol already firing. The first officer
through the door goes down. Shukhevych's
aim is still perfect. For one frozen
moment, everyone stares. They expected a
capture, not a fight. Then bullets fly
both ways. Shukhevych is hit once,
twice, three times.
He staggers, but keeps firing.
There's a legend, probably not true, but
perfect if it were, that in the final
moments before the raid, Shukhevych sat
at the piano and played Grieg. One last
performance, just as he once [music]
played Rachmaninoff at the music
conservatory. Just as he played
Ukrainian opera to stop his friends from
fighting. [music]
A musician to the end. He's wounded
badly, dying probably, but they haven't
taken him. He knows what comes next if
he surrenders.
Roman Shukhevych makes his final choice.
He refuses to be taken alive.
>> [music]
>> He's 42 years old.
The soldiers stand over his body,
uncertain what to feel. They finally
killed the wolf, but he died on his own
terms.
>> [music]
>> He denied them even the satisfaction of
taking him alive. His son Yuri, already
in a labor camp, is brought to identify
the body.
>> Father lay on straw in an embroidered
shirt. The marks of his final battle
were visible. Three wounds under his
chest.
>> This is the last time the son sees his
father. The body is reportedly taken to
Moscow. Legend says Stalin himself
wanted to see. Stalin allegedly looked
at his enemy's face for a long time.
Then gave the order.
>> Burn him.
Scatter the ashes.
>> The ashes were scattered over the Zbruch
river. No grave, no memorial.
>> [music]
>> Stalin wanted Shukhevych erased from
history completely. In 1997, the
Security Service of Ukraine destroyed 12
of 13 volumes of Shukhevych's case file.
No one explained why. The remaining
documents are presumably [music] in FSB
archives in Moscow. Russia has ignored
all requests for access. Shukhevych
wasn't a perfect man. History is
complicated, but he was right about one
thing. Ukraine exists, and no empire has
the right to decide otherwise. His ashes
were scattered over a river. No grave,
no memorial.
And yet, 74 years later, you're hearing
his story. Some things can't be erased.

title: How Vietnamese Tunnels Outsmarted the U.S. Military
