sitting in Lord Palmerston's office with
maps of the Chinese coast with battle
strategies with a complete plan for war.
Lynn thinks he's won. He destroyed the
opium. He humiliated the merchants. He
appealed to British morality. He has no
idea what's coming.
Palmerston was skeptical at first. war
with China over drug smugglers. But
Jardine was prepared. He didn't talk
about opium. Not [music] once. He talked
about British property stolen by Chinese
officials. British citizens held
hostage. British honor insulted. He
talked about markets. 400 million
Chinese consumers. The biggest untapped
market on Earth. If only they could be
forced to open their doors. He spread
his maps across Palmerston's desk,
pointed to weak spots in Chinese
defenses, explained exactly which ports
to seize, which rivers to blockade,
where to land troops. Palmerston was
impressed. This wasn't some wildeyed
merchant ranting about lost cargo. This
was a complete military operation. The
war debates in Parliament were fierce.
William Gladstone, future prime
minister, stood up and called it a war
more unjust in its origin, a war more
calculated to cover this country with
permanent disgrace. I am in dread of the
judgments of God upon England, for our
national iniquity towards China. He
pointed out the obvious hypocrisy. Opium
was illegal in Britain. The British knew
it was poison, and yet they were about
to go to war for the right to sell it to
the Chinese. But Gladstone's side lost.
The vote was close. 271 votes for war.
262 against. Nine votes. Nine votes that
would kill tens of thousands. Addict
millions. Collapse an empire, create
Hong Kong. Nine votes that would reshape
Asia for the next 200 years.
June 1840, a British fleet appears off
the Chinese coast. 16 warships, four
steamers, 4,000 soldiers, and several
vessels leased from Jardine Mat and
Company. William Jardine was making
money on both sides of the war he'd
started. The Chinese had no chance.
Their weapons were 200 years out of
date. matchlock musketss, bronze
cannons, wooden junks. The British had
explosive shells, rifled guns, and iron
hold steam ships. At Twinp, British
ships fired from beyond the range of
Chinese guns. The Chinese couldn't even
shoot back. By noon, 11 Chinese junks
were burning. Hundreds of Chinese dead.
The British moved up the coast. Amoy,
Ningbo, Shanghai. Each battle was the
same massacre. Tens of thousands of
Chinese dead, British dead, fewer than a
hundred. By August 1842, British forces
threatened Nanjing. The emperor had no
choice. Chinese officials boarded HMS
Cornwallis and signed the Treaty of Nank
King at gunpoint. The terms were almost
word for word from the Jardine paper.
China pays $21 million in reparations, 6
million for the destroyed opium, 12
million for the war. China opens five
ports to foreign trade, and Britain
takes Hong Kong, a nearly uninhabited
island off the southern coast. The
treaty forces China to hand it over
permanently, British territory. Now, the
Chinese negotiators are horrified. It's
one thing to pay money, another to open
ports, but to give up Chinese soil to a
foreign power forever, they have no
choice. British warships are at the
gates of Nanjing. Hong Kong becomes
Britain's headquarters for the opium
trade. For the next century, every chest
of opium flows through its ports. Today,
it's one of the world's financial
capitals, built on a foundation of
opium. And in 1842, the trade doesn't
stop. It explodes. William Jardine never
called himself a drug lord. History did
that for him.

En septembre 1839, un marchand écossais entre au ministère britannique des Affaires étrangères. Il porte une
mallette en cuir. À l'intérieur, des cartes des côtes chinoises, des stratégies militaires et une liste d'exigences. Ce
n'est ni un général, ni un diplomate. C'est un trafiquant de drogue. Et dans les deux heures qui suivent, il convaincra Lord
Palmerston de déclencher une guerre qui fera des dizaines de milliers de morts, des millions de toxicomanes et remodèlera l'Asie
pour les deux siècles à venir. Mais voici ce qui rend la situation encore plus tragique : il n'a jamais touché à l'opium. Il
n'a jamais mis les pieds en Chine avec de la drogue en main. Il a simplement mis en place le système et laissé
douze millions de personnes s'autodétruire. Il s'appelle William Jardine. Et c'est ainsi qu'un trafiquant de drogue
a fait s'effondrer un empire. Lord Palmerston est assis derrière son bureau. Ministre des Affaires étrangères britannique, l'un des
hommes les plus puissants du monde, il décide avec qui la Grande-Bretagne commerce, qui elle combat,
qui elle détruit. Et à cet instant précis, il écoute un trafiquant de drogue. Jardine étale
ses cartes sur le bureau. Il désigne des ports, des rivières, des fortifications. Il a passé vingt ans à naviguer
sur ces eaux. Il connaît chaque recoin des côtes chinoises. « Ici, dit-il, attaquez ici et là. Prenez
ces ports. Bloquez ce fleuve. » Il fait glisser un document. Stratégies de bataille, effectifs, nombre
exact de navires de guerre nécessaires, et voici nos exigences : une compensation intégrale pour l'opium détruit par la Chine,
l'ouverture de nouveaux ports au commerce britannique, et cette île. Il tapote la carte. Hong Kong. « Nous voulons Hong Kong. »
Palmerston étudie les cartes. Il ne s'agit pas d'un fantasme. C'est une opération militaire complète,
planifiée dans les moindres détails. « Et pourquoi la Grande-Bretagne devrait-elle faire la guerre pour des marchands d'opium ? » demande-t-il.
Jardine ne cille pas. « Pas pour l'opium, Monsieur. Pour l'honneur britannique. La Chine a emprisonné des citoyens britanniques.
Saisi des biens britanniques. Humilié la Couronne. C'est inacceptable. » Il ne mentionne jamais la dépendance.
Jamais les douze millions de Chinois accros à son produit. Il ne mentionne jamais les familles
détruites, les fortunes perdues, les cadavres s'entassant dans les fumeries d'opium à travers la Chine. Il ne parle que d'
honneur, de commerce, de prestige britannique. Et Palmerston l'écoute, car voici ce qui caractérise
les trafiquants de drogue qui changent le cours de l'histoire : ils ne parlent jamais de drogue, mais de commerce. Or, on ne rend pas
douze millions de personnes dépendantes par accident. On ne bâtit pas un tel empire par chance. Alors, comment un
jeune fermier écossais issu d'une famille misérable est-il devenu l'architecte du plus grand trafic de drogue de l'histoire ? William
Jardine est né en 1784 dans une ferme écossaise des plus pauvres. Son père est mort lorsqu'il avait neuf ans. La
famille était sans ressources. Son frère aîné a réussi à réunir suffisamment d'argent pour lui permettre d'
étudier la médecine. À dix-huit ans, Jardine a obtenu son diplôme et a rejoint la Compagnie britannique des Indes orientales comme chirurgien de bord.
La solde était misérable, mais le poste offrait un avantage : deux caisses de marchandises pour
le commerce privé. La plupart des marins n'y prêtaient pas attention. Pas Jardine. Il achetait des marchandises dans un port, les revendait dans un autre,
louait des espaces de chargement à des marins invendus, tenait des registres méticuleux et effectuait
des calculs précis. Deux devinrent quatre, puis huit. À 30 ans, il abandonna la médecine. À 40 ans,
il était l'un des marchands les plus riches d'Asie. Que vendait-il ? De l'opium. Mais voici ce qui distinguait
Jardine de tous les autres trafiquants d'opium : il ne se contentait pas de vendre de la drogue, il l'industrialisait. En 1832,
il s'associa à James Mat. Ils fondèrent la Jardine Mat and Company et lui donnèrent un nom chinois, EWO,
« Happy Harmony » (Harmonie Heureuse). Une harmonie bien malheureuse pour une entreprise qui vend du poison. D'autres négociants travaillaient seuls. Jardine, lui,
construisit une chaîne d'approvisionnement. D'autres possédaient un seul navire. Jardine, lui, construisit une flotte. D'autres concluaient
des accords. Jardine, lui, créa des systèmes. En 1838, son système permettait d'écouler 40 000 caisses d'opium par an, soit
2 500 tonnes. De quoi rendre des millions de personnes dépendantes. Mais comment faire entrer 2 500 tonnes de drogue illégale dans un
pays qui l'interdit depuis plus d'un siècle ? En construisant une machine. Et celle de Jardine était
parfaite. Voici comment fonctionnait son opération. Première étape : ses agents en Inde achètent
de l'opium brut aux cultivateurs du Bengale, de Malwa et de Patna. La Compagnie britannique des Indes orientales contrôle l'approvisionnement,
mais des trafiquants indépendants comme Jardine se chargent de la contrebande. Deuxième étape : des ouvriers transforment l'opium
dans des usines. Ils malaxent la pâte noire et collante en boules, qu'ils emballent dans des caisses en bois tapissées de
feuilles de manguier. Chaque caisse pèse 63,5 kg et contient suffisamment de poison pour rendre des centaines de toxicomanes.
Troisième étape : les clippers de Jardine, les navires les plus rapides de l'océan, transportent le coffre jusqu'en Chine.
Le voyage dure six semaines. Les navires sont armés de canons. Les équipages sont entraînés au combat,
mais ils n'accostent pas dans les ports chinois. L'opium est illégal en Chine depuis 1729. Tout navire pris en flagrant
délit de contrebande est confisqué. Tout marin surpris à en faire le trafic est passible de la peine de mort. Jardine a donc inventé
une solution : des entrepôts flottants. De vieux navires ancrés en eaux internationales à l'
île Linton, au large du delta de la rivière des Perles. L'opium est transvasé des clippers vers ces épaves,
dont les cales sont empilées du sol au plafond et gardées par des hommes armés de mousquets. Les navires restent
immobiles. Ils flottent là, tels des coffres au trésor remplis de poison. Mais imaginez un instant :
vous êtes sur un navire au milieu de l'océan avec des millions de dollars de
drogue illégale, et vos clients se trouvent sur le continent, à des kilomètres de là, derrière les patrouilles douanières chinoises qui
exécuteront quiconque se fait prendre à faire de la contrebande. Comment combler cet écart ? Comment faire passer des milliers de caisses d'
opium des eaux internationales aux rues de Canton sans se faire prendre ?
La solution de Jardine était géniale. 3 heures du matin, delta de la rivière des Perles. Une flottille de bateaux émerge des ténèbres. On les
appelle des « crabes bateliers ». Longs, profilés, bas sur l'eau. Chacun embarque 40 rameurs. Ils peuvent distancer
n'importe quelle patrouille douanière et sont lourdement armés. Les contrebandiers s'approchent de l'entrepôt flottant de Jardine,
font un signal, une échelle de corde se déploie. La transaction est simple : de l'argent contre de l'opium.
Les contrebandiers paient en argent, principalement en dollars espagnols. Ils reçoivent un reçu, un bon de livraison pour un
nombre précis de caisses. Puis ils rament jusqu'aux navires-entrepôts et récupèrent leur cargaison. Les
caisses sont descendues dans leurs bateaux et leurs filets. À l'aube, ils sont de retour sur le continent chinois.
En quelques jours, l'opium se retrouve dans les fumeries de Canton, dans les pipes, dans les poumons, dans les veines, et l'argent de Jardine
est en sécurité. Cela se produit chaque nuit. Des centaines de transactions, des milliers de caisses,
des millions de dollars : le crime parfait. Jardine ne touche jamais à la drogue lui-même, ne met jamais les pieds en
Chine avec de l'opium en poche. Ses mains sont, en théorie, propres. Si quelqu'un se fait prendre,
c'est le problème du trafiquant. En 1838, sa compagnie, Jardine Mat & Company, possède 19 clippers
pour les traversées océaniques, des centaines de bateaux plus petits pour le cabotage, des entrepôts à Canton,
Macao et dans une douzaine d'autres ports. Elle contrôle la moitié du commerce extérieur avec la Chine, et Jardine avait
plus d'un tour dans son sac. Il engage un missionnaire prussien nommé Charles Gutslaugh, un homme de Dieu qui parlait
un chinois parfait. Jardine le convainc que le meilleur moyen de répandre le christianisme est de voyager
le long des côtes sur des navires de contrebande d'opium. Le missionnaire pourrait distribuer des Bibles pendant que les marins
déchargent la drogue. Gutslaugh accepte. Pendant des années, il sert d'interprète aux capitaines de Jardine,
un prédicateur chrétien qui contribue à empoisonner des millions de personnes. Voilà qui était William Jardine. Il pouvait convaincre n'importe qui
de n'importe quoi, et l'opium continuait de couler à flots. En 1810, les marchands importèrent 4 500 caisses en Chine. En 1838,
ce nombre avait explosé pour atteindre 40 000. Cela représente 2 500 tonnes d'opium brut chaque année. Mais à quoi
ressemblent concrètement 2 500 tonnes ? Canton, 1838. Une file d'attente s'étend sur trois pâtés de maisons dans
une rue étroite. Des milliers de personnes attendent, tremblantes. Elles n'attendent pas de nourriture. Elles
attendent de l'opium. Regardez-les. Les yeux cernés, les joues creuses, les os saillants sous leurs
vêtements en lambeaux. Il y a un an, cet homme était soldat. Cette femme était institutrice. Cet adolescent allait
reprendre le commerce de son père. Aujourd'hui, ce sont des fantômes. C'est ainsi que les Chinois les appellent, les fantômes de l'opium.
Mais ce n'est pas propre à Canton. C'est partout pareil. Dans n'importe quelle ville côtière, on voit la même chose.
Des fumeries d'opium à chaque coin de rue. Une fumée si épaisse qu'on peut la goûter. Des corps gisent dans les entrées d'immeubles. Dans certaines villes,
90 % des adultes sont dépendants. La dépendance s'installe insidieusement. Un homme essaie l'opium lors d'une soirée,
sent la chaleur se répandre dans son corps, la douleur disparaître, les soucis s'estomper. Il
recommence sans cesse. En quelques mois, il n'en a plus envie. Il en a besoin. Sans opium,
son corps se rebelle. Frissons, sueurs, crampes, nausées. Certains ne supportent pas le sevrage et
continuent de consommer. Ils continuent de fumer. Ils vendent tout ce qu'ils possèdent : leurs meubles, leurs outils…
Leur terre, leur avenir. Imaginez maintenant une situation bien plus grave. Pas seulement une personne, pas seulement une ville. Des millions de
personnes à travers tout un empire. L'armée impériale, jadis la plus redoutée d'Asie,
est au bord du gouffre. Les officiers sont toxicomanes. Les soldats troquent leurs armes contre de l'opium.
Les fonctionnaires arrivent au travail incapables de réfléchir clairement. Ils ne savent plus lire les documents, ni
prendre de décisions. La collecte des impôts s'effondre. Revenons un instant en 1800. Car
pour comprendre l'ampleur de cet effondrement, il faut savoir ce qu'était la Chine avant Jardine.
En 1800, la Chine dominait le monde, non par la conquête, mais par l'économie. Elle possédait tout ce que
tout le monde désirait : thé, soie et porcelaine. Tous les Européens buvaient du thé chinois. Tous les aristocrates portaient
de la soie chinoise. Chaque foyer aisé exposait de la porcelaine chinoise. Les Britanniques en étaient obsédés. En 1800,
ils importaient 23 millions de livres de thé par an. Toute l'économie britannique en dépendait. Mais
la Chine ne voulait rien de la Grande-Bretagne. Les marchands britanniques arrivaient avec des navires chargés de laine,
de montres et de produits manufacturés. Les Chinois n'étaient pas intéressés. Les Britanniques payaient donc en argent,
des montagnes d'argent. L'argent affluait en Chine à un rythme si rapide qu'il épuisait les réserves européennes. En 1793,
le roi George III envoya une délégation commerciale à Pékin. « Ouvrez davantage de ports. Baissez les droits de douane. Laissez-nous
commercer librement. » La réponse de l'empereur fut : « Nous possédons tout. Je n'accorde aucune valeur aux objets étranges ou
ingénieux et je n'ai que faire des fabricants de votre pays. » Autrement dit : « Nous n'avons pas besoin
de vous. C'est vous qui avez besoin de nous. » Et il avait raison. L'économie chinoise était plus importante que celle de toute l'Europe réunie.
400 millions d'habitants, un tiers de l'humanité, autosuffisants, puissants, d'une richesse incommensurable
. Les Britanniques étaient face à un problème : comment commercer avec un empire qui n'a besoin de rien de
ce qu'ils possèdent ? Ils trouvèrent la solution : l'opium. Et en seulement 40 ans, la machine de William Jardine
bouleversa tout. L'argent qui affluait en Chine s'en échappe désormais. Les paysans abandonnèrent
leurs champs. Les pénuries alimentaires se répandirent. Et voici le début de la spirale infernale de l'économie. Chaque caisse d'opium
coûtait de l'argent. De l'argent chinois. En 1838, la Chine perdait 9 millions de dollars d'argent par an, qui finissaient dans
les poches de Jardine. Ce même argent qui faisait autrefois la richesse de la Chine saignait désormais l'empire
à blanc. La monnaie s'effondrait. L'inflation explosait. Un sac de riz qui coûtait une pièce d'argent en coûtait maintenant
cinq. Les paysans se révoltaient. Non pas parce qu'ils mouraient de faim, mais parce qu'ils avaient besoin d'opium et ne pouvaient plus se le procurer. Mais
voici la question : comment enrayer une crise de dépendance quand tout un pays est accro ? Comment
lutter contre les marchands étrangers quand ses propres fonctionnaires sont leurs clients ? En décembre 1838,
l'empereur prend une décision qui va changer le cours de l'histoire. Il nomme Lynn Zhu
commissaire impérial. Sa mission : éradiquer le commerce de l'opium. Lynn a 53 ans, c'est un érudit, un poète,
un haut fonctionnaire réputé pour deux choses : son intelligence brillante et son refus catégorique d'
accepter des pots-de-vin. Dans un système gangrené par la corruption, Lynn Zhu est incorruptible. Il arrive à Canton
en mars 1839. Immédiatement, il se met à recueillir des renseignements. Qui sont les trafiquants chinois ? Qui sont
les fournisseurs étrangers ? Où sont les navires ? Où sont les entrepôts ? En quelques semaines, il arrête
1 700 trafiquants d’opium chinois et confisque 70 000 pipes à opium. Mais ce n’est que le début. Lynn
connaît la véritable source du problème : les entrepôts flottants, les marchands étrangers, William Jardine
lui-même. Il envoie un message au quartier du commerce extérieur : « Rendez tout votre opium, chaque caisse,
chaque navire. » Les étrangers rient. Pour qui se prend ce bureaucrate ? Ils vont bientôt le découvrir
. Car Lynn n’est pas comme les autres fonctionnaires qu’ils ont corrompus. Il n’est pas comme les généraux qu’ils ont
achetés. Il n’est comme personne avec qui ils ont jamais traité. Et dans 24 heures, 350 étrangers vont
mourir de faim, piégés, implorant grâce. 24 mars 1839. Lindsa Shu encercle les
comptoirs étrangers de Canton. Ces comptoirs ne sont pas des navires, mais un complexe fortifié sur le front de mer
où vivent et travaillent tous les marchands étrangers. Un petit quartier à l'intérieur de Canton. Bureaux, entrepôts,
logements. 350 étrangers piégés dans leur propre quartier. Lynn n'attaque pas.
Soldats. Il attaque par l'isolement. Il ordonne à tous les domestiques chinois de quitter le quartier étranger.
Cuisiniers, femmes de ménage, interprètes, bateliers, partis du jour au lendemain. 350 étrangers se réveillent complètement
seuls. Lynn poste alors des gardes armés à chaque porte. Il construit des barricades dans les rues.
Il tend des chaînes en travers de la rivière pour bloquer les bateaux. Personne n'entre, personne ne sort. Les livraisons de nourriture sont interrompues.
Les livraisons d'eau sont interrompues. Le deuxième jour, ils abattent leurs chevaux pour la viande. Le troisième jour, l'eau est rationnée,
deux tasses par personne. Le quatrième jour, certains tentent de corrompre les gardes. Les gardes les dénoncent à Lynn. Le
cinquième jour, un marchand britannique tente de s'échapper par-dessus le mur d'enceinte pendant la nuit. Rattrapé, battu,
renvoyé à l'intérieur. Le sixième jour, l'eau est presque épuisée. Les hommes sont malades de chaleur, de stress,
de viande de cheval avariée. Lynn envoie un autre message. Rendez l'opium ou mourez de faim. Le surintendant britannique,
Charles Elliot, n'a aucune autorité pour faire ce qu'il s'apprête à faire. Aucune autorisation de Londres,
mais il n'a pas le choix. Il ordonne aux marchands de tout lui remettre. 20 283 caisses d'opium,
plus de 1 400 tonnes, d'une valeur de 2 millions de dollars. La plus importante saisie de drogue de l'histoire. Linda Shu ne se contente pas
de confisquer l'opium, il le détruit. Il ordonne à des ouvriers de creuser trois immenses tranchées près de la mer,
à Hume. Chaque tranchée mesure 45 mètres de long, 23 mètres de large et 2 mètres de profondeur. L'opium est transporté des
entrepôts dans des caisses en bois. Les ouvriers ouvrent chaque caisse, déversent la pâte noire et collante
dans les tranchées, la mélangent à du sel et de la chaux. La réaction chimique est violente. Le mélange bouillonne,
siffle et se dissout en une boue toxique. Puis ils ouvrent les vannes et la rejettent dans l'océan.
L'opération dure 23 jours et mobilise 500 ouvriers pour 20 000 caisses. Lynn écrit un poème pour présenter ses excuses aux dieux de
la mer pour avoir pollué leur royaume. Une fois son poème terminé, il écrit une lettre à la reine Victoria. La richesse
de la Chine est utilisée pour enrichir les étrangers. Il écrit : « De quel droit envoyez-vous ce poison
nuire au peuple chinois ? Où est votre conscience ? L'opium est interdit dans votre propre
pays car vous savez que c'est du poison. Alors pourquoi nous le vendez-vous ? » La lettre est envoyée à Londres.
La reine Victoria ne répond jamais. La plupart des historiens pensent qu'elle ne l'a même jamais vue. Mais voici ce que
Lynn ignore. Pendant qu'il écrit des lettres faisant appel à la conscience britannique, William Jardine
est assis dans le bureau de Lord Palmerston, des cartes des côtes chinoises, des stratégies de bataille et
un plan de guerre complet à la main. Lynn pense avoir gagné. Il a détruit l'opium. Il a humilié les marchands.
Il a fait appel à la morale britannique. Il n'a aucune idée de ce qui l'attend. Palmerston était sceptique au début.
Une guerre contre la Chine à cause des trafiquants de drogue. Mais Jardine était préparé. Il n'a pas parlé d'opium. Pas
une seule fois. Il a parlé de biens britanniques volés par des fonctionnaires chinois. De citoyens britanniques pris
en otage. De l'honneur britannique bafoué. Il a parlé de marchés. 400 millions de consommateurs chinois. Le
plus grand Un marché inexploité sur Terre. Si seulement on pouvait les forcer à ouvrir leurs portes ! Il étala
ses cartes sur le bureau de Palmerston, désigna les points faibles des défenses chinoises, expliqua précisément quels
ports s'emparer, quels fleuves bloquer, où débarquer les troupes. Palmerston était impressionné. Il
ne s'agissait pas d'un marchand exalté divaguant sur une cargaison perdue. C'était une opération militaire complète.
Les débats sur la guerre au Parlement furent féroces. William Gladstone, futur Premier ministre,
prit la parole et déclara que c'était une guerre plus injuste dès son origine, une guerre plus susceptible de couvrir
ce pays d'une honte éternelle. « Je redoute le jugement de Dieu sur l'Angleterre, pour
notre iniquité nationale envers la Chine. » Il souligna l'hypocrisie flagrante. L'opium était illégal en
Grande-Bretagne. Les Britanniques savaient que c'était du poison, et pourtant ils étaient sur le point d'entrer en guerre pour le droit de
le vendre aux Chinois. Mais le camp de Gladstone perdit. Le vote fut serré. 271 voix pour la guerre. 262 contre.
Neuf voix. Neuf voix qui allaient tuer des dizaines de milliers de personnes. Des millions. L'effondrement d'un empire,
la création de Hong Kong. Neuf votes qui allaient redessiner le paysage asiatique pour les deux siècles à venir.
En juin 1840, une flotte britannique apparaît au large des côtes chinoises : seize navires de guerre, quatre vapeurs, quatre mille soldats
et plusieurs embarcations louées à la compagnie Jardine Mat. William Jardine s'enrichissait sur les deux
fronts de cette guerre qu'il avait déclenchée. Les Chinois n'avaient aucune chance. Leur armement était obsolète depuis deux siècles.
Mousquets à mèche, canons en bronze, jonques en bois. Les Britanniques disposaient d'obus explosifs,
de canons rayés et de navires à vapeur à cales en fer. À Twinp, les navires britanniques tirèrent hors de
portée des canons chinois. Les Chinois ne purent riposter. À midi,
onze jonques chinoises brûlaient. Des centaines de Chinois étaient morts. Les Britanniques remontèrent la côte. Amoy,
Ningbo, Shanghai. Chaque bataille fut un massacre. Des dizaines de milliers de morts chinois,
moins d'une centaine de morts britanniques. En août 1842, les forces britanniques menacèrent
Nankin. L'empereur n'eut d'autre choix. Les officiels chinois montèrent à bord du HMS Cornwallis et signèrent
le traité de Nankin sous la menace des armes. Les termes étaient presque identiques à ceux du document Jardine.
La Chine paya 21 millions de dollars de réparations, 6 millions pour l'opium détruit et 12 millions pour la guerre.
La Chine ouvrit cinq ports au commerce extérieur et la Grande-Bretagne annexa Hong Kong, une
île quasi inhabitée au large de la côte sud. Le traité contraignit la Chine à céder définitivement
ce territoire britannique. À présent, les négociateurs chinois sont horrifiés. Payer une rançon,
ouvrir des ports, c'est une chose ; mais céder définitivement du territoire chinois à une puissance étrangère, c'est une obligation.
Des navires de guerre britanniques sont aux portes de Nankin. Hong Kong devient la plaque tournante du
commerce britannique de l'opium. Pendant un siècle, chaque caisse d'opium transitera par ses ports. Aujourd'hui, c'est l'une des
capitales financières mondiales, bâtie sur les fondations de l'opium. Et en 1842, le trafic ne s'arrête pas.
Il explose. William Jardine ne s'est jamais considéré comme un baron de la drogue. C'est l'histoire qui l'a fait pour lui.

on Garibaldi Street.
Two cars, engines ready, hearts
pounding. 7:40 p.m. The bus arrives, on
schedule, like always.
Eichmann doesn't get off.
The agents freeze. Is the operation
compromised? Did someone warn him?
Minutes pass. The street is silent. A
neighbor's dog barks somewhere. One
agent's hand moves toward his weapon.
7:55 p.m. Another bus appears.
This time a familiar figure steps off.
Thin, balding, carrying a small
flashlight because the street light is
broken. Peter Malkin approaches from the
front. He's rehearsed this a hundred
times. "Un momentito, senor?"
Eichmann stops, looks up. Malkin grabs
his arm. Eichmann tries to jerk away,
opens his mouth to scream. At that exact
moment, a door opens across the street.
A neighbor steps out onto his porch,
stands there, looks toward the sound.
Malkin's hand clamps over Eichmann's
face. The other agents rush from the
car. They lift him off his feet. His
legs kick in the air.
The neighbor squints into the darkness,
takes a step forward.
One agent whispers, "He's coming."
Malkin shoves Eichmann into the
backseat. The door slams.
The neighbor is still walking toward the
street.
The driver turns the key. Nothing. The
engine doesn't start. He turns it again.
Nothing.
The neighbor is 20 m away now. 15.
Third try. The engine catches. The car
lurches forward. Tires spray dirt.
Through the back window, they see the
neighbor standing in the middle of the
road watching them disappear.
Did he see their faces? The license
plate? Will he call the police? They'll
never know. But for three blocks, nobody
breathes.
Now comes the impossible part, keeping
him hidden while the largest manhunt in
Argentine history closes in.
The car drives 17 minutes through back
roads, pulls into a garage. Door closes.
Eichmann is dragged inside, handcuffed
to a bed, goggles over his eyes so he
can't see their faces or memorize the
location. For hours, he refuses to
speak. Around midnight, one agent enters
alone, speaks German. "What size shoes
do you wear?" Eichmann answers.
It matches SS records.
"Your Nazi Party membership number?"
He recites it from memory perfectly.
"Are you Adolf Eichmann?"
Long pause.
"Ja, ich bin Adolf Eichmann."
But here's what surprises the agents. He
doesn't panic, doesn't beg, doesn't try
to bargain. He asks [music] calmly, "Who
do you work for? Americans? Russians?"
"Israelis." Eichmann nods slowly, almost
relieved. "I always knew this day would
come." Then he says something that
chills them. "You know, there will have
to be negotiations, an exchange. Your
government will want something from
mine." He still thinks he has leverage,
still thinks [music] someone will save
him, still believes he's too valuable to
simply disappear.
He's wrong, but his calm is unnerving.
The next morning, one agent pulls the
team leader aside. "Eight days. Every
hour is another chance for [music] a
neighbor to hear something, another
chance for the police to get lucky."
The team leader shakes his head. "If we
kill him, he's a footnote. [music]
If we try him, he's a lesson."
Nobody argues again.
The clock is ticking.
May 18th. Eichmann's family reports him
missing. Police begin searching. 48
hours until airports might close. May
19th. The El Al plane lands. Argentine
police are now actively looking for a
missing German resident named Ricardo
Klement. 36 hours until takeoff. May
20th. Radio reports mention the search.
Police have distributed a description.
The agents sedate Eichmann, dress him in
an El Al steward's uniform, put him in a
wheelchair, apply makeup to change his
appearance. 12 hours until takeoff.
They drive to the airport in two cars.
If one gets stopped, the other
continues.
At customs, they present forged
documents. Israeli crew member, severe
food poisoning, being sent home for
medical treatment.
The officer looks at the slumped figure,
looks at the documents, looks at the
figure again. Every agent holds their
breath. One phone call and they're
finished. Prison, international scandal,
the whole operation destroyed. The
officer frowns, opens his mouth. "This
man [music] looks very sick." "Yes,
that's why we're flying him home." Three
seconds pass, [music] the longest three
seconds of their lives. The officer
stamps the papers, waves them through.
2:00 a.m., May 21st. The plane lifts off
from Buenos Aires. The agents don't
celebrate, don't cheer. They sit in
silence watching the city lights
disappear below them. Eichmann is out of
Argentina, but Argentina isn't done with
Israel yet. But here's what happens
[music] next.
Argentina explodes. Headlines across
Buenos Aires, "Israeli agents kidnap
Argentine resident. Foreign spies
operate on our soil. Sovereignty
violated. Government demands answers."
The Argentine foreign minister holds a
press conference. His words are ice.
"This is an act of aggression against
the Argentine [music] nation. We demand
the immediate return of Ricardo Klement
and the prosecution of those
responsible." He doesn't call him
Eichmann, he calls him Ricardo Klement,
an Argentine resident, a victim. Think
about that. The man who sent millions to
gas chambers [music] is now being
defended as a victim of Israeli
aggression. Argentina files a formal
complaint with the UN Security Council.
Emergency session. Delegates from around
the world. Resolution 138 passes. It
officially condemns Israel's actions as
a violation of international law and a
threat to peaceful relations between
nations. The resolution doesn't mention
the Holocaust, doesn't mention 6 million
dead, only mentions sovereignty.
Argentina recalls its ambassador. Israel
recalls theirs. Diplomatic relations
severed. Now here's the part that
terrifies Israeli leadership. Eichmann's
lawyers file motions challenging the
court's jurisdiction. Their argument is
simple. The kidnapping was illegal.
Therefore, the trial is illegitimate.
Therefore, their client must be
released. And it's working. Legal
scholars around the world debate whether
Israel has the right to try a man
captured this way.
Newspapers run op-eds questioning the
legitimacy of the whole process.
For three weeks, [music] there's a real
possibility that Eichmann could be
returned to Argentina, that he could
walk free, that the entire operation,
the risk, the sacrifice, [music] the
years of hunting could end with the
architect of the Holocaust living out
his days as a protected citizen in
Buenos Aires.
Israel doesn't back down. They
acknowledge the operation, express
regret [music] for violating
sovereignty, but refuse to return
Eichmann. The gamble pays off. The world
moves on. The trial proceeds. And in a
Jerusalem courtroom,
>> [music]
>> Adolf Eichmann finally meets the people
whose lives he erased. He has prepared
for this moment. He has a defense, and
he believes it will work. Jerusalem,
April 11th, 1961.
The courtroom is packed. Journalists
from 36 countries, diplomats, survivors,
television cameras broadcasting to
millions around the world. At the
center, a bulletproof glass booth.
Inside, Adolf Eichmann. Dark suit,
headphones for translation, taking notes
constantly. He looks like a man
attending a budget meeting, not facing
charges for the murder of millions.
The trial lasts four months. 112
witnesses. But here's the moment that
matters. A woman takes the stand,
Hungarian survivor. She describes being
loaded onto one of Eichmann's trains in
1944,
standing on the platform [music] at
Auschwitz, watching her parents walk
toward the gas chambers. Her mother
turned back once, waved, then
disappeared. She points at the man in
the glass booth.
"That is the man who sent my family to
their deaths."
Eichmann looks up from his notes, meets
her eyes.
He doesn't look away, doesn't flinch,
doesn't show a flicker of recognition or
remorse, just stares back with empty
eyes. Then returns to his notepad,
continues writing. No emotion, no guilt,
nothing.
That image, the bureaucrat who won't
look away from his victim, who feels
nothing [music] while she weeps, becomes
the face of what Hannah Arendt will call
the banality of evil.
Eichmann's defense is simple. He was
following orders. "I never killed anyone
personally. I was responsible only for
transportation. I was a small cog in a
large machine."
The prosecution responds with documents,
orders signed by Eichmann, memos
demanding faster deportations, letters
showing he didn't just follow orders, he
exceeded them. He innovated. He took
pride in his work.
December 15th, 1961.
The verdict.
Guilty. All counts. Crimes against the
Jewish people, crimes against humanity,
war crimes. Sentence, death. But
Eichmann has one last thing to say.
Ramla prison, Israel. May 31st, 1962.
11:58 p.m. Adolf Eichmann walks to the
gallows.
Refuses a hood, refuses to have his legs
bound.
A guard offers wine. He drinks half.
His last words, "Long live Germany. Long
live Argentina. Long live Austria. I had
to obey the rules of war and my flag."
[music]
1 minute past midnight, the floor drops.
His body is cremated before dawn.
>> [music]
>> Ashes scattered in the Mediterranean Sea
beyond Israeli waters.
No grave, no marker, nothing to become a
shrine.
The Holocaust was committed by men with
filing cabinets and train schedules. Men
who followed orders. Men who told
themselves they were just doing their
jobs. The architect of the Holocaust
[music]
told the world he was just following
orders.
The world didn't believe him.
That was enough.

text:
From birth to battlefield, Spartan life was an endless gauntlet of pain, deprivation, and impossible expectations. This is the unvarnished truth behind the 300's legend: a society that turned child-rearing into military programming and created warriors so fearsome precisely because they had nothing left to lose.

Borrow against your stocks. Billionaires
have most of their wealth tied up in
stocks. If they sell the stocks, they
have to pay taxes. So to get around
this, they call up the bank. They
receive a low interest rate loan with
their stocks as collateral. If the
stocks go down, the banks might ask for
more stocks to add as collateral, or the
billionaire might have to pay some cash
to keep the loan in good standing. In
normal markets, this is easy cash and a
great way to avoid taxes. Yes, they
still have to pay interest, but the low
interest rate is usually much lower than
whatever their tax bill would have been
if they sold. Also, since they didn't
sell their stock, they get to benefit
from it going up in value. It could
increase in value more than the cost of
their interest, making the whole deal a
no-brainer. They get money to spend
without losing a money-making asset.
Use mortgages to buy property. In
November 2013, Blackstone's rental home
division, Invitation Homes, bundled the
rent from 3,27
houses and used it to raise $479
million, a firstofits-kind deal at the
time. This showed how big players scale
real estate. Use a mortgage or a pool of
them. Buy assets that pay for
themselves. Then refinance and repeat.
Here's how they do it in simple terms.
Step one, borrow to buy houses. They get
mortgages to buy lots of homes. Step
two, they get renters. People move in
and pay rent every month. Step three,
they put the rent in a special box. They
make a tiny company that only collects
that rent and pays bills. Step four,
they sell IUS to investors. The rent
collecting company sells bonds.
Investors give cash now. The bond says,
"We'll pay you each month using the
rent." Step five, backup plan if things
go wrong. The houses are collateral. If
payments stop, investors can take or
sell the houses. Step six, they use the
cash to grow. With investor cash, they
pay off earlier loans and buy more
houses. And finally, step seven,
refinance and repeat. When rates are
better or house prices rise, they swap
their old debt for cheaper debt and do
it all again. Insurance float. This is
Joe, your average guy. He pays his car
insurance bill every month and hopes he
never has to use it. Meanwhile, the
insurance company is collecting Joe's
payments. They invest that money for
years and pay the claims whenever they
pop up. For Joe to use the money, he has
to have some kind of incident with his
car and hope that they approve his
claim. And even then, they're going to
be stingy with how much they give him.
See, insurance payments are called
premiums. Companies receive the premiums
upfront. This is a liability, which is
like debt, because they only pay the
claims in the future. This gap between
collecting and paying is called float.
They can use the float to invest in
stocks, bonds, or entire businesses. A
genius tool to use other people's money
for your investments. Buy companies with
debt. Billionaires and private equity
companies borrow money to buy a big cash
generating company, then use the
company's own profits to repay the loan.
That's the leverage buyout or LBO.
Owners put in some equity. Banks provide
a lot of debt. And the target company's
cash flow carries the load. If they
improve operations, sell a few non-core
pieces, and pay down debt, their small
equity stake can grow massively. It's
high stakes, but it works often enough
to create fortunes.
Sell bonds to fund growth. In April
2013, Apple sold $17 billion in bonds,
the largest corporate bond sale at the
time. Even though they were swimming in
cash, they did this because debt was
dirt cheap, interest is taxdeductible,
and issuing bonds let Apple reward
shareholders and invest without bringing
overseas cash back to the United States
and paying extra taxes. When your credit
is great, you can borrow on friendly
terms, keep control of your company, and
still bankroll expansions, acquisitions,
or shareholder payouts. Bonds are just
tradable IUS.
Borrow to buy back shares. A company
raises debt and uses the cash to
repurchase its own stock. Share count
goes down, so each remaining share
represents a bigger slice of the pie.
Earnings per share often look better,
which can nudge the price up. Founders
and early owners like this because their
percentage ownership effectively grows
without them spending a dime. Interest
is a business expense, so it can reduce
taxes, and if the stock is undervalued,
it's an efficient use of capital.
Leverage the portfolio.
You borrow from your broker to buy more
stocks than your cash alone would allow.
If your stocks rise, your gains are
multiplied. If they fall, losses are
multiplied and fast. Brokers set minimum
cushions. If markets drop below those
cushions, you get a margin call and may
be forced to sell everything to pay them
back. Billionaires use margin when they
see a clear edge or short-term
opportunity, and they typically do it
alongside other safer borrowing methods.
The appeal is obvious. Amplify returns.
But the risk is real. Leverage makes
small mistakes expensive. Some of the
biggest losses in history were due to
leverage portfolios.
Build with construction loans.
Developers don't show up with a suitcase
of cash to build a tower. They line up a
construction loan that funds most of the
cost while the building is going up.
Before a shovel ever hits the dirt, they
try to lock in tenants or pre-sales,
which reassure the bank that rent or
sales will repay the loan. When the
building is finished and leased, they
can refinance into a longerterm mortgage
at a lower rate because at this stage,
it's much less risky for the bank. With
the new loan, they pay off the
construction lender and often pull some
cash out. That cash becomes the down
payment for the next project. Rinse,
repeat. Borrow to build. Stabilize the
asset. Refinance on better terms. And
roll the equity into the next deal.
Borrow to pay yourself.
In 2010, hospital chain HCA borrowed
billions and paid a giant one-time
dividend to its private equity owners.
Cash today without selling the company.
Lenders played along because hospitals
generate steady cash. And a year later,
HCA returned to public markets. just
fine. The headline, borrow at the
company level, wire money to the owners,
and keep the business.
Let customers prepay.
You may have heard people saying that
Starbucks is really a bank. Well, this
is the exact method they use. Customers
load their money into their Starbucks
account, and this allows Starbucks to
use their money for business operations.
Deposits, annual subscriptions, and
pre-orders are a way for companies to
get cash upfront. The mechanics are
simple. Upfront customer money acts like
an interestfree loan that funds
inventory, hiring, and marketing. Gyms,
software, airlines, hotels, and event
promoters do this every day. They
collect early, record it as deferred
revenue on the books, and use the cash
to build and sell more. It also locks in
customers since they've already paid,
smooths demand, and gives you clean
signals about what to make next.

text:
Soapy Smith and the Conquest of Skagway — the true story of how a quiet drifter from Georgia with twenty borrowed dollars stepped off a steamer in October 1897 and, in nine months, came to own every saloon, every newspaper, and even the elected mayor of Alaska's richest boomtown — without ever firing a single shot.
On a cold morning in October 1897, a man named Jefferson Randolph Smith II walked off the steamer Utopia onto the muddy dock at Skagway, Alaska. Every other passenger on that ship was heading north for Klondike gold. Smith was not. He understood something the prospectors didn't. The men with the gold were going home. The men with the money — were just arriving.

Skagway was the chokepoint of the greatest gold rush in North American history. Twenty thousand men a year passed through it, each carrying his entire life savings in cash — the five hundred dollars required to outfit a Yukon claim, more money than the average American earned in a year. The nearest US Marshal was eight hundred miles away. There were no courts. No federal law. No civil government of any kind. It was the largest pile of unguarded money on the continent.
By February 1898, every man arriving in Skagway was reading Smith's newspaper. Drinking in Smith's saloon. Voting for Smith's mayor. Praying in the church Smith funded. And paying five dollars to send telegrams home — from an office whose wires connected to nothing.

This is the full story of how a small-time confidence man from Denver — known across the Rockies for a street trick involving wrapped bars of soap and hundred-dollar bills — arrived at the chokepoint of the Klondike Gold Rush and turned a frontier port into the most sophisticated criminal operation in the history of the American West. How Soapy Smith built a three-hundred-man organization in nine months, opened a fake telegraph office that sold homesick stampeders five-dollar replies from imaginary wives, ran his own Committee of Law and Order out of the back room of his saloon, bribed a US Treasury agent into writing a clean report to Washington, and was personally congratulated by the Vice President of the United States. How a single Klondiker named John Stewart, robbed of a five-pound pouch of gold dust on July 7, 1898, did what no one else had done in nine months — and called a citizens' meeting on the Juneau Company Wharf. How, the next evening, Smith walked onto that wharf with a Winchester rifle and died in four seconds of gunfire.

And how the psychological mechanisms Smith demonstrated on the streets of Skagway — the rigged prize game, the fake telegraph, the manufactured social proof — quietly became the architecture of the modern slot machine, the modern loot box, and the modern phishing scam. Bally Manufacturing patented his soap trick, by a different name, in 1976. The IT-security industry rediscovered his telegraph office in 1995. The global gambling industry that now runs on his methods is worth five hundred billion dollars a year.

He was never tried. He never spent a day in prison. He was simply shot.
He is buried outside the cemetery in Skagway, behind a wooden fence — under a wooden marker that tourists keep stealing pieces of.

Skagway, Alaska, October 1897. A drifter
from Georgia steps off the steamer
Utopia,
>> [music]
>> 20 borrowed dollars in his pocket. His
name is Jefferson Smith.
Every other man on the dock is heading
north for gold. Smith isn't. In 9
months, he will own this town, every
saloon, every newspaper, even the
elected mayor, and he will not fire a
single shot to do it. Skagway is the
choke point of the Klondike gold rush.
20,000 men a year, each carrying their
entire life savings in cash. The nearest
US Marshall, 800 miles away. No courts,
no federal law. The largest pile of
unguarded money in North America.
By February, every man arriving in
Skagway is reading Smith's newspaper,
voting for Smith's mayor, praying in
Smith's church, and paying $5 to send a
telegram home from an office with no
wires.
The most profitable thing Smith ever
sold was a bar of soap. To understand
what happened in Skagway, you need to
understand the man who walked off that
steamer, Jefferson Randolph Smith II,
born 1860, Coweta County, Georgia. A
wealthy family before the Civil War, a
ruined one after. By 18, Smith was
driving cattle through Texas. By 20, he
was working the saloons in Fort Worth,
>> [music]
>> watching men with experienced hands take
money from drunk cowboys with three-card
monte. He learned the trade by watching.
He didn't talk much. He listened. By 25,
Smith had moved to Denver, Colorado, and
it was in Denver in 1881 that he
invented the trick that would give him
his name, and eventually an empire.
He set a small wooden case on a street
corner in downtown Denver. On the case,
bars of ordinary soap. He started
wrapping them in paper, one at a time,
in front of a crowd. Into some of the
wrappers, in plain view, he slipped
paper money, $1 bills, $5 bills, 10, 20,
and once, for the audience, a $100 bill.
In 1881, $100 was 4 months wages for a
working man. He mixed the wrapped soaps
together in the case. He looked up at
the crowd that had started to gather,
and he offered them for $5 each. A man
stepped out of the crowd, bought a bar,
unwrapped it, pulled out a $100 bill,
shouted in disbelief, held it up so
everyone could see. The crowd surged
forward. By sundown, Smith had sold
every bar in the case. The man who won
the $100 was his cousin. The other
winners, three or four small bills
scattered through the case to keep
momentum, went to his employees. The
rest of the bars went to strangers who
paid $5 for 10 cents worth of soap. The
Denver papers called him Soapy Smith.
Over the next 15 years, he ran that
trick and a dozen variants of it across
Denver, Leadville, Creed, and the small
mining towns of the Rockies. He built a
small organization, maybe 30 men. He
paid bribes to police. He survived three
murder accusations. By 1896, Denver had
cleaned up. The new mayor wanted Smith
gone. Smith was running out of cities,
and then the newspapers started printing
a single word, Klondike. In August 1897,
the steamer Portland docked in Seattle
carrying 68 prospectors. Among them, 3/4
of a ton of gold. Within a month, 10,000
men had packed everything they owned and
bought tickets north. Soapy Smith bought
one, too. He wasn't going to the gold
fields. He understood something the
prospectors didn't. The men with the
gold were going home. The men with the
money were just arriving.
To understand why Soapy Smith ended up
owning Skagway, you need to understand
the geography of the Klondike gold rush.
The gold was in the Yukon, 600 miles
inland, behind two mountain passes,
White Pass and Chilkoot Pass, that
killed 3,000 pack animals in a single
winter. To get to the gold, you had to
start at the coast. There were two
ports, Dyea, at the foot of Chilkoot,
and Skagway, at the foot of White Pass.
In the summer of 1897, neither port
existed in any real sense. Skagway was a
few cabins on a mud flat. By December,
it had 10,000 people and 125 businesses.
By spring 1898, it was the largest city
in Alaska. The Canadian Mounted Police,
on the other side of the mountains, were
enforcing a rule. To enter the Yukon,
every prospector had to bring exactly 1
ton of supplies, flour, bacon, picks,
tents, stove, rifle, ammunition, boots.
It cost approximately $500 per man to
outfit. In 1897, the average American
annual wage was around $440.
So, every stampeders in Skagway carried,
in cash, in bank drafts, in gold coins,
more money than he had ever held in his
life, often more than he would ever hold
again.
And he had to stay in Skagway for
[music] weeks, sometimes months. The
federal government of the United States
was not there. Alaska had been purchased
from Russia in 1867.
It had no civil government, no courts,
no US marshals stationed within reach.
The closest federal authority was in
Sitka, 600 miles by boat, no telegraph
connection. The army garrison at Fort
St. Michael was 800 miles away. In
practice, Skagway had no law. What it
had was 20,000 men with cash in their
pockets, no civil structure, no
families, and weeks of empty time to
fill. The men who got rich in Skagway
were not the prospectors. The
prospectors went north and most of them
came back with nothing. The men who got
rich were the men who sold to the
prospectors, the hotel owners, the pack
horse renters, the saloon keepers, the
boot makers, the bankers. By the time
Soapy Smith stepped off the Utopia in
October 1897, that economy was already
worth more per day than most cities in
continental America. Smith looked at it
and saw something the saloon keepers
didn't. The hotels were selling beds.
The saloons were selling whiskey. The
banks were selling drafts. Nobody was
selling certainty. Nobody was selling
hope. Nobody was selling the feeling of
home. And in Skagway in 1897, those were
the three most expensive things in the
world.
In the first 3 months, Smith built five
operations. The first was the prize soap
racket, the same trick from Denver, 20
years older and refined. Smith would set
his case on a busy corner near the
docks. A crowd would gather. A
confederate, what Smith called a capper,
would buy a bar, unwrap it, find a $50
bill, and shout. What happened next is
the part that modern psychologists have
a name for. It's called social proof.
When a person doesn't know what to do,
the brain looks at what others nearby
are doing and copies faster than
thinking, faster than logic. The crowd
doesn't decide to buy soap. the crowd
watches one man win, and individual
brains in the crowd register the event
as a personal missed opportunity. The
technical term for the feeling is fear
of missing out. Smith didn't know the
term. He didn't need to. What he had
built on that wooden case was the
world's first slot machine. Modern slot
machine designers, the people who design
the casino floor in Las Vegas today,
describe their job in three words: loss
disguised as win. The machine pays you
back 10 cents on a $5 bet, plays a sound
that signals victory, lights up, and
your brain releases dopamine. You have
lost $4.90.
Your nervous system experiences a
triumph. Smith built that effect with
humans in 1879.
The capper's shout was the bell. The
$100 bill was the jackpot light. The
crowd's surge forward was the cascade of
new bets. Most stampeder's who bought a
bar of soap walked away with a piece of
ordinary soap, $5 poorer. Many of them
returned the next day.
The second operation was the saloon.
Smith opened a place called Jeff Smith's
Parlor on Holly Street. Mahogany bar,
imported whiskey, an ornate gold leaf
mirror behind the counter. From the
street, it looked like the most
respectable establishment in town.
Inside, every game was rigged. The faro
tables had marked cards. The roulette
wheels were brake-controlled. The poker
games used cappers, Smith's men, who
would befriend a stampeder, take him for
whiskey, and then for everything in his
pocket. But, that's not what made the
parlor an empire. What made the parlor
an empire was the back office.
The third operation, the back office,
was the information system. When a
steamer docked in Skagway, three men
were waiting before the gangplank
lowered. One dressed as a clergyman, one
as a newspaperman, one as an old
prospector with a friendly face. They
would walk up to the new arrivals,
introduce themselves, offer to help
carry bags, recommend a hotel, ask how
the trip was, make jokes, inquire about
wives, offer condolences for the cold,
ask casually how much the man had
brought. By the time the stampeders
reached his hotel, three men in Soapy
Smith's organization knew his name, his
hometown, his approximate cash, and
where he was staying.
That information went directly to the
parlor. Within a day, the stampeder
would find himself in a card game, or
buying a bar of soap, or being
approached by another friendly stranger
with a business opportunity.
The fourth operation was the most
psychologically refined. It was a
telegraph office. Smith opened it on
Trail Street in early 1898. Sign on the
door, counter inside, a telegraph key on
the desk, a line going out the window,
up the side of the building, across the
roof, and ending out of view of any
customer at nothing.
The line was not connected to anywhere.
The telegraph key was a prop. Skagway
had no overland telegraph connection to
the rest of the world until 1901. But
for $5, a customer could send a message
anywhere. Within an hour, an operator
would deliver a reply. "Yes, your wife
is well. The children miss you. Send
money home if you can. Mother is
unwell."
The replies were written in the back
room by Smith's clerks. Most stampeders
had been gone from home for two to four
months. They had not heard their wives'
voices since they left. They were
sleeping in shared tents with strangers.
They were exhausted, cold, and afraid.
For $5, they could touch home for an
hour. This was Smith's most lucrative
operation per minute of work ever. It
was also, in modern terms, fishing. Not
the technical kind, he wasn't stealing
passwords, but the psychological
architecture is identical. A trusted
communication channel that does not
exist. A reply that exploits emotional
vulnerability. A request that the victim
fulfills because the false context felt
real.
The IT security industry has a name for
the technique today. They date it to
1995 with the first AOL fishing scams.
Soapy Smith was running it in 1898.
The fifth operation was politics.
Skagway tried to organize a vigilance
committee in March 1898, citizens who
would enforce order in the absence of
federal law. Smith found out within
hours. By the time the committee held
its first meeting, Smith had already
established his own committee, calling
itself the committee of law and order,
with himself as chairman. He published a
notice in the Daily Alaskan. He warned
the public against the unauthorized
vigilance committee. He pledged that his
committee, meeting at Jeff Smith's
parlor, would protect Skagway from
disorder. He donated money to the local
church. He paid for stray dog shelters.
He sponsored a brass band. By April
1898, the Skagway News, funded in part
by Smith, was calling him the uncrowned
king of Skagway. By May, he had 300 men
working for him. By June, he was
officially the marshal of the 4th of
July parade. He rode at the head of the
procession on a white horse.
The Vice President of the United States,
Garret Hobart, sent him a personal
letter of congratulation.
For 9 months between October 1897 and
July 1898, Jefferson Smith ran Skagway
the way the Block family ran Monte
Carlo, completely. His organization
counted by then between 200 and 300 men,
cappers at the docks, card sharps at the
parlor,
bouncers,
lookouts, spies inside the rival hotels,
bribed clerks inside the bank. The
deputy sheriff was on his payroll. The
actual federal authorities were aware. A
US Treasury agent, sent by Washington to
investigate complaints, arrived in
Skagway in May 1898. Within 4 days, the
agent had been wined, dined, escorted to
the parlor, befriended by Smith
personally, and put on a steamer south
with a report that nothing was unusual
in Skagway.
Smith funded the agent's return ticket.
The amount of money moving through
Smith's organization in spring 1898, by
the lowest estimate from his bookkeeper,
was approximately $10,000 per week,
about $15 million per year in today's
money. It was not a fortune by gold rush
standards. The actual Klondike fortunes
were larger, but Smith was extracting
his money without ever picking up a
pickaxe, freezing on a mountain pass, or
drowning in the Yukon River. He took it
from the men who were doing all those
things. By June, the formal structure of
Skagway was, for any practical purpose,
Smith's. The mayor would consult him
before signing ordinances. The newspaper
editors would check stories with him.
The pastor of the largest church would
meet with him weekly. He had achieved a
thing that, in the history of the
American West, almost no other criminal
had managed. He had not robbed a town.
He had become one. And then, on July
7th, 1898, a Klondiker named John
Douglas Stewart walked off a returning
steamer. Stewart had spent the previous
winter in the Yukon. He was a small
operator from British Columbia. He had
not struck rich, but he had washed
enough gold dust from his claim to fill
a small pouch. The pouch weighed 5 lb.
At the market price, the pouch was worth
about $2,700.
Stewart walked into Skagway looking for
a bank. Three of Smith's men intercepted
him. Friendly conversation, drinks at
the parlor, a demonstration of three
card monte at a back table, a small bet,
a win, a larger bet, a larger win, a
still larger bet for the dust. A switch
of the card, Stewart lost the pouch.
Stewart did what almost no one had done
in 9 months. He went to the steamer
dock. He found other Klondikers waiting
to board. He told them what had
happened. He showed them his empty
pouch. He told them the names. By that
evening, a meeting had been called at
Sylvester Hall. Around 100 citizens of
Skagway showed up, then 200, then 500.
The hall was too small. They moved to
the Juno Company Wharf. For the first
time in 9 months, the people of Skagway
were assembled in one place without a
member of Smith's organization in the
room. Smith heard about the meeting at
the parlor. He picked up a Winchester
rifle from the rack behind the bar. He
buckled on a Colt revolver. He drank a
glass of whiskey. He stepped out into
the street. It was around 9:00 in the
evening, July 8th, 1898.
A heavy wooden door blocked the entrance
to the wharf where the citizens were
meeting. A small man stood in front of
it. His name was Frank Reid, a civil
engineer, a man who had laid out the
original streets of Skagway. Reid was
armed. The two men walked toward each
other on the wooden planks.
What happened on the Juno Company Wharf
at 9:00 on the evening of July 8th, 1898
is one of the most documented gun fights
in the American West. There were 47
sworn witnesses.
The transcript runs 380 pages.
What happened is this.
Smith walked onto the wharf with his
Winchester rifle held at port arms. Reed
raised his cult. They arguing. Smith
said something to Reed. The exact words
have never been agreed on. Some
witnesses heard, "Get back." Some heard,
"Damn you. Don't you pull that on me."
Reed said something back. Both men fired
within 2 seconds from a distance of
approximately 3 ft. Smith died on the
wharf, a bullet through the heart. Reed
was shot in the leg and groin. He lived
for 12 more days before dying of his
wounds.
The fight on the wharf lasted, by every
witness account, less than 4 seconds. In
those 4 seconds, every operation Smith
had built collapsed. By the next
morning, the vigilance committee, the
real one, had assembled 300 men. They
went door-to-door in Skagway. They
arrested Smith's cappers. They closed
Jeff Smith's parlor and seized the
books. They closed the telegraph office.
They emptied the committee of law and
order from the back room of the parlor.
The ringleaders of Smith's organization
were rounded up and forced onto a
steamer south to the actual federal
authorities in Sitka. The rest of the
gang fled into the Yukon and were caught
by the mounted police who knew exactly
who they were because Smith had spent 9
months making himself famous.
Within 72 hours of Smith's death, the
criminal empire of Skagway was over. But
the most important thing about that gun
fight is not who died. It's what the
people of Skagway did next. The day
after Smith was killed, the citizens
committee held a public memorial for
Reed. They commissioned a granite
headstone. They wrote on it, "He gave
his life for the honor of Skagway. The
marker still stands today in Skagway's
Gold Rush Cemetery. It is the largest
marker in the cemetery. A hundred yards
away behind a wooden fence is a smaller
marker. It reads in three lines,
Jefferson R. Smith died July 8th, 1898,
age 38. A pauper's grave. Outside the
cemetery itself, the town of Skagway
voted that Smith would not be buried in
the same ground as the man who shot him.
The Klondike Gold Rush ended in 1899.
Within two years, Skagway shrank from
20,000 people to less than a thousand.
The federal government finally arrived
in 1900. By 1901, there was an overland
telegraph. By 1903, there was a US
courthouse.
By 1910, Skagway was a small port town.
Today, it has 800 year-round residents.
Most of the buildings from 1898 are
gone.

text:
Berlin — once the beating heart of global club culture — is facing an existential crisis. The city that gave us Berghain, Tresor, and a generation of free-spirited nightlife is being reshaped by gentrification, rising rents, and changing attitudes toward clubbing itself.

In this episode, we dive deep into how Berlin’s legendary scene was born from the fall of the Wall, how real estate speculation fueled its rise — and now, how those same forces threaten to destroy it. From Watergate to SchwuZ, iconic venues are closing one by one, as the city’s cultural core begins to crumble.

This is the story of how Berlin’s freedom became its greatest export — and why that freedom is now under siege.

🎧 Featuring stories from the city’s most iconic clubs
🏙️ Exploring how gentrification and housing policy reshaped nightlife
💡 A look at what it means for Berlin’s identity — and its future

If Berlin wants to keep its soul, something has to change.

[Music]
This is Berlin, a city worldrenowned for
its night life, its beating heart of
electronic music and freedom. At the
center lies the ring barn, a boundary
encircling nearly every major nightclub
at the core of the capital's party
scene. Over 90% of Berlin's nightife is
concentrated in just 10 of the city's 96
neighborhoods. A cultural core unlike
anywhere else in the world. That
concentration shapes more than just the
city's identity. It drives its economy.
Before the pandemic, tourism related to
the club scene generated around€ 1.5
billion in a single year for the city.
More than twice the revenue of Germany's
most famous football powerhouse, Bayern
Munich made in the same year. But
beneath the surface, that core is
crumbling.
Electronic clubs like Watergate and
Ranata announced they will close by the
end of the year.
>> Last year, two of Berlin's best known
techno institutions, Watergate and
Ranata, announced they would be closing.
And now the city's oldest LGBT
nightclub, Schvutz, has declared
bankruptcy. Rising rents, relentless
gentrification, and shifting
demographics are forcing even the city's
most iconic venues to close their doors.
Like other major cities, Berlin is
grappling with rapid population growth
and aggressive real estate speculation,
creating a shortage of affordable space
and driving up the cost of living across
the board. The result is a nightlife
culture under siege. A scene once
celebrated worldwide as a symbol of
freedom and self-expression now faces an
existential crisis. A battle to survive
in the very city that built its legend.
To understand how Berlin got here, we
need to rewind 30 years or so.
>> East German authorities have said in
essence that the Berlin wall doesn't
mean anything anymore. The wall of the
East Germans will now be breached by
anybody one who wants to leave.
Occasionally they shout, "Da Musvec, the
wall must go." Thousands and thousands
of West Germans come to make the point
that the wall has suddenly become
irrelevant.
The roots of today's crisis stretch all
the way back to the fall of the Berlin
Wall when cheap rents and empty
buildings first created the conditions
for the city's legendary nightlife
scene. The fall of the wall in 1989
didn't just reunite a city. It also
planted the seeds of a modern problem,
gentrification.
[Applause]
Berlin was in an unusual financial bind.
Decades of division had driven most of
its industry to West Germany, leaving
the East starving for money. Investors
quickly cottoned on. Berlin soon became
a magnet for international capital and
powerful housing corporations. Compared
to the other parts of Western Europe,
property here was astonishingly cheap.
Take the example of Deutsch Von, a real
estate company that snapped up 60,000
apartments for just €450 million. That's
roughly €7,000
per property. 15 years later, the deal
came full circle with Berlin's
government forced to buy back part of
that same stock, about 14,000 apartments
at an average of 163,000
each. That's a staggering return of more
than 2,000%.
Now, we're talking about nightclubs, not
residential real estate, but the housing
example shows how the city's once
affordable property market became a gold
mine for investors. However, these very
forces would also help lay the
foundations for the impending explosion
in club culture. In the early 1990s, the
city's eastern districts were dotted
with empty factories, warehouses, and
power plants. Vast, inexpensive, and
largely isolated, they became ideal
breeding grounds for an underground rave
movement. Traor opened up in 1991 inside
the abandoned vaults of the Vatheim
department store. Bergheim took over a
cavernous East German power plant, and
Sysifos transformed a derelict dog
biscuit factory into a sprawling openair
playground. While most venues relied on
short-term leases, a few clubs secured
ownership early, protecting them from
the rent hikes and redevelopment that
would eventually suffocate others. 15
years ago, the owners of Burghine
promised the premises from the Swedish
energy company Vatenfall for €1.5
million, a bargain by today's standards.
By owning its building, the club stands
among the few in the city insulated from
rising rents and the pressures of
profit-driven foreign investors. This
independence enabled its parent company
to report annual profits of more than €2
million, which may explain why they can
be so particular about who gets in.
Those without such protection weren't so
fortunate, and over the years, one by
one, Berlin's clubs have begun to
vanish. Knack club in VMF in 2010.
Maria A Obnoff in 2011.
Delicious Donuts Icon and Tape in 2012,
Horitzburg in 2013,
Cookies Weekend, Magdalena and Picnic in
2014,
Magnet Club and Statbad Wedding in 2015,
Rosies, Bassie Club and Barbetta in
2018,
followed by Shalet, Zank Gayorg, and
Ruml's B in 2019.
Behind many of these closures runs a
common thread, the rising influence of
powerful real estate interests. And in
Berlin, one name surfaces repeatedly
when the conversation turns to
gentrification and the disappearance of
nightclubs. Guora Pedovitz.
In the '90s, Pedovitz began to
systematically purchase occupied
buildings in Citzburg. Today, his empire
has been ties to the closure of some of
the most controversial cultural
hotspots, including nightclubs Ranata
and the world famous Watergate.
Ranata has been especially direct,
publicly naming Padovitz's company as
the reason for its demise. Watergate's
explanation for ending its 22-year run
was both more nuanced and concerning.
Along with rising rent, wage and energy
costs, its management pointed to shifts
in the relevance of Berlin club culture
for young people.
>> March, we had a weekend which had three
soldout shows and then the news came
like there's this pandemic and like
everything's going to be forbidden and
everything.
>> It seems that during the pandemic of
2020, habits shifted. People filled
their nights with other pursuits and
music itself shifted into new spaces.
Streaming and digital platforms became
the main stage, reshaping not just how
music was consumed, but how entire
communities around it formed. Clubbing
has always been generational. Most
people live that life for 3 or 4 years
before studies, work, or new
responsibilities pull them away, leaving
room for the next wave. But with venues
closed for 2 and 1/2 years, that cycle
was broken. A whole generation never
stepped onto the dance floor, and the
gap they left behind is one the scene is
still struggling to recover from.
But perhaps the most telling sign of
change isn't just which clubs survive,
it's how long the nights last. A study
by the FD found that the share of nights
running past 3:00 a.m. has fallen in 12
of 15 major cities since 2014. And this
is perhaps the biggest threat of all, a
lack of appetite for club culture.
Today's younger clubbers simply aren't
going out for the same marathon sessions
that defined Berlin's reputation.
Instead of disappearing into a club for
12 or even 24 hours, many prefer shorter
nights, or they save their energy for
the occasional festival.
The culture of staying out until sunrise
once the heartbeat of the city's night
life is fading with each new generation.
Whether Berlin chooses to protect what
it made special, the authenticity, the
raw creativity, the sense of community
will determine if the city continues to
stand as the global capital of club
culture, or if it becomes just another
metropolis that lost its edge to
gentrification.
The next chapter isn't written yet, but
if Berlin wants to preserve the very
heartbeat that gave it identity, action
will be needed to ensure the night can
go on.

text:
How One Aviator Built Stalin's WWII Women's Air Force in Six Weeks — the true story of how a twenty-nine-year-old Soviet flight navigator walked into a private office on the second floor of the Kremlin on October 8, 1941, and walked out seventy minutes later with three combat aviation regiments and six hundred biplanes.

On a Wednesday afternoon in October 1941, with the Wehrmacht one hundred and ten kilometres from Moscow and three Red Army bomber regiments already destroyed, Marina Raskova walked into Stalin's office carrying a folded sheet of paper inside her overcoat. On it were three thousand names — Soviet women who had written to her that summer asking how to volunteer for the air war. Twelve hundred already held civilian flying qualifications. The Soviet Union had fewer than four thousand military pilots left alive.

Raskova was not a soldier. She was the most famous woman in the country — a record-setting navigator who, three years earlier, had jumped from a doomed transport over Siberian taiga and walked one hundred and thirty kilometres through trackless forest on cranberries and stream water before a rescue team found her. Stalin had pinned the title Hero of the Soviet Union on her chest. He had also, twice in 1941, refused to allow women into combat.

This is the full story of how she changed his mind in seventy minutes. How she selected eighty-six college students out of one thousand applicants with three questions. How she trained them at a freezing airfield on the Volga in men's overcoats and boots stuffed with newspaper, flying Polikarpov U-2 biplanes designed in 1928 to spray pesticide on collective farms — wood, fabric, steel cable, no armour, no radio, slower at full throttle than a Messerschmitt 109 at stall. How a navigator named Polina Gelman discovered that a Polikarpov with its engine cut would glide silently for seven hundred metres — and how the Wehrmacht began to hear, instead of an engine, only the sound of eight bracing wires against the night wind, like the sweeping of a broom. The Germans named them Nachthexen. Night Witches.

The regiment flew twenty-three thousand six hundred and seventy-two combat sorties between June 1942 and May 1945. The pilots flew without parachutes — a unanimous regimental decision in writing on June 14, 1942 — because two parachutes weighed twenty kilograms, and twenty kilograms was an additional bomb fragment. On the worst night, July 31 to August 1, 1943, eight women were lost in six minutes over the Taman Peninsula, their combined ages one hundred and seventy-one. Marina Raskova herself died on January 4, 1943, when a transport carrying her to her new day bomber regiment struck the bank of the Volga in heavy fog. She was thirty. Her ashes were interred in the Kremlin Wall. Bershanskaya, the regiment's commander, was back at the operating airfield twelve days after the funeral. She told her squadron commanders one sentence: Marina Mikhailovna would expect us to fly tonight.

The regiment flew that night, and almost every night for the next twenty-eight months — through Ukraine, Belarus, East Prussia, Pomerania, until the last sortie on May 4, 1945, over a Wehrmacht ammunition depot near Świnoujście. They were not invited to the Moscow Victory Parade. The official Soviet histories did not mention them. Twelve years later, four years after Stalin's death, their commander published four thousand words in Krasnaya Zvezda and listed every name.

The most decorated women's combat aviation unit in the history of any war the world has fought — built by one Soviet aviator who walked into the Kremlin with a folded list in her overcoat.
