Kremlin, Moscow, October 8th, 1941,
3:00 in the afternoon. A 29-year-old
Soviet aviator named Marina Raskova
walks into a private office on the
second floor. The man behind the desk is
Joseph Stalin.
Raskova is not a soldier. She is not a
general. She is not a party member. She
is the most famous woman in the Soviet
Union.
A record-setting flight navigator who, 3
years earlier, flew 6,000 km without a
man on board. She has come to ask Stalin
to build him an air force entirely out
of college students.
The Wehrmacht is 110 km from Moscow.
Three of the Red Army's bomber regiments
have been shot down in the past 4 weeks.
Stalin has refused, twice [music]
already in 1941, to allow women into
combat. The military doctrine does not
provide for it. The aircraft are not
configured for them. Raskova has 6 weeks
to change his mind. Two questions decide
the next 3 years. How does a 29-year-old
flight navigator change Joseph Stalin's
[music] mind in 6 weeks? And how does
she train 100 college students to outfly
the German air force in aircraft no
general in any army would take into a
war?
To understand how a civilian aviator
walked into Stalin's office and walked
out with an army, you have to understand
who Marina Raskova was. Marina
Mikhailovna, born March 1912, Moscow.
[music]
She studied chemistry, married, had a
daughter at 18, took a draftswoman
position at the Air Force's Zhukovsky
Academy.
>> [music]
>> She was 20. She wanted to fly. In 1932,
she enrolled in the Civil Aviation
Academy at Tushino, the second woman
ever admitted.
>> [music]
>> Within 18 months, she She completed the
navigator program. By 25, [music]
she was one of the top aerial navigators
in the Soviet Union.
In September, 1938, Raskova was the
senior navigator on a flight that, if it
succeeded, would set the world record
for the longest non-stop flight ever
flown by a woman. The crew was all
female.
Pilot, Polina Osipenko. Second pilot,
Valentina Grizodubova.
Raskova as the navigator.
They flew an aircraft called the Rodina,
Motherland, Moscow to
Komsomolsk-on-Amur.
6,450
km. 26 hours and 29 minutes. In the last
90 minutes, in heavy fog, [music]
Raskova made a navigational error. They
drifted south over uninhabited Siberian
taiga, almost out of fuel. Grizodubova,
the senior pilot, told Raskova to bail
out before the crash. So that, if the
rest of the crew died, the navigator
could survive to report what had gone
wrong. Raskova jumped at 4,000 ft. She
landed in marshland. No map, no rations.
She walked for 10 days. She lived on
cranberries and stream water. She walked
130 km through trackless [music] forest
before she encountered a Soviet rescue
team. When she walked out, she had lost
14 kg. She had also become the most
famous woman in the Soviet Union. Stalin
personally awarded Raskova, Osipenko,
and Grizodubova the title [music] Hero
of the Soviet Union. The first three
women ever to receive it.
By October of 1941, the country itself
was eight weeks from possibly ceasing to
exist. And Marina Raskova was walking
into Stalin's office.
The meeting was scheduled for 15
minutes. It lasted approximately 70.
Raskova began by reading aloud the
contents of a single sheet of paper she
had brought with her folded inside her
overcoat, a list approximately 3,000
names. Each one a Soviet woman who had
between June and October 1941 written
personally to Raskova [music] at the
Zhukovsky Academy asking how to
volunteer for the air war. Teachers,
factory workers, engineering students,
doctors, daughters of dead soldiers,
wives of dead soldiers. The list,
Raskova [music] told Stalin, contained
1,200 women who already held civilian
flying qualifications.
The Soviet Union had at that [music]
moment fewer than 4,000 military pilots
remaining alive. She was offering him an
additional 1,200. She had three
conditions.
First, women-only regiments, not
auxiliary positions, not ground crews,
not nurses, combat regiments, pilots,
navigators, mechanics, armorers, all
female.
Second, she, Raskova, would personally
command the recruitment, training, and
formation. No male officer above her
until the regiments were operational.
Third, the regiments would not be sent
into combat until she had certified them
ready.
Stalin listened for approximately 20
minutes without interrupting. When she
had finished, he asked one question.
>> How long?
>> Raskova answered,
>> Six weeks for selection, six months for
training,
eight months until the first regiment is
in combat.
>> Stalin paused. He looked at Molotov. He
looked back at Raskova.
He said,
>> Take what you need.
>> The order, Soviet Air Force Directive
number 0099,
was signed the same evening. It
authorized three women's regiments,
fighter, day bomber, night bomber.
Raskova was given the temporary rank of
major. 600 Polikarpov U-2 biplanes, a
training base at Engels on the Volga.
She left the Kremlin at 4:34 p.m. She
walked to the Metropol Hotel. She placed
a phone call to her deputy. She said
three sentences.
>> Start the recruitment. Start it tonight.
We have eight months.
>> By midnight, the first telegram had gone
out to every Komsomol committee in the
Soviet Union. By the end of the week,
the first 100 volunteers had arrived at
Engels.
The volunteers were selected from
approximately 1,000 applicants. The
criteria, as Raskova explained to her
deputy, "We need girls who are clever,
[music] who do not faint at the sight of
blood, who can carry a 50-kg bomb, and
who will not cry when their commander
dies."
She asked each candidate the same three
questions. "What is your age? What is
your education? Why are you [music]
here?"
She accepted, at the first round, every
applicant who answered the third with
the words, "Because no one else will let
me."
The first 100 were, on average, 20 years
old. The youngest was 16. Galia
Dokutovich, a Belarusian medical student
who had lied about her age.
Most had never held a firearm. None,
when they arrived, had [music] a
military uniform. There had never been a
Soviet woman in active combat service,
so there were no women's uniforms. The
supply officers issued the girls men's
overcoats, boots in sizes 42 through 45,
fur hats designed for men's heads. The
girls stuffed newspaper into the boots
to make them fit. They cut their hair,
by Raskova's order, to within 2 cm of
their scalps.
The aircraft they would fly was the
Polikarpov U-2, designed in 1928 as a
training plane. By 1941, it was being
used to spray pesticide on collective
farms.
Wood, fabric, steel cable. Two open
cockpits, no armor, no radio. Maximum
speed 120 km/h.
Slower than the stall speed [music] of
the German Messerschmitt Bf 109. It
carried two bombs, no bomb bay. The
navigator pulled a wire by [music] hand
to release them. It was an aircraft no
senior officer in any major air force in
the [music] world would willingly have
taken into combat in 1941.
Raskova chose it for one reason.
There were 30,000 of them in Soviet
inventory.
Training began November 2nd, 1941.
The Engels airfield dropped to minus 28°
C. There were no heated flight
There were no heated flight suits. In
the first 6 weeks, 14 of the original
100 were medically discharged with
severe frostbite. The remaining 86
continued.
By April 1942, 8 months ahead of
Raskova's schedule, she certified the
night bomber regiment as combat-ready,
the 588th.
She gave its command to a 30-year-old
former civilian aviator from Stavropol
named Yevdokiya Bershanskaya.
The 588th flew its first combat mission
on the night of June 8th, 1942.
It was the first time in the history of
organized warfare that an entirely
female combat regiment had flown into
action.
The Germans heard the engines before
they saw the planes.
The Polikarpov U-2 produced a sound the
Luftwaffe pilots described as like a
sewing machine.
The German nickname for the regiment, Na
Maschinen, appeared in intelligence
reports as early as July 1942. What the
Germans were not prepared for was what
the U-2 did 1 minute before it dropped
its bombs.
Bershanskaya's pilots had developed a
tactic Raskova had not taught them. It
emerged from a single suggestion by a
navigator named Polina Gelman, who had
observed during their second combat
mission that the Polikarpov, with its
engine cut and trimmed correctly, would
glide for approximately 700 m before
losing critical altitude.
700 m of silent flight.
By the third week of operations, every
crew was practicing the maneuver. At 2
km from the target, the pilot cut the
engine. The aircraft descended in
silence.
The bombs released at 300 m above the
ground. The first sound the Germans
heard was not the engine. It was the
wires of the wings. Eight bracing cables
against the night wind, making a sound
that, in the testimony of two Wehrmacht
prisoners captured at Krasnodar,
resembled the sweeping of a broom.
The Germans gave the regiment a second
nickname. Nachthexen, night witches. The
Germans knew the regiment existed. They
could not stop it. The Messerschmitt Bf
110 night fighter had a minimum
operational speed of 190 km/h.
The Polikarpov U-2 cruised at 115.
A Bf 110 attacking from behind would
overshoot before the gunner could fire.
Attacking from above, it lost so much
speed in the dive that the U-2 could
turn 90° and disappear into the dark.
The Germans deployed dedicated night
fighter [music] squadrons to combat the
regiment. The squadrons did not succeed.
By the spring of 1943, every crew in the
588th was flying between five and eight
combat sorties per night. On some
nights, individual [music] crews flew
18
The pilots did this with no parachutes.
By informal regulation, adopted
unanimously in writing by the regiment
on June 14th, 1942, they did not carry
them. Two parachutes weighed 20 kg. 20
kg was an additional bomb fragment. The
crews chose the bombs.
If a U-2 [music] was hit over an enemy
position, there was no jump. The pilot
and navigator would attempt to glide to
a clear field. If they could not, they
did not. There was only the night and
the next target. And if the navigator
did her work, the small, sure motion of
pulling the wire.
The names of the women who flew in the
588th by spring 1943, redesignated the
46th Guards, were partly preserved by
Bershanskaya's regimental record
keeping. The names that survived include
Polina Gelman,
>> [music]
>> navigator from Gomel, 860 sorties.
Irina Zbrova, pilot from the Volga,
1,008 sorties, the highest individual
count in the [music] regiment. Nadezhda
Popova, 852 sorties, would survive being
shot down over Belarus
>> [music]
>> and would meet her future husband, a
downed Soviet fighter pilot, in the
underbrush behind enemy lines.
Galina Dokutovich, the 16-year-old who
had lied about her age. The regiment,
between June 1942 and May 1945, [music]
flew 23,672
combat sorties. It dropped approximately
3,000 tons of munitions. 32 of its
personnel [music] did not return.
The single worst night was July 31st to
August 1st, 1943.
Operations [music] over the Taman
Peninsula. The Wehrmacht had, by then,
identified the regiment's standard
approach corridor. They moved four Bf
110 night fighters from the Crimea
specifically to interdict it. They
positioned three searchlight batteries
to illuminate the approach. The
regiment's standard response was paired
sorties. One aircraft as a decoy to draw
the searchlights, the second making the
strike. The decoy assumed it could
escape within 90 seconds. On the night
of July 31st, the German searchlight
crews had been instructed not to release
the decoy. Four aircraft were lost
[music] in the space of approximately 6
minutes.
The pilots and navigators who did not
return that night were Polina Belkina
and Tamara Frolova, Yevgeniya Krutova
and Yelena Salikova, Sofia Rogova and
Yevgeniya Sukhorukova,
>> [music]
>> Anna Vysotskaya and Galina Dokutovich.
Eight women. The combined ages were 171.
The youngest was Dokutovich, who would
have turned 18 [music] in October. The
aircraft had no radios. The decoy crews
flew [music] into the searchlight
illumination, knowing by the third
aircraft that the trap had been sprung.
[music]
They flew in anyway because the strike
crews were behind them. And the strike
crews could only complete the run if the
decoys [music] held the lights. The
strike crews destroyed three German
artillery positions that night.
Six months earlier, on January 4th,
1943, in a snowstorm above the Volga, 60
km west of Saratov, a separate Soviet
transport aircraft had been flying to
deliver Marina Raskova to her newly
forming 587th Day Bomber Regiment. The
aircraft was caught in a downdraft. It
struck the bank of the Volga in heavy
fog. All six on board did not survive
the impact. Marina Raskova was 30 years
old. Her funeral, on January 12th, was
the first state funeral of the war for
an aviator. Her ashes were interred in
the Kremlin wall. Bershanskaya was given
temporary leave from the front to
attend. She was back at the regiment's
operating airfield by January 16th. She
told her squadron commanders one
sentence.
>> Marina Mikhailovna would expect us to
fly tonight.
>> The regiment flew that night. It would
fly almost [music] every night for the
next 28 months.
By the autumn of 1943, the 46th Guards
had become in the operational reports of
three different Soviet front
headquarters the most reliable night
strike asset in the southern theater.
The regiment moved with the Red Army,
liberated Ukraine in November 1943,
Belarus in March 1944, supporting
Operation Bagration, captured Polish
airfields by August, East Prussia by
December, Pomerania by February 1945.
The crews had developed by 1944 a
private regimental tradition. Each night
before takeoff, they gathered at the
edge of the airfield. Bershinskaya
called out the targets. The crews
acknowledged in pairs. There was then a
short silence, approximately 10 seconds,
during which no one spoke. It was, in
the words of Polina Gelman, "For those
who had flown before us and for those
who would not fly again after."
The crews walked to their aircraft. The
regiment's last combat mission was flown
on the night of May 4th to 5th, 1945,
3 days before the German surrender. The
target was a Wehrmacht ammunition depot
near Swinemünde.
The pilot was Irina Zhuravleva. The
aircraft was the same Polikarpov [music]
U-2 she had been assigned at Engels in
March 1942.
The depot was destroyed. It was the
1,008th combat sortie of Zhuravleva's
war. It was the last sortie any aircraft
of the 46th Guards would ever [music]
fly. The war in Europe four days later.
The Moscow Victory [music] Parade was
held on Red Square on June 24th, 1945.
200 Soviet military units marched. The
46th Guards Night Bomber Aviation
Regiment was not invited. The reason
given to Bershanskaya in a written
communication dated June 12th was that
the regiment had no parade uniforms in
stock [music] and would in any event be
undergoing reorganization within 60
days.
The reorganization did not occur. The
regiment was disbanded by ministerial
order on October 15th, 1945.
Most of the surviving pilots returned to
the universities they had left in 1941.
The official Soviet history of the air
war published in 1948 did not mention
the 46th Guards. [music]
The official Soviet history of women in
the war the same year devoted six pages
to female nurses, two to female
partisans, and a single paragraph to
women pilots who in some cases performed
valuable auxiliary service.
Bershanskaya, who returned to Stavropol,
[music] was given a desk position in the
regional civil aviation office. She held
it for 12 years.
In May 1957,
12 years after the war, four years after
the death of Stalin, Bershanskaya
published an article in Krasnaya [music]
Zvezda. It was titled Our Regiment. It
ran to 4,000 words. It listed the eight
women who had not returned from the
night of July 31st, [music] 1943.
It listed every additional pilot,
navigator, mechanic, and armorer who had
served between 1942 and 1945.
It was the first time most of those
names had been published in any Soviet
publication.
Bershanskaya was not punished. She was,
in the same month, awarded the Order of
the Red Banner, 12 years after the
regiment had earned it collectively.
Nadezhda Popova, the pilot who had
survived being shot down and married the
fighter pilot she had met in the
underbrush, gave her first international
interview to the BBC in 1990. She would
give 32 more in 11 countries before her
death in Moscow on July 8th, 2013 at the
age of 91.
>> [music]
>> Irina Sanbrova, who had flown the
regiment's last combat mission, spent
the 55 years between the war and her
death [music] working as an engineer at
a Moscow aircraft factory. She did not,
[music] in any surviving interview,
discuss her wartime service. Yevdokia
Bershanskaya died in Moscow on September
16th, [music] 1982.
She is buried, not at the Kremlin Wall,
where her commander Marina Raskova had
been interred 39 years earlier, but at
Kuntsevo Cemetery, beside the husband
and the daughter she had outlived.
Of the 86 women who [music] had
completed Raskova's training at Engels,
the regiment returned at the end of the
war with 54. 23 had been awarded the
title Hero of the Soviet Union. But
Raskova had, on the afternoon of October
8th, [music] 1941, in a private office
on the second floor of the Kremlin, in
front of Joseph Stalin and Vyacheslav
Molotov, built the regiment.
>> [music]
>> And the regiment had done exactly what
she told Stalin it would do. Six weeks
for selection, six months for [music]
training, eight months until combat, and
then three more years of flying.
>> [music]
>> The most decorated women's combat
aviation unit in the history of any war
the world has [music] fought. Built by
one Soviet aviator who had walked into
the Kremlin with a folded list in her
overcoat and walked out 70 minutes later
with an air force.

Level one. Ashigaru.
Your feet are sore again. The straw
sandals fell apart two days ago.
Somewhere between home and here. You
walk barefoot now, like you did in the
rice patties back home. The spear across
your shoulder weighs nothing. You've
carried heavier rice bales, your drunk
father, and your baby sister when she
had the fever. The spear is bamboo with
a cheap iron tip. The armorer laughed
when he handed it to you. Said it would
break on the first impact. You're
walking in a column of 300 men. Some are
farmers like you. Others are fishermen,
charcoal [music] burners, a monk who
stopped believing. None of you know each
other's names. Names don't matter to
Ashigaru. Your foot soldiers, peasants
with sharp sticks. The samurai ride past
on horses. Their swords cost more than
your entire village earns in a year.
They don't look at you, your furniture
to them. The march stops at midday. A
supply wagon rolls up and someone throws
rice balls into the crowd. You catch
one. You shove half in your mouth before
anyone can take it and you save the
other half in your sleeve. The man next
to you didn't catch one. He's maybe 16.
He's shaking. You break your half in two
and hand him a piece. He looks at you
like you've handed him gold. Tonight
you'll sleep in the mud beside 10,000
others. Tomorrow you'll march into the
great valley to face the enemy. Your
only job is to not die. Level two,
Ronin. The knife comes out of nowhere.
Your two drinks into a bad night at a
gambling house when the ronin across the
table decides he doesn't like your face.
Maybe it's the way you're still wearing
your swords when you clearly can't
afford to eat. Maybe he's just mean. It
doesn't matter. The knife is already in
the air. You move before you think. The
knife buries itself in sheep wood beside
you. The ronin draws his sword. So do
two of his friends. Three against one.
Three Ronin just like you. Samurai who
lost their masters and became drifters.
6 months ago, you had a lord, a stipen,
a name. Then your master backed the
wrong side, and the shogunate erased his
domain. All retainers were dismissed.
Retainers are samurai that serve a lord.
Now you're a wave man tossed by the
tide, guarding gambling dens for rice
money. Your katana clears its sheath.
The first man lunges. He's sloppy. You
side step and let his momentum carry him
past you. Then you strike his arm. He
drops his sword and stumbles. One down,
two to go. They're smarter now, circling
you. The one distracts you while the
other commits. You step to him. Your
blade finds the gap in [music] his
armor. He falls. One left. The leader.
He's calculating. He sees you favor your
left leg from an old injury. He smiles.
He comes in fast, targeting that leg. He
presses you. Your short blade clears its
sheath. You catch him under the chin and
he goes down. You stand in the silence.
Three men down. The owner emerges,
shaking. He looks at the wreckage, then
at you. He reaches under the counter and
pulls out a string of coins. He needs a
new guard. You take the coins. You don't
ask about the men on the floor. Nothing
is your problem anymore except eating
tomorrow. Level three. Goken. The
appointment letter arrived yesterday.
You read it four times. Your hands
shook. Goken. Direct retainer to the
shogunate. The lowest rank, yes, but you
serve the shogun now, not some regional
lord. Your stipend is small, enough to
[music] rent a modest house in the
capital and keep two servants. Barely
enough to maintain your armor and
horses. But the stipend isn't the point.
The point is the audience. Today, you
enter the great castle for the first
